topics.summary: When to use a, an and the: I saw a dog. The dog was huge. She's a doctor. The sun is hot.
intro: ***A / an*** (the **indefinite** article) talk about one thing that isn't specific: *I need **a** pen.* ***The*** (the **definite** article) talks about something specific that the listener knows: *Can you pass me **the** pen?* (the one on the table)

Articles are difficult for many learners because some languages don't have them. This page goes step by step. For when to use **no article**, see [The or No Article](/blog/grammar/the-or-no-article/).

points.title: A or an?
points.summary: Use **a** before a consonant **sound** (*a car, a university*) and **an** before a vowel **sound** (*an apple, an hour*). Only with singular countable nouns.

blocks.md: The choice depends on the **sound**, not the letter: *an hour* (silent *h*), *a uniform* (/juː/).
Use *a / an* only with **singular countable** nouns: *a chair*. Not *a chairs* or *a water*.

examples.text: I've got **a** brother and **an** older sister.
She's waiting for **an** hour.
He goes to **a** university in Toronto.
Would you like **an** ice cream?

mistakes.wrong: I have a apple.
mistakes.right: I have an apple.

mistakes.wrong: She's an university student.
mistakes.right: She's a university student.

mistakes.wrong: I need a informations.
mistakes.right: I need some information.

points.title: A or the? First mention and things we both know
points.summary: Use **a / an** the first time you mention something. Use **the** when it's clear which one: *I saw a cat. The cat was black.* Also **the** for things there's only one of: *the sun, the moon*.

blocks.md: ***A / an*** = one of many; the listener doesn't know which one yet: *There's **a** man at the door.*
***The*** = the listener knows which one, because:

items: we mentioned it before: *A man called. **The** man said he was your uncle.*
it's clear from the situation: *Close **the** door, please.* (the door of this room)
there's only one: ***the** sun, **the** sky, **the** internet, **the** world*.

examples.text: I bought **a** jacket and **a** shirt. **The** jacket was cheap.
Can you turn off **the** light?
**The** moon is very bright tonight.
There's **a** good film on TV tonight.

mistakes.wrong: I saw a film yesterday. A film was great.
mistakes.right: I saw a film yesterday. The film was great.

mistakes.wrong: Look at a sun!
mistakes.right: Look at the sun!

points.title: A / an for jobs, descriptions, prices and frequency
points.summary: Use **a / an** for jobs (*She's a nurse*), descriptions (*It's a beautiful day*), **what a…!** and to mean **per** (*twice a week, $5 a kilo*).

blocks.md: ***A / an*** is used:

items: for **jobs** and **roles**: *My father is **an** engineer.* (not *My father is engineer*)
in **descriptions** with *be*: *It's **a** great idea. She's **a** very kind person.*
in **exclamations** with a singular countable noun: ***What a** beautiful view!*
to mean ***per*** (each): *three times **a** day, 60 km **an** hour, $3 **a** kilo*.

blocks.md: With uncountable or plural nouns, *what* has no article: ***What** lovely weather! **What** nice people!*

examples.text: My sister is **a** teacher.
That's **a** good question.
**What a** lovely garden!
I go to the gym three times **a** week.

mistakes.wrong: She is doctor.
mistakes.right: She is a doctor.

mistakes.wrong: What a beautiful weather!
mistakes.right: What beautiful weather!

mistakes.wrong: I drink coffee two times in day.
mistakes.right: I drink coffee twice a day.

points.title: The cinema, the piano, the same, the best
points.summary: Use **the** with common places in town (*the bank, the cinema*), instruments (*play the guitar*), superlatives (*the best*), *the same, the first, the only*.

rows: *go to **the** bank / **the** post office / **the** cinema / **the** doctor's*

blocks.md: With these, *the* doesn't mean one specific building: *I'm going to **the** bank* (any branch).
Sports and games have **no article**: *play football, play chess* (not *play the football*).

examples.text: I'm going to **the** dentist tomorrow.
She plays **the** violin beautifully.
It was **the** best day of my life.
We were in **the** same class at school.

mistakes.wrong: He plays the football every weekend.
mistakes.right: He plays football every weekend.

mistakes.wrong: She's best student in the class.
mistakes.right: She's the best student in the class.

mistakes.wrong: We go to same school.
mistakes.right: We go to the same school.

points.title: General statements: the tiger, a doctor, tigers; the rich
points.summary: To talk about a type in general: **plural** with no article (*Tigers are…*), **the + singular** (formal: *The tiger is…*), or **a + singular** (*A tiger can…*). **the + adjective** = a group of people (*the rich, the elderly*).

blocks.md: ***The*** + singular is also used for **inventions** and **musical instruments** in general: ***The** smartphone changed our lives.*

***The*** + adjective describes a **group of people**: *the young, the old, the elderly, the unemployed, the homeless, the blind*. It takes a **plural** verb and has no *-s*: ***The** unemployed **need** help.*

examples.text: **Elephants** are very intelligent.
**The** computer has changed the world.
**A** doctor must be patient.
**The** elderly often feel lonely.

mistakes.wrong: The elephants are very intelligent animals. (in general)
mistakes.right: Elephants are very intelligent animals.

mistakes.wrong: The poors need more help.
mistakes.right: The poor need more help.

points.title: Advanced article use: a coffee, a good knowledge, the French, a Mr Smith
points.summary: Articles can change uncountable nouns into countable ones (*a coffee, a knowledge of*), refer to nationalities (*the French*), and show you don't know someone (*a Mr Smith called*).

blocks.md: **Uncountable nouns with *a / an***: with an adjective or a specific type or amount: *She has **a** good **knowledge** of history. I need **a** good night's **sleep**. Two **coffees**, please.*
**Nationalities**: ***the*** + nationality adjective for the whole people: ***the** French, **the** Chinese, **the** British*. For a person: *a Frenchman / a French woman*.
**Names**: ***a*** + name = someone with that name you don't know: ***A** Mr Ahmadi called while you were out.* ***The*** + name for emphasis: *Is that **the** Taylor Swift?* (the famous one)
**Illnesses**: *a cold, a headache, a sore throat* (countable); *flu* or *the flu* (both correct); *cancer, diabetes* (no article).

examples.text: He has **a** deep **understanding** of the problem.
**The** Japanese are famous for their politeness.
**A** Ms Lopez is waiting for you in reception.
I think I've got **a** cold.

mistakes.wrong: She has good knowledge of Spanish.
mistakes.right: She has a good knowledge of Spanish.

mistakes.wrong: Japanese are very polite.
mistakes.right: The Japanese are very polite.

items.prompt: ___ are very loyal animals.
Who invented ___?
The government should do more to help ___ homeless. (one word)

topics.summary: Where adjectives go (a big house, not a house big) and their order when there are several: a lovely old wooden table.
intro: In English, adjectives usually go **before** the noun (*a **red** car*) or after verbs like *be, look* and *seem* (*The car is **red***).
When there are two or more adjectives, there's a usual order: ***opinion*** first, then facts like **size, age, colour, origin** and **material**: *a **beautiful old Persian** carpet*.

points.title: Adjectives before nouns and after be
points.summary: Adjectives go **before a noun** (*a small flat*) or **after** *be, look, feel, seem, sound, taste, get* (*The flat is small*). They **don't** take *-s* in the plural: *two small flats*.

rows: after *be, look, feel, seem, sound, taste, get*

blocks.md: A few adjectives are used **only after** the verb: *afraid, alone, asleep, awake, alive*: *The baby is **asleep**.* (Before a noun, say *a **sleeping** baby*.)

examples.text: I bought a **new** phone.
Your idea **sounds good**.
They live in a **beautiful** house.
The children are **asleep**.

mistakes.wrong: I have a car red.
mistakes.right: I have a red car.

mistakes.wrong: They are very kinds people.
mistakes.right: They are very kind people.

mistakes.wrong: There was an afraid child in the corner.
mistakes.right: There was a frightened child in the corner.

points.title: Opinion, size, age, colour: a lovely big old house
points.summary: With more than one adjective, put **opinion** first, then **facts**, usually in this order: **size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose** + noun: *a lovely small old round wooden table* (but two or three adjectives are more natural).

blocks.md: In real English, we rarely use more than **three** adjectives before a noun: *a **lovely old wooden** house*.
**Opinion** adjectives (*nice, beautiful, terrible*) come before **fact** adjectives (*big, old, red*): *a **nice big** room* (not *a big nice room*).

examples.text: She has **beautiful long black** hair.
We bought a **small round wooden** table.
It's a **lovely old Persian** carpet.
He was wearing **new white running** shoes.

mistakes.wrong: a black big dog
mistakes.right: a big black dog

mistakes.wrong: a wooden old chair
mistakes.right: an old wooden chair

mistakes.wrong: an Italian beautiful car
mistakes.right: a beautiful Italian car

points.title: And between adjectives: big and bright, black and white
points.summary: After a verb, join two adjectives with ***and***: *The room was big **and** bright.* With three, use commas and *and*: *clever, kind **and** funny*. Use ***and*** between colours of one thing: *a black **and** white photo*.

rows: *a long, boring meeting* or *a long **and** boring meeting*
*a black **and** white photo, a red **and** white flag*

blocks.md: Before a noun, you can put a comma or *and* between two adjectives of the **same type** (two opinions: *a long, boring film*), but not between adjectives of **different types** (*a big black dog*).

examples.text: The hotel was clean **and** comfortable.
It was a long, tiring journey.
She has a **black and white** cat.
My grandfather is wise, patient **and** kind.

mistakes.wrong: The food was cheap delicious.
mistakes.right: The food was cheap and delicious.

mistakes.wrong: She's clever and kind and funny and.
mistakes.right: She's clever, kind and funny.

points.title: Adjectives after nouns: something new, the people involved
points.summary: Some adjectives go **after** the noun: after ***something, anyone, nowhere*** (*something interesting*), with some participles and *available* (*the people involved, the seats available*), and with measurements (*two metres long*).

rows: *Let's do **something different**. Is there **anyone famous** here?*
*The wall is three metres **high**. She's six years **old**.*
*the people **present*** (= there) / *the **present** situation* (= now); *the people **concerned*** (= involved) / *a **concerned** mother* (= worried)
*a bag **full of money**, people **interested in art***

blocks.md: When an adjective has its own phrase after it, the whole thing goes **after** the noun: *a room **full of people*** (not *a full of people room*).

examples.text: I want to try **something new**.
All the people **involved** were interviewed.
The river is 200 metres **wide**.
Are there any seats **available**?

mistakes.wrong: I'd like to eat new something.
mistakes.right: I'd like to eat something new.

mistakes.wrong: The involved people were questioned.
mistakes.right: The people involved were questioned.
mistakes.why: involved (= taking part): after the noun

items.prompt: The flat is ___.
items.explanation: After a verb: two adjectives with *and*.

items.prompt: She took a ___ photo of her grandparents.
items.explanation: Colours of one thing: *black and white*.

items.prompt: The hotel was clean ___ comfortable. (one word)

topics.summary: Which preposition comes after an adjective: good at, afraid of, interested in, kind to, famous for.
intro: Many adjectives are followed by a **fixed preposition**: *She's good **at** maths. I'm afraid **of** spiders. Are you interested **in** art?* There's no simple rule, so it's best to learn the adjective and the preposition **together**.

After the preposition, use a **noun**, a **pronoun** or an ***-ing*** form: *I'm good at **cooking**.* For verbs with prepositions (*wait for, depend on*), see [Verbs and Prepositions](/blog/grammar/verbs-and-prepositions/).

points.title: Good at, afraid of, interested in
points.summary: Common pairs: **good / bad at**, **afraid / scared / proud / tired / full of**, **interested in**, **worried / excited about**, **keen on**, **famous for**.

rows: afraid, scared, frightened, proud, tired, fond, full, jealous

blocks.md: The preposition belongs to the adjective, so learn them as **pairs**: *good **at***, *afraid **of***, *interested **in***.

examples.text: My son is very **good at** maths.
Are you **afraid of** spiders?
I'm not **interested in** football.
We're really **excited about** the trip.

mistakes.wrong: I'm interested on music.
mistakes.right: I'm interested in music.

mistakes.wrong: She's afraid from dogs.
mistakes.right: She's afraid of dogs.

mistakes.wrong: He's very good in tennis.
mistakes.right: He's very good at tennis.

points.title: Kind to, married to, similar to, good for
points.summary: **kind / nice / rude / polite to** someone; **angry / annoyed with** someone **about** something; **similar to**, **different from**, **married to**, **responsible for**, **aware of**, **capable of**, **good / bad for**.

rows: *Life here is **different from** life in Iran.*

blocks.md: *Married **to*** someone, not *married with*: *He's married **to** a teacher.*
Compare: *good **at*** (a skill) and *good **for*** (healthy or useful): *She's good at tennis. Tennis is good for you.*

examples.text: Be **nice to** your sister!
My phone is **similar to** yours.
He's **responsible for** the whole team.
Fruit is **good for** you.

mistakes.wrong: She's married with an engineer.
mistakes.right: She's married to an engineer.

mistakes.wrong: The film is very different of the book.
mistakes.right: The film is very different from the book.

mistakes.wrong: He was rude with the waiter.
mistakes.right: He was rude to the waiter.

points.title: Adjective + preposition + -ing
points.summary: After a preposition, use a **noun** or the **-ing** form, never the base verb: *I'm good at **cooking**. She's tired of **waiting**. Are you interested in **joining**?*

blocks.md: A preposition is followed by a noun, a pronoun or ***-ing***: *I'm good at **swimming*** (not *good at swim*). *He's interested in **learning** Chinese.*
With ***afraid***, both patterns are possible: *I'm **afraid of flying**. I'm **afraid to fly**.*
Use **not** before the *-ing*: *I'm sorry for **not calling** you.*

examples.text: She's good at **making** friends.
I'm tired of **hearing** the same excuses.
Are you interested in **joining** our team?
He's keen on **playing** chess.

mistakes.wrong: I'm good at speak English.
mistakes.right: I'm good at speaking English.

mistakes.wrong: She's interested in learn Japanese.
mistakes.right: She's interested in learning Japanese.

points.title: Good at, good with, good for; sorry about, sorry for
points.summary: Some adjectives take **different prepositions** with **different meanings**: *good at* (skill), *good with* (handling), *good for* (healthy), *kind of you* (an action); *sorry about* (a situation), *feel sorry for* (pity).

rows: skilful at handling people or things
*He's **good with** children. She's **good with** her hands.*
*I'm **responsible for** sales. I'm **responsible to** the director.*
*We're **concerned about** safety. The book is **concerned with** politics.*

blocks.md: ***Sorry for*** + *-ing* (your own action) is also common: *I'm sorry **for shouting**.*

examples.text: She's brilliant **at** languages but not very good **with** money.
It was really nice **of** you to remember my birthday.
I feel sorry **for** people who live alone.
This article is **concerned with** climate policy.

mistakes.wrong: It was very nice to you to call.
mistakes.right: It was very nice of you to call.

mistakes.wrong: I'm sorry of the delay.
mistakes.right: I'm sorry about the delay.

mistakes.wrong: I feel sorry about him.
mistakes.right: I feel sorry for him.

points.title: Prone to, devoid of, consistent with: formal pairs
points.summary: Formal and academic pairs: **prone / susceptible / conducive / averse to**, **devoid / indicative / wary of**, **consistent / compatible / synonymous with**, **reliant / contingent on**, **exempt from**, **adept at**.

rows: prone, susceptible, conducive, averse, akin, immune
exempt from, adept at, inherent in
*Books are **exempt from** VAT in the UK.*

blocks.md: These are common in **academic** and **business** English.
In ***averse to***, ***prone to*** and ***conducive to***, *to* is a preposition, so it's followed by a noun or ***-ing***: *He isn't **averse to taking** risks.*

examples.text: The area is **prone to** flooding.
The results are **consistent with** earlier research.
She's **adept at** handling difficult clients.
The offer is **contingent on** a successful interview.

mistakes.wrong: He isn't averse to take risks.
mistakes.right: He isn't averse to taking risks.

mistakes.wrong: The app isn't compatible to older phones.
mistakes.right: The app isn't compatible with older phones.

items.prompt: He's a great nurse. He's very good ___ elderly patients.
It was very kind ___ you to drive me home.
I feel really sorry ___ him. He lost his job. (one word)

topics.summary: Words that connect ideas across sentences: the former, anyway, mind you, in other words, namely, hence, thus, that said, let alone.
intro: **Cohesion** means making a text **hang together**: each sentence connects clearly to the next. We do this with **reference words** (*this, the former*), **discourse markers** in speech (*anyway, mind you*) and **linkers** in writing (*in other words, hence, that said*).

For basic linkers like *however* and *therefore*, see [And, But, Or, So, Because](/blog/grammar/and-but-or-so-because/#abo-however-therefore). For leaving words out and *do so*, see [Ellipsis and Substitution](/blog/grammar/ellipsis-substitution/).

points.title: This, such, the former and the latter
points.summary: Refer back to earlier ideas with ***this / that / these*** (+ noun), ***such*** (+ noun), ***the former*** (the first of two) and ***the latter*** (the second of two), so you don't repeat words.

rows: *He never says thank you. **This** really annoys me.*
*I'd never seen **such a** mess.* / *We need to avoid **such problems**.*
*I visited Rome and Paris. **The former** was hotter; **the latter** was more expensive.*

blocks.md: ***This*** + a **summary noun** (*this problem, this decision, this change*) is very common in good writing: it tells the reader exactly what you're referring to.
Use ***the former / the latter*** only when there are **two** things. For three or more, use *the first, the last*.

examples.text: Some people work from home. **This** saves them time and money.
The company cut 500 jobs. **This decision** was criticised.
Tea and coffee are both popular, but **the latter** has more caffeine.
**Such** behaviour is not acceptable.

mistakes.wrong: I like tea and coffee and juice, but the latter is my favourite.
mistakes.right: I like tea, coffee and juice, but the last is my favourite.

mistakes.wrong: I've never seen a such beautiful place.
mistakes.right: I've never seen such a beautiful place.

points.title: Anyway, by the way, actually, mind you
points.summary: Spoken **discourse markers** help you manage a conversation: ***anyway*** (back to the main topic / ending), ***by the way*** (a new topic), ***actually*** (a correction or surprise), ***mind you*** (BrE: adding a contrast), ***I mean*** (explaining), ***as I was saying*** (returning to a topic).

rows: return to the main point; finish
***By the way**, have you seen Sara?*
***As I was saying**, the plan is ready.*

blocks.md: ***Actually*** means *in fact*, not *now*: ***Actually**, I don't like coffee.* For *now*, use ***currently*** or ***at the moment***.

examples.text: **By the way**, your phone is ringing.
**Actually**, I've changed my mind.
**Anyway**, let's get back to work.
The hotel was old. **Mind you**, it was very cheap.

mistakes.wrong: Actually I'm working in a bank. (= now)
mistakes.right: Currently I'm working in a bank.

mistakes.wrong: By the way, as I was saying, the plan is ready.
mistakes.right: As I was saying, the plan is ready.
mistakes.why: returning to the topic: as I was saying

points.title: In other words, namely, to sum up, that is to say
points.summary: Signposting in writing: **order** (*firstly, to begin with, lastly*), **rephrasing** (*in other words, that is to say, i.e.*), **examples** (*for instance, e.g., namely*), **summing up** (*to sum up, in conclusion, overall*).

rows: ***To begin with**, the method is cheap.*
*in other words, that is to say, i.e.*
*The test was optional; **in other words**, you didn't have to do it.*
*for instance, for example, e.g., such as*
*Two students, **namely** Ali and Sara, got full marks.*
*to sum up, in conclusion, overall, all in all*
***To sum up**, the plan has more benefits than risks.*

blocks.md: ***Namely*** gives the **exact** items you mean; ***for instance / e.g.*** give **examples** from a larger group.
***i.e.*** = *that is* (it explains); ***e.g.*** = *for example*. Don't mix them up.

examples.text: **To begin with**, let's look at the costs.
He's economical with the truth; **in other words**, he lies.
Three cities, **namely** Paris, Rome and Madrid, were chosen.
**In conclusion**, both options have advantages.

mistakes.wrong: Many fruits, i.e. apples and bananas, are cheap. (examples)
mistakes.right: Many fruits, e.g. apples and bananas, are cheap.

mistakes.wrong: To summarise up, the results were positive.
mistakes.right: To sum up, the results were positive.

points.title: Hence, thus, consequently, accordingly
points.summary: Formal **result** linkers: ***consequently***, ***as a consequence***, ***thus***, ***hence***, ***accordingly***. ***Hence*** can be followed by just a **noun**: *He's from Rome, **hence** his name, Romano.*

rows: *The road was closed, **thus** causing long delays.*
*The town is built on a hill, **hence** the name Hilltown.*
*The data is old; **hence**, the results may not be accurate.*
*The rules have changed. Please act **accordingly**.* (= in a suitable way)

blocks.md: ***Thus*** + *-ing* shows a direct result: *Prices rose, **thus making** life harder for families.*
***Accordingly*** can mean *therefore* or *in a way that suits the situation*.

examples.text: The project ran out of money; **consequently**, it was cancelled.
She's a doctor, **hence** her interest in health.
The bridge was damaged, **thus** cutting off the village.
The guests are VIPs, so please treat them **accordingly**.

mistakes.wrong: The town is by the sea, hence it's called Seaside.
mistakes.right: The town is by the sea, hence its name, Seaside.

mistakes.wrong: Prices rose, thus made life harder.
mistakes.right: Prices rose, thus making life harder.

points.title: That said, admittedly, let alone, if anything
points.summary: Very advanced markers: **concession** (*admittedly, granted, that said, be that as it may, all the same*), **emphasis** (*indeed, if anything, not to mention, let alone*).

rows: ***Admittedly**, it's expensive, but it lasts for years.*
*The hotel was noisy. **That said**, the staff were lovely.*
*You may be right. **Be that as it may**, we can't change the plan now.*
*It was raining. **All the same**, we went out.*
*The task was difficult; **indeed**, it was almost impossible.*
the opposite, if there's any difference
*The new model isn't cheaper. **If anything**, it's more expensive.*
*I can't afford a bike, **let alone** a car.*

blocks.md: ***Let alone*** follows a **negative** idea and introduces something even **less** likely: *He can't boil an egg, **let alone** cook a meal.*

examples.text: **Granted**, the course is short, but it's very intensive.
The film was long. **Having said that**, I enjoyed it.
She doesn't speak French, **let alone** Russian.
The traffic wasn't better. **If anything**, it was worse.

mistakes.wrong: I can afford a car, let alone a bike.
mistakes.right: I can't afford a car, let alone a house.
mistakes.why: let alone: after a negative, something even less likely

mistakes.wrong: That saying, I still think we should try.
mistakes.right: That said, I still think we should try.

items.prompt: We can take the bus or the train. ___ is cheaper, but the train is faster.
Unemployment has risen sharply. ___ is a serious problem for the government.
Ali and Reza both applied, but only the ___ got the job. Reza was very disappointed. (one word)
___, did you remember to buy milk? I forgot to ask you earlier.
I thought she was American. ~ No, she's Canadian, ___.
Sorry about that phone call. ___ I was saying, the meeting is on Friday. (one word)

topics.summary: Saying how often you do things: I always get up early. She's never late. We go to the gym twice a week.
intro: **Adverbs of frequency** say **how often** something happens: *always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never*.
The key thing is **word order**: they go **before** most verbs (*I **often** cook*) but **after** *be* (*I'm **often** tired*).

points.title: Always, usually, often, sometimes, never
points.summary: From most to least often: ***always*** (100%) > ***usually*** > ***often*** > ***sometimes*** > ***rarely / hardly ever*** > ***never*** (0%).

blocks.md: ***Never*** is already negative, so use a **positive** verb: *I **never** eat meat.* (not *I don't never eat meat*)
Use them with the **present simple** for habits: *I **usually** get up at 7.*

examples.text: I **always** brush my teeth before bed.
My dad **often** cooks dinner.
We **sometimes** go to the beach.
She **never** eats meat.

mistakes.wrong: I don't never watch TV.
mistakes.right: I never watch TV.

mistakes.wrong: I go always to school by bus.
mistakes.right: I always go to school by bus.

points.title: Word order: I always go, I'm always tired
points.summary: Adverbs of frequency go **before the main verb** (*I often go*) but **after** *be* (*I'm often late*) and **after** the first **auxiliary** (*I have never been, I can't always come*).

rows: *I **have never** seen it. You **can always** call me.*
***Do** you **often** go out? **Are** you **always** this busy?*
*I **don't usually** eat meat. She **isn't often** late.*

blocks.md: ***Sometimes, usually*** and ***often*** can also go at the **start** or **end**: ***Sometimes** I walk to work. I walk to work **sometimes**.*
***Always*** and ***never*** don't usually go at the start (except *Never…* for emphasis in formal English).

examples.text: I **usually** go to bed at 11.
She's **always** cheerful.
Have you **ever** been to Japan?
I don't **often** see him.

mistakes.wrong: Always I am tired.
mistakes.right: I am always tired.

mistakes.wrong: We usually are at home on Sundays.
mistakes.right: We are usually at home on Sundays.

mistakes.wrong: I never have been to Paris.
mistakes.right: I have never been to Paris.

points.title: How often? Once a week, every day, twice a month
points.summary: Ask ***How often…?*** and answer with **expressions of frequency**: *every day, once a week, twice a month, three times a year, every other day*. These usually go at the **end** of the sentence.

rows: *We eat out **once a week**. She calls **twice a day**.*
*I wash my hair **every other day**.* (= every second day)
*from time to time / now and then*

blocks.md: Say ***once*** (1) and ***twice*** (2), then ***three times, four times***…: *I've been there **twice**.* (*two times* is common in speech, but *twice* is better)

examples.text: How often do you go to the dentist? ~ **Twice a year**.
I see my grandparents **every weekend**.
The bus comes **every ten minutes**.
I go swimming **once a week**.

mistakes.wrong: I go to the gym three times in a week.
mistakes.right: I go to the gym three times a week.

mistakes.wrong: How many often do you travel?
mistakes.right: How often do you travel?

mistakes.wrong: Every days I walk to school.
mistakes.right: Every day I walk to school.

points.title: Seldom, rarely, frequently, invariably; Rarely have I…
points.summary: More formal adverbs: ***frequently*** (often), ***occasionally*** (sometimes), ***seldom / rarely*** (not often), ***invariably*** (always, without exception). ***Rarely, seldom*** and ***never*** at the start of a sentence need **inversion**: *Rarely do we see such talent.*

rows: ***Rarely have** I seen such a beautiful view.*

blocks.md: For inversion, use **auxiliary + subject**: *Seldom **does she** complain. Never **have I** felt so happy.* See [Inversion After Negative Adverbials](/blog/grammar/inversion-negative-adverbials/).
***Hardly ever*** = rarely (informal): *I **hardly ever** watch TV.*

examples.text: The trains are **frequently** late.
I **occasionally** work from home.
**Seldom do** we get snow here.
She **invariably** orders the same dish.

mistakes.wrong: Rarely I have seen such a mess.
mistakes.right: Rarely have I seen such a mess.

mistakes.wrong: I hardly never go out.
mistakes.right: I hardly ever go out.

items.prompt: ___ seen such a beautiful sunset.
He ___ arrives late. In ten years, he has never been on time.
I hardly ___ eat red meat. Maybe once a year. (one word)

topics.summary: Words that describe how we do something: She drives carefully. He speaks English well. They work hard.
intro: **Adverbs of manner** describe **how** something happens: *She sings **beautifully**. Drive **carefully**!* Most are formed from an adjective + ***-ly***: *slow → slowly*.
Adjectives describe **nouns** (*a careful driver*); adverbs describe **verbs** (*He drives carefully*).

points.title: Adjective or adverb? Quick or quickly?
points.summary: Use an **adjective** with a noun (*a quick lunch*) and an **adverb** with a verb (*She ate quickly*). Most adverbs = adjective + **-ly**.

blocks.md: Adverbs of manner usually go **after the verb** or **after the object**: *She speaks **quietly**. He opened the door **slowly**.* (not *He opened slowly the door*)

examples.text: He's a **careful** driver. He drives **carefully**.
The children played **happily** in the garden.
Please speak **slowly**.
She closed the window **quietly**.

mistakes.wrong: She sings beautiful.
mistakes.right: She sings beautifully.

mistakes.wrong: He drives very careful.
mistakes.right: He drives very carefully.

mistakes.wrong: I read quickly the email.
mistakes.right: I read the email quickly.

points.title: Good or well? Hard, fast, late, early
points.summary: The adverb of ***good*** is ***well***. Some adverbs are the **same** as the adjective: ***hard, fast, late, early, straight***. ***Hardly*** and ***lately*** have different meanings.

blocks.md: ***Hardly*** = almost not: *I **hardly** slept.* ***Lately*** = recently: *Have you seen him **lately**?* They are **not** the adverbs of *hard* and *late*.
***Well*** is also an adjective meaning **healthy**: *I don't feel **well**.*

examples.text: You speak English very **well**.
She works very **hard**.
Don't drive so **fast**!
I **hardly** know him.

mistakes.wrong: He plays the guitar very good.
mistakes.right: He plays the guitar very well.

mistakes.wrong: She works hardly.
mistakes.right: She works hard.

mistakes.wrong: He drives fastly.
mistakes.right: He drives fast.

points.title: Friendly, lively, lovely; look good, feel tired
points.summary: Some words ending in ***-ly*** are **adjectives**: *friendly, lovely, lonely, lively, silly, ugly*. For an adverb meaning, use ***in a … way***: *in a friendly way*. After **linking verbs** (*be, look, feel, sound, taste, smell, seem*), use an **adjective**: *You look tired.*

rows: *The soup **smells good**. You **sound happy**. I **feel tired**.*

blocks.md: Compare: *She **looks** angry.* (= she seems angry: adjective) / *She **looked** at me **angrily**.* (= how she looked at me: adverb).

examples.text: Our neighbours are very **friendly**.
He spoke to me **in a friendly way**.
This cake **tastes delicious**.
You **seem** a bit **sad** today.

mistakes.wrong: She talked to me friendly.
mistakes.right: She talked to me in a friendly way.

mistakes.wrong: The flowers smell beautifully.
mistakes.right: The flowers smell beautiful.

mistakes.wrong: You look tiredly.
mistakes.right: You look tired.

points.title: Hard or hardly? Free or freely? Wide or widely?
points.summary: Some pairs have **different meanings**: ***hard*** (with effort) / ***hardly*** (almost not); ***free*** (without paying) / ***freely*** (without limits); ***wide*** (fully) / ***widely*** (in many places); ***high*** / ***highly*** (very much); ***deep*** / ***deeply*** (very); ***near*** / ***nearly*** (almost).

blocks.md: In writing, adverbs of manner can go **before the main verb** for emphasis: *She **quietly** left the room.* But never between a verb and its object (*She left quietly the room* ✗).

examples.text: The museum is **free** on Sundays.
You can move **freely** around the city.
She's a **highly** paid lawyer.
I **nearly** missed the train.
She **quietly** closed the door.

mistakes.wrong: I hard ever see him.
mistakes.right: I hardly ever see him.

mistakes.wrong: This book is high recommended.
mistakes.right: This book is highly recommended.

mistakes.wrong: Spanish is wide spoken in the USA.
mistakes.right: Spanish is widely spoken in the USA.

items.prompt: English is ___ used in international business.
Children under five travel ___ on the bus.
I ___ (near) fell off my bike this morning. (one word)

topics.h1: Although, Despite and In Spite Of
topics.summary: Showing contrast: although + subject + verb, despite / in spite of + noun or -ing, even though, whereas, albeit.
intro: We use these words to show a **contrast**: something is surprising because of something else. ***Although** it was raining, we went out. **Despite** the rain, we went out.*

The key difference is **grammar**: *although* + a **clause** (subject + verb), *despite / in spite of* + a **noun** or ***-ing***. For *but* and *however*, see [And, But, Or, So, Because](/blog/grammar/and-but-or-so-because/).

points.title: Although and though + clause
points.summary: ***Although*** (or ***though***) + subject + verb shows a surprising contrast: ***Although** it was cold, we went swimming.* Don't use *although* and *but* together.

rows: ***Although** I was tired, I finished my homework.*
*I finished my homework **although** I was tired.*
***Though** it was late, she called me.*

blocks.md: Use **one** linker, not two: ***Although** it was expensive, I bought it.* or *It was expensive, **but** I bought it.* (not *Although it was expensive, but I bought it.*)
When the *although* clause comes **first**, use a **comma** after it.

examples.text: **Although** he's rich, he lives in a small flat.
We enjoyed the trip **although** the weather was bad.
**Though** it was raining, they played tennis.
**Although** she's only six, she can read very well.

mistakes.wrong: Although it was late, but I wasn't tired.
mistakes.right: Although it was late, I wasn't tired.

mistakes.wrong: Although the rain, we went out.
mistakes.right: Although it was raining, we went out.

points.title: Despite / in spite of + noun or -ing
points.summary: ***Despite*** and ***in spite of*** mean the same as *although*, but they're followed by a **noun**, a **pronoun** or ***-ing***: ***Despite** the rain… **In spite of** being tired…* Use ***despite the fact that*** + clause.

rows: ***In spite of** being tired, she kept working.*
*despite / in spite of the fact that* + clause
***Despite the fact that** it was raining, we went out.*
***Although** it was raining, we went out.*

blocks.md: Say ***despite*** (no *of*) or ***in spite of*** (with *of*). Not *despite of*.
You can't use *despite* + subject + verb: not *Despite it was raining*. Use *although*, or *despite the fact that*.

examples.text: **Despite** the traffic, we arrived on time.
**In spite of** his injury, he finished the race.
She passed **despite** not studying much.
**Despite the fact that** he's 70, he's very fit.

mistakes.wrong: Despite of the rain, we played.
mistakes.right: Despite the rain, we played.

mistakes.wrong: Despite it was cold, we swam.
mistakes.right: Although it was cold, we swam.

mistakes.wrong: In spite the noise, I slept well.
mistakes.right: In spite of the noise, I slept well.

points.title: Even though, even if, and though at the end
points.summary: ***Even though*** = a stronger *although* (a real fact). ***Even if*** = it doesn't matter whether it happens (a possible situation). ***Though*** can also go at the **end** of a sentence, meaning *however*.

rows: *She went to work **even though** she was ill.*
whether or not; it may happen

blocks.md: Compare: ***Even though** I'm tired, I'll help you.* (I am tired.) / ***Even if** I'm tired, I'll help you.* (Maybe I'll be tired, maybe not.)
Don't say *even although* or *even despite*.

examples.text: He didn't stop **even though** he was exhausted.
**Even if** you apologise, she won't forgive you.
The food was expensive. It was delicious, **though**.
**Even though** she lives near me, I rarely see her.

mistakes.wrong: Even although it was late, we stayed.
mistakes.right: Even though it was late, we stayed.

mistakes.wrong: Even if he's my brother, I don't trust him. (He is my brother.)
mistakes.right: Even though he's my brother, I don't trust him.

points.title: Whereas, while, on the other hand
points.summary: To compare **two different facts**, use ***whereas*** or ***while*** (*I like tea, **whereas** my wife likes coffee*) or ***On the other hand*** at the start of a new sentence. ***On the contrary*** is different: it means *that's not true; the opposite is true*.

rows: *The flat is small. **On the other hand**, it's very cheap.*
*on the contrary* (= the opposite is true)
*You're not boring. **On the contrary**, you're very interesting!*

blocks.md: ***Whereas*** and ***while*** join two clauses in **one** sentence. ***On the other hand*** usually starts a **new** sentence.
Often ***on the one hand … on the other hand***: ***On the one hand**, it's cheap. **On the other hand**, it's far from the city.*

examples.text: Ali loves sport, **whereas** his sister hates it.
**While** some people enjoy the heat, others hate it.
City life is exciting. **On the other hand**, it can be stressful.
I'm not angry. **On the contrary**, I'm happy for you.

mistakes.wrong: The flat is small. On the contrary, it's cheap.
mistakes.right: The flat is small. On the other hand, it's cheap.
mistakes.why: comparing two facts: on the other hand

mistakes.wrong: My father is calm, whereas my mother is calm too.
mistakes.right: My father is calm, whereas my mother is very nervous.

points.title: Albeit, much as, notwithstanding, tired as I was
points.summary: Formal concession: ***albeit*** + adjective / adverb / noun phrase, ***much as*** + clause (= although I really), ***notwithstanding*** (= despite), ***adjective / adverb + as / though*** + clause (*Tired **as** I was, …*), ***however*** + adjective (*However hard I try, …*).

rows: ***Much as** I like him, I can't agree.*
***Notwithstanding** the cost, the project went ahead.*
***Tired as** she was, she kept going.*
***However hard** I try, I can't do it.*

blocks.md: ***Albeit*** is never followed by a full clause: *a small, **albeit** important, change* (not *albeit it was important*).
***Notwithstanding*** can also come **after** the noun: *The cost **notwithstanding**, the project went ahead.*

examples.text: It was a success, **albeit** a small one.
**Much as** I'd love to come, I'm too busy.
**Strange as** it may seem, I've never seen the sea.
**However much** you earn, you'll always want more.

mistakes.wrong: The plan worked, albeit it was slow.
mistakes.right: The plan worked, albeit slowly.

mistakes.wrong: Much as I like him, but I can't agree.
mistakes.right: Much as I like him, I can't agree.

items.prompt: I'll be at your party ___ it snows. Nothing will stop me!
She didn't wear a coat ___ it was freezing.
The hotel was a bit noisy. The staff were really friendly, ___. (one word)
My sister likes horror films, ___ I prefer comedies.
The job is well paid. ___, the hours are very long.
Some students prefer online classes, ___ others prefer classes in person. (one word)

topics.h1: And, But, Or, So and Because
topics.summary: The basic linking words: and (adding), but (contrast), or (choice), so (result) and because (reason).
intro: **Linking words** (conjunctions) join ideas: *I like tea **and** coffee. It's cheap **but** good. Tea **or** coffee? It was late, **so** I went home. I went home **because** it was late.*

This page starts with the basics and goes up to formal linkers like *however* and *therefore*. For *although* and *despite*, see [Although, Despite and In Spite Of](/blog/grammar/although-despite-in-spite-of/).

points.title: And, but, or
points.summary: ***And*** adds information. ***But*** shows a **contrast** (a different or surprising idea). ***Or*** gives a **choice**.

blocks.md: You can join **words** (*bread **and** butter*) or **sentences** (*I called her, **but** she didn't answer*).
Use ***or*** in negative sentences: *I don't like tea **or** coffee.* (not *and coffee* here)
We often put a comma before *but* when it joins two sentences: *It was sunny**, but** it was cold.*

examples.text: I play football **and** tennis.
My flat is small **but** comfortable.
Would you like rice **or** potatoes?
She doesn't eat meat **or** fish.

mistakes.wrong: I like coffee but I like tea.
mistakes.right: I like coffee and I like tea.

mistakes.wrong: Do you want water and juice? (one of them)
mistakes.right: Do you want water or juice?

points.title: So or because? Result and reason
points.summary: ***Because*** gives the **reason** (why?). ***So*** gives the **result** (what happened next?): *I was hungry, **so** I ate a sandwich. I ate a sandwich **because** I was hungry.*

rows: *It was raining, **so** we stayed at home.*
*We stayed at home **because** it was raining.*
*I was tired, **so** I went to bed.*
*I went to bed **because** I was tired.*

blocks.md: ***Because*** can also start the sentence; then use a comma: ***Because** it was raining, we stayed at home.*
Don't use *so* and *because* together: *Because it was late, I went home.* (not *Because it was late, so I went home.*)

examples.text: I'm learning English **because** I want a better job.
The shop was closed, **so** I went home.
**Because** he was ill, he didn't come to work.
It's cold, **so** take a jacket.

mistakes.wrong: Because I was hungry, so I made a sandwich.
mistakes.right: Because I was hungry, I made a sandwich.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't go out so I was ill.
mistakes.right: I didn't go out because I was ill.

points.title: Because or because of? So, that's why
points.summary: ***Because*** + a **clause** (subject + verb): *because **it was** raining*. ***Because of*** + a **noun**: *because of **the rain***. ***That's why*** = so (in speaking).

rows: *It was raining. **That's why** we stayed in.*

blocks.md: After ***because of***, use a noun, a pronoun or *-ing*: *because of **him**, because of **the traffic***.

examples.text: The flight was cancelled **because of** the snow.
The flight was cancelled **because** it was snowing.
I failed the test **because of** you!
I missed the bus. **That's why** I'm late.

mistakes.wrong: I was late because the traffic.
mistakes.right: I was late because of the traffic.

mistakes.wrong: I was late because of the traffic was bad.
mistakes.right: I was late because the traffic was bad.

points.title: Also, too, as well, either
points.summary: ***Also*** goes **before** the main verb (after *be*): *I **also** play tennis.* ***Too*** and ***as well*** go at the **end**: *I play tennis **too / as well**.* In negatives, use ***either***: *I don't like it **either**.*

rows: before the main verb, after *be* and auxiliaries
*She doesn't speak German, and I don't **either**.*

blocks.md: ***Also*** is more common in writing; ***too*** and ***as well*** are more common in speaking.
Don't use *too* in negatives: *I don't like it **either*** (not *I don't like it too*).

examples.text: I **also** have a car.
He's a singer, and he's **also** an actor.
I love pizza. ~ Me **too**!
I can't swim. ~ I can't **either**.

mistakes.wrong: I like also football.
mistakes.right: I also like football.

mistakes.wrong: I don't eat meat too.
mistakes.right: I don't eat meat either.

mistakes.wrong: Too I speak Spanish.
mistakes.right: I speak Spanish too.

points.title: However, therefore, in addition, as a result
points.summary: In more formal writing, use linkers between sentences: ***However*** (contrast), ***Therefore / As a result*** (result), ***In addition / Moreover*** (adding). They usually start a new sentence, followed by a **comma**.

blocks.md: *But* and *so* join two parts of **one** sentence. ***However*** and ***therefore*** usually link **two sentences**: *The plan was good. **However**, it was too expensive.*
You can also put *however* in the middle, between commas: *The plan, **however**, was too expensive.* With a semicolon: *The plan was good; **however**, it was expensive.*
Don't use ***however*** like *but* with only a comma: not *It was good, however it was expensive.* Use a full stop or a semicolon.

examples.text: The hotel was lovely. **However**, the food was terrible.
Sales fell by 20%. **As a result**, 50 jobs were lost.
The job is well paid. **In addition**, it offers flexible hours.
He didn't study. **Therefore**, he failed.

mistakes.wrong: The weather was bad. But however, we went out.
mistakes.right: The weather was bad. However, we went out.

mistakes.wrong: It's cheap. Moreover it's bad quality. (contrast)
mistakes.right: It's cheap. However, it's bad quality.

topics.h1: Be About To, Be Due To and Be To
topics.summary: More ways to talk about the future: The film is about to start. The train is due to arrive at 6. The President is to visit Canada.
intro: Apart from *will* and *going to*, English has other phrases for the future. They add meaning: ***be about to*** (very soon), ***be due to*** (scheduled), ***be to*** (official plans and orders).
Many of them are common in the news and in formal writing. For the main future forms, see [Will vs Going To](/blog/grammar/will-vs-going-to/).

points.title: Be about to: very soon
points.summary: **be about to + base verb** = something will happen very soon: *Hurry up! The film is about to start.* **was about to** = I was just going to.

blocks.md: ***Be about to*** + base verb means something will happen **in a very short time**: *Turn off your phones. The plane **is about to** take off.*
We don't usually add a time phrase like *tomorrow*; the meaning is already *immediately*.
***Was / were about to*** describes something that was going to happen immediately in the past, often when something interrupted it: *I **was about to** call you when you knocked on the door.*

examples.text: Quick, get inside! It**'s about to** rain.
The shop **is about to** close. Please make your final purchases.
I **was about to** leave when the phone rang.
We **were about to** give up when we found the key.

mistakes.wrong: The film is about starting.
mistakes.right: The film is about to start.

mistakes.wrong: The bus is about to leave tomorrow.
mistakes.right: The bus leaves tomorrow. / The bus is about to leave.
mistakes.why: about to = immediately (no future time phrase)

points.title: Be due to: scheduled events
points.summary: **be due to + verb** = it's planned or expected at a particular time: *The train is due to arrive at 6.15.* **be due** + time: *The baby is due in May.*

blocks.md: ***Be due to*** + base verb describes something **scheduled** or **expected**: *The new hospital **is due to** open next year. The meeting **was due to** start at nine.*
Without a verb, ***be due*** + time: *The rent **is due** on Friday. Our baby **is due** in March.*
***Was due to*** often suggests the plan didn't happen as expected: *The flight **was due to** land at 6, but it was delayed.*
Don't confuse it with ***due to*** + noun = *because of*: *The match was cancelled **due to** the rain.*

examples.text: The President **is due to** arrive at noon.
Your essay **is due** next Monday.
The film **was due to** start at 8, but it started late.
When **is** the baby **due**?

mistakes.wrong: The train is due arriving at six.
mistakes.right: The train is due to arrive at six.

points.title: On the point of, on the verge of, be set to
points.summary: **be on the point / verge of + -ing** = very close to doing something. **be set to + verb** (news) = expected to happen soon: *Prices are set to rise.*

rows: *I was **on the point of leaving** when she arrived.*
very close to (often emotional or major)
*The team **is poised to** win the title.*

blocks.md: These phrases are more formal or dramatic than *be about to*. *Be set to* and *be poised to* are typical of **news headlines and reports**.

examples.text: The company is **on the point of closing** down.
Scientists are **on the verge of** a major discovery.
Unemployment **is set to** fall this year.
The government **is poised to** announce new rules.

mistakes.wrong: I was on the point to leave.
mistakes.right: I was on the point of leaving.

mistakes.wrong: Prices are set rising.
mistakes.right: Prices are set to rise.

points.title: Be to: official plans and orders
points.summary: **be to + base verb** for official arrangements (*The President is to visit Japan*) and for orders (*You are to stay here*). **If … is to** = if … wants to / is going to.

blocks.md: ***Be to*** + base verb is a formal way to describe **official plans**, often in the news: *The Prime Minister **is to** visit Brazil next month. Two hundred workers **are to** lose their jobs.*
It can also give **orders or instructions**: *You **are to** report to the manager at 9. Nobody **is to** leave the building.* See [Must and Have To](/blog/grammar/must-have-to/#mht-formal).
***If … is / are to*** = *if … wants to / is going to succeed*: ***If** we **are to** finish on time, we need more staff.*

examples.text: The Queen **is to** open the new hospital on Monday.
You **are not to** tell anyone about this.
**If** the city **is to** grow, it needs better transport.
The two leaders **are to** meet in Geneva.

mistakes.wrong: The President is to visiting Canada.
mistakes.right: The President is to visit Canada.

points.title: Was to and was to have done: destiny and plans that failed
points.summary: **was to + verb** = something that happened later, seen from the past (*He was to become president*). **was to have + past participle** = a plan that didn't happen.

blocks.md: In stories and history, ***was / were to*** + base verb describes what **happened later** (destiny): *In 1990 she met the man who **was to** become her husband.* (He became her husband later.)
***Was / were to have*** + past participle describes a plan that **didn't happen**: *The wedding **was to have taken** place in June, but it was cancelled.*
***Was to*** + base verb can also mean *was planned to*: *We **were to** meet at noon, but she didn't come.*
For more ways to describe the future from the past, see [Future in the Past](/blog/grammar/future-in-the-past/).

examples.text: Little did he know that this **was to** be his last match.
The hotel **was to have opened** in 2020, but the pandemic stopped it.
They **were to** marry the following spring.
It **was to** change her life forever.

mistakes.wrong: The meeting was to have take place on Monday.
mistakes.right: The meeting was to have taken place on Monday.

items.prompt: The plane is ___ to land in ten minutes.
What does *The report is due on Friday* mean?
options: The report was finished on Friday.

items.prompt: The new metro line ___ (be / due / open) in 2027.

topics.h1: Because, As, Since and Due To
topics.summary: Ways to give a reason: because, as, since, now that, seeing as, due to, owing to, thanks to, given that.
intro: ***Because*** is the most common way to give a **reason**: *I stayed at home **because** I was ill.* ***As*** and ***since*** mean the same, and they often start the sentence when the reason is already **known**: ***As** it's late, let's go home.*
***Due to, owing to*** and ***thanks to*** are followed by a **noun**, like *because of*. For the basics of *so* and *because*, see [And, But, Or, So, Because](/blog/grammar/and-but-or-so-because/).

points.title: Because, as and since
points.summary: ***Because***, ***as*** and ***since*** all give a reason + clause. ***Because*** puts more focus on the reason and is the usual answer to *Why?* ***As*** and ***since*** often start the sentence when the reason is clear or already known.

rows: the reason is the important new information
*I'm learning Spanish **because** I'm moving to Madrid.*
a known reason, often at the start
***As** it was raining, we took a taxi.*
a known reason, often at the start
***Since** you're here, can you help me?*

blocks.md: To answer a ***Why?*** question, use ***because***: *Why are you late? ~ **Because** I missed the bus.* (not *As I missed the bus*)
***Since*** can also mean *from a time* (*since 2010*), and ***as*** can mean *while* or *like*, so check the meaning in the sentence.

examples.text: **As** we have time, let's have a coffee.
**Since** it's your birthday, I'll pay.
I couldn't sleep **because** the neighbours were noisy.
Why are you so happy? ~ **Because** I got the job!

mistakes.wrong: Why did you leave early? ~ As I was tired.
mistakes.right: Why did you leave early? ~ Because I was tired.

mistakes.wrong: As it was late, so we went home.
mistakes.right: As it was late, we went home.

points.title: Now that, seeing as, in case
points.summary: ***Now that*** = because of a **new** situation (*Now that I've retired, I have more time*). ***Seeing as / seeing that*** (informal) = because. Don't confuse reasons with ***in case*** (a precaution: *Take an umbrella **in case** it rains*).

rows: ***Now that** the kids have left home, the house is quiet.*
***Seeing as** you're here, you can help.*
*Take some water **in case** you get thirsty.*

blocks.md: ***Now that*** often goes with the **present perfect** or a present tense: ***Now that** I've passed my test, I can drive to work.*
After ***in case***, use a **present** tense for the future: *in case it **rains*** (not *in case it will rain*).

examples.text: **Now that** I live near work, I walk every day.
**Seeing as** it's Friday, let's order pizza.
Write down my number **in case** you need it.
**Now that** you mention it, I do feel a bit cold.

mistakes.wrong: Take a coat in case it will be cold.
mistakes.right: Take a coat in case it's cold.

mistakes.wrong: Now as I've finished, I can relax.
mistakes.right: Now that I've finished, I can relax.

points.title: Due to, owing to, thanks to, because of
points.summary: ***Because of, due to, owing to*** and ***thanks to*** + **noun** or ***-ing***. ***Due to*** often follows *be* (*The delay **was due to** the snow*). ***Thanks to*** is usually for **good** results. Use ***due to the fact that*** + clause.

rows: *The flight was cancelled **due to** bad weather.* / *The delay **was due to** a strike.*
***Owing to** illness, the concert was cancelled.*
***Thanks to** your help, we finished on time.*
*due to / owing to the fact that* + clause
*…**due to the fact that** prices have risen.*

blocks.md: Like *because of*, these are followed by a **noun**, not a clause: *due to **the rain*** (not *due to it was raining*).

examples.text: The match was postponed **due to** heavy rain.
The accident **was due to** driver error.
**Owing to** a technical problem, the website is down.
**Thanks to** the new bridge, the journey is much shorter.

mistakes.wrong: The train was late due to it was snowing.
mistakes.right: The train was late due to the snow.

mistakes.wrong: Thanks to the storm, our house was damaged.
mistakes.right: Because of the storm, our house was damaged.

points.title: Given that, in that, inasmuch as, for, in view of
points.summary: Formal ways to give reasons: ***given (that)***, ***in view of***, ***on account of***, ***in that*** (= because, explaining in what way), ***inasmuch as***, and literary ***for*** (= because, after the main clause).

rows: ***Given that** he's only 18, his success is amazing.* / ***Given** his age, …*
***In view of** the bad weather, the event has been cancelled.*
*He retired early **on account of** ill health.*
*The plan is risky **in that** it depends on one supplier.*
*He is guilty **inasmuch as** he knew about it.*

blocks.md: Literary ***for*** never starts a sentence and always follows a **comma**: *We hurried home**, for** it was getting dark.*
***Given*** can be followed by a **noun** or ***that*** + clause: ***Given** the cost, … / **Given that** it costs so much, …*

examples.text: **Given that** it's his first job, he's doing very well.
**In view of** recent events, security has been increased.
The results are surprising **in that** they contradict earlier research.
He said nothing, **for** he knew it was hopeless.

mistakes.wrong: For she was tired, she went to bed.
mistakes.right: She went to bed, for she was tired.
mistakes.why: literary for: never at the start

mistakes.wrong: In view the weather, we stayed in.
mistakes.right: In view of the weather, we stayed in.

items.prompt: ___ I've found a job, I can rent my own flat.
Take your phone ___ you get lost.
___ that the exams are over, we can finally relax. (one word)
items.explanation: *Now that* = because of a new situation.

items.prompt: The concert was cancelled ___ the singer's illness.
___ my teacher, I passed the exam with a high mark.
The delay was ___ to a problem with the engine. (one word)

topics.h1: Both… And, Either… Or, Neither… Nor, Not Only… But Also
topics.summary: Joining two ideas: both Ali and Sara, either tea or coffee, neither Monday nor Tuesday, not only clever but also kind.
intro: These **paired conjunctions** join two words, phrases or clauses: *I speak **both** English **and** Persian. We can go **either** today **or** tomorrow.*
For *both, either* and *neither* on their own (*both of them, either day*), see [Quantifiers](/blog/grammar/quantifiers/#qn-both-either-neither).

points.title: Both… and
points.summary: ***Both X and Y*** = X and Y, the two together: *Both my mother and my father are teachers.* With two subjects, use a **plural** verb.

blocks.md: ***Both… and*** adds emphasis: the two things are true: *She speaks **both** French **and** Spanish.*
Two subjects with *both… and* take a **plural** verb: ***Both** Ali **and** Sara **are** coming.*
Put *both* directly before the first item: *She's **both** clever **and** funny.*

examples.text: **Both** my brother **and** my sister live in Vancouver.
The film was **both** funny **and** sad.
I like **both** tea **and** coffee.

mistakes.wrong: Both Ali and Sara is coming.
mistakes.right: Both Ali and Sara are coming.

mistakes.wrong: She is both intelligent or kind.
mistakes.right: She is both intelligent and kind.

points.title: Either… or: one or the other
points.summary: ***Either X or Y*** = X or Y, one of the two: *We can either take the bus or walk.* In negatives, ***not… either… or*** = not X and not Y. With two subjects, the verb agrees with the **nearest** one.

rows: *I **don't** speak **either** French **or** German.* (= I speak neither)
*Either Ali or **his sisters are** coming. Either his sisters or **Ali is** coming.*

blocks.md: With two subjects, the verb agrees with the **nearest** subject: *Either my parents or **my brother is** going to pick you up.*
Use *either… or* for a choice between **two** things. With more items, *or* alone is usual: *You can pay by cash, card **or** cheque.*

examples.text: You can **either** call me **or** send an email.
**Either** you leave now, **or** I call the police.
She doesn't eat **either** meat **or** fish.
**Either** Monday **or** Tuesday is fine.

mistakes.wrong: You can have either tea and coffee.
mistakes.right: You can have either tea or coffee.

mistakes.wrong: Either Ali or Reza are coming.
mistakes.right: Either Ali or Reza is coming.

points.title: Neither… nor: not one and not the other
points.summary: ***Neither X nor Y*** = not X and not Y: *Neither my brother nor my sister can swim.* Use a **positive** verb, because *neither… nor* is already negative.

blocks.md: Use a **positive** verb: *I **have** neither time nor money.* (= I don't have time or money), not *I don't have neither…*
With two subjects, the verb agrees with the **nearest** subject: *Neither the teacher nor **the students were** ready.*
*Neither… nor* is a little formal. In conversation, *not… either… or* is common: *I **don't** like **either** coffee **or** tea.*

examples.text: **Neither** my mum **nor** my dad speaks English.
The hotel was **neither** clean **nor** cheap.
She **neither** smiled **nor** said hello.
**Neither** the bus **nor** the trains **were** running.

mistakes.wrong: Neither Ali nor Reza didn't come.
mistakes.right: Neither Ali nor Reza came.

mistakes.wrong: I like neither fish or meat.
mistakes.right: I like neither fish nor meat.

points.title: Not only… but also
points.summary: ***Not only X but (also) Y*** = X and also Y, with emphasis on the **second** idea: *She's not only clever but also very kind.* At the **start** of a sentence, use **inversion**: *Not only did he forget my birthday, but he also…*

rows: *She **not only** sings **but also** writes her own songs.*
***Not only is** it cheap, **but** it's **also** fast.*
*Not only did we miss the train, but we lost our tickets **as well**.*

blocks.md: ***Also*** can be left out, or you can use *as well / too* at the end: *Not only is he rich, but he's famous **too**.*

When *not only* starts the sentence, use **question order** (auxiliary + subject): ***Not only did she** win, she broke the record.* See [Inversion After Negative Adverbials](/blog/grammar/inversion-negative-adverbials/).

examples.text: The app is **not only** free **but also** easy to use.
She **not only** works full-time **but also** studies at night.
**Not only did** he arrive late, **but** he **also** forgot the documents.
**Not only is** this hotel cheap, it's **also** very central.

mistakes.wrong: Not only he forgot my birthday, but he also lied.
mistakes.right: Not only did he forget my birthday, but he also lied.

mistakes.wrong: She is not only clever and also kind.
mistakes.right: She is not only clever but also kind.

points.title: Parallel structure, nor after a negative, whether… or
points.summary: Paired conjunctions join **parallel** items (the same grammar): *either **to stay** or **to leave***. ***Nor*** can start a new clause after a negative, with **inversion**: *He didn't call, **nor did he** write.* ***Whether… or*** = it doesn't matter which.

rows: *She was praised **both** for her courage **and** for her honesty.*
*I have never been to Spain, **nor do I** want to go.*
***Whether** you like it **or** not, you have to go.*

blocks.md: In formal writing, place each conjunction **directly before** the parallel items: *He is **either** in Tehran **or** in Isfahan* or *He is in **either** Tehran **or** Isfahan*.
***Nor*** after a negative clause uses **inversion**: *The plan isn't cheap, **nor is it** practical.* See also [So Do I, Neither Do I](/blog/grammar/so-do-i-neither-do-i/).

examples.text: You must **either** pay now **or** cancel the order.
The report was **neither** accurate **nor** complete.
He didn't apologise, **nor did he** explain.
**Whether** we win **or** lose, we'll enjoy the game.

mistakes.wrong: The job is both challenging and it pays well.
mistakes.right: The job is both challenging and well paid.

mistakes.wrong: She didn't call, nor she wrote.
mistakes.right: She didn't call, nor did she write.

items.prompt: She speaks not only Persian ___ also Turkish.
Not only ___ late, but he also forgot the tickets.
items.explanation: At the start: inversion (*did he arrive*).

items.prompt: Not only ___ (be) the food delicious, but it was also cheap.
items.explanation: At the start: inversion (*was the food*).

topics.h1: Causative Have and Get (I had my hair cut)
topics.summary: When someone else does something for you: I had my hair cut. We're getting the kitchen painted.
intro: We use ***have something done*** when we arrange for **another person** to do something for us, usually a service: *I **had my car repaired**.* (A mechanic repaired it; I didn't do it myself.)
Compare: *I repaired my car* (I did it) / *I **had** my car **repaired*** (someone did it for me). For the passive in general, see [Passive Voice](/blog/grammar/passive-voice/).

points.title: Have something done: services
points.summary: **have + object + past participle** = arrange for someone to do it: *I have my hair cut every month. We had the house painted.*

rows: *I **have my hair cut** every six weeks.*

blocks.md: The word order is important: ***have + thing + past participle***. *I had **my car washed*** (someone washed it). *I had washed my car* (past perfect: I washed it myself).
*Have* is a normal verb here, so questions and negatives use *do / does / did*: ***Did** you **have** the TV **repaired**?*

examples.text: I **had my hair cut** yesterday.
We're **having a new kitchen fitted** next month.
She **has her nails done** every Friday.
You should **have your eyes tested**.

mistakes.wrong: I had cut my hair at the hairdresser's.
mistakes.right: I had my hair cut at the hairdresser's.

mistakes.wrong: I cut my hair yesterday. (the hairdresser did it)
mistakes.right: I had my hair cut yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: Did you had your car washed?
mistakes.right: Did you have your car washed?

points.title: Get something done
points.summary: **get + object + past participle** means the same as *have something done*, but it's more informal: *I need to get my phone fixed.* It can also mean *finish*: *get the work done*.

blocks.md: In everyday speech, ***get*** is very common instead of *have*: *I **got my hair cut**. I must **get my passport renewed**.*
*Get something done* can also mean **finish it** (do it yourself or make sure it happens): *I need to **get this report done** by Friday.*
With *get*, there's often a feeling of effort or of something we need to deal with: *I finally **got the washing machine fixed**.*

examples.text: I'm going to **get my teeth checked** next week.
We **got the heating repaired** before winter.
Let's **get this job done** and go home.
Where can I **get my shoes repaired**?

mistakes.wrong: I need to get fix my laptop.
mistakes.right: I need to get my laptop fixed.

mistakes.wrong: I got my car to wash.
mistakes.right: I got my car washed.

points.title: Had my phone stolen: things that happen to you
points.summary: **have / get + object + past participle** also describes bad things that **happen** to you, not things you arrange: *I had my bag stolen. He got his nose broken.*

blocks.md: The same structure can describe an **unpleasant experience** caused by someone else: *We **had our car broken into** last night.* (We didn't arrange it!)
Compare: *My bag **was stolen*** (passive) and *I **had my bag stolen*** (focus on me as the victim). Both are correct.
*Get* is also used, especially for injuries and accidents: *He **got his arm broken** playing rugby.*

examples.text: She **had her passport stolen** in Rome.
We **had our flight cancelled**.
He **got his fingers trapped** in the door.
They **had their house broken into** while they were on holiday.

mistakes.wrong: I stole my wallet on the bus. (someone stole it)
mistakes.right: I had my wallet stolen on the bus.

mistakes.wrong: She had stolen her phone. (it happened to her)
mistakes.right: She had her phone stolen.

points.title: Have someone do, get someone to do, make and let
points.summary: **have + person + base verb** and **get + person + to + verb** = arrange for someone to do something: *I'll have the porter carry your bags. I got my brother to help me.*

rows: *I **got my sister to lend** me her car.*

blocks.md: Note the difference: *have / make / let* + **base verb** (no *to*); *get* + person + ***to*** + verb.
In the passive, *make* takes *to*: *I **was made to** wait for an hour.* *Let* has no passive: use *be allowed to*.

examples.text: The manager **had the staff work** late.
I **got a friend to fix** my computer.
The teacher **made us rewrite** the essay.
My parents **let me stay** up late.

mistakes.wrong: I got my brother help me.
mistakes.right: I got my brother to help me.

mistakes.wrong: She made me to apologise.
mistakes.right: She made me apologise.

mistakes.wrong: They let us to go.
mistakes.right: They let us go.

points.title: Have someone doing, I won't have it, get things going
points.summary: **have + person + -ing** = cause an ongoing result (*He had us laughing*). **won't have + person + -ing** = won't allow (*I won't have you talking like that*). **get + object + -ing** = start something (*get the car going*).

blocks.md: ***Have + person + -ing*** describes an effect someone causes: *The comedian **had** everyone **laughing**. In ten minutes she **had** the kids **dancing**.*
***I won't have*** + person + *-ing* (or + noun) = I won't accept or allow it: *I **won't have** you **speaking** to your mother like that!* *I **won't have** any arguments in this house.*
***Get + object + -ing*** = make something start working or moving: *It took an hour to **get the engine running**. Let's **get things moving**.*
***Have something done*** can also mean *finish by a time*: *I'll **have the report finished** by Monday.* (I'll make sure it's finished.)

examples.text: Her stories **had us laughing** all evening.
I **won't have** people **smoking** in my house.
We finally **got the old car going**.
I'll **have it done** by five o'clock.

mistakes.wrong: He had us laugh all night. (an ongoing effect)
mistakes.right: He had us laughing all night.

mistakes.wrong: I won't have you to shout at me.
mistakes.right: I won't have you shouting at me.

items.prompt: Poor Ahmad! He ___ on the train yesterday.
items.explanation: A bad experience: *had his laptop stolen*.

items.prompt: What does *We had our car damaged* mean?
options: We paid someone to damage our car.
items.explanation: A bad experience caused by someone else.

items.prompt: She ___ (have / her handbag / snatch) in the market.
items.explanation: A bad experience: *had her handbag snatched*.

items.prompt: I couldn't open the jar, so I ___ my husband to do it.
The doctor ___ me wait for two hours!
I'll have my secretary ___ (send) you the contract.

topics.summary: Ways to put emphasis on one part of a sentence: I do like it. It was Ali who called. What I need is a holiday.
intro: A **cleft sentence** splits one sentence into two parts to **focus** on the most important information: *Ali broke the window.* → ***It was Ali who** broke the window.* (not someone else) / ***What I need is** a holiday.*
We also use stressed ***do / does / did*** for emphasis: *I **do** like it!* See also [So Do I, Neither Do I](/blog/grammar/so-do-i-neither-do-i/#sdn-formal).

points.title: Emphatic do: I do like it! Do sit down.
points.summary: Put ***do / does / did*** before the base verb in a **positive** sentence to add **emphasis** or **contrast**: *I **do** like your dress! She **did** call you. I don't eat meat, but I **do** eat fish.* ***Do*** + imperative is polite and warm: ***Do** come in!*

rows: *I don't drive, but I **do** have a licence.*

blocks.md: After ***do / does / did***, use the **base verb**: *She **does** work hard* (not *does works*). *He **did** tell me* (not *did told*).

examples.text: I **do** hope you can come.
He doesn't say much, but he **does** listen.
I **did** send the email. Check your spam folder.
**Do** have some more cake!

mistakes.wrong: She does works very hard.
mistakes.right: She does work very hard.

mistakes.wrong: I did told you about it!
mistakes.right: I did tell you about it!

points.title: It was Ali who…: it-clefts
points.summary: ***It is / It was*** + the focused part + ***who / that*** + the rest: ***It was Ali who** broke the window* (not someone else). ***It's the price that** worries me* (not the size).

rows: ***It was Ali who** broke the window.*
***It was in Paris that** I met her.*
***It was on Friday that** we left.*

blocks.md: Use ***who*** or ***that*** for people, ***that*** for things, places and times. Use ***It is*** for present and ***It was*** for past.
It-clefts are often used to **correct** someone: *No, it wasn't me who called. **It was** my brother.*

examples.text: **It was** my mother **who** taught me to cook.
**It's** the traffic **that** makes me late.
**It was** in 2019 **that** we moved to Canada.
**It wasn't** me **who** told her!

mistakes.wrong: It was Ali which broke the window.
mistakes.right: It was Ali who broke the window.

mistakes.wrong: Was in Paris that I met her.
mistakes.right: It was in Paris that I met her.

points.title: What I need is a holiday: what-clefts
points.summary: ***What*** + clause + ***is / was*** + the focused part: ***What I need is** a holiday. **What I like about her is** her honesty.* The focus comes **at the end**.

rows: ***What I love is** his sense of humour.*

blocks.md: The verb after *what…* is usually ***is*** (or ***was*** for the past), even when the focus is plural: ***What we need is** more teachers.*
You can reverse it: *A holiday **is what** I need.*

examples.text: **What** I really want **is** a cup of tea.
**What** worries me **is** the cost.
**What** I liked most **was** the food.
**What** you need to do **is** practise every day.

mistakes.wrong: The thing what I need is time.
mistakes.right: What I need is time. / The thing that I need is time.

mistakes.wrong: What I need it is a holiday.
mistakes.right: What I need is a holiday.

points.title: All I want is, the thing is, the reason why
points.summary: Other cleft patterns: ***All I want is…*** (= the only thing), ***The thing (that) I…is***, ***The reason (why)…is that***, ***The place where…***, ***The person who…***, ***The first / last / only thing…***.

rows: ***All I want is** a quiet life.* (= the only thing)
***The reason I'm late is that** the bus broke down.*
***The place where** we met **is** now a bank.*
***The person who** helped me **was** a stranger.*
***The only thing** I can do **is** wait.*

blocks.md: After ***The reason (why)…***, use ***is that*** (not *is because* in careful writing): ***The reason** I called **is that** I need help.*
After ***All*** and ***The only thing***, a verb focus can be a base verb: ***All I did was** ask a question.*

examples.text: **All I did was** ask a simple question!
**The thing I like most is** the food.
**The reason why** she left **is that** she was unhappy.
**The only thing** I can't eat **is** fish.

mistakes.wrong: All what I want is peace.
mistakes.right: All I want is peace. / All that I want is peace.

mistakes.wrong: The reason I'm late is because the bus was slow. (careful writing)
mistakes.right: The reason I'm late is that the bus was slow.

points.title: What she did was call the police; what happened was
points.summary: To focus on an **action**, use ***What*** + subject + ***do / did*** + ***is / was*** + (*to*) + base verb: ***What she did was (to) call** the police.* To focus on a whole event: ***What happened was (that)…***

rows: ***What she did was (to) call** the police.*
***What happened was (that)** the car broke down.*
***What I'm going to do is sell** the house.*

blocks.md: After ***What … did was***, use the **base verb** (with or without *to*): *What he did was **leave** / **to leave**.* Not *What he did was left*.

examples.text: **What** we **did was** take a taxi.
**What** you **need to do is** fill in this form.
**What happened was** that the bridge collapsed.
**What** I'm **going to do is** call him tomorrow.

mistakes.wrong: What she did was called her lawyer.
mistakes.right: What she did was call her lawyer.

mistakes.wrong: What was happened was an accident.
mistakes.right: What happened was an accident.

points.title: It wasn't until, it's not that…it's that, that's what
points.summary: Advanced patterns: ***It wasn't until*** + time + ***that*** (= only then), ***It's not that … , it's (just) that…***, and **reversed** clefts: ***That's what** I mean. **This is where** the problem starts. **Here's why**…*

rows: ***It wasn't until** I moved abroad **that** I appreciated my family.*
***It's not that** I don't like you**; it's that** I'm busy.*
***That's why** I left. **That's exactly what** I meant.*
***It is** the customers **who** are affected most.*

blocks.md: ***It wasn't until*** can also start with ***Not until*** + inversion in very formal English: ***Not until** I moved abroad **did** I appreciate my family.* See [Inversion After Negative Adverbials](/blog/grammar/inversion-negative-adverbials/).

examples.text: **It wasn't until** midnight **that** they finally arrived.
**It's not that** the job is hard; **it's that** the hours are long.
**That's what** I've been trying to tell you!
**This is how** you open the file.

mistakes.wrong: It wasn't until I was 30 when I learned to drive.
mistakes.right: It wasn't until I was 30 that I learned to drive.

mistakes.wrong: It's not that I'm angry, but I'm tired.
mistakes.right: It's not that I'm angry; it's that I'm tired.

items.prompt: You never believe me, but I ___ tell you the truth.
I know you think he's lazy, but he ___ work very hard.
Please ___ come in and sit down. You're very welcome. (one word: emphatic auxiliary)
It was my brother ___ found the money.
I don't mind the work. ___ the long hours that I don't like.
It was in Rome ___ they first met. (one word)
___ I need right now is a long sleep.
What I love about this city ___ the food.
___ surprised me was how friendly everyone was. (one word)

topics.summary: Comparing things: bigger, more interesting, the best, as tall as, much faster, the sooner the better.
intro: Use **comparatives** to compare two things (*Toronto is **bigger than** Ottawa*) and **superlatives** to say which is the most in a group (*It's **the biggest** city in Canada*).
This page also covers *as… as* and how to make a comparison stronger or weaker (*much bigger, a bit cheaper, by far the best*).

points.title: Bigger, more expensive, the biggest, the most expensive
points.summary: Short adjectives take **-er / the -est** (*cheap → cheaper → the cheapest*). Long adjectives take **more / the most** (*expensive → more expensive → the most expensive*). Use **than** after a comparative.

blocks.md: Use ***than*** after a comparative: *My brother is taller **than** me.* Use ***the*** before a superlative, often with *in* or *of*: *the tallest **in** the class, the best day **of** my life*.
Some two-syllable adjectives can take both forms: *quieter / more quiet, simpler / more simple, cleverer / more clever*.

examples.text: My flat is **smaller than** yours.
This is **the most beautiful** beach in Iran.
Today is **hotter than** yesterday.
Maths is **easier than** physics for me.

mistakes.wrong: She is more tall than her sister.
mistakes.right: She is taller than her sister.

mistakes.wrong: This is the most cheap hotel.
