mistakes.right: This is the cheapest hotel.

mistakes.wrong: He's older that me.
mistakes.right: He's older than me.

mistakes.wrong: It's the biggest city of the world.
mistakes.right: It's the biggest city in the world.

points.title: Good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; far, further
points.summary: Irregular forms: **good → better → the best**, **bad → worse → the worst**, **far → farther / further → the farthest / the furthest**. The adverbs **well** and **badly** also become **better** and **worse**.

blocks.md: ***Further*** also means **more, extra**: *For **further** information, call us.* (not *farther* here)

examples.text: Your English is **better** than mine.
That was **the worst** meal I've ever had.
The station is **further** than I thought.
She earns **more** money than me.

mistakes.wrong: This film is more good than the book.
mistakes.right: This film is better than the book.

mistakes.wrong: It was the baddest day of my life.
mistakes.right: It was the worst day of my life.

mistakes.wrong: I feel more bad today.
mistakes.right: I feel worse today.

points.title: As… as, not as… as, the same as
points.summary: Use ***as + adjective + as*** to say two things are **equal**: *She's as tall as her mother.* ***Not as / not so… as*** = less: *Ottawa isn't as big as Toronto.* Use ***the same as*** for things that are equal.

rows: *This hotel **isn't as expensive as** the other one.*
*Your phone is **the same as** mine. She's **the same age as** me.*
*Their house is **twice as big as** ours.*

blocks.md: After *as… as*, everyday English uses an object pronoun: *as tall as **me***. Careful English: *as tall as **I am***.

examples.text: The new film is **as good as** the first one.
Ottawa **isn't as big as** Toronto.
My bag is **the same as** yours.
This laptop is **twice as expensive as** that one.

mistakes.wrong: She's as taller as me.
mistakes.right: She's as tall as me.

mistakes.wrong: My phone is the same like yours.
mistakes.right: My phone is the same as yours.

mistakes.wrong: It isn't as cold than yesterday.
mistakes.right: It isn't as cold as yesterday.

points.title: Much bigger, a bit cheaper, by far the best
points.summary: Make comparatives stronger with ***much, a lot, far*** (*much bigger*) and weaker with ***a bit, a little, slightly*** (*a bit cheaper*). Make superlatives stronger with ***by far*** (*by far the best*).

rows: *It's **even** colder today.* (and it was already cold)

blocks.md: Don't use ***very*** with comparatives: *much better* (not *very better*).
***Even*** + comparative shows the first thing was already high: *Yesterday was hot, but today is **even hotter**.*

examples.text: The train is **much faster** than the bus.
Could you speak **a bit more slowly**?
This is **by far the best** café in town.
Today is **even colder** than yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: My new flat is very bigger.
mistakes.right: My new flat is much bigger.

mistakes.wrong: This is far the best hotel.
mistakes.right: This is by far the best hotel.

points.title: The more, the better; colder and colder
points.summary: ***The + comparative…, the + comparative*** shows two things changing together: *The more you practise, the better you get.* ***Comparative + and + comparative*** shows a continuing change: *It's getting colder and colder.*

rows: ***The more** I read, **the more** I learn.*

blocks.md: In *the… the…* sentences, keep normal word order after each comparative: *The older he gets, the quieter **he becomes**.*
Long adjectives repeat *more*: ***more and more** popular* (not *more and more popular-er*).

examples.text: **The more** you sleep, **the better** you feel.
**The faster** you drive, **the more** dangerous it is.
My son is getting **taller and taller**.
Online shopping is becoming **more and more popular**.

mistakes.wrong: More you practise, better you get.
mistakes.right: The more you practise, the better you get.

mistakes.wrong: It's getting more and more cold.
mistakes.right: It's getting colder and colder.

mistakes.wrong: Prices are getting more expensive and more expensive.
mistakes.right: Prices are getting more and more expensive.

points.title: Superior to, nowhere near as, twice the size of, the latter
points.summary: Formal and advanced comparison: ***superior / inferior / preferable to*** (not *than*), ***nowhere near as / not nearly as*** (much less), ***twice the size of***, ***the former / the latter***, and ***more + adjective + than + adjective*** for two qualities.

rows: *This model is **superior to** the old one.* (not *superior than*)
*The sequel is **nowhere near as good as** the original.*
*Their house is **twice the size of** ours.*
*I visited Rome and Paris. **The latter** was my favourite.* (= Paris)
*He's **more lucky than clever**.* (two qualities of one person)

blocks.md: When comparing two **qualities** of the same thing, use ***more***, even with short adjectives: *The task was **more long than difficult**.*
***Junior, senior*** and ***prior*** also take ***to***: *She's **senior to** me.*

examples.text: Walking is **preferable to** driving in the city centre.
The new version is **nowhere near as fast as** we hoped.
The new stadium is **twice the size of** the old one.
I like tea and coffee, but **the former** is better for my sleep.

mistakes.wrong: This method is superior than the old one.
mistakes.right: This method is superior to the old one.

mistakes.wrong: The sequel is nowhere near good as the original.
mistakes.right: The sequel is nowhere near as good as the original.

items.prompt: ___ you start, the sooner you'll finish.
The weather is getting ___. Winter is coming.
I love history. The more I learn about it, the ___ interested I become. (one word)

topics.h1: Unless, As Long As, Provided, In Case and Even If
topics.summary: Other ways to make conditions: unless (= if not), as long as, provided, in case, even if.
intro: *If* isn't the only word for conditions. English uses ***unless, as long as, provided (that), in case*** and ***even if*** to add different meanings: an exception, a strict condition, a precaution, or *it doesn't matter*.

After all of these, we use a **present** tense for the future, just like after *if*: *I'll come **unless** it **rains**.* For the basic patterns, see [Zero and First Conditional](/blog/grammar/zero-and-first-conditional/).

points.title: Unless = if … not
points.summary: **unless** = *if … not*. Use a **positive** verb after it: *I'll go **unless** it rains* (= if it doesn't rain).

blocks.md: ***Unless*** means *except if* or *if … not*: *You can't come in **unless** you have a ticket.* = You can't come in **if** you **don't** have a ticket.
The verb after *unless* is **positive** in form, but the meaning is negative. Don't add *not*: ***unless** it **rains*** (not *unless it doesn't rain*).
Like *if*, *unless* takes a **present** tense for the future: ***Unless** you **hurry**, you'll miss the bus.*

examples.text: I'll be there at eight **unless** the train **is** late.
**Unless** you **book** now, there won't be any seats.
Don't call me **unless** it**'s** an emergency.
He won't help you **unless** you **ask** him.

mistakes.wrong: I'll come unless it doesn't rain.
mistakes.right: I'll come unless it rains.

mistakes.wrong: Unless you will study, you'll fail.
mistakes.right: Unless you study, you'll fail.

points.title: As long as, provided (that), providing
points.summary: **as long as / provided (that) / providing** = only if: *You can borrow my car **as long as** you're careful.*

blocks.md: These phrases mean ***only if*** or ***on condition that***. They make a strict condition: *You can go out **as long as** you're back by ten.* = You can go out, but only if you're back by ten.

***Provided (that)*** and ***providing (that)*** mean the same, but they're more formal. ***On condition that*** is very formal: *The loan was approved **on condition that** it was repaid within a year.*
Use a **present** tense for the future: ***As long as** you **work** hard, you'll pass.* Not *as long as you will work*.

examples.text: You can stay **as long as** you **don't make** a mess.
**Provided that** the weather **is** good, the match will go ahead.
I'll lend you the money **providing** you **pay** me back next week.
You can use the photos **on condition that** you **credit** the photographer.

mistakes.wrong: You can come as long as you will be quiet.
mistakes.right: You can come as long as you're quiet.

mistakes.wrong: Provided you don't hurry, you'll miss the train.
mistakes.right: Unless you hurry, you'll miss the train.
mistakes.why: provided = only if, not if not

points.title: In case: a precaution
points.summary: **in case** = because something **might** happen: *Take an umbrella **in case** it rains.* It's different from *if*.

blocks.md: We do something ***in case*** something happens = as a precaution, because it **might** happen: *I'll take an umbrella **in case** it rains.* (I'll take it now, because it might rain.)
Compare: *I'll take an umbrella **if** it rains* = I'll only take it if it is raining when I leave.
Use a **present** tense for the future after *in case*: *in case it **rains*** (not *in case it will rain*). For the past, use the past simple: *I took my coat **in case** it **got** cold.*
***In case of*** + noun is used on signs and in formal English: ***In case of** fire, use the stairs.* (= if there is a fire)

examples.text: Write down the address **in case** you **forget** it.
I'll give you my number **in case** you **need** help.
We left early **in case** there **was** traffic.
**In case of** emergency, break the glass.
examples.note: formal: if there is an emergency

mistakes.wrong: Take a jacket in case it will be cold.
mistakes.right: Take a jacket in case it's cold.

mistakes.wrong: I'll call you in case I'm late.
mistakes.right: I'll call you if I'm late.
mistakes.why: Call only when you're late: if.

points.title: Even if, even though and whether or not
points.summary: **even if** = it doesn't matter if: *I'll go **even if** it rains.* **even though** = although (a fact). **whether or not** = in both cases.

blocks.md: ***Even if*** says that the result will be the same **whatever happens**: *I'll finish this report **even if** I have to work all night.* (Maybe I'll have to, maybe not. It doesn't matter.)

***Even though*** is different: it introduces a **fact**, like *although*: ***Even though** it was raining, we went for a walk.* (It really was raining.) See [Although, Despite and In Spite Of](/blog/grammar/although-despite-in-spite-of/).
***Whether or not*** (or *whether … or not*) = in both cases: *I'm going, **whether or not** you come.* / *…**whether** you come **or not**.*

examples.text: **Even if** you apologise, she won't forgive you.
**Even though** he's rich, he lives in a tiny flat.
We'll play the match **whether or not** it rains.
I wouldn't tell you **even if** I knew.

mistakes.wrong: Even it rains, we'll go.
mistakes.right: Even if it rains, we'll go.

mistakes.wrong: Even if I was tired, I finished the work. (I really was tired)
mistakes.right: Even though I was tired, I finished the work.

points.title: When unless doesn't work, and only if
points.summary: *Unless* = *except if*. Don't use it for feelings or results of *not* happening (*I'd be upset if you didn't come*). **Only if** makes the condition the one and only condition.

blocks.md: *Unless* means *except if*. It doesn't work when the sentence is about the **effect of something not happening**, especially feelings: *I'll be very upset **if** you **don't** come.* Not *unless you come*. *She'd be surprised **if** he **didn't** call.* Not *unless he called*.
*Unless* is also unusual in **questions**: *What will you do **if** she **doesn't** agree?* Not *unless she agrees*.
*Unless* is often added as an **afterthought**: *Let's take the bus, **unless** you'd rather walk.*

***Only if*** = in this one case and no other: *I'll lend you money **only if** you promise to pay it back.* In formal English it can start the sentence with inversion: ***Only if** you promise **will** I lend you the money.*

examples.text: I'll be really disappointed **if** you **don't** pass.
What happens **if** the payment **doesn't** go through?
We could eat out, **unless** you're too tired.
You'll get a refund **only if** you keep the receipt.

mistakes.wrong: I'll be sad unless you come to my party.
mistakes.right: I'll be sad if you don't come to my party.

mistakes.wrong: What will you do unless you get the visa?
mistakes.right: What will you do if you don't get the visa?

items.prompt: I'm going to the concert ___ I have to go alone.
items.explanation: It doesn't matter if I have to go alone: *even if*.

items.prompt: ___ she had a cold, she went to work. (She really had a cold.)
We're leaving at nine, whether you like it ___ not.

topics.summary: Which nouns you can count (an apple, two apples) and which you can't (water, advice, information), and how to talk about them.
intro: ***Countable*** nouns can be counted: *one apple, two apples*. ***Uncountable*** nouns can't: *water, rice, advice*. You can't say *two rices* or *an advice*.
The difference changes the words you use with them: *a, some, much, many, a few, a little*. See also [Much, Many, A Few, A Little](/blog/grammar/much-many-a-few-a-little/).

points.title: Countable or uncountable?
points.summary: **Countable** nouns have a singular and a plural (*an apple, two apples*). **Uncountable** nouns have no plural and no *a / an* (*water, rice, money*), and they take a singular verb.

blocks.md: Uncountable nouns are often **liquids** (*water, juice*), **materials** (*wood, paper, gold*), **food in a mass** (*rice, sugar, cheese*) and **ideas** (*love, help, time*).
Uncountable nouns take a **singular verb**: *The milk **is** in the fridge. Money **isn't** everything.*

examples.text: I'd like **an** orange and **some** bread.
There **is** some cheese in the fridge.
How **many** eggs do we need?
How **much** sugar do you take?

mistakes.wrong: I need some moneys.
mistakes.right: I need some money.

mistakes.wrong: The rice are ready.
mistakes.right: The rice is ready.

mistakes.wrong: I eat a bread every morning.
mistakes.right: I eat bread every morning.

points.title: Tricky uncountable nouns: advice, information, news
points.summary: Some nouns are **uncountable** in English but countable in many other languages: *advice, information, news, furniture, luggage, homework, equipment, traffic, weather, work, travel*.

rows: *a piece of news, a news story*
*a chair, a table, a piece of furniture*

blocks.md: These nouns take a **singular verb** and no *-s*: *The information **is** on the website. Your advice **was** very helpful.*
Use *some, any, much, a lot of* or *a piece of* with them: *Can I give you **some advice**? I don't have **much homework**.*

examples.text: Can you give me **some information** about the course?
I have **a lot of homework** tonight.
Our luggage **is** in the car.
I'm looking for **a job**. I need **work**.

mistakes.wrong: She gave me a good advice.
mistakes.right: She gave me some good advice.

mistakes.wrong: We bought new furnitures.
mistakes.right: We bought new furniture.

mistakes.wrong: The news are on at six.
mistakes.right: The news is on at six.

mistakes.wrong: I had a nice travel.
mistakes.right: I had a nice trip.

points.title: A piece of, a slice of, a bottle of
points.summary: To count uncountable nouns, use a **unit**: *a piece of cake, a slice of bread, a bottle of water, a cup of coffee, a bar of chocolate, a loaf of bread*.

blocks.md: The **unit** is countable, so it can be plural: *two **slices** of bread, three **bottles** of water*. The uncountable noun stays singular: *two slices of **bread*** (not *breads*).

examples.text: Could I have **a glass of** water, please?
I bought **two loaves of** bread.
She gave me **a useful piece of** advice.
We need **a carton of** milk.

mistakes.wrong: Two breads, please.
mistakes.right: Two loaves of bread, please.

mistakes.wrong: three bottles of waters
mistakes.right: three bottles of water

points.title: Nouns that can be both: paper or a paper, coffee or a coffee
points.summary: Many nouns can be **countable or uncountable** with a different meaning: *paper* (material) / *a paper* (a newspaper); *glass* / *a glass*; *time* / *a time*; *experience* / *an experience*. With drinks, *a coffee* = a cup of coffee.

rows: *a paper*: a newspaper or an essay
*a glass*: for drinking; *glasses*: for your eyes
*hair*: all the hair on your head
*a time*: an occasion: *I've been there three times.*
*an experience*: something that happened to you
*coffee, tea, juice*: the drink in general
*a coffee*: a cup or glass of it

examples.text: I need some **paper** to print this.
I bought **a paper** at the station.
Two **coffees**, please.
She has a lot of **experience** in marketing.
Travelling alone was **an** amazing **experience**.

mistakes.wrong: I have a lot of experiences in sales.
mistakes.right: I have a lot of experience in sales.

mistakes.wrong: She has long black hairs.
mistakes.right: She has long black hair.

mistakes.wrong: Is there a room for one more person in the car?
mistakes.right: Is there room for one more person in the car?

points.title: Formal uncountable nouns: research, evidence, feedback
points.summary: In formal and academic English, *research, evidence, feedback, knowledge, progress, accommodation, equipment* are **uncountable**. Use *a piece of*, *a study* or another countable word for one. Some uncountable nouns become countable for **kinds** (*French wines*).

rows: *a tool, a device / a program, an app*

blocks.md: These nouns take a **singular verb** and have **no plural**: *The evidence **is** clear. Recent research **has** shown…*
**Kinds**: some uncountable nouns are countable when we mean **types**: *This shop sells **French wines** and **Italian cheeses**. There are **many different teas** from China.*

examples.text: There **is** no **evidence** that the drug works.
She's doing **research** into childhood memory.
Thank you for your **feedback**.
We tasted **three local cheeses**.

mistakes.wrong: Recent researches show that sleep matters.
mistakes.right: Recent research shows that sleep matters.

mistakes.wrong: We found an evidence.
mistakes.right: We found a piece of evidence.

mistakes.wrong: You've made a good progress.
mistakes.right: You've made good progress.

items.prompt: Is there ___ room in your car for my bag?
I've been to London three ___.
She has ten years of ___ (experience) as a nurse.

topics.h1: Defining Relative Clauses (the man who…, the book that…)
topics.summary: Clauses that say which person or thing we mean: The woman who lives next door is a doctor. The book that I lent you is mine.
intro: A **defining relative clause** tells us **which** person or thing we're talking about: *The man **who called you** is my uncle.* Without the clause, the sentence isn't complete or clear.
Defining clauses don't use commas. For clauses that add **extra** information (*My uncle, who is a doctor, …*), see [Non-Defining Relative Clauses](/blog/grammar/non-defining-relative-clauses/).

points.title: Who, which and that
points.summary: **who** for people, **which** for things, **that** for both: *the girl who / that won*, *the car which / that I bought*.

rows: *The woman **who** works here is very kind.*
*The bus **which** goes to the airport is the 10.*
*The man **that** called you… / The bus **that** goes…*

blocks.md: The relative pronoun **replaces** a word. Don't repeat it: *The man who **he** lives next door* ✗ → *The man who lives next door* ✓.
No commas in defining relative clauses: *The book **that** you gave me is great.*

examples.text: I know a girl **who** speaks five languages.
Where's the cake **that** was in the fridge?
The film **which** we saw last night was boring.
People **who** exercise live longer.

mistakes.wrong: The man which lives next door is a doctor.
mistakes.right: The man who lives next door is a doctor.

mistakes.wrong: The phone who I bought is broken.
mistakes.right: The phone that / which I bought is broken.

mistakes.wrong: The woman who she called me is my aunt.
mistakes.right: The woman who called me is my aunt.

points.title: Leaving out who, which or that: the people we met
points.summary: When the relative pronoun is the **object** of the clause, you can leave it out: *the book (that) I'm reading, the people (who) we met*.

blocks.md: Look at the word after the pronoun. If it's a **subject** (*I, we, she, the teacher…*), the pronoun is the **object** and you can leave it out: *The film **(that) we saw** was great.*
If the pronoun is the **subject** (it's followed directly by a verb), you **can't** leave it out: *The man **who called** you…* (not *The man called you…*, which has a different meaning).

examples.text: The cake **(that) you made** was delicious.
The people **(who) we met** on holiday were lovely.
The man **who lives** next door is a pilot.
Is this the jacket **(which) you wanted**?

mistakes.wrong: The woman lives next door is a doctor.
mistakes.right: The woman who lives next door is a doctor.

mistakes.wrong: The book I'm reading it is great.
mistakes.right: The book I'm reading is great.

points.title: Whose, where and when
points.summary: **whose** = of whom / of which (*the man whose car was stolen*). **where** = in / at which (*the town where I grew up*). **when** = time (*the day when we met*).

rows: *The girl **whose** bag was stolen called the police.*
*This is the house **where** I was born.*
*I remember the day **when** we first met.*

blocks.md: ***Whose*** is followed by a **noun**: *the man **whose wife** is a judge*. It's used for people and sometimes things: *a company **whose** products are famous*.
***Where*** can't be left out, but you can use *which / that … in*: *the house **where** I live* = *the house (that) I live **in***.
***When*** can be left out after *the day, the year, the time*: *the day **(when)** we met*.

examples.text: That's the man **whose** dog bit me.
The café **where** we first met has closed.
Summer is the time **when** most people travel.
I have a friend **whose** father is a famous actor.

mistakes.wrong: The man who's car was stolen called the police.
mistakes.right: The man whose car was stolen called the police.

mistakes.wrong: The hotel which we stayed was lovely.
mistakes.right: The hotel where we stayed was lovely. / The hotel which we stayed at was lovely.

points.title: Prepositions in relative clauses: the house I live in
points.summary: In everyday English, the preposition goes at the **end**: *the house I live in, the person I spoke to*. In formal English: *the person to whom I spoke*.

blocks.md: Many verbs and adjectives have a preposition (*live in, talk to, look for, interested in*). In a relative clause, it usually stays **after the verb**: *That's the man **I was talking to**. Is this the job **you applied for**?*
The pronoun is often left out: *the music **(that) I listen to***.

In **formal** English, the preposition can move to the front, followed by ***which*** (things) or ***whom*** (people): *the house **in which** I live*, *the person **to whom** I spoke*. Never use *that* or *who* after a preposition.

examples.text: That's the girl **I told you about**.
Is this the book **you were looking for**?
The hotel **we stayed at** was by the sea.
The committee **to which** we applied rejected the plan.

mistakes.wrong: The person to who I spoke was rude.
mistakes.right: The person (who) I spoke to was rude. / The person to whom I spoke was rude.

mistakes.wrong: The house in that I live is old.
mistakes.right: The house (that) I live in is old. / The house in which I live is old.

points.title: Who or whom?
points.summary: **whom** is the formal object form of *who*: *the man whom I met*. In everyday English, people use **who** or **that**, or leave it out. After a preposition, always **whom**.

blocks.md: ***Whom*** is used for the **object** of the relative clause in formal English: *The candidate **whom** we interviewed was excellent.* In normal speech: *The candidate **(who / that) we interviewed**…*
After a **preposition**, ***whom*** is the only choice: *the people **with whom** I work*. (Informal: *the people **(who) I work with***)
Never use *whom* as the **subject**: *the man **who** called* (not *the man whom called*).

examples.text: The doctor **whom** I saw was very kind.
The doctor **(who) I saw** was very kind.
The colleague **with whom** I share an office is on holiday.
The woman **who** called you is here.

mistakes.wrong: The man whom lives next door is noisy.
mistakes.right: The man who lives next door is noisy.

mistakes.wrong: The friend with who I travelled was ill.
mistakes.right: The friend with whom I travelled was ill.

points.title: What or that? Everything that, all that, what you need
points.summary: **what** = *the thing(s) that*. Don't use *what* after a noun or after *everything, all, something, nothing*: use **that**: *Everything that he said was true.*

blocks.md: ***What*** is not a normal relative pronoun. It means ***the thing that***, so it has no noun before it: ***What** you need is a holiday.* = *The thing that you need…*
After a noun or after *all, everything, something, anything, nothing, the only thing*, use ***that*** (or leave it out): *Is there **anything (that)** I can do? **All (that)** I want is some sleep.*

examples.text: **What** I love about Toronto is the people.
**Everything that** you told me was true.
The **only thing (that)** I need is a coffee.
She didn't understand **what** I said.

mistakes.wrong: Everything what he said was a lie.
mistakes.right: Everything (that) he said was a lie.

mistakes.wrong: The thing what I like most is the music.
mistakes.right: The thing that I like most is the music. / What I like most is the music.

points.title: Reduced relative clauses: the woman talking to Tom, a car made in Japan
points.summary: Shorten relative clauses with **-ing** (active: *the man sitting there* = who is sitting) or a **past participle** (passive: *the car stolen yesterday* = which was stolen).

rows: *The woman **who is talking** to Tom is my aunt.*
*The woman **talking** to Tom is my aunt.*
*The car **which was stolen** yesterday was found.*

blocks.md: Use ***-ing*** for an **active** meaning (the noun does the action) and the **past participle** for a **passive** meaning (something is done to the noun).
Don't use *-ing* for a single completed action in the past: *The man **who broke** the window ran away* (not *The man breaking the window ran away*, which means he was in the middle of breaking it).

examples.text: Who's the boy **wearing** the red hat?
Most of the people **invited** to the party came.
Students **wishing** to join should email the club.
The new bridge, **built** in 2020, is very modern.

mistakes.wrong: The man stood at the door is my father.
mistakes.right: The man standing at the door is my father.

mistakes.wrong: A letter writing in English is easier to read.
mistakes.right: A letter written in English is easier to read.

points.title: The first to arrive, nothing to do, the reason why, the way
points.summary: Infinitive relative clauses: **the first / last / only / next + to + verb** (*the first person to arrive*), **something / nothing + to + verb** (*nothing to do*). Also **the reason (why / that)** and **the way (that / in which)**.

blocks.md: After ***the first, the last, the only, the next*** and superlatives, a *to*-infinitive can replace a relative clause: *She was **the first woman to win** the prize.* (= who won)

After ***something, anything, nothing, a lot, somewhere*** and some nouns, *to* + verb shows **purpose** or **possibility**: *There's **nothing to eat**. I need **somewhere to stay**. Is there **anything to drink**?*
***The reason (why / that)*** and ***the way (that / in which)***: *That's **the reason (why)** I left. I like **the way (that)** she talks.* Don't say *the way how*.

examples.text: Neil Armstrong was **the first person to walk** on the Moon.
I've got **a lot of work to do** today.
Is there **anywhere to park** near here?
**The reason (why)** I called is to say thank you.

mistakes.wrong: She was the first woman who to fly across the Atlantic.
mistakes.right: She was the first woman to fly across the Atlantic.

mistakes.wrong: I don't like the way how he speaks.
mistakes.right: I don't like the way (that) he speaks.

items.prompt: The woman ___ answered the phone was very polite.
Formal: *The man ___ the police arrested was released.*
The person with ___ I work is very organised. (one word)
I didn't believe a word of ___ he said.
Is there anything ___ I can do to help?
___ I need now is a good night's sleep. (one word)
The girl ___ next to Mina is my sister.
Most of the goods ___ in this shop are imported.
The police are looking for a man ___ (wear) a black jacket. (one word)

topics.summary: Avoiding repetition by leaving words out (ellipsis) or using short words like one, do so and so (substitution).
intro: Good English avoids **repeating** words. We can **leave words out** (*ellipsis*): *I wanted to go, but I couldn't (go).* Or we can **replace** them with a short word (*substitution*): *I don't like this shirt. Can I see a different **one**?*
For short answers and *so do I*, see [So Do I, Neither Do I](/blog/grammar/so-do-i-neither-do-i/). For *I think so*, see the same page.

points.title: One and ones: the red one, these ones
points.summary: Use ***one*** (singular) and ***ones*** (plural) instead of repeating a **countable noun**: *I don't like this jacket. I prefer the black **one**. These shoes are nicer than the old **ones**.*

rows: *My phone is broken. I need a new **one**.*
*The **one** on the left is mine. The **ones** I bought were cheap.*

blocks.md: Don't use *one* for **uncountable** nouns: *I like white wine more than red* (not *red one*).
After *this / that*, *one* is often used: *I'll take **this one***. After *these / those*, *ones* is optional in BrE: *I prefer **those (ones)**.*

examples.text: This cup is dirty. Can I have a clean **one**?
The **ones** in the window are on sale.
I'd like a coffee. A large **one**, please.
**Which one** is your house?

mistakes.wrong: My bike is old. I want a new.
mistakes.right: My bike is old. I want a new one.

mistakes.wrong: I like green tea more than black one.
mistakes.right: I like green tea more than black.

points.title: I'd love to, I didn't want to: to instead of the whole verb
points.summary: Use ***to*** alone instead of repeating the **whole infinitive**: *Would you like to come? ~ I'd love **to**. I didn't want to go, but I had **to**.*

rows: *Would you like to dance? ~ I'd love to dance.*
*I meant to call you, but I forgot to call you.*
*You can stay if you want to stay.*
*He didn't go, although he promised to go.*

blocks.md: Keep ***to***: *I'd love **to**.* (not *I'd love.*) But after ***want*** and ***like*** in clauses with *if, when, what*, *to* is often left out: *Do what you **want**. Come whenever you **like**.*
With ***be*** and ***have***, keep them after *to*: *I'm not rich, and I don't want **to be**. I haven't finished, but I'd like **to have** by Friday.*

examples.text: Can you come tomorrow? ~ I'll try **to**.
I didn't want to leave, but I had **to**.
You don't have to help, but you can if you'd like **to**.
She isn't a doctor, but she'd like **to be**.

mistakes.wrong: Would you like to come? ~ Yes, I'd love.
mistakes.right: Would you like to come? ~ Yes, I'd love to.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't call her. I forgot it.
mistakes.right: I didn't call her. I forgot to.

points.title: She went out and bought milk: leaving out repeated words
points.summary: After ***and, but, or***, we often leave out a **repeated subject**, **auxiliary** or **verb**: *She went out and (she) bought some milk. I can sing but (I) can't dance. Ali ordered fish and Sara (ordered) chicken.*

rows: *He opened the door and he went in.*
*He opened the door and went in.*
*I've finished the report and I've sent it.*
*I've finished the report and sent it.*
*She plays tennis and she plays golf.*
*Ali drinks tea and Sara drinks coffee.*

blocks.md: You can only leave out words that are **the same** in both parts: *I'll call you and (I'll) explain.*
After a **comparison**, leave out the repeated verb: *She's taller than her brother (is).*

examples.text: We went to the beach and **swam** in the sea.
I've washed the dishes and **dried** them.
He can speak French but not **Spanish**.
My brother is older than **me**.

mistakes.wrong: She's tired and she's tired of her job. (repeated)
mistakes.right: She's tired of her job.

mistakes.wrong: I've cleaned the kitchen and I've cleaned the bathroom.
mistakes.right: I've cleaned the kitchen and the bathroom.

points.title: Do so, do that, if so, if not, I'm afraid so
points.summary: Substitute a whole verb phrase with ***do so*** (formal), ***do that / do it*** (informal). Replace a whole clause with ***so*** (*If so…, I'm afraid so*) or ***not*** (*If not…, I hope not*).

rows: *He was asked to leave, but he refused to **do so**.*
*I'll clean the car. ~ No, I'll **do it**.*
*Are you free? **If so**, come over. **If not**, call me.*
*Is it true? ~ I believe **so**. I told you **so**!*
*Will it rain? ~ I hope **not**. I'm afraid **not**.*

blocks.md: ***Do so*** replaces a verb + its object or complement: *Anyone who wants to leave early may **do so*** (= may leave early).
Use ***so*** and ***not*** after *think, hope, believe, suppose, expect, be afraid* and in *if so / if not*.

examples.text: Visitors may take photos, but they must not **do so** with flash.
Do you need help? **If so**, let me know.
Is the shop open? ~ I don't think **so**.
Have you finished? **If not**, keep working.

mistakes.wrong: She promised to call, but she didn't do.
mistakes.right: She promised to call, but she didn't do so.

mistakes.wrong: Is it going to rain? ~ I hope no.
mistakes.right: Is it going to rain? ~ I hope not.

points.title: Want a coffee? Sounds good. Seen Ali?
points.summary: In **informal speech**, we often leave out words at the **start** of a sentence (subjects and auxiliaries) when the meaning is clear: *(Do you) **Want** a coffee? (It) **Sounds** good. (Have you) **Seen** Ali? (I'm) **Sorry** I'm late.*

blocks.md: This is normal in **conversation**, text messages and emails to friends, but **not** in formal writing.

examples.text: **Looks** like rain.
**Got** a minute?
**See** you later!
**Anyone** want a sandwich?

mistakes.wrong: Dear Sir, Hope you are well. Want to apply for the job. (formal letter)
mistakes.right: Dear Sir, I hope you are well. I would like to apply for the job.

mistakes.wrong: Sounds like good.
mistakes.right: Sounds good.

points.title: As did we, than do most people, so would I
points.summary: Formal **comparative and additive** patterns use an auxiliary (often with **inversion**): *She was tired, **as were** we. They earn more **than do** most people. He loved the film, **as did** I.*

blocks.md: Inversion after ***as*** and ***than*** is **formal**; the normal order is also correct: *…than men **do**. …as I **did**.*
Make sure the **auxiliary** matches the tense of the first verb: *He **had** finished, as **had** I. She **will** win, as **will** you.*

examples.text: Ali left early, **as did** Sara.
City dwellers spend more on rent **than do** people in villages.
My parents were born in Iran, **as were** my grandparents.
He has passed, and **so have** I.

mistakes.wrong: She loves jazz, as does I.
mistakes.right: She loves jazz, as do I.
mistakes.why: auxiliary agrees with the subject: do I

mistakes.wrong: He had already left, as did I.
mistakes.right: He had already left, as had I.

items.prompt: Do you want to come to the cinema with us? ~ I'd love ___!
I didn't want to work on Saturday, but I had ___.
Did you call your mother? ~ No, I forgot ___. I'll call her now. (one word)
She opened the letter and ___ it quickly.
I've packed my bag and ___ my ticket.
I can play the guitar but ___ the piano. (one word)

topics.summary: For + a period (for two years), since + a starting point (since 2022), ago + past simple (two years ago).
intro: ***For*** and ***since*** both answer the question *How long?*, usually with the present perfect: *I've lived here **for** five years. I've lived here **since** 2020.* ***Ago*** tells us **when** something happened: *I moved here five years **ago**.*
This page goes from the basic difference to useful patterns like *It's two years since…* and *over the last few years*.

points.title: For + a period, since + a starting point
points.summary: **for** + a length of time (*for three hours, for ten years*); **since** + the time it started (*since 9 am, since Monday, since 2019*).

blocks.md: With the present perfect, both describe a situation that **started in the past and continues now**: *She**'s worked** here **for** two years / **since** 2023.*
To choose, ask: is it a **length** of time (how much time)? → *for*. Is it a **point** on the calendar or the clock? → *since*.

examples.text: I've known Maryam **for** fifteen years.
I've known Maryam **since** we were at school.
We've been here **since** 8 o'clock.
They've been married **for** a long time.

mistakes.wrong: I've lived here since three years.
mistakes.right: I've lived here for three years.
mistakes.why: three years is a period: for

mistakes.wrong: She's been ill for Monday.
mistakes.right: She's been ill since Monday.
mistakes.why: Monday is a starting point: since

mistakes.wrong: I live here for five years.
mistakes.right: I've lived here for five years.

points.title: Ago, for or since?
points.summary: **ago** = how long before now something happened (past simple): *I came two years ago.* **for / since** = how long a situation has continued (present perfect).

blocks.md: ***Ago*** goes **after** the time: *three days ago, a long time ago, ten minutes ago*. It is used with the **past simple**.
These three sentences can describe the same situation: *I **met** him five years **ago**. I**'ve known** him **for** five years. I**'ve known** him **since** 2020.*
Don't use *ago* with the present perfect: *I came here two years ago* or *I've been here for two years*. Not *I've been here two years ago*.

examples.text: The film started twenty minutes **ago**.
The film has been on **for** twenty minutes.
We moved here **in** 2021. We've lived here **since** 2021.

mistakes.wrong: I've started this job three months ago.
mistakes.right: I started this job three months ago.

mistakes.wrong: I came here before two years.
mistakes.right: I came here two years ago.

points.title: How long have you…? or When did you…?
points.summary: *How long **have** you **been** here?* (up to now) vs *When **did** you **arrive**?* (a point in the past). Don't use the present simple for *how long* up to now.

blocks.md: To ask about the **length** of a situation up to now, use ***How long*** + present perfect (simple or continuous):

items: ***How long have** you **known** each other?*
***How long have** you **been learning** English?*

blocks.md: To ask about a **point** in the past, use ***When / What time*** + past simple: ***When did** you **meet**?*
A very common mistake is the present simple: *How long are you here?* means *How long will you stay?* (about the future), not *How long have you been here?*

State verbs (*know, have, be, like*) use the present perfect simple: *How long **have** you **had** this phone?* Activities often use the continuous: *How long **have** you **been waiting**?* See [Present Perfect Continuous](/blog/grammar/present-perfect-continuous/).

examples.text: **How long have** you **lived** in Toronto? ~ For six years.
**When did** you **move** to Toronto? ~ In 2019.
**How long have** they **been** married?
**How long are** you **staying** in Paris? ~ Until Friday.

mistakes.wrong: How long do you know him?
mistakes.right: How long have you known him?

mistakes.wrong: How long are you married?
mistakes.right: How long have you been married?

mistakes.wrong: When have you arrived?
mistakes.right: When did you arrive?
mistakes.why: A point in the past: past simple.

points.title: It's two years since… and I haven't… for…
points.summary: Three ways to say the same thing: *It's two years since I saw her. I haven't seen her for two years. The last time I saw her was two years ago.*

blocks.md: These patterns are useful for talking about how long it is since something happened:

rows: **It's / It has been** + period + **since** + past simple
**The last time** + past simple + **was** + ago / time
***The last time** I **saw** her **was** two years **ago**.*

blocks.md: After ***It's … since***, the **past simple** is the usual choice: *It's ages since we **went** out.*
In American English, *in* is common after a negative: *I haven't seen her **in** two years.* Both *for* and *in* are correct here.

examples.text: **It's** five years **since** they **moved** to Canada.
We **haven't been** to the cinema **for** months.
**The last time** I **ate** meat **was** in 2020.
I **last saw** him at your wedding.

mistakes.wrong: It's three years since I visit my aunt.
mistakes.right: It's three years since I visited my aunt.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't see him for a long time. (and I still haven't)
mistakes.right: I haven't seen him for a long time.

points.title: Since + a clause, ever since, and since meaning because
points.summary: **since** + past simple clause for the starting point: *since I left school*. **ever since** = all the time from then until now. **since** can also mean *because*.

blocks.md: ***Since*** can be followed by a **clause** (subject + verb). The clause usually uses the **past simple**, because it refers to a moment in the past: *I've lived here **since** I **was** ten.* *A lot has changed **since** we last **met**.*
When the *since* clause describes a situation that **continues now**, the present perfect is possible: *I've felt much better **since** I**'ve been** doing yoga* (I'm still doing it).

***Ever since*** emphasises *all the time from then until now*: *We've been friends **ever since** we met at university.* It can also go at the end: *We met at university and we've been friends **ever since**.*
***Since*** can also mean ***because*** (a reason that both people know): ***Since** it's raining, let's stay in.*
Don't confuse *since* and *for* + a clause: *I've worked here **since** I graduated.* Not *for I graduated*.

examples.text: She's been much happier **since** she **changed** jobs.
**Ever since** I was a child, I've loved music.
He hasn't called **since** he **moved** to Dubai.
**Since** you're here, can you help me with this?

mistakes.wrong: I've lived here since I am a child.
mistakes.right: I've lived here since I was a child.
mistakes.why: since + past simple for the starting point

mistakes.wrong: She has been sad for her cat died.
mistakes.right: She has been sad since her cat died.

points.title: Over the last few years, in years, during, throughout
points.summary: **over / in the last** + period with the present perfect for a period up to now; **in years / for ages** after negatives; **during / throughout** for a period.

blocks.md: To describe a **period up to now**, these phrases are very common with the present perfect:

items: ***Over the last / past** ten years, the population **has doubled**.*
***In the last** few months, we**'ve had** three new clients.*
***Recently / Lately / So far** …*

blocks.md: With a negative, we can use ***for*** or ***in*** (more common in American English): *I haven't been to a concert **for / in** years.* ***Not … for ages*** is informal.

***During*** + noun = at some time or all the time in a period: *I woke up twice **during** the night.* ***Throughout*** = from the beginning to the end: *It rained **throughout** the match.* ***For*** says **how long**, not when: *It rained **for** two hours.*
Don't use *during* for *how long*: *I stayed there **for** two weeks.* Not *during two weeks*.

examples.text: **Over the past** decade, smartphones **have changed** the way we live.
Our sales **have risen** by 15% **in the last** quarter.
I haven't heard that song **in years**.
He was in hospital **for** a week, and **during** that time he read five books.
examples.note: for = how long; during = in that period

mistakes.wrong: I stayed in Rome during three weeks.
mistakes.right: I stayed in Rome for three weeks.

mistakes.wrong: During two years I lived in Paris.
mistakes.right: For two years I lived in Paris.

items.prompt: Things have changed a lot since I ___ this job.
We met in 2010 and we've been close friends ___.
items.explanation: At the end of the sentence: *ever since*.

items.prompt: How much weight have you lost since you ___ (start) running?
items.explanation: *Since* + past simple for the starting point.

topics.h1: Future Continuous and Future Perfect (will be doing, will have done)
topics.summary: Seeing the future from a point in time: This time tomorrow I'll be flying. By Friday I'll have finished.
intro: The **future continuous** (*will be doing*) describes an action **in progress** at a time in the future: *This time tomorrow I**'ll be lying** on a beach.*

The **future perfect** (*will have done*) describes an action that will be **complete** before a time in the future: *By June I**'ll have finished** my course.* For assumptions like *He'll be sleeping now*, see [Modals of Deduction](/blog/grammar/modals-of-deduction/#md-will-assumption).

points.title: Future continuous: will be doing
points.summary: **will be + -ing** for an action in progress at a particular time in the future: *At 8 tonight I'll be watching the match.*

blocks.md: The future continuous puts you **in the middle** of a future action: *Don't call at 9. I**'ll be having** dinner.* (I'll start before 9 and finish after.)
Typical time phrases: *this time tomorrow / next week, at 6 o'clock tomorrow, all day tomorrow, when you arrive*.
Compare with the past continuous, which does the same for the past: *At 8 last night I **was watching** TV.* See [Past Continuous](/blog/grammar/past-continuous/).

examples.text: This time next week we**'ll be skiing** in the Alps.
Don't phone between 2 and 4. I**'ll be sleeping**.
When you arrive, I**'ll be waiting** at the gate.
**Will** you **be working** late tonight?

mistakes.wrong: At 10 tomorrow I will working.
mistakes.right: At 10 tomorrow I will be working.

mistakes.wrong: This time tomorrow I'll be fly to Rome.
mistakes.right: This time tomorrow I'll be flying to Rome.

points.title: Will you be using…? Polite questions and things that will happen anyway
points.summary: **Will you be + -ing?** asks politely about someone's plans: *Will you be using the car tonight?* It also describes things that will happen as a matter of course: *I'll be seeing Ali tomorrow.*

blocks.md: ***Will you be + -ing?*** is a polite way to ask about someone's plans, often before asking for something: ***Will you be using** your laptop this afternoon? If not, could I borrow it?*
It sounds less direct than *Will you use…?*, which can sound like a request or an order.

The future continuous also describes things that will happen **anyway**, as part of a routine or arrangement: *I**'ll be passing** the post office, so I can post your letter.* (I'm going that way anyway.)

examples.text: **Will** you **be going** to the shops later? I need some milk.
**Will** you **be staying** for dinner?
I**'ll be seeing** Mina at work tomorrow, so I'll give her the book.
The train **will be stopping** at all stations.

mistakes.wrong: Will you use the printer this afternoon? (just asking about plans politely)
mistakes.right: Will you be using the printer this afternoon?

points.title: Future perfect: will have done by…
points.summary: **will have + past participle** for something that will be **complete** before a time in the future: *By 2030 I'll have paid off my loan.*

blocks.md: The future perfect looks **back** from a point in the future: *By the end of the month, I**'ll have worked** here for two years.*
It often goes with ***by*** (+ time) or ***by the time*** (+ present): ***By the time** you get home, I**'ll have cooked** dinner.*
*By* means *not later than*. *By Friday* = on or before Friday. It's different from *until*: *I'll be here **until** Friday* (all the time up to Friday).

examples.text: By next summer, I**'ll have saved** enough for a car.
The film **will have started** by the time we arrive.
**Will** you **have finished** the report by Monday?
Don't worry, they **won't have forgotten** your birthday.

mistakes.wrong: By 2030 I will finish university.
mistakes.right: By 2030 I will have finished university.
mistakes.why: complete before a future time: will have + past participle

mistakes.wrong: By the time you will come, I'll have left.
mistakes.right: By the time you come, I'll have left.

points.title: Future perfect continuous: will have been doing
points.summary: **will have been + -ing** for the duration of an activity up to a point in the future: *By June, I'll have been working here for ten years.*

blocks.md: The future perfect continuous measures **how long** an activity will have continued by a future time: *In March, we**'ll have been living** in Toronto for five years.*
It's often used with ***for*** + a period and ***by*** / ***in*** + a future time.
Like other continuous forms, it's not used with **state** verbs: *By May, I**'ll have known** her for ten years.* (not *will have been knowing*)
Compare: *By 6 pm I**'ll have written** 3 chapters* (how much: future perfect simple) / *By 6 pm I**'ll have been writing** for 8 hours* (how long: continuous).

examples.text: Next month I**'ll have been learning** English for a year.
By the time we get there, we**'ll have been driving** for ten hours.
In September, she**'ll have been teaching** at this school for 20 years.
By 2030, I**'ll have known** him for half my life.

mistakes.wrong: Next year I will be working here for five years. (meaning the length of time up to then)
mistakes.right: Next year I will have been working here for five years.
mistakes.why: duration up to a future time: will have been + -ing

mistakes.wrong: By June we'll have been knowing each other for a year.
mistakes.right: By June we'll have known each other for a year.

items.prompt: ___ the meeting room this afternoon? If not, we'd like to use it.
items.explanation: Polite question about plans: *Will you be using…?*

items.prompt: What does *I'll be driving past your house, so I can pick you up* suggest?
options: I've decided to drive to your house specially.
I'll be going that way anyway.
items.explanation: The future continuous = it will happen anyway.

items.prompt: ___ (you / stay) at the hotel again next week?
items.explanation: Polite question about plans: *Will you be staying…?*

items.prompt: By the end of the year, I ___ ten books.
items.explanation: Complete before a future time: *will have read*.

items.prompt: Hurry up! By the time we get there, the concert ___.
By Friday, the builders ___ (finish) the kitchen.

topics.h1: Future in the Past (was going to, would…)
topics.summary: Talking about the future from a point in the past: I knew you would come. We were going to leave, but it rained.
intro: Sometimes we look at the future **from a point in the past**: *In 2010 I didn't know I **would** live in Canada one day.* Each future form has a past version: *will → would*, *am going to → was going to*, *am leaving → was leaving*, *am about to → was about to*.
These forms are common in stories and in reported speech. For *was going to* on its own, see [Be Going To](/blog/grammar/be-going-to/#bgt-was-going-to).

points.title: The future seen from the past: four forms
points.summary: **would** (from *will*), **was going to** (from *going to*), **was + -ing** (from present continuous), **was about to** (from *be about to*).

rows: *He was excited because he **was flying** to Japan the next day.*
*I **was about to** leave when you called.*

blocks.md: Choose the form the same way you would for the future, but put it in the past: a prediction or promise → *would*; a plan → *was going to*; an arrangement → past continuous; something very soon → *was about to*.

examples.text: I was sure you **would** pass.
We **were going to** buy a house, but prices went up.
She couldn't come because she **was meeting** a client.
The film **was about to** start when the power went off.

mistakes.wrong: I knew she will help us.
mistakes.right: I knew she would help us.

mistakes.wrong: Yesterday I'm going to call you, but I forgot.
mistakes.right: Yesterday I was going to call you, but I forgot.

points.title: Would as the future in the past (reported speech and thoughts)
points.summary: After past reporting and thinking verbs (*said, thought, knew, hoped*), **will** becomes **would**: *She said she would come. I thought it would rain.*

blocks.md: When we report what someone **said or thought** in the past about the future, *will* usually becomes ***would***: *I'll help you* → *She said she **would** help me.*
The same happens with *thought, knew, hoped, expected, was sure*: *We **hoped** the weather **would** be good.*
*Won't* becomes ***wouldn't***: *He promised he **wouldn't** be late.* See [Reported Speech](/blog/grammar/reported-speech/).
If the future is **still** in the future when you speak, *will* is also possible: *She said she**'ll** call tomorrow.* (Tomorrow hasn't come yet.)

examples.text: He said he **would** be home by six.
I thought the test **would** be easier.
They were sure they **wouldn't** lose.
Did you know he **would** be there?

mistakes.wrong: He said he will come yesterday.
mistakes.right: He said he would come yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: I hoped you will win.
mistakes.right: I hoped you would win.

points.title: Little did she know she would…: hints about the future in stories
points.summary: In stories, **would** and **was to** look ahead from the past to what happened later: *It was a decision she **would** regret for the rest of her life.*

blocks.md: Writers use the future in the past to **foreshadow**, to tell the reader what will happen later in the story: *This **would** be the last time they saw each other.* *Years later, he **would** become a famous architect.*
***Was to*** gives a similar, more formal effect: *It **was to** be her greatest success.* See [Be About To, Be Due To and Be To](/blog/grammar/be-to-be-about-to/#btb-was-to).
***Little did … know*** (with inversion) is a dramatic way to introduce it: ***Little did she know** that the letter **would** change her life.*

examples.text: He left home at 18. He **would** never return.
It was a small mistake, but it **would** cost the company millions.
That summer **was to** be the happiest of her life.
**Little did** they **know** that they **would** win the lottery a week later.

mistakes.wrong: Little they knew that the storm would destroy the town.
mistakes.right: Little did they know that the storm would destroy the town.

mistakes.wrong: She said goodbye. She will never see him again. (in a past story)
mistakes.right: She said goodbye. She would never see him again.

points.title: Plans that didn't happen: was going to, was hoping to, had intended to
points.summary: Several forms describe past plans that **didn't happen**: *was going to, was supposed to, was hoping to, had intended to, was to have done, would have liked to*.

rows: *I **was going to** call you, but I forgot.*
*I **was hoping to** see you at the party.*
*The talks **were to have taken** place in May.*

blocks.md: These forms often come with ***but*** and a reason: *We **had planned to** go camping, **but** the weather was terrible.*
The past perfect forms (*had hoped, had intended*) stress that the plan was made earlier and didn't work out. See [Past Perfect](/blog/grammar/past-perfect/#ppf-unfulfilled).

examples.text: I **had intended to** write back, but I was too busy.
You **were supposed to** be here an hour ago!
We **were hoping to** buy a house this year.
The match **was to have been** played yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: I was going to called you.
mistakes.right: I was going to call you.

mistakes.wrong: I had intended finish it.
mistakes.right: I had intended to finish it.

items.prompt: I was nervous because I ___ my first presentation the next day.
items.explanation: An arrangement seen from the past: *was giving*.

items.prompt: I knew you ___ like this restaurant.
We ___ (be / about / leave) when it started to snow.
items.explanation: Very soon, from the past: *were about to*.

items.prompt: She told me she ___ me later, but she never did.
We expected the train ___ late, but it was on time.
I was sure you ___ (not / forget) my birthday.
items.explanation: Past certainty about the future: *wouldn't forget*.

topics.h1: Future Time Clauses (When I get home, I'll…)
topics.summary: After when, as soon as, before, after and until, use a present tense for the future: I'll call you when I get home.
intro: In sentences about the future, words like ***when, as soon as, before, after, until*** introduce a **time clause**. In the time clause, we use a **present** tense, not *will*: *I'll call you **when** I **get** home.* Not *when I will get home*.
This is the same rule as for *if* in the first conditional. For the difference between *if* and *when*, see [Zero and First Conditional](/blog/grammar/zero-and-first-conditional/#zfc-if-or-when).

points.title: When, as soon as, before, after + present
points.summary: For the future, use **present simple** after *when, as soon as, before, after, until*: *I'll text you **as soon as** I **arrive**.*

blocks.md: The **main clause** uses a future form (*will, going to*) or an imperative. The **time clause** uses the present: *I'll be ready **when** you **come**.*
Use a comma when the time clause comes first: ***When** I get home, I'll call you.* / *I'll call you **when** I get home.*

examples.text: I'll call you **when** I **get** to the hotel.
**As soon as** the shop **opens**, I'm going to buy that dress.
Please lock the door **before** you **leave**.
We'll have dinner **after** the kids **go** to bed.

mistakes.wrong: I'll call you when I will arrive.
mistakes.right: I'll call you when I arrive.

mistakes.wrong: As soon as she will finish, we'll go.
mistakes.right: As soon as she finishes, we'll go.

points.title: When I've finished…: present perfect in time clauses
points.summary: Use the **present perfect** in a time clause to show that the first action will be **complete** before the second: *I'll call you when I've finished work.*

blocks.md: *When I **finish** work, I'll call you* and *When I**'ve finished** work, I'll call you* both refer to the future. The present perfect stresses that the first thing will be **completely done** first.
The present perfect is common with *when, after, as soon as, until, once*: *You can go out **after** you**'ve done** your homework.*
Don't use the present perfect when the two actions happen at the **same time**: *When I **see** him, I'll tell him.* (not *When I've seen him* if you mean at that moment)

examples.text: I'll lend you the book **when** I**'ve read** it.
**As soon as** I**'ve saved** enough money, I'll buy a car.
Don't go **until** you**'ve signed** the contract.
**After** she**'s had** lunch, she'll call you back.

mistakes.wrong: I'll give it back when I will have read it.
mistakes.right: I'll give it back when I've read it.
mistakes.why: no will in the time clause

points.title: Until, once, by the time, the moment, next time
points.summary: Other time words follow the same rule: *I'll wait **until** you **arrive**. **Once** you **know** the rules, it's easy. **By the time** we **get** there, the film **will have started**.*

rows: ***By the time** you **arrive**, I**'ll have left**.*

blocks.md: ***By the time*** often goes with the **future perfect** in the main clause: *By the time we get there, the shop **will have closed**.* See [Future Continuous and Future Perfect](/blog/grammar/future-continuous-future-perfect/).
Don't use *until* with a negative meaning in the time clause: *I'll wait **until** you come* (not *until you don't come*).

examples.text: I won't stop **until** I **find** it.
**Once** you**'ve tried** it, you'll love it.
**By the time** the guests **arrive**, dinner **will be** ready.
Tell me **the moment** you **hear** anything.

mistakes.wrong: I'll wait until you will come back.
mistakes.right: I'll wait until you come back.

mistakes.wrong: By the time we will get there, the film will have started.
mistakes.right: By the time we get there, the film will have started.

points.title: When will is correct after when and if
points.summary: *Will* is correct after *when* in **questions and noun clauses** (*I don't know when he'll come*), and after *if* for **willingness** (*if you'll wait*). Only time clauses take the present.

blocks.md: The *no will* rule is only for **time clauses** (*when* = at the time that). When *when* introduces a **question** or a **noun clause** (the object of a verb like *know, ask, wonder*), use the normal future: ***When will** the results be ready? I don't know **when** they**'ll** be ready.*
Compare: *Tell me **when** he **arrives*** (= at the time he arrives; time clause) and *Tell me **when** he**'ll arrive*** (= tell me the time of his arrival; noun clause).

After *if*, *will* is possible for **willingness** or **insistence**: *If you**'ll** follow me, I'll show you your room.* See [Zero and First Conditional](/blog/grammar/zero-and-first-conditional/#zfc-will-in-if).

examples.text: I wonder **when** she**'ll** call.
Do you know **when** the shop **will** open?
I'll call you **when** the shop **opens**.
**If** you**'ll** just wait a moment, I'll find the manager.

mistakes.wrong: I don't know when he arrives tomorrow. (asking about the time)
mistakes.right: I don't know when he'll arrive tomorrow.
mistakes.why: noun clause: will (the present is possible for timetables)

items.prompt: By the time we ___ to the station, the train will have left.
I'll wait here ___ you finish. Take your time.
___ you understand the basics, the rest is easy. (one word: as soon as)

topics.summary: Which verb form comes next? I enjoy swimming. I want to swim. I'm good at swimming. I saw him swim.
intro: When one verb follows another, the second verb is often either an **-ing form** (*gerund*) or **to + base verb** (*infinitive*): *I enjoy **cooking**. I want **to cook**.* The first verb decides which form you need.

There's no simple rule for every verb, but there are useful patterns. This page goes from the basics to advanced forms. Some verbs change meaning with *-ing* or *to*: see [Verbs that Change Meaning](/blog/grammar/verbs-change-meaning-ing-infinitive/).

points.title: Like, love, hate + -ing
points.summary: After **like, love, hate, enjoy**, use **-ing**: *I like swimming. She loves reading. They hate getting up early.* (*Like / love / hate + to* is also correct.)

blocks.md: To talk about things you like or don't like doing, use ***like / love / enjoy / hate / don't mind*** + **-ing**: *I **love dancing**. My dad **hates waiting**.*

After *like, love* and *hate*, ***to*** + verb is also correct, especially in American English: *I **like to swim** / I **like swimming**.* But after ***enjoy*** and ***don't mind***, only *-ing* is possible: *I **enjoy swimming*** (not *enjoy to swim*).
**Spelling**: *swim → swimming, make → making, run → running, lie → lying*. The rules are the same as for the present continuous.

examples.text: I **like playing** football.
My sister **loves watching** films.
We **enjoy travelling**.
I **don't mind cooking**.

mistakes.wrong: I enjoy to swim.
mistakes.right: I enjoy swimming.

mistakes.wrong: She likes play tennis.
mistakes.right: She likes playing tennis. / She likes to play tennis.

mistakes.wrong: I don't mind to wait.
mistakes.right: I don't mind waiting.

points.title: Want to, need to, decide to, hope to
points.summary: After **want, need, would like, decide, hope, plan, try, learn, forget, promise**, use **to + base verb**: *I want to travel. She decided to leave.*

blocks.md: Many verbs that talk about wishes, plans and decisions take ***to*** + base verb: *I **want to** learn Spanish. We **hope to** see you soon. They **decided to** move.*
The negative is ***not to***: *I **decided not to** go.* (not *decided to not go* in careful English, though it's common in speech)

examples.text: I **need to** buy some milk.
She **would like to** visit Japan.
They **plan to** get married next year.
He **promised not to** be late.

mistakes.wrong: I want go home.
mistakes.right: I want to go home.

mistakes.wrong: She decided moving to Spain.
mistakes.right: She decided to move to Spain.

mistakes.wrong: I hope seeing you soon.
mistakes.right: I hope to see you soon.

points.title: Enjoy, finish, mind, stop, avoid + -ing
points.summary: After **enjoy, finish, mind, stop, avoid, keep, suggest, miss, practise**, use **-ing**: *Have you finished eating? I can't stop laughing.*

blocks.md: Some verbs are always followed by **-ing**, never *to*: *I **finished working** at six. He **kept talking**. Do you **mind waiting**?*
***Keep (on) -ing*** = continue or repeat: *She **keeps** **asking** me the same question.*

***Stop + -ing*** means you don't do it any more: *I **stopped smoking** last year.* *Stop + to* has a different meaning. See [Verbs that Change Meaning](/blog/grammar/verbs-change-meaning-ing-infinitive/#vcm-stop-go-on).

examples.text: Have you **finished reading** the book?
I **miss living** near the sea.
Try to **avoid eating** late at night.
You need to **practise speaking** every day.

mistakes.wrong: Have you finished to eat?
mistakes.right: Have you finished eating?

mistakes.wrong: I can't avoid to see him.
mistakes.right: I can't avoid seeing him.

mistakes.wrong: Would you mind to close the window?
mistakes.right: Would you mind closing the window?

points.title: Want someone to do: verb + object + to
points.summary: **want / would like / ask / tell / expect / help + person + to + verb**: *I want you to come. She asked me to help her.* Not *I want that you come*.

blocks.md: To talk about what you want **another person** to do, use ***want + person + to*** + verb: *I **want you to** listen. My parents **want me to** study medicine.*
Other verbs with this pattern: *would like, ask, tell, expect, help, teach, allow, advise, remind, encourage*: *She **taught me to** drive.*
***Help*** can also be followed by the base verb with no *to*: *Can you **help me (to) carry** this?*
Don't use a *that* clause after *want*: *I want **you to** come* (not *I want that you come*). See [Reporting Verbs](/blog/grammar/reporting-verbs/#rv-verb-object-to).

examples.text: I **want you to** be happy.
My boss **expects us to** work hard.
She **asked me to** call her back.
Can you **help me move** this table?

mistakes.wrong: I want that you come with me.
mistakes.right: I want you to come with me.

mistakes.wrong: My mum wants me study more.
mistakes.right: My mum wants me to study more.

mistakes.wrong: He told me go home.
mistakes.right: He told me to go home.

points.title: After prepositions: -ing (interested in learning, before leaving)
points.summary: After a **preposition** (*in, at, of, for, about, before, after, without*), use **-ing**: *I'm interested in learning Chinese. Think before speaking.*

blocks.md: A verb after a preposition is always in the ***-ing*** form: *She's good **at drawing**. Thank you **for coming**. **After finishing** work, I went home.*

Be careful with ***to*** when it's a **preposition**, not part of an infinitive: *I look forward **to seeing** you. I'm used **to getting** up early.* (Test: you can put a noun after it: *I look forward to the party.*)

examples.text: I'm tired **of waiting**.
She left **without saying** goodbye.
Are you interested **in joining** our club?
I'm looking forward **to meeting** you.

mistakes.wrong: I'm good at cook.
mistakes.right: I'm good at cooking.

mistakes.wrong: I look forward to hear from you.
mistakes.right: I look forward to hearing from you.

mistakes.wrong: Before to leave, check the windows.
mistakes.right: Before leaving, check the windows.

points.title: Common verbs + -ing and verbs + to
points.summary: Learn the most common patterns: **+ -ing**: *admit, avoid, consider, deny, imagine, keep, mind, miss, practise, risk, suggest*. **+ to**: *afford, agree, arrange, decide, expect, fail, hope, manage, offer, plan, promise, refuse, seem*.

blocks.md: Some verbs take **both** with little or no difference in meaning: *begin, start, continue, like, love, hate, prefer*: *It started **raining** / **to rain**.*

A useful tip: many *to* verbs look to the **future** (*hope, plan, promise, decide*); many *-ing* verbs talk about something that is **real or happening** (*enjoy, finish, avoid, admit*). It's not a perfect rule, but it helps.

examples.text: Have you **considered moving** abroad?
I can't **afford to buy** a car.
She **pretended to be** asleep.
He **admitted making** a mistake.

mistakes.wrong: I can't afford buying a new phone.
mistakes.right: I can't afford to buy a new phone.

mistakes.wrong: We considered to sell the house.
mistakes.right: We considered selling the house.

mistakes.wrong: She managed finishing on time.
mistakes.right: She managed to finish on time.

points.title: -ing as a subject; it's worth -ing; it's no use -ing
points.summary: **-ing** can be the subject: *Swimming is good for you.* Useful phrases: **it's worth -ing, it's no use -ing, there's no point (in) -ing, have difficulty / trouble (in) -ing**.

blocks.md: An *-ing* form can be the **subject** of a sentence: ***Learning** a language **takes** time. **Smoking** is bad for you.* The verb is singular.
We can also say ***It is*** + adjective + ***to*** + verb: ***It's** hard **to learn** a language.* (more common in speech)
Fixed phrases with *-ing*:

items: ***it's worth / it isn't worth -ing***: *This museum **is worth visiting**.*
***it's no use / it's no good -ing***: ***It's no use complaining**.*
***there's no point (in) -ing***: ***There's no point waiting**. The bus has gone.*
***have difficulty / trouble / problems (in) -ing***: *I **had trouble finding** the hotel.*

examples.text: **Running** every morning keeps me healthy.
**It's** easy **to get** lost in this city.
This book **is worth reading**.
**There's no point arguing** with him.

mistakes.wrong: Swim is good exercise.
mistakes.right: Swimming is good exercise.

mistakes.wrong: It's worth to visit the old town.
mistakes.right: It's worth visiting the old town.

mistakes.wrong: I had difficulty to understand him.
mistakes.right: I had difficulty understanding him.

points.title: See someone do or see someone doing?
points.summary: After **see, hear, watch, notice, feel**: **object + base verb** = the whole action (*I saw him cross the road*). **object + -ing** = part of an action in progress (*I saw him crossing the road*).

rows: the complete action, start to finish
the action in progress (maybe not finished)

blocks.md: Use the **base verb** (no *to*) for a short or complete action: *I **heard** someone **shout**. We **watched** the plane **land**.*
Use ***-ing*** when you saw or heard the action **in progress**: *I **heard** the children **playing** in the garden.* (They were playing; I didn't hear the whole game.)
In the **passive**, *see / hear* + *to*: *He **was seen to leave** the building.* (formal)

examples.text: I **saw** her **drop** her phone.
I **saw** her **talking** to the manager.
Did you **hear** the baby **cry**?
I could **smell** something **burning**.

mistakes.wrong: I saw him to cross the road.
mistakes.right: I saw him cross the road.

mistakes.wrong: I heard someone to knock.
mistakes.right: I heard someone knock. / I heard someone knocking.

points.title: Perfect and passive forms: having done, to have done, being done
points.summary: **having + past participle** and **to have + past participle** show an earlier action: *He denied having stolen it. She seems to have left.* **being + past participle** and **to be + past participle** are passive.

rows: perfect passive: *having been done* / *to have been done*

blocks.md: The perfect forms show that the action happened **before** the main verb. They're often optional: *He admitted **taking** / **having taken** the money.* (same meaning)
After *seem, appear, claim, pretend, be said*, the perfect infinitive is needed for a past action: *She **seems to have lost** weight.* (not *seems to lose*, which means something different)

examples.text: **Having finished** the report, she went home.
He **claims to have met** the President.
Nobody likes **being ignored**.
The house **appears to have been** empty for years.

mistakes.wrong: She seems to forget my name yesterday.
mistakes.right: She seems to have forgotten my name.
mistakes.why: past action: to have + past participle

mistakes.wrong: He was proud of having chose.
mistakes.right: He was proud of having been chosen.

items.prompt: ___ too much sugar is bad for your teeth.
The film is long, but it's worth ___.
There's no point ___ (call) him. He never answers.
I watched the sun ___ behind the mountains. It was beautiful.
When I walked past, I heard them ___ about me.
Did you see anyone ___ (leave) the building?

topics.summary: Why we say very cold but absolutely freezing, and very good but absolutely amazing.
intro: **Gradable** adjectives can be more or less: *cold, big, good*. Use ***very, a bit*** and ***extremely*** with them: *very cold*. **Extreme** adjectives already mean “very”: *freezing, huge, amazing*. Use ***absolutely*** or ***really*** with them: *absolutely freezing*.
Using the right word before an adjective is one of the easiest ways to sound more natural.

points.title: Very cold, absolutely freezing
points.summary: Use ***very / extremely / a bit*** with **gradable** adjectives (*very big*). Use ***absolutely*** or ***really*** with **extreme** adjectives (*absolutely huge*). ***Really*** works with both.

blocks.md: Avoid *very freezing* or *absolutely cold*. ***Really*** is fine with both: *really cold, really freezing*.

examples.text: It's **very cold** today.
It's **absolutely freezing**!
The hotel was **really** amazing.
I'm **extremely** tired.

mistakes.wrong: The film was very fantastic.
mistakes.right: The film was absolutely fantastic.

mistakes.wrong: I'm absolutely hungry.
mistakes.right: I'm absolutely starving.

mistakes.wrong: Their house is very enormous.
mistakes.right: Their house is absolutely enormous.

points.title: Absolute adjectives: completely different, almost empty
points.summary: **Absolute** adjectives describe all-or-nothing qualities: *impossible, perfect, unique, dead, empty, full, finished, different, wrong, right*. Use ***completely, totally, absolutely, entirely*** with them, and ***almost / nearly*** for “not quite”: *almost empty*.

rows: *absolutely perfect* (*very unique* is common but avoided in careful English)

blocks.md: ***Almost, nearly*** and ***practically*** go well with absolute adjectives: *The bottle is **almost** empty.*
Some adjectives can be gradable or absolute with different meanings: *The party was **really** dead* (= boring, informal) / *The battery is **completely** dead.*

examples.text: Her new job is **completely different** from her old one.
You're **absolutely right**.
The cinema was **almost empty**.
It's **totally impossible** to finish today.

mistakes.wrong: This painting is very unique.
mistakes.right: This painting is unique.
mistakes.why: unique: no very in careful English

mistakes.wrong: The task was very impossible.
mistakes.right: The task was completely impossible.

points.title: Highly unlikely, deeply concerned: adverb + adjective pairs
points.summary: Advanced English uses natural **adverb + adjective** pairs instead of *very*: ***highly** unlikely, **deeply** concerned, **bitterly** disappointed, **fully** aware, **perfectly** normal, **seriously** injured*.

blocks.md: These pairs are **collocations**: they aren't grammar rules, but native speakers use them far more often. *Highly unlikely* is natural; *highly cheap* is not.
Don't use *highly* with simple physical words: *very tall* (not *highly tall*).

examples.text: It's **highly unlikely** that it will snow in June.
I was **deeply moved** by her speech.
The fans were **bitterly disappointed**.
I'm **fully aware** of the risks.

mistakes.wrong: The hotel comes strongly recommended.
mistakes.right: The hotel comes highly recommended.

mistakes.wrong: He was heavily injured in the accident.
mistakes.right: He was seriously injured in the accident.

items.prompt: The two brothers are ___ identical. Nobody can tell them apart.
The petrol tank is ___ empty. We need to stop soon.
You're ___ right. I should apologise. (one word)

topics.summary: Making claims more careful and less direct in academic and professional English: This may suggest… It would appear that… The results seem to show…
intro: **Hedging** means making a statement **less certain** or **less direct**, so you don't claim more than you can prove: *Coffee **causes** heart disease.* → *Coffee **may contribute** to heart disease.* **Distancing** shows the idea comes from **someone else**: *The minister **is said to** be resigning.*

Hedging is essential in academic writing, reports and polite business English. For *It is said that…* and *is thought to…*, see also [Passive Reporting Structures](/blog/grammar/passive-reporting-structures/).

points.title: May, might, could, tend to, seem to
points.summary: Soften claims with **modal verbs** (*may, might, could*), ***tend to*** (= usually), and ***seem / appear to***: *This **may** be the reason. Young people **tend to** spend more online. The plan **seems to** work.*

blocks.md: ***Tend to*** + base verb describes a general tendency: *Men **tend to** be taller than women.*
***Be likely to*** + base verb = probably will: *It **is likely to** rain.* ***Be unlikely to*** = probably won't.

examples.text: Stress **may** cause sleep problems.
Older drivers **tend to** drive more slowly.
The new medicine **appears to** be effective.
Costs **are likely to** increase next year.

mistakes.wrong: Young people tend spend more time online.
mistakes.right: Young people tend to spend more time online.

mistakes.wrong: The results seem showing an improvement.
mistakes.right: The results seem to show an improvement.

points.title: Probably, possibly, largely, to some extent
points.summary: **Adverbs** and phrases soften or limit a claim: ***probably, possibly, perhaps, apparently, arguably, generally, largely, relatively, to some extent, in some cases***.

rows: ***Apparently**, the meeting has been cancelled.* (I heard this)
*She is **arguably** the best player in the world.* (you could say this)
***To some extent**, the plan was successful.*

blocks.md: Position: these adverbs usually go **before the main verb** or **after** *be*: *It **is probably** true. It **probably** works.*

examples.text: The decline is **largely** due to lower prices.
This is **arguably** the most important discovery of the century.
**To some extent**, the results support the theory.
**Apparently**, she's moving to Spain.

mistakes.wrong: The results are probable correct.
mistakes.right: The results are probably correct.

mistakes.wrong: In some extent, I agree.
mistakes.right: To some extent, I agree.

points.title: It would appear that, it could be argued that
