points.summary: Impersonal ***it*** patterns make claims more **careful** and **objective**: ***It would appear that…, It seems likely that…, It could be argued that…, There is some evidence that…, This suggests that…***

rows: ***It would appear that** the data is incomplete.*
***It seems likely that** prices will rise.*
***It could be argued that** the law is unfair.*
***There is some evidence that** diet affects mood.*
***It is possible that** the results are wrong.*

blocks.md: ***Would*** makes *appear* and *seem* even more tentative: *It **would seem** that…* is more cautious than *It seems that…*
Use ***suggest*** (not *prove*) when evidence is not complete: *The results **suggest** that…*

examples.text: **It would appear that** there has been a mistake.
**It could be argued that** social media does more harm than good.
**There is little evidence that** the treatment works.
These findings **suggest that** more research is needed.

mistakes.wrong: It would appears that the plan failed.
mistakes.right: It would appear that the plan failed.

mistakes.wrong: It could argue that the plan is too expensive.
mistakes.right: It could be argued that the plan is too expensive.

points.title: Is said to have, would seem to suggest, reportedly
points.summary: **Distancing** shows that a claim comes from **others**, not from you: ***is said / thought / believed to (have)…***, ***reportedly, allegedly, supposedly***, ***according to***. Combine hedges for very careful claims: ***would seem to suggest***.

rows: *The company **is thought to** be in trouble.*
*He **is said to have** left the country.*
***According to** the report, crime has fallen.*
*The data **would seem to suggest** a link.*

blocks.md: ***Allegedly*** is used for **crimes** or wrongdoing that hasn't been proved: *He **allegedly** stole £1m.*
Don't combine ***according to*** with ***I*** or with opinion verbs: *According to the report…* (not *According to me…*; say *In my opinion…*).

examples.text: The painting **is believed to be** worth millions.
She **is said to have** written the letter herself.
The president **reportedly** refused to comment.
The findings **would seem to suggest** that diet plays a role.

mistakes.wrong: According to me, the plan is bad.
mistakes.right: In my opinion, the plan is bad.

mistakes.wrong: He is said to leave the country last week.
mistakes.right: He is said to have left the country last week.

items.prompt: (Cautious claim) Lack of sleep ___ affect your memory, but more research is needed.
People in cities ___ to have smaller families.
The new policy ___ (appear) to be working.
The increase in sales is ___ due to the new advertising campaign.
She is ___ the greatest writer of her generation. Many critics think so.
___ some extent, I agree with you, but not completely. (one word)

topics.summary: Giving instructions, orders, advice and invitations: Sit down. Don't worry. Let's go. Hurry up, or we'll be late.
intro: The **imperative** is the **base form** of the verb with no subject: ***Open** the window. **Sit** down. **Don't** touch that!* We use it for **instructions**, **orders**, **advice**, **warnings** and **invitations**.
To make an imperative more polite, add ***please*** or use a question like *Could you…?* See [Requests, Offers and Permission](/blog/grammar/requests-offers-permission/).

points.title: Open the door. Don't run.
points.summary: **Positive**: base verb (*Sit down. Be quiet.*). **Negative**: ***Don't*** + base verb (*Don't worry. Don't be late.*). Use it for instructions, orders, advice and warnings.

blocks.md: The imperative is the **same** for one person or many: *Sit down, Ali. Sit down, everyone.*
With ***be***, the negative is ***Don't be***: ***Don't be** silly.* (not *Be not silly*)

examples.text: **Close** the door, please.
**Don't** worry. Everything will be OK.
**Be** careful! The floor is wet.
**Don't** touch the oven. It's hot.

mistakes.wrong: Closes the door, please.
mistakes.right: Close the door, please.

mistakes.wrong: Not run in the corridor!
mistakes.right: Don't run in the corridor!

mistakes.wrong: Don't to be late.
mistakes.right: Don't be late.

points.title: Let's go, let's not, shall we?
points.summary: ***Let's*** + base verb makes a **suggestion** that includes **you and me**: ***Let's** go to the beach.* Negative: ***Let's not*** + verb (*Let's not argue*). Add ***shall we?*** to make it softer.

blocks.md: ***Let's*** = *let us*. The full form *let us* is formal: ***Let us** pray.*
***Let me*** + verb is an **offer** or a polite way to say what you're going to do: ***Let me** explain.*

examples.text: **Let's** order a pizza tonight.
**Let's not** tell anyone yet.
**Let's** go for a walk, **shall we**?
**Let me** carry that bag for you.

mistakes.wrong: Let's to go to the cinema.
mistakes.right: Let's go to the cinema.

mistakes.wrong: Let's don't argue. (BrE, formal)
mistakes.right: Let's not argue.

mistakes.wrong: Let's going home.
mistakes.right: Let's go home.

points.title: Please, make sure, don't forget to
points.summary: Make imperatives friendlier with ***please***, ***just***, and phrases like ***Make sure you…***, ***Don't forget to…***, ***Remember to…***, ***Feel free to…***, ***Have a…***

blocks.md: Imperatives can sound **rude** if you say them to strangers or your boss. Use ***please***, or a question: *Could you close the door, **please**?*

examples.text: **Please** don't smoke here.
**Make sure** you drink enough water.
**Don't forget to** bring your passport.
**Have a** nice day!

mistakes.wrong: Don't forget calling me.
mistakes.right: Don't forget to call me.

mistakes.wrong: Make sure to you lock the door.
mistakes.right: Make sure you lock the door. / Make sure to lock the door.
mistakes.why: make sure + clause or to + verb

points.title: You sit here. Somebody call a doctor!
points.summary: Sometimes imperatives have a **subject** for **emphasis** or **contrast**: ***You** sit here, and **I'll** sit there.* With ***someone / everybody***: ***Somebody** call an ambulance! **Everyone** listen.* And ***Don't you dare…!*** (a strong warning).

rows: ***You** wait here. I'll get the car.*

blocks.md: A subject with an imperative can sound **impatient** or **strong**, so use it with care.

examples.text: **You** stay here. I'll be back in a minute.
**Everybody** sit down, please.
**Somebody** open the window. It's too hot!
Pass me the salt, **will you**?

mistakes.wrong: Don't you to worry.
mistakes.right: Don't you worry.

mistakes.wrong: Somebody calls a doctor!
mistakes.right: Somebody call a doctor!

points.title: Study hard and you'll pass; hurry up, or we'll be late
points.summary: **Imperative + *and*** = *if you do this, the result will happen*: ***Study** hard **and** you'll pass.* **Imperative + *or / or else*** = *if you don't, something bad will happen*: ***Hurry** up, **or** we'll miss the train.*

rows: ***Press** this button **and** the door will open.*

blocks.md: These are common in **advice**, **warnings** and **adverts**: ***Buy** two **and** get one free!*

examples.text: **Practise** every day **and** you'll improve quickly.
**Wear** a coat, **or** you'll catch a cold.
**Never** tell anyone your password.
**Call** before 6 pm **and** we'll deliver today.

mistakes.wrong: Hurry up, and we'll miss the bus.
mistakes.right: Hurry up, or we'll miss the bus.

mistakes.wrong: Study hard or you'll pass.
mistakes.right: Study hard and you'll pass.

items.prompt: Work hard, ___ you'll get a promotion.
Turn the music down, ___ the neighbours will complain.
Don't be late, ___ else you'll miss the start of the film. (one word)

topics.summary: Questions inside other sentences, with normal word order: Do you know where the station is? I wonder if she's coming.
intro: An **indirect question** is a question inside another sentence: *Where is the station?* → *Do you know **where the station is**?* Indirect questions are more polite and very common in conversation.

The rule: after the question word (or *if / whether*), use **statement word order** and no *do / does / did*. For direct questions, see [Question Words and Question Forms](/blog/grammar/question-words-and-forms/).

points.title: Do you know where…? I don't know what…
points.summary: After **Do you know…? / I don't know…**, use **statement order**: *Do you know where she **lives**?* (not *where does she live*)

blocks.md: The question word stays, but the word order changes to **subject + verb**, and *do / does / did* disappear: *Where **is** the bank?* → *Do you know where **the bank is**?*
Use a question mark only if the whole sentence is a question: *Do you know where it is**?*** / *I don't know where it is**.***

examples.text: **Do you know where** the post office **is**?
**I don't know what** her name **is**.
**I have no idea why** he **said** that.
**Can you remember when** the film **starts**?

mistakes.wrong: Do you know where is the station?
mistakes.right: Do you know where the station is?

mistakes.wrong: I don't know where does he work.
mistakes.right: I don't know where he works.

mistakes.wrong: Do you know what time is it?
mistakes.right: Do you know what time it is?

points.title: If and whether: indirect yes/no questions
points.summary: For yes/no questions, use **if** or **whether**: *Is she coming?* → *Do you know **if / whether** she's coming?*

blocks.md: When the direct question has **no question word** (a yes/no question), use ***if*** or ***whether***: *Are you free?* → *I wonder **if** you're free.* *Did he pass?* → *Do you know **whether** he passed?*
***Whether*** is a little more formal, and it's the usual choice with ***or not*** and after **prepositions**: *I'm not sure **whether or not** to go. It depends **on whether** it rains.*

examples.text: **Do you know if** the bank is open today?
**I wonder whether** she got my message.
**I'm not sure if** I locked the door.
It depends **on whether** we have time.

mistakes.wrong: Do you know is the shop open?
mistakes.right: Do you know if the shop is open?

mistakes.wrong: I wonder if does she like me.
mistakes.right: I wonder if she likes me.

mistakes.wrong: It depends on if it rains.
mistakes.right: It depends on whether it rains.

points.title: Could you tell me…? Polite indirect questions
points.summary: Indirect questions make requests for information more **polite**: *Could you tell me where the toilets are? Would you mind telling me how old you are?*

rows: ***Could you tell me** where the station is?*
***Do you happen to know** what time it closes?*
***Can I ask** how much this is?*
***I was wondering why** my card was refused.*

blocks.md: Use these phrases with strangers, at work, in shops and in formal situations. The question inside always uses **statement order**.
*I was wondering…* and *I'd like to know…* are statements, so they end with a full stop: *I was wondering if you could help me.*

examples.text: **Could you tell me** where the lifts are?
**Do you happen to know** if there's a pharmacy near here?
**Would you mind telling me** what your name is?
**I'd like to know** why the flight was cancelled.

mistakes.wrong: Could you tell me where is the exit?
mistakes.right: Could you tell me where the exit is?

mistakes.wrong: I was wondering if could you help me?
mistakes.right: I was wondering if you could help me.

points.title: What to do, whether to go: question word + to-infinitive
points.summary: After verbs like **know, decide, wonder, ask, explain**, a question word + **to + verb** can replace a full clause: *I don't know what to say. She can't decide whether to go.*

blocks.md: ***Question word + to-infinitive*** talks about what someone should or could do: *I don't know **what to do**.* = I don't know what I should do.
It works with *what, where, when, how, who, which* and ***whether*** (but not *if* or *why*): *Can you show me **how to use** this? I'm not sure **whether to call** her.*
The subject of the infinitive is the same as the subject of the sentence, or people in general: *She told me **where to park**.* (= where I should park)

examples.text: I don't know **what to wear** to the wedding.
Can you tell me **how to get** to the station?
We couldn't decide **whether to stay** or **go**.
She showed me **where to sign**.

mistakes.wrong: I don't know what should I do.
mistakes.right: I don't know what to do. / I don't know what I should do.

mistakes.wrong: I'm not sure if to accept.
mistakes.right: I'm not sure whether to accept.

mistakes.wrong: I don't know why to go.
mistakes.right: I don't know why I should go.

points.title: What he said is true: question-word clauses as subjects and objects
points.summary: A clause like **what he said, where she lives, how it works** can act as a noun: as a **subject** (*What he said is true*) or an **object** (*I understand why you're upset*).

blocks.md: Clauses beginning with *what, where, how, why, whether, who* can be used like a noun phrase. They keep **statement order**:

items: as **subject**: ***What you need** is a holiday. **How he did it** is a mystery. **Whether we win** doesn't matter.*
as **object**: *I can't believe **what she told me**. I understand **why you left**.*
after **prepositions**: *It depends on **how much it costs**. We talked about **where to live**.*

blocks.md: A clause as subject takes a **singular** verb: ***What they want** **is** more money.*
*What* clauses are also used for emphasis: ***What I love about Toronto** is the diversity.* See [Cleft Sentences](/blog/grammar/cleft-sentences/).

examples.text: **What happened next** was amazing.
**Why she left** remains unclear.
I can't remember **where I parked**.
It depends on **whether** the weather improves.

mistakes.wrong: What did he say is true.
mistakes.right: What he said is true.

mistakes.wrong: Where does she live is a secret.
mistakes.right: Where she lives is a secret.

mistakes.wrong: I can't believe what did she tell me.
mistakes.right: I can't believe what she told me.

items.prompt: I've never used this machine. Can you show me ___ it?
He can't decide ___ to take the job or not.
I didn't know what ___ (say), so I said nothing.

topics.h1: Infinitive of Purpose (to, for, so that, in order to)
topics.summary: Saying why you do something: I went to the shop to buy milk. I saved money so that I could travel.
intro: To say **why** someone does something, we usually use ***to*** + base verb: *I went to the bank **to get** some money.* This is called the **infinitive of purpose**.
We can also use ***for*** + noun, ***so that*** + clause, and the more formal ***in order to / so as to***. This page shows when to use each one.

points.title: To + verb: I went to the shop to buy bread
points.summary: Use **to + base verb** to say why: *I'm saving money to buy a car. She called to say sorry.*

blocks.md: The infinitive with *to* answers the question **Why?**: *Why did you go to the shop? ~ **To buy** some bread.*
It usually comes after the main action: *I went to the library **to study**. We use a knife **to cut** bread.*
Don't use *for* + verb to give a purpose: *I came here **to learn** English.* Not *for learn* or *for to learn*.

examples.text: I'm learning English **to get** a better job.
She went to the airport **to meet** her sister.
We turned on the heating **to keep** warm.
Why did you call? ~ **To ask** about the party.

mistakes.wrong: I went to the shop for buy milk.
mistakes.right: I went to the shop to buy milk.

mistakes.wrong: He came to Canada for study.
mistakes.right: He came to Canada to study.

points.title: To or for? For + noun, for + -ing
points.summary: **to + verb** for an action: *I went out to get some milk.* **for + noun**: *I went out for some milk.* **for + -ing** for what a thing is used for: *a knife for cutting bread.*

rows: *I went to the shop **to buy** bread.*
*I went to the shop **for** some bread.* / *Let's go out **for** dinner.*

blocks.md: ***For + -ing*** describes the general **function** of a thing: *A thermometer is used **for measuring** temperature.* For a person's purpose, use ***to***: *I used the thermometer **to measure** the baby's temperature.*
***For + person + to + verb***: *There's a bus **for students to** get to campus.*

examples.text: Let's go out **for** a walk.
I went to the café **for** breakfast.
These scissors are **for cutting** paper.
I bought some scissors **to cut** the paper.

mistakes.wrong: I went to the shop for buying bread.
mistakes.right: I went to the shop to buy bread.

mistakes.wrong: We went out for eat.
mistakes.right: We went out to eat. / We went out for dinner.

points.title: So that + can / could / will / would
points.summary: Use **so that** + subject + **can / could / will / would** for a purpose, especially when the subject changes: *I'll write it down so that I don't forget. She spoke slowly so that we could understand.*

blocks.md: ***So that*** introduces a full **clause** with a purpose. It's especially useful when the second subject is **different**: *I gave him my number **so that he could** call me.*
Use ***can / will*** for the present and future, and ***could / would*** for the past: *I'm leaving early **so that I can** catch the train. I left early **so that I could** catch the train.*
*That* is often dropped in speech: *Speak louder **so** everyone can hear.*
For a **negative** purpose, *so that … won't / don't* is often more natural than *to*: *I wrote it down **so that I wouldn't** forget.* (not *to not forget* in careful English)

examples.text: Turn the light on **so that** I **can** see.
I set two alarms **so that** I **wouldn't** oversleep.
She saved money **so that** her children **could** go to university.
Close the door **so** the cat **doesn't** get out.

mistakes.wrong: I gave her my number so that she call me.
mistakes.right: I gave her my number so that she could call me.

mistakes.wrong: He spoke slowly so that we can understand. (past)
mistakes.right: He spoke slowly so that we could understand.

points.title: In order to, so as to (and the negative)
points.summary: **in order to / so as to + verb** are more formal ways to give a purpose. For a negative purpose, use **in order not to / so as not to** (not *not to* alone).

blocks.md: ***In order to*** and ***so as to*** mean the same as *to*, but they're more **formal** and make the purpose clearer: *We left early **in order to** avoid the traffic.*

For a **negative** purpose, use ***in order not to*** or ***so as not to***: *We walked quietly **so as not to** wake the baby.* Simple *not to* alone usually sounds wrong: not *We walked quietly not to wake the baby*.
*In order to* can go at the start of a sentence for emphasis: ***In order to** apply, you must be over 18.*

examples.text: **In order to** get a visa, you need a letter from your employer.
I took notes **so as to** remember the details.
He spoke quietly **so as not to** disturb anyone.
She left early **in order not to** miss the train.

mistakes.wrong: I went out quietly not to wake anyone.
mistakes.right: I went out quietly so as not to wake anyone.
mistakes.why: negative purpose: so as not to / in order not to

mistakes.wrong: In order to pass, you need study hard.
mistakes.right: In order to pass, you need to study hard.

points.title: With a view to, with the aim of, for fear of, lest
points.summary: Formal purpose expressions: **with a view to / with the aim of + -ing**, **for fear of + -ing / for fear that**, and very formal **lest** (= so that … not).

rows: *They bought land **with a view to building** a hotel.*
*The course was designed **with the aim of improving** skills.*
*She didn't speak **for fear of making** a mistake.*
*He hid the letter **for fear that** someone would read it.*

blocks.md: Note that ***to*** in *with a view to* is a **preposition**, so it's followed by *-ing*: *with a view to **buying*** (not *to buy*).
***Lest*** is rare in modern speech; it appears in formal or literary writing. In everyday English, use *so that … not* or *in case*.

examples.text: She's taking evening classes **with a view to** changing careers.
The law was passed **with the aim of** reducing pollution.
I didn't mention it **for fear of** upsetting her.
They spoke in whispers **lest** they **be** overheard.

mistakes.wrong: They bought the house with a view to sell it.
mistakes.right: They bought the house with a view to selling it.

mistakes.wrong: He didn't move for fear to wake her.
mistakes.right: He didn't move for fear of waking her.

items.prompt: We turned off our phones ___ disturb the other guests.
___ to register, please complete the form below.
items.explanation: *In order to* at the start of a sentence.

items.prompt: She left early in order ___ (not / miss) the last train.

topics.summary: Using it as an empty subject or object: It's raining. It's easy to learn. I find it hard to believe.
intro: English sentences need a **subject**, so we often use ***it*** as an “empty” subject: ***It**'s raining. **It**'s five o'clock.* We also use ***it*** to **introduce** a long idea that comes later: ***It**'s important **to drink water**.* (= To drink water is important.)

This page goes from the basics to advanced patterns like *I find it hard to…* and *It goes without saying that…* For *It is said that…*, see [Passive Reporting Structures](/blog/grammar/passive-reporting-structures/).

points.title: It's raining, it's 5 o'clock, it's 10 km
points.summary: Use ***it*** as the subject for **weather**, **time**, **dates**, **days** and **distance**: ***It**'s cold. **It**'s half past six. **It**'s Monday. **It**'s 3 km to the station.*

rows: ***It**'s 5 km from here to the beach.*

blocks.md: Don't leave out ***it***: ***It**'s raining* (not *Is raining*).

examples.text: **It**'s very hot today.
**It**'s ten past nine.
**It**'s my birthday tomorrow.
How far is **it** to the airport?

mistakes.wrong: Is cold today.
mistakes.right: It's cold today.

mistakes.wrong: What time is?
mistakes.right: What time is it?

points.title: It is or there is?
points.summary: ***There is / are*** says that something **exists** or is in a place (first mention): ***There's** a problem.* ***It is*** describes or identifies something **already known**: ***It's** a big problem.*

blocks.md: Use ***there*** to **introduce** something new; then use ***it*** (or *they*) to talk about it: ***There's** a new film at the cinema. **It**'s really funny.*

examples.text: **There's** a bank on the corner. **It** opens at 9.
**There are** two bedrooms. **They**'re quite small.
Who's at the door? ~ **It**'s Ali.
**There's** no milk in the fridge.

mistakes.wrong: It's a supermarket near here. (first mention)
mistakes.right: There's a supermarket near here.

mistakes.wrong: There's very cold today.
mistakes.right: It's very cold today.

points.title: It's easy to learn, it's nice to meet you
points.summary: ***It's*** + **adjective** + ***to*** + verb: ***It's easy to** use. **It's nice to** meet you.* Add ***for*** + person: ***It's hard for me to** understand.* Also ***It takes*** + time + ***to***: ***It takes** an hour **to** get there.*

rows: ***It's difficult for children to** sit still.*
***It was kind of you to** help.*

blocks.md: This is more natural than starting with *to*: ***It's** easy **to** cook pasta* (not usually *To cook pasta is easy*).

examples.text: **It's** dangerous **to** swim here.
**It's** hard **for** me **to** wake up early.
**It was** nice **of** you **to** call.
**It takes** 20 minutes **to** walk to school.

mistakes.wrong: Is easy to learn English.
mistakes.right: It's easy to learn English.

mistakes.wrong: It's difficult to me to understand.
mistakes.right: It's difficult for me to understand.

points.title: It's a shame that, it seems that, it doesn't matter
points.summary: ***It*** + *be* + adjective / noun + ***that***-clause: ***It's a shame that** you can't come. **It's obvious that** he's lying.* With verbs: ***It seems / appears / turns out that…*** ***It doesn't matter whether / what…***

rows: ***It's a pity that** you missed the party.*
***It turned out that** she was right.*

blocks.md: ***That*** can often be left out in speech: ***It's a shame** you can't come.*

examples.text: **It's** a shame **that** the concert was cancelled.
**It seems that** the train is late again.
**It turned out that** we were in the wrong room.
**It doesn't matter** if you're late.

mistakes.wrong: Seems that we're lost.
mistakes.right: It seems that we're lost.

mistakes.wrong: It's a pity what you can't come.
mistakes.right: It's a pity that you can't come.

points.title: I find it hard to, I'd appreciate it if, make it clear
points.summary: ***It*** can also be a **preparatory object**: ***I find it hard to** believe. **I'd appreciate it if** you could help. **She made it clear that** she was unhappy. **I take it** you're not coming.*

rows: ***I'd appreciate it if** you didn't smoke here.*
***I hate it when** people are late.*
***I take it** you've heard the news.*

blocks.md: Don't leave out ***it***: *I find **it** hard to sleep* (not *I find hard to sleep*). *I'd appreciate **it** if…* (not *I'd appreciate if…*).

examples.text: I **find it** easy **to** talk to her.
The teacher **made it clear that** phones weren't allowed.
**I'd appreciate it if** you could reply soon.
**I love it when** it snows.

mistakes.wrong: I find difficult to wake up early.
mistakes.right: I find it difficult to wake up early.

mistakes.wrong: I'd appreciate if you could call me.
mistakes.right: I'd appreciate it if you could call me.

points.title: It's no use, it's worth, it goes without saying
points.summary: Fixed patterns: ***It's no use / no good*** + *-ing*, ***It's worth*** + *-ing*, ***It goes without saying that…***, ***It remains to be seen whether…***, ***It stands to reason that…***, ***It's not for me to…***

rows: ***It goes without saying that** safety comes first.*
***It remains to be seen whether** the plan will work.*
***It stands to reason that** prices will rise.*

blocks.md: After ***no use / no good / worth***, use ***-ing***: *It's no use **complaining*** (not *to complain*).

examples.text: **It's no use** arguing with him. He never listens.
**It's** really **worth seeing** the museum.
**It goes without saying that** you'll be paid.
**It remains to be seen whether** he'll accept the offer.

mistakes.wrong: It's no use cry about it.
mistakes.right: It's no use crying about it.

mistakes.wrong: It's worth to visit the castle.
mistakes.right: It's worth visiting the castle.

items.prompt: ___ that the shop is closed today.
It's a pity ___ you can't stay longer.
It doesn't ___ what you think. I've already decided. (one word)

topics.summary: Formal word order for emphasis: Never have I seen such a mess. Not only is it cheap, but it's also good.
intro: In formal or dramatic English, when a **negative or limiting word** starts the sentence (*never, rarely, not only, only when, under no circumstances*), we **invert** the subject and the auxiliary, like in a question: *I have **never** seen such a mess.* → ***Never have I** seen such a mess.*

If there's no auxiliary, add ***do / does / did***: *We rarely go out.* → ***Rarely do we** go out.* For inverted conditionals (*Had I known…*), see [Inverted Conditionals](/blog/grammar/inverted-conditionals/).

points.title: Never have I…, rarely do we…, little did I know
points.summary: After ***never, rarely, seldom, little*** at the start, use **auxiliary + subject**: ***Never have I** felt so happy. **Rarely do we** see snow here. **Little did she know** what would happen.*

rows: ***Little did I know** what would happen.*

blocks.md: The auxiliary comes **before** the subject, as in a question: *Never **have I**… / Rarely **do we**… / Seldom **does she**…*
With ***be***, invert *be* itself: ***Rarely is** the city so quiet.*

examples.text: **Never have I** eaten such delicious food.
**Rarely do** tourists visit this village.
**Seldom has** the team played so well.
**Little did we know** that our lives were about to change.

mistakes.wrong: Never I have seen such a beautiful view.
mistakes.right: Never have I seen such a beautiful view.

mistakes.wrong: Rarely we go to the cinema.
mistakes.right: Rarely do we go to the cinema.

points.title: Not only … but also, not until, not once
points.summary: ***Not only*** + auxiliary + subject + ***but (also)***: ***Not only is** it cheap, **but** it's **also** fast.* ***Not until*** + time / clause, then inversion in the main clause: ***Not until** midnight **did** they arrive.* ***Not once*** + inversion.

rows: ***Not only is it** cheap, **but** it's **also** fast.*
***Not only does she** speak French, **but** she **also** speaks Spanish.*

blocks.md: With ***Not until***, the inversion is in the **main** clause, not in the *until* part: ***Not until** I got home **did I** realise* (not *Not until did I get home…*).

examples.text: **Not only did** he forget my birthday, **but** he **also** forgot our anniversary.
**Not until** the end of the film **did** I understand the story.
**Not once has** she been late.
**Not only is** this phone light, **but** it's **also** waterproof.

mistakes.wrong: Not only he forgot, but he also lied.
mistakes.right: Not only did he forget, but he also lied.

mistakes.wrong: Not until did I see the photos I believed it.
mistakes.right: Not until I saw the photos did I believe it.

points.title: Only when, only after, only then, only by
points.summary: ***Only*** + time / condition expression at the start, then **inversion** in the main clause: ***Only when** I got home **did I** realise… **Only after** the meeting **did** we know… **Only then did** she understand.*

rows: ***Only when** you leave home **do you** appreciate your parents.*
*I read the letter again. **Only then did I** understand.*
***Only if** you pay in advance **will you** get a discount.*
***Only in** Japan **have I** seen such clean streets.*

blocks.md: As with *not until*, the inversion comes in the **main** clause: *Only when I arrived **did I** see…* (not *Only when did I arrive…*).

examples.text: **Only when** it started to rain **did** we go inside.
**Only by** practising every day **can** you improve.
**Only then did** I realise my mistake.
**Only after** he left **did** I find his note.

mistakes.wrong: Only when I got home I realised.
mistakes.right: Only when I got home did I realise.

mistakes.wrong: Only by work hard can you succeed.
mistakes.right: Only by working hard can you succeed.

points.title: Under no circumstances, on no account, in no way
points.summary: Strong negative phrases at the start take **inversion**: ***Under no circumstances should** you open this door. **On no account must** you tell her. **At no time did** he say that. **Nowhere have I** seen…*

rows: ***Under no circumstances should** you leave the building.*
***On no account must** you touch the wires.*
***At no time was** the public in danger.*
***In no way is** this your fault.*
***Nowhere** else **will** you find such good coffee.*

blocks.md: These are common in **rules**, **warnings** and **official statements**.

examples.text: **Under no circumstances should** you share your password.
**On no account must** the children play near the river.
**At no time did** I promise you a pay rise.
**In no way does** this change our plans.

mistakes.wrong: Under no circumstances you should open the box.
mistakes.right: Under no circumstances should you open the box.

mistakes.wrong: At no time I said that.
mistakes.right: At no time did I say that.

points.title: Hardly had I, no sooner, not a word did he say
points.summary: Very formal patterns: ***Hardly / Scarcely had*** + subject … ***when***, ***No sooner had*** + subject … ***than***, ***Not a (single)*** + noun + inversion (*Not a word did he say*), and ***So / Such*** + inversion (*So strong was the wind that…*).

rows: ***Hardly had** we sat down **when** the phone rang.*
***No sooner had** she arrived **than** she started complaining.*
***Not a single word did** he say.*
***So strong was** the wind **that** trees fell down.*
***Such was** the demand **that** the tickets sold out.*

blocks.md: Remember the pairs: ***hardly / scarcely … when*** and ***no sooner … than***. These patterns are mostly used in **writing** and storytelling.
Inversion is a **choice** for emphasis; the normal order is always correct: *We had hardly sat down when…*

examples.text: **Scarcely had** the film started **when** the power went off.
**No sooner had** I paid **than** I saw it cheaper online.
**Not a single person** **did** I recognise at the party.
**So loud was** the music **that** we couldn't talk.

mistakes.wrong: Hardly had I arrived than it started to rain.
mistakes.right: Hardly had I arrived when it started to rain.

mistakes.wrong: Not a word he said. (formal inversion)
mistakes.right: Not a word did he say.

items.prompt: Never ___ such a beautiful sunset.
Rarely ___ to bed before midnight.
Little ___ she know that he was planning a surprise party. (one word)

topics.summary: When to use like (similar to), as (in the role of, in the same way) and as if (it seems that).
intro: ***Like*** means **similar to**: *She sings **like** a professional.* ***As*** means **in the role of** (*He works **as** a waiter*) or **in the same way** + clause (*Do **as** I say*). ***As if*** describes how something **seems**: *It looks **as if** it's going to rain.*
For unreal *as if* + past (*He talks as if he knew everything*), see [Unreal Past](/blog/grammar/unreal-past/#up-as-if).

points.title: Like (similar to) or as (a job or role)?
points.summary: ***Like*** + noun = **similar to** (but not really): *He swims **like** a fish.* ***As*** + noun = a **real job, role or use**: *She works **as** a nurse. I used my scarf **as** a blanket.*

rows: *He talks **like** a teacher.* (He isn't a teacher.)
*He works **as** a teacher.* (He is a teacher.)

blocks.md: After ***like***, use a **noun** or **pronoun**: *like **me**, like **a child***.

examples.text: My brother eats **like** a horse.
I worked **as** a waiter when I was a student.
She looks **like** a film star.
We used the sofa **as** a bed.

mistakes.wrong: He works like a taxi driver. (it's his job)
mistakes.right: He works as a taxi driver.

mistakes.wrong: My son is as his father.
mistakes.right: My son is like his father.

points.title: As I said, as usual, do as I say
points.summary: ***As*** + clause = **in the same way** or **in agreement with**: *Do **as** I say. **As** I said, … **As** you know, …* Fixed phrases: ***as usual***, ***as expected***. In informal English, ***like*** + clause is common (*like I said*).

rows: *as I said / as you know / as we agreed*
***As** I said, the meeting is at 3.*
***Like** I said, it's not my problem.*

blocks.md: In careful or formal English, use ***as*** before a clause: ***As** I mentioned in my email, …* In informal speech, *like* is very common: *Nobody cooks **like** my mum does.*

examples.text: **As** you can see, the room is very small.
She was wearing black, **as usual**.
Please do **as** you're told!
The project was finished **as planned**.

mistakes.wrong: Like usual, he forgot his keys.
mistakes.right: As usual, he forgot his keys.

mistakes.wrong: As I've told you before, but you don't listen.
mistakes.right: As I've told you before, you need to listen.
mistakes.why: as + clause, then the main clause

points.title: Look like, look happy, what's it like?
points.summary: ***Look / sound / feel / taste / smell*** + **adjective** (*You look **tired***), but ***look like*** + **noun** (*You look **like** your dad*). ***What's it like?*** asks for a description; ***What does it look like?*** asks about appearance.

rows: *That sounds **like a good idea**. She looks **like her sister**.*
***What does** he **look like**?* ~ *He's tall with dark hair.*

blocks.md: Don't use *like* before an adjective: *You look **tired*** (not *You look like tired*).

examples.text: You **look** worried. Is everything OK?
This **sounds like** a great plan.
**What's** the weather **like** in Toronto?
**What does** your brother **look like**?

mistakes.wrong: You look like tired.
mistakes.right: You look tired.

mistakes.wrong: How is your new teacher like?
mistakes.right: What is your new teacher like?

points.title: Look as if, sound as though, feel like
points.summary: ***Look / sound / seem / feel*** + ***as if / as though / like*** + **clause** describes how something seems: *It looks **as if** it's going to rain. You sound **as though** you've got a cold.* ***Like*** + clause is informal.

rows: *It looks as if / as though* + clause
*I feel **like** I've known you for years.* (informal)

blocks.md: Use a **normal tense** when the situation is probably **true**: *It looks as if it's going to rain* (the sky is dark).
For something **unreal** or untrue, use a past form: *He acts **as if** he **owned** the place.* See [Unreal Past](/blog/grammar/unreal-past/#up-as-if).

examples.text: It **looks as if** the shop is closed.
You **sound as though** you need a holiday.
It **feels like** it's going to be a long day.
She **looked as if** she'd seen a ghost.

mistakes.wrong: It looks as it's going to snow.
mistakes.right: It looks as if it's going to snow.

mistakes.wrong: You seem as you're worried.
mistakes.right: You seem as if you're worried.

points.title: Such as, unlike, alike, likewise, as is often the case
points.summary: ***Such as*** (and *like*) introduce **examples**. ***Unlike*** = different from. ***Alike*** = similar (after the noun or verb). ***Likewise*** = in the same way. Formal ***as*** clauses: ***as is often the case***, ***as was expected***, ***as can be seen***.

rows: *I love fruit **such as** mangoes and kiwis.*
*The twins look **alike**. Students and teachers **alike** enjoyed it.*
***As is often the case**, the cheapest option was the worst.*
***As can be seen** in Figure 2, sales rose.*

blocks.md: ***Alike*** is never used **before** a noun: *The houses are **alike*** (not *the alike houses*). Use ***similar*** before a noun: ***similar** houses*.
In formal writing, ***such as*** is preferred to *like* for examples.

examples.text: Big cities, **such as** Tokyo and London, are expensive.
**Unlike** most of my friends, I don't have a car.
My sister and I think **alike**.
**As was expected**, the team won easily.

mistakes.wrong: The two brothers are very like.
mistakes.right: The two brothers are very alike.

mistakes.wrong: Alike his father, he became a doctor.
mistakes.right: Like his father, he became a doctor.

items.prompt: The sky is very dark. It looks ___ it's going to rain.
You sound ___ you've got a cold.
There are no lights on. It looks as ___ they've gone away. (one word)

topics.summary: When to use make (create, produce) and do (activities, work), with the most common collocations.
intro: ***Make*** usually means **create** or **produce** something new: ***make** a cake, **make** a plan*. ***Do*** is for **activities**, **work** and **tasks**: ***do** your homework, **do** the dishes*.
Many expressions don't follow the rule, so learn them as **pairs**: ***make** a mistake* (not *do a mistake*), ***do** someone a favour* (not *make a favour*).

points.title: Make a cake, do your homework
points.summary: ***Make*** = create or produce (*make a cake, make tea, make a mess*). ***Do*** = activities, work and jobs (*do homework, do the dishes, do sport*), and general actions with *something, anything, nothing, what*.

rows: *do the dishes / the shopping / the cleaning*

blocks.md: For general activities, use ***do***: *What are you **doing**? I'm not **doing** anything. What do you **do**?* (= What's your job?)

examples.text: I'll **make** some coffee.
Have you **done** your homework?
Don't **make** a mess in the kitchen!
Who **does** the shopping in your family?

mistakes.wrong: I need to make my homework.
mistakes.right: I need to do my homework.

mistakes.wrong: Can you do a cake for the party?
mistakes.right: Can you make a cake for the party?

mistakes.wrong: I always do my bed in the morning.
mistakes.right: I always make my bed in the morning.

points.title: Make a mistake, do me a favour
points.summary: Common **fixed** pairs. **make**: *a mistake, a decision, money, progress, an effort, friends, a plan, an appointment, an excuse, a complaint, a suggestion*. **do**: *a favour, business, your best, damage, good, harm, research, a course, an exam* (BrE).

blocks.md: These are **collocations**: there's no strict rule, so learn the whole phrase.

examples.text: Everyone **makes** mistakes.
Could you **do** me a favour?
She's **making** good progress with her English.
The storm **did** a lot of damage.

mistakes.wrong: I did a big mistake.
mistakes.right: I made a big mistake.

mistakes.wrong: Can you make me a favour?
mistakes.right: Can you do me a favour?

mistakes.wrong: He does a lot of money.
mistakes.right: He makes a lot of money.

points.title: It made me laugh; she made me wait
points.summary: ***Make*** + person + **base verb** = cause or force someone to do something: *The film **made me laugh**. My boss **made me work** late.* ***Make*** + person + **adjective**: *It **made me happy**.* Passive: *I **was made to wait**.*

rows: *We **were made to wait** for an hour.*

blocks.md: In the **active**, there's **no *to***: *She made me **stay***. In the **passive**, ***to*** comes back: *I was made **to stay***.

examples.text: That joke **made me laugh**.
The long wait **made everyone tired**.
The teacher **made us rewrite** the essay.
He **was made to apologise**.

mistakes.wrong: My mum made me to clean my room.
mistakes.right: My mum made me clean my room.

mistakes.wrong: The story made me sadly.
mistakes.right: The story made me sad.

points.title: Make sense, make do with, could do with
points.summary: Useful expressions: ***make sense*** (be logical), ***make sure*** (check), ***make up your mind*** (decide), ***make the most of*** (use well), ***make do with*** (manage with less), ***make it*** (arrive / succeed), ***could do with*** (want, need), ***do without*** (manage without), ***have (nothing) to do with***.

rows: *We'll have to **make do with** a small flat.*
*We **made it** just in time. She **made it** as a singer.*

blocks.md: ***Could do with*** is very common in British English for something you'd like or need: *This room **could do with** a clean.*

examples.text: Your story doesn't **make sense**.
I **could do with** a holiday.
We missed the bus, but we still **made it** to the concert.
His job **has something to do with** computers.

mistakes.wrong: It doesn't do sense.
mistakes.right: It doesn't make sense.

mistakes.wrong: I can't make without coffee in the morning.
mistakes.right: I can't do without coffee in the morning.

items.prompt: I can't decide which dress to buy. I can't ___ up my mind.
I'm so tired. I ___ a long sleep.
The train leaves in five minutes. We'll never ___ it! (one word)

topics.summary: Saying something is possible but not certain: I might go out tonight. It may rain. She might be working.
intro: We use ***might*** and ***may*** to say that something is **possible**, but we're not sure: *I **might** go to the gym later. It **may** rain tomorrow.*

For being sure or almost sure (*must, can't*), and for possibility in the past (*might have done*), see [Modals of Deduction](/blog/grammar/modals-of-deduction/). For *May I…?*, see [Requests, Offers and Permission](/blog/grammar/requests-offers-permission/).

points.title: Might and might not: perhaps
points.summary: **might / might not + base verb** = perhaps (now or in the future): *I **might** go to the party. It **might not** rain.*

blocks.md: ***Might*** + base verb means *perhaps*, about the present or the future: *Take an umbrella. It **might** rain.* = Perhaps it will rain.
The negative is ***might not*** (*mightn't* is rare and only British): *I **might not** come.* = Perhaps I won't come.
Like other modals, *might* is the same for every person and has no *to*: *She **might** call.* Not *She mights call* or *might to call*.
Compare: *I**'m going to** visit Ali* (a plan) / *I **might** visit Ali* (perhaps, I'm not sure). For questions, we usually say *Do you think…?*: ***Do you think** it'll rain?* (not *Might it rain?*)

examples.text: I **might** buy a new laptop next month.
We **might not** have enough time.
Ask Sara. She **might** know the answer.
The shop **might** be closed now. It's late.

mistakes.wrong: I might to go to the beach.
mistakes.right: I might go to the beach.

mistakes.wrong: He mights be late.
mistakes.right: He might be late.

mistakes.wrong: It might rains.
mistakes.right: It might rain.

points.title: May or might?
points.summary: **may** and **might** both mean *perhaps*. *May* is a little more formal and can sound a little more certain. Use *might* for unreal situations.

blocks.md: In most sentences, ***may*** and ***might*** are both possible with the same meaning: *She **may / might** be at home.* *We **may / might** move to Vancouver.*
***May*** is a little more **formal** and is common in writing: *Some medicines **may** cause sleepiness.* Many speakers feel it is slightly more likely than *might*.
In **unreal** (second conditional) sentences, use ***might***, not *may*: *If I had more money, I **might** buy a house.* Not *I may buy*.
*May not* means *perhaps not*: *He **may not** know.* (In formal rules, *may not* can also mean *not allowed*: *Visitors **may not** take photos.*)

examples.text: The meeting **may** finish late.
Side effects **may** include headaches.
If you asked her nicely, she **might** help you.
I **may not** be able to come.

mistakes.wrong: If I won the lottery, I may stop working.
mistakes.right: If I won the lottery, I might stop working.

mistakes.wrong: May it rain tomorrow?
mistakes.right: Do you think it will rain tomorrow?
mistakes.why: questions about possibility: Do you think…?

points.title: Might be doing: now or in the future
points.summary: **might / may be + -ing** = perhaps something is happening now, or is planned: *Don't call now. She **might be sleeping**. I **might be working** late tonight.*

blocks.md: ***Might / may + be + -ing*** shows that perhaps an action is **in progress now**: *Where's Tom? ~ He **might be having** a shower.*
It can also be about a **possible future arrangement**: *I **may be going** to Paris next week.* (It isn't decided.)
Compare: *She **might work** at home* (perhaps that's her job situation) / *She **might be working** at home today* (perhaps she is right now).
For possibility in the past (*might have done*), see [Modals of Deduction](/blog/grammar/modals-of-deduction/).

examples.text: Don't phone him now. He **might be driving**.
The kids are quiet. They **may be watching** TV.
I **might be moving** to Calgary next year.
We **might be getting** a new manager soon.

mistakes.wrong: She might sleeping.
mistakes.right: She might be sleeping.

mistakes.wrong: He might is working.
mistakes.right: He might be working.

points.title: Might as well, may as well
points.summary: **might / may as well + base verb** = there's no better option, so let's do it: *The bus isn't coming. We **might as well** walk.*

blocks.md: We say ***might as well*** or ***may as well*** when we do something because there's **no good reason not to** or **nothing better to do**: *There's nothing on TV. I **might as well** go to bed.*
It often sounds a little unenthusiastic. *We **might as well** take a taxi* = it's not ideal, but it's the best option.
***Might as well*** can also compare two bad options: *This phone is so slow, I **might as well** use a pigeon!* (= it would be just as good)

examples.text: The film has already started. We **might as well** go home.
We've got an hour before the train. We **may as well** have a coffee.
Nobody listens to me. I **might as well** talk to the wall.

mistakes.wrong: We might as well to walk.
mistakes.right: We might as well walk.

mistakes.wrong: We might as good stay here.
mistakes.right: We might as well stay here.

points.title: He may be rich, but…: may and might for concession
points.summary: **may / might … but** = I accept this is true, but something else is more important: *He **may** be rich, **but** he isn't happy.*

blocks.md: We use ***may*** or ***might*** + **but** to **admit** that something is true before making a contrasting point. The *may* clause is not uncertain here; it's a concession: *It **may** be expensive, **but** it's worth it.* = I agree it's expensive, but…
The structure is common in arguments and discussions. ***Might*** is a little more tentative: *You **might** think it's easy, **but** it isn't.*
For the past: ***may / might have*** + past participle: *She **may have been** tired, **but** that's no excuse.*

examples.text: The hotel **may** be old, **but** it's very comfortable.
You **might** not like him, **but** he's a good manager.
He **may have** studied law, **but** he's never worked as a lawyer.
I **may** be wrong, **but** I think she's lying.

mistakes.wrong: The test may be difficult, so I passed it.
mistakes.right: The test may have been difficult, but I passed it.
mistakes.why: concession + but; past: may have been

points.title: You might want to…, may well, might have told me
points.summary: **might** for polite suggestions (*You **might want to** check that*) and annoyance (*You **might have** told me!*). **may / might well** = probably.

blocks.md: ***You might (want to)…*** makes a suggestion very polite and indirect: *You **might want to** save your work before you close the file. You **might** try calling them again.*

***You might have*** + past participle expresses **annoyance** about something someone didn't do: *You **might have** told me you were bringing friends!* (You didn't, and I'm annoyed.) Compare *could have* (same meaning).
***May well / might well / could well*** + base verb = it's **quite likely**: *Prices **may well** rise next year.* *It **might well** be the best film of the year.*

examples.text: You **might want to** check the address before you go.
You **might have** warned me about the traffic!
The company **may well** close its London office.
She **could well** be right.

mistakes.wrong: You might want check your answers.
mistakes.right: You might want to check your answers.

mistakes.wrong: He may well to win.
mistakes.right: He may well win.

items.prompt: The last bus has gone. We ___ walk home.
What does *I may as well finish the work tonight* mean?
options: There's no reason not to, so I'll do it.

items.prompt: Nobody else wants the last piece of pizza, so I might as ___ eat it. (one word)

topics.summary: Mix past and present: If I had taken that job, I would be rich now.
intro: **Mixed conditionals** combine two different times. The condition is in one time and the result is in another: *If I **had taken** that job (past), I **would be** rich now (present).*

They're built from the second and third conditionals. If you need to review those first, see [Second Conditional](/blog/grammar/second-conditional/) and [Third Conditional](/blog/grammar/third-conditional/).

points.title: Past condition, present result
points.summary: **if + past perfect, would + base verb**: an imaginary past and its result **now**: *If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.*

rows: *I **would be** able to buy a house now.*

blocks.md: The condition is about the **past** (it didn't happen). The result is about the **present** (it isn't true now).
Words like ***now, today, still, by now*** often show the present result.
Compare with the third conditional, where both parts are past: *If I had studied medicine, I **would have become** a doctor* (then). *…I **would be** a doctor **now**.*

examples.text: If I **hadn't missed** the bus, I **would be** at work now.
If she **had accepted** the offer, she **would live** in Dubai today.
If you **had listened** to me, we **wouldn't be** lost.
If they **hadn't moved** away, we**'d** still **be** neighbours.

mistakes.wrong: If I learned to drive last year, I would have a car now.
mistakes.right: If I had learned to drive last year, I would have a car now.

mistakes.wrong: If you had gone to bed earlier, you wouldn't have been tired now.
mistakes.right: If you had gone to bed earlier, you wouldn't be tired now.

points.title: Present condition, past result
points.summary: **if + past simple, would have + past participle**: a present (or general) situation that would have changed the past: *If I spoke French, I would have understood him.*

blocks.md: The condition is about something that is **generally or always** not true (a permanent fact about a person, an ability, a feeling). The result is in the **past**.
*If I **were** a better cook, I **would have made** a cake for the party.* = I'm not a good cook (now and always), so I didn't make a cake.
This mix is less common. Use it when the *if* clause describes a **permanent** situation, not a single past event.

examples.text: If I **weren't** so shy, I **would have spoken** to her.
If he **knew** the area, he **wouldn't have got** lost.
If you **were** more organised, you **wouldn't have forgotten** the meeting.
If we **didn't have** kids, we **would have gone** on the trip.

mistakes.wrong: If I was braver, I would ask her out last week.
mistakes.right: If I was braver, I would have asked her out last week.
mistakes.why: Past result: would have + past participle.

points.title: Mixed conditionals with continuous forms and modals
points.summary: Mixed conditionals can use **could, might** and **continuous** forms: *If I hadn't missed the flight, I'd be lying on a beach now.*

blocks.md: The result can use ***could*** or ***might*** instead of *would*: *If I had learned Arabic as a child, I **could** read this now. If you hadn't upset her, she **might** be here.*
Continuous forms describe actions in progress: *If it **weren't raining**, we **would have gone** out.* / *If I **hadn't changed** jobs, I **would be working** in London now.*

examples.text: If we hadn't missed the flight, we **would be lying** on a beach right now.
If I'd brought my laptop, I **could** work on the train.
If you **weren't working** tonight, we **would have invited** you.
If she hadn't been so rude, he **might** still **be** her friend.

mistakes.wrong: If I hadn't lost my keys, I could have been inside now.
mistakes.right: If I hadn't lost my keys, I could be inside now.

points.title: Choosing the right conditional
points.summary: Ask two questions: Is the condition real or imaginary? Is each part about the past, the present or the future? Then choose the forms.

rows: *If I'd had time, I'd have helped.*
*If I'd taken the job, I'd be rich.*
*If I were braver, I'd have said something.*

blocks.md: Look for time clues: *now, today, still* (present), *yesterday, last year, then* (past), *always, in general* (permanent).

In real conditionals any sensible tense combination is possible: *If he left at six, he'll be here soon.* (I don't know if he left.) See [Zero and First Conditional](/blog/grammar/zero-and-first-conditional/#zfc-other-tenses).

examples.text: If I **had** a car, I**'d drive**.
If I**'d had** a car, I**'d have driven**.
If I**'d bought** a car, I**'d drive** to work now.
If I **didn't hate** driving, I**'d have driven**.

mistakes.wrong: If I didn't miss the train this morning, I would be at work now.
mistakes.right: If I hadn't missed the train this morning, I would be at work now.
mistakes.why: A past event in the if clause: past perfect.

items.prompt: If I had booked the tickets earlier, we ___ in the front row now.
items.explanation: Past condition, present result: *would be sitting*.

items.prompt: If she hadn't broken her leg, she ___ in the race today.
If you had taken the medicine, you ___ (feel) better now.
If I ___ afraid of flying, I would have visited you last summer.
items.explanation: A permanent situation: *If I weren't afraid…*

items.prompt: If she spoke better English, she ___ the interview last week.
He's a careless person. If he ___ (be) more careful, he wouldn't have broken his phone last week.
items.explanation: A permanent quality: *were / was* (mixed); *had been* (third conditional) is also correct.

topics.summary: How sure are you? It must be true. It might be true. It can't be true. She must have left.
intro: We use modal verbs to show **how sure** we are about something, based on what we know: *She **must** be at home* (I'm sure). *She **might** be at home* (perhaps). *She **can't** be at home* (I'm sure she isn't).

The same verbs talk about the **past** with *have* + past participle: *She **must have left** early.* This page also covers stronger and more formal ways to talk about probability, like *bound to* and *likely to*. For *might* as perhaps in general, see [May and Might](/blog/grammar/may-might/).

points.title: Must and can't: I'm sure
points.summary: **must** = I'm sure it's true. **can't** = I'm sure it isn't true. *He's been working all day. He **must** be tired. That **can't** be Tom. He's in Paris.*

rows: *The lights are on. They **must** be at home.*

blocks.md: We use ***must*** when we have a good reason (evidence) to be sure: *You've been travelling for 20 hours. You **must** be exhausted.*
For the negative, use ***can't*** (or *couldn't*), not *mustn't*: *That **can't** be right.* Not *That mustn't be right* (in British English, *mustn't* means *not allowed*).
In American English, ***must not*** is also used for negative deductions: *He **must not** be home. His car is gone.* In British English, *can't* is the usual choice.

examples.text: You **must** be Mina's brother. You look just like her.
This **can't** be the right address. It's a car park!
There **must** be a mistake on the bill.
He **can't** be hungry. He's just eaten a huge pizza.

mistakes.wrong: He mustn't be at home. The lights are off. (British English)
mistakes.right: He can't be at home. The lights are off.

mistakes.wrong: She must to be tired.
mistakes.right: She must be tired.

points.title: Might, may, could: it's possible
points.summary: **might / may / could** = it's possible (perhaps true). **couldn't** = I'm sure it isn't. *He might be at work. It could be a virus.*

rows: *She **might / may / could** be at the library.*
*She **couldn't** be at home. I saw her at the gym.*

blocks.md: Use *might, may* or *could* when you think something is possible but you **don't have enough evidence** to be sure: *Where's my phone? ~ It **could** be in the car.*

Careful with the negatives: ***might not / may not*** = perhaps not. ***Couldn't*** = I'm sure it isn't (like *can't*). *He **might not** be at home* (perhaps he isn't) is different from *He **couldn't** be at home* (impossible).

examples.text: The noise **might** be the wind.
Don't eat that. It **could** be poisonous.
She **may not** know the answer.
It **couldn't** be John. He's in hospital.

mistakes.wrong: She could not be at home, I'm not sure.
mistakes.right: She might not be at home. I'm not sure.

mistakes.wrong: It can be the postman at the door.
mistakes.right: It might / could be the postman at the door.

points.title: Must be doing, might be doing, can't be doing
points.summary: For actions **in progress now**, use **must / might / can't + be + -ing**: *She isn't answering. She **must be driving**.*

blocks.md: To make a deduction about what is **happening now**, use *modal + be + -ing*: *Listen! Someone **must be playing** the piano. He **can't be sleeping**. The light is on.*
It also works for future arrangements: *They **might be coming** tomorrow.*

examples.text: The phone's busy. She **must be talking** to her mother.
Why is he smiling? He **might be thinking** about his girlfriend.
You **can't be working** already! You only woke up five minutes ago.
They **could be waiting** for us at the other entrance.

mistakes.wrong: She must sleeping.
mistakes.right: She must be sleeping.

mistakes.wrong: He can't be work now. It's Sunday.
mistakes.right: He can't be working now. It's Sunday.

points.title: Must have done, can't have done: sure about the past
points.summary: **must have + past participle** = I'm sure it happened. **can't / couldn't have + past participle** = I'm sure it didn't happen.

rows: *The ground is wet. It **must have rained**.*
*He **can't have seen** me. He didn't say hello.*

blocks.md: For deductions about the **past**, use *modal + have + past participle*: *She **must have left** early. Her coat isn't here.*
*Can't have* and *couldn't have* mean the same in deductions: *You **can't / couldn't have finished** already!*
*Must have* is often pronounced /ˈmʌstəv/. Don't write *must of*: *She **must have** forgotten.*

examples.text: The window is broken. Someone **must have thrown** a ball.
You **must have been** so happy when you heard the news.
She **can't have driven** here. She doesn't have a car.
They **couldn't have heard** us. We were very quiet.

mistakes.wrong: He must went home.
mistakes.right: He must have gone home.

mistakes.wrong: She can't have saw it.
mistakes.right: She can't have seen it.

mistakes.wrong: You must of been tired.
mistakes.right: You must have been tired.

points.title: Might have done, could have done: possible in the past
points.summary: **might / may / could have + past participle** = perhaps it happened. **might not have** = perhaps it didn't. *She might have missed the bus.*

blocks.md: When we think something **possibly** happened in the past, use *might / may / could have* + past participle: *Where's Leila? ~ She **might have gone** home. She **could have missed** the train.*
For *perhaps it didn't happen*, use ***might not have / may not have***: *He **may not have received** my email.* (Remember: *couldn't have* = I'm sure it didn't.)
***Could have*** also describes something that was **possible but didn't happen**: *You were lucky. You **could have been** killed!* (but you weren't)

examples.text: I can't find my wallet. I **might have left** it in the taxi.
She **may not have heard** the doorbell.
Be careful! You **could have fallen**!
They **could have taken** a different road.

mistakes.wrong: He might not have came.
mistakes.right: He might not have come.

mistakes.wrong: She couldn't have got my message, but I'm not sure.
mistakes.right: She might not have got my message. I'm not sure.

points.title: That'll be the postman: will and should for assumptions
points.summary: **will / won't** for confident assumptions (*That'll be Ali at the door*). **should** for what we expect (*He should be home by now*).

blocks.md: ***Will*** can make a confident assumption about the **present**, based on what we know about routines and habits: *The doorbell's ringing. **That'll be** the postman.* (He always comes at this time.)
***Will have*** + past participle does the same for the past: *You**'ll have heard** the news, I suppose.*

***Should*** shows what we **expect**, often based on plans: *The flight **should** have landed by now.* (That's what's expected.) See [Should and Ought To](/blog/grammar/should-ought-to/#soa-expectation).
From most to least sure: *must / will* → *should* → *may / might / could* → *can't / won't* (sure it isn't).

examples.text: Someone's at the door. **That'll be** my sister.
Don't call him now. He**'ll be** asleep.
You**'ll have seen** the photos on Instagram.
It's 6 pm. Dad **should** be leaving work about now.

mistakes.wrong: That will to be John.
mistakes.right: That will be John.

points.title: Bound to, likely to, may well: other ways to show probability
points.summary: **be bound to / be sure to** = certain. **be likely to** = probable. **be unlikely to** = not probable. **may well / could well** = quite possible.

rows: *be bound to / be sure to / be certain to*
*It**'s bound to** rain at the weekend.*
*be likely to / there's a good chance (that)*

blocks.md: These phrases are common in news, reports and formal discussions about the future.

Word order: ***likely*** is an adjective (*She is **likely** to win*), but ***probably*** is an adverb (*She will **probably** win*). Don't say *She will likely win* in British English (it is common in American English).
***Bound to*** can also suggest *it always happens*: *If you leave food out, the dog**'s bound to** eat it.*

examples.text: You've studied so hard. You**'re bound to** pass.
The new law **is unlikely to** change much.
**There's a good chance** we'll be late.
The final **could well** be the best match of the year.

mistakes.wrong: She is likely win.
mistakes.right: She is likely to win.

mistakes.wrong: It's bound rain.
mistakes.right: It's bound to rain.

items.prompt: The kids are very quiet. They ___ something naughty!
Sara ___. I can hear her singing in the shower.
items.explanation: Sure it isn't happening: *can't be sleeping*.

items.prompt: Don't call Ali now. He ___ (might / have) dinner.
The streets are wet. It ___ in the night.
Tom didn't study at all, but he got 98%. He ___ the answers before the exam!
I can't find my keys. I ___ (must / leave) them at the office.
Hassan isn't here yet. He ___ the earlier train.
What does *You could have been hurt!* mean?
options: It was possible, but you weren't hurt.

items.prompt: I'm not sure why she's angry. I ___ (might / say) something wrong.

topics.h1: Much, Many, A Lot Of, A Few, A Little
topics.summary: Talking about quantity: How much money? How many people? A lot of time, a few friends, a little sugar.
intro: Use ***many*** and ***a few*** with **plural countable** nouns (*many books, a few friends*), and ***much*** and ***a little*** with **uncountable** nouns (*much time, a little milk*). ***A lot of*** works with both.
See also [Countable and Uncountable Nouns](/blog/grammar/countable-uncountable-nouns/) and [Some and Any](/blog/grammar/some-any/).

points.title: Much, many, a lot of; how much, how many
points.summary: Use ***many*** + plural nouns and ***much*** + uncountable nouns, mostly in **questions and negatives**. Use ***a lot of / lots of*** with both, especially in **positive** sentences. Ask ***How many…?*** and ***How much…?***

blocks.md: In positive sentences, ***a lot of*** sounds more natural than *much*: *I drink **a lot of** coffee.* (not *I drink much coffee*). *Many* is fine in positive sentences, but *a lot of* is more common in speech.
***How much*** also asks about **price**: *How much is this jacket?*

examples.text: How **many** brothers do you have?
I don't have **much** money.
There are **a lot of** people here.
How **much** is a coffee?

mistakes.wrong: How much people came?
mistakes.right: How many people came?

mistakes.wrong: I don't have many time.
mistakes.right: I don't have much time.

mistakes.wrong: There is a lot of cars.
mistakes.right: There are a lot of cars.

points.title: A few and a little: some, but not a lot
points.summary: ***A few*** + plural nouns and ***a little*** + uncountable nouns mean **some, a small amount**: *I have a few friends here. Can I have a little sugar?*

rows: *a few eggs, a few days, a few people*
*a little milk, a little time, a little money*

blocks.md: *A few* and *a little* are **positive**: they mean *some*, often *enough*: *I have **a few** friends in Toronto, so I'm not lonely.*
***A little*** can also mean *a bit* before an adjective: *I'm **a little** tired.*

examples.text: I'll be ready in **a few** minutes.
Add **a little** salt.
We stayed in Paris for **a few** days.
She speaks **a little** French.

mistakes.wrong: I have a little friends here.
mistakes.right: I have a few friends here.

mistakes.wrong: Can I have a few milk?
mistakes.right: Can I have a little milk?

points.title: Few or a few? Little or a little?
points.summary: ***A few / a little*** = **some** (positive). ***Few / little*** (without *a*) = **not many / not much** (negative): *I have a few friends* (I'm OK). *I have few friends* (I'm lonely).

rows: *There's **a little** time left. Let's have a coffee.*

blocks.md: *Few* and *little* (without *a*) are quite **formal**. In conversation, people usually say *not many / not much*: *Not many people came.*
***Very few / very little*** are common: *There's **very little** money left.*
***Quite a few*** = quite a lot: *Quite a few people came.*

examples.text: **Few** tourists visit this area in winter.
He has **little** patience with lazy students.
**A few** of my friends came to help.
**Quite a few** people complained.

mistakes.wrong: Unfortunately, a few people came, so the party was boring.
mistakes.right: Unfortunately, few people came, so the party was boring.

mistakes.wrong: Don't hurry. There's little time.
mistakes.right: Don't hurry. There's a little time.

points.title: Too much, too many, plenty of, a large number of
points.summary: ***Too much / too many*** = more than you want. ***Plenty of*** = more than enough. In formal English: ***a large number of*** + plural nouns, ***a great deal of / a large amount of*** + uncountable nouns.

rows: *a great deal of money, a large amount of data*

blocks.md: ***Plenty of*** is positive: *Don't worry, we have **plenty of** time.* (= more than enough)
In formal writing, use ***a large number of*** with countable nouns and ***a great deal of / a large amount of*** with uncountable nouns. Don't use *a great deal of* with plural nouns.

examples.text: There are **too many** cars in the city centre.
I spend **too much** time on my phone.
Help yourself. There's **plenty of** food.
The project requires **a great deal of** effort.

mistakes.wrong: There's too many noise.
mistakes.right: There's too much noise.

mistakes.wrong: A large number of money was stolen.
mistakes.right: A large amount of money was stolen.

mistakes.wrong: A great deal of people agree.
mistakes.right: A large number of people agree.

points.title: Much in formal writing, many a, a great many
points.summary: In **formal** English, ***much*** and ***many*** are common in positive sentences: *Much has been written about this.* ***Many a*** + singular noun = many (literary). ***A good / great many*** = a very large number.

rows: ***Much** research has been done on this topic. There is **much** debate about…*
***Much** of the city was destroyed. **Many** believe that…*

blocks.md: In everyday speech, *a lot of* is more natural in positive sentences. In academic and formal writing, ***much*** and ***many*** are common: *There has been **much** discussion of…*
***As much as / as many as*** + number emphasises that the number is **large**: *As many as 10,000 people were affected.* Use *as much as* for money and uncountable amounts.

examples.text: **Much** has changed since the 1990s.
**Many a** traveller has got lost in these mountains.
She has written **a great many** articles.
**As many as** 500 jobs could be lost.

mistakes.wrong: Many a students have tried.
mistakes.right: Many a student has tried.
mistakes.why: many a + singular noun + singular verb

mistakes.wrong: A great many people was there.
mistakes.right: A great many people were there.

mistakes.wrong: It can cost as many as $1,000.
mistakes.right: It can cost as much as $1,000.

items.prompt: I can't sleep. There's ___ noise outside.
Don't rush. We have ___ time.
There were too ___ people on the bus, so I walked. (one word)

topics.h1: Narrative Tenses: Telling Stories in the Past
topics.summary: The four past tenses working together to tell a story: events, background, earlier events and earlier activities.
intro: When we tell a story or describe past events, we use four **narrative tenses** together. Each one has a different job.

This page shows how to combine them, how to move back in time and forward again, and how to make a story clear and lively. For each tense on its own, see [Past Simple](/blog/grammar/past-simple/), [Past Continuous](/blog/grammar/past-continuous/), [Past Perfect](/blog/grammar/past-perfect/) and [Past Perfect Continuous](/blog/grammar/past-perfect-continuous/).

points.title: The four narrative tenses and their jobs
points.summary: Past simple = the main events; past continuous = the background; past perfect = earlier events; past perfect continuous = earlier activities.

rows: activities that continued up to the main story
*She**'d been waiting** for that letter for weeks.*

blocks.md: Read how they work together: *It **was raining** when Sara **got** home. She **was** wet and tired because she**'d been walking** for an hour. When she **opened** the door, she **saw** that someone **had been** in the house.*
The **past simple** carries the story forward. The other three tenses give extra information around the main events. If you are not sure, the past simple is usually the safest choice.

examples.text: We **were having** lunch when the earthquake **started**.
When we **got** to the cinema, the film **had** already **started**.
He **was** angry because he**'d been waiting** for two hours.

mistakes.wrong: I was waking up at 7, had a shower and left.
mistakes.right: I woke up at 7, had a shower and left.
mistakes.why: The main events in order: past simple.

mistakes.wrong: When I arrived, the train already left.
mistakes.right: When I arrived, the train had already left.
mistakes.why: Earlier than the main event: past perfect.

points.title: Going back in time and coming back
points.summary: Use the past perfect to go back to an earlier time, then return to the past simple. Don't put the whole flashback in the past perfect.

blocks.md: Sometimes a story needs to go back to something that happened **earlier**. The past perfect shows this jump back:
*The plane **took off**. I **was** nervous. I **had** never **flown** before, and I **had heard** stories about accidents.*
When the flashback is long, use the past perfect for the first verb or two to show the jump, then go on in the **past simple**:
*I **had met** Ali ten years earlier. We **were** both students then, and we **shared** a flat for two years…*
When the order of events is already clear (for example with *before* or *after*), the past simple is often enough: *I **checked** the doors **before** I **left**.*
Using the past perfect for every verb makes a story heavy. Use it to make the order clear, not by habit.

examples.text: When I saw him, I knew him at once. We**'d worked** together years before.
She **opened** the box. Her grandmother **had given** it to her when she **was** a child.
I **phoned** the hotel after I **saw** the advert.
examples.note: order clear: past simple is fine

mistakes.wrong: I had met him at a party. I had liked him and we had talked all night and we had danced.
mistakes.right: I had met him at a party. I liked him and we talked all night and danced.
mistakes.why: After the first verb, return to the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: When I arrived at the station, my train left. (it left earlier)
mistakes.right: When I arrived at the station, my train had left.
mistakes.why: The earlier event needs the past perfect.

points.title: Time linkers in stories
points.summary: Linkers show when things happened: *when, as soon as, after, before, by the time, until, while, during, eventually, in the end, at last*.

rows: *By the time we **arrived**, the shop **had closed**.*
two things at the same time
after a long time or difficulties

blocks.md: ***By the time*** + past simple is usually followed by the **past perfect**: *By the time I **got** there, everyone **had left**.*
***At last*** shows relief after waiting: ***At last** the bus came!* ***In the end*** introduces the final result: ***In the end**, we decided to stay.*
***During*** needs a noun (*during the meeting*), not a clause. Before a clause, use ***while***: ***while** we were in the meeting*.

examples.text: **By the time** the ambulance **arrived**, the man **had stopped** breathing.
We **didn't leave until** the storm **had passed**.
**During** the night, the temperature **fell** to −20.
**Eventually**, after three hours, we **reached** the top.

mistakes.wrong: During we were travelling, we met a lot of people.
mistakes.right: While we were travelling, we met a lot of people.

mistakes.wrong: By the time we arrived, the film already started.
mistakes.right: By the time we arrived, the film had already started.

mistakes.wrong: At the end we found a taxi.
mistakes.right: In the end we found a taxi.

points.title: Choosing the right tense in a story
points.summary: For each verb, ask: is it the next event, the background, an earlier event, or an earlier activity? The answer gives you the tense.

blocks.md: Use these questions to choose the tense of each verb:

items: Is it the **next event** in the story? → past simple: *I **ran** to the door.*
Was it **in progress** at that moment? → past continuous: *Someone **was knocking**.*
Did it happen **before** the moment we're talking about? → past perfect: *I **had** never **seen** him before.*
Was it an **activity going on up to** that moment? → past perfect continuous: *He **had been driving** all night.*

blocks.md: Example: *Last winter I **was staying** with friends in the mountains. One evening, while we **were having** dinner, the lights **went** out. We **had heard** that a storm was coming, but we **hadn't expected** it so soon. It **had been snowing** all day, and the roads **were** closed.*
State verbs (*be, know, have* for possession, *want*) are not normally continuous, even in the background: *Everyone **knew** him.* Not *Everyone was knowing him.*

examples.text: The phone **rang**. I **was** in the shower.
I **had been working** for ten hours, so I **was** exhausted.
She **didn't recognise** me because I**'d changed** so much.

mistakes.wrong: I was getting up, I was having breakfast and I was leaving.
mistakes.right: I got up, had breakfast and left.

mistakes.wrong: Everyone was knowing the answer.
mistakes.right: Everyone knew the answer.

points.title: Making stories lively: other tenses in narratives
points.summary: Good storytellers also use the present for drama (*So I walk in and…*), *would* for repeated actions, and *was about to / was going to* for plans that changed.

blocks.md: **The present for drama.** In jokes, anecdotes and spoken stories, many speakers use the present simple and continuous to make the story feel immediate: *So I**'m standing** at the bus stop, and this man **comes** up to me and **says**…* See [Present Simple vs Present Continuous](/blog/grammar/present-simple-vs-present-continuous/#psc-stories-commentary).
**Would for repeated actions.** In memories, *would* describes things that happened again and again: *Every morning, my grandfather **would make** tea and **would sit** by the window.*

**Plans that changed.** *was going to, was about to, was on the point of* describe what was planned or about to happen: *I **was about to** leave when the phone **rang**. We **were going to** fly, but we **took** the train in the end.*
Choose one time frame and keep it. If you start an anecdote in the present, stay in the present; don't switch to the past in the middle without a reason.

examples.text: So she **looks** at me and **says**, *Who are you?*
Every summer we **would spend** weeks at the lake.
I **was about to** give up when I **saw** the sign.
We **were going to** have a party, but it **was** cancelled.

mistakes.wrong: So I walk into the room and everybody looked at me.
mistakes.right: So I walk into the room and everybody looks at me.

mistakes.wrong: I was about leaving when she arrived.
mistakes.right: I was about to leave when she arrived.

items.prompt: ___ the summer, we visited my cousins in Rasht.
By the time we got to the restaurant, the kitchen ___.
items.explanation: *By the time* + past simple → past perfect.

items.prompt: We waited ___ the last guest had gone, then we started cleaning.
It was midnight. I ___ for hours and my eyes were tired.
