items.explanation: An activity up to that moment: *had been studying*.

items.prompt: I ran outside to see what ___.
When I opened my eyes, the nurse ___ (stand) next to my bed.
items.explanation: In progress at that moment: *was standing* (in written stories, *stood* is also possible).

topics.summary: Turning verbs and adjectives into nouns for a formal, academic style: decide → decision, prices rose → the rise in prices.
intro: **Nominalisation** means using a **noun** where we could use a verb or an adjective: *They **decided** quickly.* → *Their **decision** was quick.* It makes writing more **formal** and helps you pack more information into a sentence.

Nominalisation is common in academic essays, reports and the news. But too much of it makes a text heavy, so use it with care. For other formal features, see [Hedging and Distancing](/blog/grammar/hedging-distancing/).

points.title: Decide → decision, important → importance
points.summary: Many **verbs** and **adjectives** have a related **noun**. Common endings: ***-tion / -sion*** (*decision*), ***-ment*** (*development*), ***-al*** (*arrival*), ***-ure*** (*failure*), ***-ance / -ence*** (*importance*), ***-ity*** (*ability*), ***-ness*** (*awareness*).

blocks.md: Some nouns are **irregular** and must be learned: *grow → **growth**, high → **height**, long → **length**, strong → **strength**, die → **death**, succeed → **success**, choose → **choice***.

examples.text: The **reduction** in costs was welcome.
We noticed a big **improvement** in his work.
The **arrival** of the train was delayed.
Nobody understood the **importance** of the meeting.

mistakes.wrong: The decide was made yesterday.
mistakes.right: The decision was made yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: There was a big grow in sales.
mistakes.right: There was a big growth in sales.

points.title: Because prices rose → because of the rise in prices
points.summary: In formal writing, a **clause** (subject + verb) often becomes a **noun phrase**: *Because prices **rose** sharply…* → *Because of **the sharp rise in prices**…* *When he **arrived**…* → ***On his arrival**…*

rows: *Because of / Due to **the sharp rise in prices**, …*
*The government decided to close the school.*
***The government's decision to close the school** …*
*They introduced new rules. This caused problems.*
***The introduction of new rules** caused problems.*

blocks.md: When you change the verb into a noun, an **adverb** often becomes an **adjective** (*rose sharply → a sharp rise*), and the **subject** becomes a possessive or an *of*-phrase (*the government decided → the government's decision / the decision of the government*).

examples.text: **The closure of the factory** led to many job losses.
**Failure to follow** the rules will result in a fine.
**On completion of** the course, you'll receive a certificate.
**The rapid growth of** the city has caused traffic problems.

mistakes.wrong: Due to prices rose, sales fell.
mistakes.right: Due to the rise in prices, sales fell.

mistakes.wrong: The quickly growth of the city surprised everyone.
mistakes.right: The rapid growth of the city surprised everyone.

points.title: Make a decision, carry out research, reach an agreement
points.summary: Formal English often uses a **general verb + noun** instead of a single verb: *decide → **make a decision**, investigate → **carry out an investigation**, agree → **reach an agreement***. Learn the right **verb + noun** partners.

blocks.md: These partners (collocations) are **fixed**: *carry out research* (not *make research*), *take action* (not *do action*).

examples.text: The police **carried out an investigation**.
After hours of talks, they **reached an agreement**.
The government must **take action** now.
She **gave a clear explanation** of the problem.

mistakes.wrong: We made a research on social media.
mistakes.right: We carried out research on social media.

mistakes.wrong: The team did a decision quickly.
mistakes.right: The team made a decision quickly.

points.title: Dense noun phrases, and when to avoid them
points.summary: Academic writing uses **dense noun phrases** with pre-modifiers (*a three-year government study*) and *of*-phrases. But **too many** nouns make a text hard to read: *There was an increase in the level of unemployment* is weaker than *Unemployment rose*.

rows: *There was a significant increase in the level of unemployment.*
*The implementation of the plan was carried out by the team.*
*A decision was made to conduct a review.*

blocks.md: Good academic writers **balance** nouns and verbs: use nominalisation to **summarise** or **refer back** (*This increase…*), and verbs to describe **actions** clearly.
**Pre-modifiers** pack information before the noun: *a study that lasted three years → **a three-year study***; *changes to government policy → **government policy changes***.

examples.text: The **three-year research project** was funded by the EU.
Prices fell. **This fall** surprised analysts.
Unemployment **rose sharply**.
**Recent government policy changes** have helped small businesses.

mistakes.wrong: We did an analysis of the data and a comparison of the results. (heavy)
mistakes.right: We analysed the data and compared the results.

mistakes.wrong: A three-years study was carried out.
mistakes.right: A three-year study was carried out.

items.prompt: The ___ of the new hospital will take three years.
There has been a sharp ___ in the number of tourists.
The company's repeated ___ (fail) to pay its staff caused a strike.

topics.h1: Non-Defining Relative Clauses (My sister, who lives in Paris, …)
topics.summary: Clauses that add extra information, with commas: My brother, who is a doctor, lives in Vancouver.
intro: A **non-defining relative clause** adds **extra information** about a person or thing that is already clear: *My mother, **who is 70**, still works.* If you remove the clause, the sentence still makes sense.

These clauses always have **commas**, use *who* or *which* (never *that*), and you can't leave out the pronoun. For clauses that identify which person or thing, see [Defining Relative Clauses](/blog/grammar/defining-relative-clauses/).

points.title: Extra information: commas, who and which
points.summary: Use **commas** and **who / which** (not *that*). The pronoun can't be left out: *Tom, who I met at school, is a pilot.*

rows: *Tehran, **which** is the capital of Iran, is very big.*
*My boss, **who** is very kind, …* / *My car, **which** is ten years old, …*
you can't leave out the pronoun
*Tom, I met at school, …* ✗ → *Tom, **who** I met at school, …*

blocks.md: Non-defining clauses are common with **names**, **unique** things and nouns with *my / your / this*: *My father, who…* (I have only one father), *The Eiffel Tower, which…*
In speech, these clauses are less common; they're typical of writing.

examples.text: My sister, **who** lives in Rome, is visiting next week.
The Nile, **which** flows through eleven countries, is very long.
Mr Ahmadi, **who** I've known for years, is retiring.
Our new flat, **which** we bought last year, has a big balcony.

mistakes.wrong: My brother, that is a doctor, lives in Calgary.
mistakes.right: My brother, who is a doctor, lives in Calgary.

mistakes.wrong: Paris, I love, is beautiful.
mistakes.right: Paris, which I love, is beautiful.

mistakes.wrong: My mother who is 60 loves dancing.
mistakes.right: My mother, who is 60, loves dancing.

points.title: Defining or non-defining? The commas change the meaning
points.summary: Without commas = **which one** (*My brother who lives in Rome* = I have more than one brother). With commas = **extra information** (*My brother, who lives in Rome,* = I have one brother).

rows: *My sister **who lives in London** is a nurse.*
I have more than one sister; this is the one in London.
*My sister, **who lives in London**, is a nurse.*
I have one sister. By the way, she lives in London.

blocks.md: Ask yourself: Does the clause tell us **which** one? → defining, no commas. Is it just **extra** information? → non-defining, commas.

examples.text: The passengers **who had tickets** got on the train.
The passengers, **who had tickets**, got on the train.
My daughter **who is at university** is coming home.
examples.note: I have more than one daughter

examples.text: My daughter, **who is at university**, is coming home.

mistakes.wrong: My mother who is a teacher lives in Isfahan. (you have one mother)
mistakes.right: My mother, who is a teacher, lives in Isfahan.

points.title: Which for a whole idea: He was late, which annoyed me
points.summary: **which** can refer to the **whole previous clause**, not just a noun: *She passed all her exams, which was a big surprise.*

blocks.md: A non-defining clause with ***which*** can comment on everything said before: *The train was cancelled, **which** meant we had to take a taxi.* (*which* = the fact that the train was cancelled)
Only ***which*** works here. Not *that* or *what*: *He didn't call, **which** was strange* (not *what was strange*).

examples.text: It rained all week, **which** was disappointing.
He forgot my birthday, **which** really upset me.
The hotel was full, **which** meant we had to find another one.
She apologised, **which** was nice of her.

mistakes.wrong: He passed the exam, what surprised everyone.
mistakes.right: He passed the exam, which surprised everyone.

mistakes.wrong: The shop was closed, that was annoying.
mistakes.right: The shop was closed, which was annoying.

points.title: Whose, where and when in non-defining clauses
points.summary: **whose, where, when** also work in non-defining clauses: *My neighbour, whose dog barks all night, …* *Rome, where I studied, …* *In 2020, when we moved, …*

blocks.md: The rules are the same as for defining clauses, but with **commas**: *Our teacher, **whose** husband is a writer, gave us his book.*
***Where*** and ***when*** after a place or time that is already clear: *I went back to Shiraz, **where** I grew up.* *She was born in 1995, **when** her parents lived in Paris.*

examples.text: Mina, **whose** brother is a doctor, wants to study medicine.
We stayed in Kyoto, **where** we visited many temples.
I'll call you on Monday, **when** I'm back at work.
The company, **whose** CEO resigned last week, is in trouble.

mistakes.wrong: My friend, who's mother is a teacher, helped me.
mistakes.right: My friend, whose mother is a teacher, helped me.

mistakes.wrong: We went to Lisbon, which we stayed for a week.
mistakes.right: We went to Lisbon, where we stayed for a week.

points.title: Most of whom, some of which, all of whom
points.summary: After **quantifiers** (*some, many, most, all, none, both, neither, a few*) + **of**, use **whom** (people) or **which** (things): *I have two brothers, both of whom live abroad.*

blocks.md: This structure is common in formal writing to give information about part of a group: *The company employs 500 people, **most of whom** work part-time.*

Use ***whom*** for people and ***which*** for things after *of*. Not *of who* or *of them*: *…three cars, **all of which** are electric* (not *all of them are electric* in one sentence without *and*).
Also: ***the majority of whom, half of which, one of which, the best of which***.

examples.text: I invited twenty friends, **most of whom** came.
She wrote ten novels, **two of which** became films.
The tourists, **many of whom** were from Japan, loved the city.
We tried three restaurants, **none of which** was open.

mistakes.wrong: I have two sisters, both of who are married.
mistakes.right: I have two sisters, both of whom are married.

mistakes.wrong: He has three cars, all of them are red.
mistakes.right: He has three cars, all of which are red.

points.title: Formal patterns: in which, at which point, by which time
points.summary: In formal English, a preposition can come before **which / whom**: *the house, in which he was born*. Fixed phrases: **at which point, by which time, in which case**.

blocks.md: In formal writing, put the preposition **before** *which* or *whom*: *The hall, **in which** the concert was held, was full.* (Informal: *The hall, which the concert was held in, …*)
Useful fixed phrases that link to the previous idea:

items: ***at which point*** = at that moment: *He started shouting, **at which point** I left.*
***by which time*** = by that time: *We arrived at midnight, **by which time** everyone was asleep.*
***in which case*** = if that happens: *It may rain, **in which case** the match will be cancelled.*

examples.text: The report, **to which** I referred earlier, is online.
The music got louder, **at which point** the neighbours called the police.
The film ended at 11, **by which time** I was very tired.
You might miss the bus, **in which case** call me.

mistakes.wrong: The hotel, in that we stayed, was lovely.
mistakes.right: The hotel, in which we stayed, was lovely.

mistakes.wrong: She might be late, in what case we'll start without her.
mistakes.right: She might be late, in which case we'll start without her.

items.prompt: My grandfather, ___ is 90, still drives.
The Amazon, ___ is the largest rainforest in the world, is in danger.
Shakespeare, ___ wrote Hamlet, was born in 1564. (one word)
*My brother, who lives in Spain, is a chef.* How many brothers do I probably have?
*The players who were injured didn't play.* What does this mean?
options: Only the injured players didn't play.
items.explanation: Defining: it tells us which players.

items.prompt: My father, ___ is a pilot, travels a lot. (one word)
My flight was delayed by six hours, ___ meant I missed my meeting.
In *He sold his car, which surprised me*, what does *which* refer to?
options: the fact that he sold his car

items.prompt: She won the competition, ___ meant she could study abroad for free. (one word)
My uncle, ___ farm is in the north, grows rice.
We spent a week in Barcelona, ___ we saw the Sagrada Família.
In 1998, ___ I was six, my parents moved to Canada. (one word)

topics.summary: Using one noun to describe another: a bus stop, a tennis ball, a ten-minute walk, a five-star hotel.
intro: In English, a noun can work like an adjective in front of another noun: *a **bus** stop, a **coffee** cup, a **city** map*. The **second** noun is the main one: a *bus stop* is a kind of stop.
These are called **compound nouns** or **noun modifiers**. They're very common in everyday English, and even more common in news and formal writing.

points.title: Noun + noun: a bus stop, a shoe shop
points.summary: Put a noun **before** another noun to describe it: *a bus stop, a tennis ball, a shoe shop*. The first noun is usually **singular**, and the **second** noun is the main one.

blocks.md: The **first** noun works like an adjective, so it's usually **singular**: *a shoe shop* (not *a shoes shop*).
The **second** noun is the main noun and takes the plural: *two bus **stops**, three shoe **shops***.
Order matters: *a **flower garden*** is a garden; *a **garden flower*** is a flower.

examples.text: Let's meet at the **bus station**.
I need a new **tennis racket**.
There are three **car parks** near here.
What's your **email address**?

mistakes.wrong: I work in a toys shop.
mistakes.right: I work in a toy shop.

mistakes.wrong: Where's the stop bus?
mistakes.right: Where's the bus stop?

mistakes.wrong: We have two bus stop near our house.
mistakes.right: We have two bus stops near our house.

points.title: One word, two words or a hyphen?
points.summary: Compound nouns can be written as **one word** (*toothbrush, bedroom*), **two words** (*bus stop, credit card*) or with a **hyphen** (*mother-in-law, check-in*). There's no fixed rule, so check a dictionary.

rows: *bus stop, credit card, swimming pool, post office, phone call*

blocks.md: Very common compounds often become **one word** over time: *email, website, weekend*.
The stress is usually on the **first** part: ***BUS** stop, **BED**room, **SWIM**ming pool*.
***-ing* + noun** compounds often describe a **purpose**: *a **swimming** pool* (a pool for swimming), *a **washing** machine, a **parking** space*.

examples.text: I need a new **toothbrush**.
Can I pay by **credit card**?
My **mother-in-law** lives with us.
Is there a **parking space** near your house?

mistakes.wrong: I need a new machine washing.
mistakes.right: I need a new washing machine.

mistakes.wrong: Our hotel has a pool swimming.
mistakes.right: Our hotel has a swimming pool.

points.title: A ten-minute walk, a five-star hotel
points.summary: Use **number + noun** with a **hyphen** before a noun to describe time, age, size or value: *a ten-minute walk, a five-star hotel, a three-year-old girl*. The noun is **singular**: *a two-hour film* (not *two-hours*).

rows: *a ten-minute break, a two-hour meeting, a three-week course*
*a six-year-old boy* (but: *The boy is six years old.*)
*a ten-dollar bill, a 500-page book, a two-bedroom flat*

blocks.md: Before a noun, the measurement word is **singular** and joined with a **hyphen**: *a **five-minute** walk*. After the verb, it's **plural** with no hyphens: *The walk is **five minutes** long.*
Compare: *a **ten-minute** walk* = *ten **minutes'** walk* (possessive). Both are correct.

examples.text: It's **a ten-minute** walk to the station.
We stayed in **a five-star** hotel.
They have **a two-year-old** daughter.
She wrote **a 300-page** novel.

mistakes.wrong: It's a two-hours flight.
mistakes.right: It's a two-hour flight.

mistakes.wrong: My son is ten-years-old.
mistakes.right: My son is ten years old.

mistakes.wrong: a three-weeks holiday
mistakes.right: a three-week holiday

points.title: A coffee cup or a cup of coffee?
points.summary: **Noun + noun** describes the **type or purpose** (*a coffee cup* = a cup for coffee). ***Of*** describes the **contents** (*a cup of coffee*). ***'s*** is for things that **belong to** a person or are **made for** a group of people (*Ali's cup, a children's book*).

rows: *a **glass of wine**, a **box of shoes**, a **cup of tea***
belongs to a person; made for people

blocks.md: Compare: *a **matchbox*** (a box for matches, maybe empty) / *a **box of matches*** (a box with matches in it).
For things **made for** a group of people, use *'s*: *a **children's** hospital, a **men's** shirt, a **girls'** school*.

examples.text: Can you pass me a **wine glass**?
She drank **a glass of wine**.
I bought a **children's** book for my nephew.
The **car door** won't open.

mistakes.wrong: I'd like a coffee cup with milk, please. (to drink)
mistakes.right: I'd like a cup of coffee with milk, please.

mistakes.wrong: He reads a mens magazine.
mistakes.right: He reads a men's magazine.

points.title: Compound adjectives and long noun phrases
points.summary: **Compound adjectives** with hyphens are common before nouns: *a well-known writer, a long-term plan, a part-time job, a high-quality product*. News and formal English also use **long noun + noun phrases**: *a government housing policy*.

rows: *a **long-term** plan, a **part-time** job, a **last-minute** decision, a **high-quality** product*
*a **government education reform** plan* = a plan by the government to reform education

blocks.md: Use a **hyphen** when the compound comes **before** the noun: *a **well-known** writer*. After the verb, there's often no hyphen: *The writer is **well known**.*
Adverbs ending in *-ly* usually don't take a hyphen: *a **highly paid** job* (you'll also see *badly-paid* in British writing).
Long noun strings are compact but can be hard to read. Read them **from the end**: the last noun is the main one. In clear writing, you can unpack them: *a plan **for** reforming education*.

examples.text: She's a **well-known** journalist.
I'm looking for a **part-time** job.
Writing reports is very **time-consuming**.
The **city council parking** rules changed this year.

mistakes.wrong: It's a long term plan.
mistakes.right: It's a long-term plan.

mistakes.wrong: a high quality's product
mistakes.right: a high-quality product

items.prompt: It's a ___ drive from here to the airport.
items.explanation: Before a noun: singular with a hyphen.

items.prompt: Which is correct?
options: She has a five year's old son.

items.prompt: We booked a ___ (three / course) meal for the party.
I'm thirsty. Can I have ___?
We keep our old photos in a ___.
items.explanation: Purpose / type: *a shoebox* (it has photos in it, not shoes).

items.prompt: She works at a ___ (children) hospital. (one word)

topics.summary: Which preposition goes with a noun: the reason for, the cause of, a solution to, an increase in, on purpose, by mistake.
intro: Many nouns are followed by a **fixed preposition**: *the **reason for** the delay, the **cause of** the fire, a **solution to** the problem*. Learn the noun and its preposition **together**.

There are also fixed **preposition + noun** phrases: *on purpose, by mistake, in advance*. For prepositions after verbs and adjectives, see [Verbs and Prepositions](/blog/grammar/verbs-and-prepositions/) and [Adjectives and Prepositions](/blog/grammar/adjectives-and-prepositions/).

points.title: The reason for, a solution to, a problem with
points.summary: Common pairs: **reason for**, **cause of**, **solution / answer / key to**, **invitation to**, **increase / rise in**, **demand / need for**, **problem with**, **relationship with**, **difference between**, **interest in**, **damage to**, **effect on**.

rows: solution, answer, key, invitation, damage, reply

blocks.md: The noun often has a different preposition from its verb: *They **solved** the problem* (no preposition) / *a **solution to** the problem*.

examples.text: Nobody knows the **reason for** his decision.
Hard work is the **key to** success.
There's a big **demand for** nurses.
What's the **difference between** a crocodile and an alligator?

mistakes.wrong: What's the reason of the delay?
mistakes.right: What's the reason for the delay?

mistakes.wrong: Hard work is the key of success.
mistakes.right: Hard work is the key to success.

mistakes.wrong: I have a problem in my car.
mistakes.right: I have a problem with my car.

points.title: On purpose, by mistake, in advance, on holiday
points.summary: Fixed **preposition + noun** phrases: **on purpose**, **by mistake / accident / chance**, **in advance**, **in a hurry**, **on holiday / business**, **for sale**, **on sale**, **in danger**, **at risk**, **out of order**, **out of date**, **in charge of**.

rows: on purpose, on holiday, on business, on sale, on fire, on foot
by mistake, by accident, by chance, by car, by hand
in advance, in a hurry, in danger, in love, in charge of, in tears
at risk, at first, at least, at the moment
out of order, out of date, out of work, out of stock
for sale, for rent, for a change

blocks.md: ***For sale*** = someone wants to sell it. ***On sale*** = available in shops, or (especially in AmE) at a lower price.

examples.text: Sorry, I deleted your email **by mistake**.
We met **by chance** at the airport.
Please pay **in advance**.
The milk is **out of date**.

mistakes.wrong: She did it by purpose.
mistakes.right: She did it on purpose.

mistakes.wrong: I'm in holiday next week.
mistakes.right: I'm on holiday next week.

mistakes.wrong: He's on a hurry.
mistakes.right: He's in a hurry.

points.title: An increase in or of? Attitude to, advantage over
points.summary: ***Increase / rise / fall in*** + the thing that changes (*a rise **in** prices*), but ***of*** + the **amount** (*a rise **of** 5%*). Other pairs: **attitude to / towards**, **advantage of / over**, **respect for**, **connection between / with**, **in contrast to / with**.

rows: *the **advantages of** online learning; an **advantage over** other players*
*He has a lot of **respect for** his teachers.*
***In contrast to** last year, sales are up.*

blocks.md: You can use both in one phrase: *an **increase of** 10% **in** the price of fuel*.

examples.text: There's been a big **rise in** house prices.
Prices went up by 3%: a **rise of** 3%.
Speaking two languages gives you an **advantage over** other candidates.
Children learn **respect for** others at home.

mistakes.wrong: There was an increase of unemployment.
mistakes.right: There was an increase in unemployment.

mistakes.wrong: Salaries rose. There was a rise in 4%.
mistakes.right: Salaries rose. There was a rise of 4%.

points.title: Impact on, insight into, emphasis on: formal pairs
points.summary: Formal and academic pairs: **impact / emphasis / influence on**, **insight into**, **approach / contribution / commitment / access / threat / alternative / exposure to**, **implications for**, **preference for**; and phrases like **in the light of**, **with regard to**, **on behalf of**, **in terms of**.

rows: *The book gives an **insight into** village life.*
approach, contribution, commitment, access, threat, alternative, exposure

blocks.md: Useful formal phrases: ***in the light of*** (because of), ***with regard to*** (about), ***on behalf of*** (representing), ***in terms of*** (when we talk about), ***by means of*** (using).

examples.text: The internet has had a huge **impact on** education.
Her research gives new **insight into** the disease.
We need a fresh **approach to** the problem.
I'm writing **on behalf of** my company.

mistakes.wrong: The new law will have a big impact to small businesses.
mistakes.right: The new law will have a big impact on small businesses.

mistakes.wrong: Everyone should have access for clean water.
mistakes.right: Everyone should have access to clean water.

items.prompt: Last year there was a 10% fall ___ the number of car accidents.
The company reported an increase ___ 15% in profits.
Young people often have a different attitude ___ money. (one word)

topics.h1: Object Pronouns: Me, Him, Her, Us, Them
topics.summary: Using me, you, him, her, it, us and them after verbs and prepositions: Call me. I like her. Come with us.
intro: **Object pronouns** (*me, you, him, her, it, us, them*) come **after** a verb or a preposition: *Can you help **me**? I'm waiting for **them**.*
For *I, he, she, they*, see [Subject Pronouns and Possessive Adjectives](/blog/grammar/subject-pronouns-possessive-adjectives/).

points.title: Me, you, him, her, it, us, them after a verb
points.summary: Use an **object pronoun** after a verb: *I love **her**. She called **me**. We saw **them**.*

blocks.md: The subject does the action; the object receives it: ***She** helps **me**. **I** help **her**.*
*You* and *it* don't change.

examples.text: Can you help **me**?
I know **him**. He's my neighbour.
Where are my keys? I can't find **them**.
We love **you**!

mistakes.wrong: Can you help I?
mistakes.right: Can you help me?

mistakes.wrong: I like she.
mistakes.right: I like her.

mistakes.wrong: I bought a new phone, but I don't like.
mistakes.right: I bought a new phone, but I don't like it.
mistakes.why: the verb needs an object: it

points.title: Object pronouns after prepositions: with me, for them
points.summary: Use **object pronouns** after **prepositions**: *with me, for her, about him, to us, from them*.

blocks.md: Prepositions (*with, for, to, about, at, from, without, near, behind*) are followed by **object** pronouns: *Come **with us**! This is **for you**. Look **at me**.*
Some verbs need a preposition before the object: *listen **to** me, wait **for** him, look **at** them, talk **to** her*.

examples.text: This present is **for her**.
I often talk **to them** on the phone.
Can you come **with us**?
Don't worry **about me**.

mistakes.wrong: This is for she.
mistakes.right: This is for her.

mistakes.wrong: Come with we!
mistakes.right: Come with us!

mistakes.wrong: Listen me!
mistakes.right: Listen to me!

points.title: Me too, it's me, my friend and I
points.summary: In short answers and after ***be***, use **object pronouns** in everyday English: *Me too! Who's there? ~ It's me.* In a subject with **two people**, use the **subject** form, and put yourself **last**: *My friend and I went to the cinema.*

rows: *I do / I am* is also possible
*Me and my friend went out* is very informal

blocks.md: To check the pronoun, remove the other person: *My friend and **I** went out* → ***I** went out*. *She invited my friend and **me*** → *She invited **me***.
*Me and my friend went…* is common in casual speech, but it's considered incorrect in writing and exams.

examples.text: I love pizza. ~ **Me too**!
Who broke the window? ~ Not **me**!
**Ali and I** are best friends.
Our teacher gave **Ali and me** extra homework.

mistakes.wrong: Me and Sara are going to the cinema.
mistakes.right: Sara and I are going to the cinema.
mistakes.why: subject: I, and put yourself last

mistakes.wrong: She invited Ali and I.
mistakes.right: She invited Ali and me.

mistakes.wrong: I like this song. ~ I too.
mistakes.right: I like this song. ~ Me too.

points.title: Than me or than I am? Between you and me
points.summary: After ***than*** and ***as***, use an **object pronoun** in everyday English (*She's taller than me*) or **subject + verb** in careful English (*She's taller than I am*). After prepositions like ***between*** and ***except***, always use the **object** form: *between you and me*.

rows: *He's older **than me**. She's as tall **as him**.*
*He's older **than I am**. She's as tall **as he is**.*

blocks.md: *Than I* without a verb (*He's older than I*) is very formal and sounds old-fashioned. Use *than me* or *than I am*.
***Between you and me*** = this is a secret. *Between you and I* is a common mistake.

examples.text: My sister is younger **than me**.
My sister is younger **than I am**.
**Between you and me**, I don't like the new boss.
Everyone passed **except her**.

mistakes.wrong: Between you and I, he's leaving the company.
mistakes.right: Between you and me, he's leaving the company.

mistakes.wrong: She's taller than me am.
mistakes.right: She's taller than I am.

mistakes.wrong: Nobody except he knew the answer.
mistakes.right: Nobody except him knew the answer.

items.prompt: ___, I think the plan is a bad idea.
My brother is much taller than ___.
She speaks English better than I ___. (one word)

topics.summary: Shorter, more formal clauses with -ing, past participles and having + past participle: Feeling tired, she went to bed. Built in 1900, the house is beautiful.
intro: A **participle clause** is a short clause with an ***-ing*** form (*walking*), a **past participle** (*built*) or ***having*** + past participle (*having finished*), and **no subject or conjunction**: ***Feeling tired**, she went to bed.* (= Because she felt tired…)
Participle clauses are common in **writing** and make sentences shorter and smoother. The most important rule: the clause must have the **same subject** as the main clause.

points.title: -ing clauses: at the same time, or because
points.summary: An ***-ing*** clause can show an action **at the same time** (*Walking home, I met Ali*) or a **reason** (*Feeling ill, she stayed in bed*). The subject is the same as in the main clause.

rows: ***Walking** home, I met an old friend.*
***Feeling** tired, she went to bed early.*
*She sat by the window, **reading** a book.*
***Not knowing** what to do, I called my dad.*

blocks.md: For the **negative**, put ***not*** before the *-ing*: ***Not having** a car, we took the bus.*
The clause can go **before** or **after** the main clause. Use a **comma** to separate them.

examples.text: **Hearing** a noise, he went downstairs.
**Being** a doctor, she knew what to do.
He left the room, **slamming** the door.
**Not wanting** to wake the baby, we spoke quietly.

mistakes.wrong: Not knew what to say, I stayed quiet.
mistakes.right: Not knowing what to say, I stayed quiet.

mistakes.wrong: Knowing not the answer, she guessed.
mistakes.right: Not knowing the answer, she guessed.

points.title: Past participle clauses: built in 1900
points.summary: A **past participle** clause has a **passive** meaning: ***Built** in 1900, the house is now a museum.* (= The house was built in 1900.) ***Written** in simple English, the book is easy to read.*

rows: ***Built** in 1900, the bridge is still in use.*
***Shocked** by the news, she couldn't speak.*
***Made** in Italy, these shoes are expensive.*
These shoes are made in Italy…
***Asked** about the plan, he said nothing.*

blocks.md: Compare: ***Seeing** the dog, the boy ran.* (the boy saw: active) / ***Seen** from the air, the city looks small.* (the city is seen: passive)

examples.text: **Painted** by Leonardo da Vinci, the Mona Lisa is very famous.
**Surprised** by the question, she didn't answer.
**Located** in the centre, the hotel is perfect for tourists.
**Given** the chance, I'd travel the world.

mistakes.wrong: Building in 1850, the church is very old.
mistakes.right: Built in 1850, the church is very old.

mistakes.wrong: Writing by a famous author, the book sold well.
mistakes.right: Written by a famous author, the book sold well.

points.title: The man sitting there, the car parked outside
points.summary: Participle clauses can replace **relative clauses**: *the man **sitting** there* (= who is sitting), *the car **parked** outside* (= which is parked), *people **living** in cities* (= who live).

rows: *The woman **who is talking** to Ali is my boss.*
*The woman **talking** to Ali is my boss.*
*The car **which was stolen** last week was found.*
*Goods **which are made** in China are cheap.*

blocks.md: Use ***-ing*** for an **active** meaning and the **past participle** for a **passive** meaning.
Don't use an *-ing* clause for a single finished action in the past: *The man **who broke** the window ran away* (not *The man breaking the window ran away*).

examples.text: Who's the girl **wearing** the red dress?
The houses **built** last year are already sold.
Anyone **needing** help should call this number.
The money **found** in the street was given to the police.

mistakes.wrong: The people waited for the bus were cold.
mistakes.right: The people waiting for the bus were cold.

mistakes.wrong: The book writing by her grandfather is in the library.
mistakes.right: The book written by her grandfather is in the library.

points.title: Having finished, having been told
points.summary: ***Having*** + **past participle** shows that one action happened **before** another: ***Having finished** my work, I went home.* Passive: ***Having been told** the news, she called her mother.*

rows: ***Having finished** lunch, we went for a walk.*
***Not having seen** the film, I can't comment.*
***Having been warned** about the storm, they stayed home.*

blocks.md: Use ***having*** + past participle when the first action is **finished** before the second, or to show a **reason** based on an earlier action.
With **conjunctions**: ***After finishing** / **After having finished** work, I went to the gym.*

examples.text: **Having lived** in Japan, she speaks Japanese well.
**Having been** invited, we had to go.
**Not having** studied, he failed the test.
**Having saved** enough money, they bought a house.

mistakes.wrong: Having finish the report, she sent it.
mistakes.right: Having finished the report, she sent it.

mistakes.wrong: Having been invite to the wedding, we bought a gift.
mistakes.right: Having been invited to the wedding, we bought a gift.

points.title: Dangling participles, and after / while / when + -ing
points.summary: The participle clause must have the **same subject** as the main clause. ***Walking** down the street, **the rain** started* is wrong (the rain wasn't walking). You can keep a conjunction: ***After leaving**, **while waiting**, **when using**, **once finished***.

rows: *Walking home, **I** got caught in the rain.* / *While I was walking home, the rain started.*
***While** I was driving to work, an accident happened.*

blocks.md: Conjunction + participle is common and clear: ***After finishing** the course, you'll get a certificate. **When using** this app, keep your phone charged. **Once opened**, keep in the fridge.*

examples.text: **While waiting** for the bus, I read a book.
**Before signing** the contract, read it carefully.
**Once opened**, the bottle should be kept cold.
**If stored** correctly, the medicine lasts for years.

mistakes.wrong: Arriving at the station, the train had left.
mistakes.right: Arriving at the station, we found that the train had left.

mistakes.wrong: Having eaten lunch, the bill was paid.
mistakes.right: Having eaten lunch, we paid the bill.

points.title: With prices rising, the work done, weather permitting
points.summary: **Absolute** clauses have their **own subject**: ***The work done**, we went home.* ***With*** + noun + participle: ***With prices rising**, people spend less.* Fixed expressions: ***weather permitting***, ***all things considered***, ***generally speaking***.

rows: ***The meeting over**, everyone left.* / ***The work done**, we relaxed.*
***weather permitting**, **all things considered**, **generally speaking**, **strictly speaking**, **judging by**, **considering**…*

blocks.md: Absolute clauses are formal or literary. ***With*** + noun + participle is common in both speech and writing.
Fixed expressions like ***judging by / from***, ***considering***, ***generally speaking*** are accepted even when the subjects are different: ***Judging by** his face, he's angry.*

examples.text: **The sun having set**, we lit a fire.
**With** the kids **asleep**, the house was quiet.
We'll have the party outside, **weather permitting**.
**All things considered**, it was a successful year.

mistakes.wrong: With prices rise, people are spending less.
mistakes.right: With prices rising, people are spending less.

mistakes.wrong: Weather permits, we'll eat outside.
mistakes.right: Weather permitting, we'll eat outside.

items.prompt: ___ late for work, she ran to the bus stop.
items.explanation: Reason: *Being late* = because she was late.

items.prompt: ___ what to say, he just smiled.
___ (look) out of the window, I saw a strange light in the sky.
___ in 1889, the Eiffel Tower is the symbol of Paris.
___ from the top of the mountain, the village looks tiny.
___ (make) from recycled plastic, these bags are good for the environment.
The man ___ next to the window is my uncle.
Most of the cars ___ in this factory are exported.
The children ___ (play) in the park are from the local school.

topics.h1: Passive Reporting Structures (It is said that…, He is believed to…)
topics.summary: Reporting what people say or believe without saying who: It is said that… The suspect is believed to be in Spain.
intro: In news, reports and academic writing, we often report what **people in general** say, think or believe, without saying who. We use passive structures: ***It is said that** the house is haunted.* / *The house **is said to be** haunted.*
These structures sound objective and formal. For the passive in general, see [Passive Voice](/blog/grammar/passive-voice/).

points.title: It is said that…, It is believed that…
points.summary: **It + passive reporting verb + that** + clause: *It is said that he is very rich. It was reported that the minister had resigned.*

rows: ***It is said that** he is rich.*
*Experts believe that the drug is safe.*
***It is believed that** the drug is safe.*
*They reported that the fire was under control.*
***It was reported that** the fire was under control.*

blocks.md: Common verbs: *say, believe, think, report, know, expect, claim, estimate, consider, understand, allege*.
The tense of *be* changes with the time of the reporting: *It **is** thought… / It **was** thought… / It **has been** reported…*

examples.text: **It is said that** the castle is 800 years old.
**It is estimated that** 2 million people visited the festival.
**It was reported that** two people were injured.
**It is expected that** prices will rise.

mistakes.wrong: It says that he is rich. (meaning people say)
mistakes.right: It is said that he is rich.

mistakes.wrong: It is believed the drug safe.
mistakes.right: It is believed that the drug is safe.

points.title: He is said to be…, She is believed to live…
points.summary: **subject + passive reporting verb + to-infinitive**: *He is said to be very rich. The suspect is believed to live in Spain.*

rows: ***It is said that** he is rich.*
***It is believed that** she lives abroad.*
***It is expected that** the strike will end soon.*

blocks.md: This pattern starts with the **person or thing** we're talking about, so it's very common in news: *The president **is expected to arrive** tomorrow.*
Use ***to*** + base verb when the reported situation is at the **same time** as the reporting (or later): *He **is thought to be** in London.*

examples.text: The singer **is said to be** very shy.
Two climbers **are reported to be** missing.
The new phone **is expected to cost** $1,000.
Mozart **is considered to be** a genius.

mistakes.wrong: He is said being very rich.
mistakes.right: He is said to be very rich.

mistakes.wrong: She is believed that she lives abroad.
mistakes.right: She is believed to live abroad. / It is believed that she lives abroad.

points.title: Is thought to have done, is believed to be doing
points.summary: Use **to have + past participle** for an earlier action (*He is believed to have left the country*) and **to be + -ing** for an action in progress (*She is thought to be working on a new book*).

rows: *She **is said to be writing** a new novel.*
*He **is believed to have left** the country.*
*They **are thought to have been living** in Paris.*
*The painting **is thought to have been stolen** in 1990.*

blocks.md: The infinitive shows the time of the reported action compared with the time of reporting: *He **is said to have been** a great dancer when he was young.*

examples.text: The robbers **are believed to have escaped** in a blue car.
The actor **is reported to be recovering** in hospital.
The temple **is thought to have been built** 2,000 years ago.
She **is said to have been working** on it for years.

mistakes.wrong: He is believed to left the country.
mistakes.right: He is believed to have left the country.

mistakes.wrong: The man is thought to have stole the car.
mistakes.right: The man is thought to have stolen the car.

points.title: There is said to be…, There are thought to be…
points.summary: With *there*, use **there + is / are + reporting verb + to be**: *There are said to be ghosts in the house.*

blocks.md: When the reported sentence starts with *there is / there are*, use ***there + passive reporting verb + to be***: *People say that there is a secret tunnel.* → ***There is said to be** a secret tunnel.*
For the past: ***there + is / are + verb + to have been***: ***There are thought to have been** over 1,000 people at the meeting.*
The verb agrees with the noun after it: ***There is** said to be **a** problem. / **There are** said to be **some** problems.*

examples.text: **There are said to be** wolves in these forests.
**There is thought to be** a link between diet and sleep.
**There are believed to have been** survivors.
**There is reported to be** a delay on the line.

mistakes.wrong: There is said to be many problems.
mistakes.right: There are said to be many problems.

mistakes.wrong: It is said to be a tunnel under the castle.
mistakes.right: There is said to be a tunnel under the castle.

points.title: Be supposed to, allegedly, reportedly
points.summary: **be supposed to** = people say (*This café is supposed to be great*). In news: **allegedly, reportedly, apparently** and **according to** report information without claiming it's true.

blocks.md: ***Be supposed to*** + infinitive is an informal way to say *it is said*: *The new restaurant **is supposed to be** very good.* (people say so)
Adverbs like ***reportedly, allegedly, apparently, supposedly*** give a similar meaning in one word: *The minister **allegedly** accepted money.* (Someone says so; it isn't proven.)
***According to*** + source names who said it: ***According to** the police, the man was armed.*
*Allegedly* is used for accusations of crimes or wrongdoing that haven't been proven. *Reportedly* simply means *according to reports*.

examples.text: This beach **is supposed to be** the most beautiful in Greece.
The actor is **reportedly** planning to retire.
He **allegedly** stole $2 million.
**According to** the forecast, it'll snow tomorrow.

mistakes.wrong: According to me, the film is great.
mistakes.right: In my opinion, the film is great.
mistakes.why: according to + another source, not me

mistakes.wrong: This museum is suppose to be interesting.
mistakes.right: This museum is supposed to be interesting.

items.prompt: ___ that the new law will reduce crime.
It ___ that the company lost $10 million last year.
It ___ (believe) that the painting is a fake.
The thief is believed ___ in the city centre.
This hotel ___ to be the best in town.
The new bridge is expected ___ (open) in May.

topics.h1: Passive Voice (It was made in China)
topics.summary: When the action matters more than who does it: English is spoken here. The bridge was built in 1932.
intro: In a **passive** sentence, the person or thing that the action happens **to** becomes the subject: *The bridge **was built** in 1932.* We don't need to say who built it.
The passive is made with **be** + **past participle**, in any tense: *is made, was made, has been made, will be made*. Compare the active: *Engineers **built** the bridge in 1932.*

points.title: Present simple passive: is made, are sold
points.summary: **am / is / are + past participle**: *Cheese **is made** from milk. These phones **are made** in Korea.*

blocks.md: Use *is* with a singular subject and *are* with a plural subject. Then add the **past participle** (*made, spoken, cleaned*).
Negative and questions work like *be*: *Breakfast **isn't included**. **Is** breakfast **included**?*

examples.text: Rice **is grown** in many Asian countries.
The museum **is visited** by thousands of people every year.
These shoes **are made** of leather.
**Is** this seat **taken**?

mistakes.wrong: English is speak in Australia.
mistakes.right: English is spoken in Australia.

mistakes.wrong: The rooms is cleaned every day.
mistakes.right: The rooms are cleaned every day.

mistakes.wrong: Coffee grown in Brazil.
mistakes.right: Coffee is grown in Brazil.

points.title: Past simple passive: was built, were invited
points.summary: **was / were + past participle**: *The castle **was built** in 1450. We **were invited** to the wedding.* Add **by** to say who did it.

blocks.md: Use ***was*** with *I / he / she / it* and ***were*** with *you / we / they*: *The car **was repaired**. The cars **were repaired**.*
Add ***by*** + the person or thing only when it's important to say who did it: *The telephone **was invented by** Bell.*

examples.text: My phone **was stolen** on the bus.
The Mona Lisa **was painted by** Leonardo da Vinci.
The match **was cancelled** because of the rain.
**Were** you **born** in Tehran?

mistakes.wrong: The bridge was build in 1990.
mistakes.right: The bridge was built in 1990.

mistakes.wrong: The letters was sent yesterday.
mistakes.right: The letters were sent yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: This book was written from Hafez.
mistakes.right: This book was written by Hafez.

points.title: When do we use the passive? And when do we need by?
points.summary: Use the passive when **who does it** is unknown, obvious or unimportant, or when we want to focus on the **action or result**. Use **by** only when the agent adds useful information.

blocks.md: We use the passive when:

items: we **don't know** who did it: *My wallet **has been stolen**.*
it's **obvious** or **unimportant**: *The rubbish **is collected** on Mondays.* (by the council, obviously)
we want to **focus** on the thing, not the person: *This song **was written** in 1965.*
in **formal, scientific or news** writing: *The samples **were heated** to 100°C.*

blocks.md: Leave out *by* + agent when it says nothing new: *The thief **was arrested*** (not *by the police*, which is obvious). Keep it when it's important: *The film **was directed by** a 19-year-old.*
Don't overuse the passive. In everyday speech, the active is usually more natural: *Someone stole my bike* or *My bike was stolen* are both fine; *My bike was stolen by someone* is not natural.

examples.text: Our flat **was broken into** last week.
The new hospital **will be opened** by the Prime Minister.
Mistakes **were made**.
examples.note: focus on the action, not the person

examples.text: The water **is then filtered** and **bottled**.

mistakes.wrong: My bag was stolen by someone.
mistakes.right: My bag was stolen.

mistakes.wrong: The criminal was arrested by the police yesterday. (the police is obvious)
mistakes.right: The criminal was arrested yesterday.

points.title: Continuous and perfect passives: is being done, has been done
points.summary: Continuous: **is / was being + past participle**. Perfect: **has / had been + past participle**: *The road is being repaired. My bike has been stolen.*

rows: *The house **had been sold** before we saw it.*

blocks.md: Choose the tense as you would for an active sentence, then make it passive with a form of ***be*** + past participle.
Don't confuse ***being*** (continuous) and ***been*** (perfect): *is **being** built* (now) / *has **been** built* (finished).

examples.text: A new school **is being built** near our house.
I felt I **was being watched**.
Your order **has been sent**.
When we arrived, the food **had been eaten**.

mistakes.wrong: The house is been painted.
mistakes.right: The house is being painted.

mistakes.wrong: The parcel has being delivered.
mistakes.right: The parcel has been delivered.

points.title: Future and modal passives: will be done, can be done, must be done
points.summary: After **will, can, must, should, might**, use **be + past participle**: *The results will be announced tomorrow. This can't be done.*

blocks.md: The pattern is always ***modal + be + past participle***: *will be built, can be seen, must be paid, might be cancelled*.
*Be going to* works the same way: *The match **is going to be shown** on TV.*
For the past, use ***modal + have been + past participle***: *It **should have been fixed** last week.* *The letter **might have been lost**.*

examples.text: The winners **will be announced** on Friday.
This medicine **must be kept** in the fridge.
The meeting **might be postponed**.
The work **should have been finished** yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: The money must pay by Friday.
mistakes.right: The money must be paid by Friday.

mistakes.wrong: It can be did easily.
mistakes.right: It can be done easily.

points.title: Passive infinitives and -ing forms: to be done, being done
points.summary: After verbs that take **to**, use **to be + past participle**: *I want to be told.* After verbs that take **-ing**, use **being + past participle**: *I hate being interrupted.*

rows: *She expects **to be promoted**. The car needs **to be washed**.*
*I don't like **being told** what to do. He's afraid of **being laughed at**.*

blocks.md: Choose *to be done* or *being done* according to the verb pattern: *want / hope / expect / need **to be** + pp*; *enjoy / hate / avoid / remember / after / without **being** + pp*.
***Need + -ing*** has the same meaning as *need to be done* (mainly British): *The windows **need cleaning**.* = *need **to be cleaned**.*

examples.text: Everyone wants **to be loved**.
I can't stand **being kept** waiting.
She left the room without **being seen**.
The project is expected **to be finished** by June.

mistakes.wrong: I don't like to being told what to do.
mistakes.right: I don't like being told what to do.
mistakes.why: like + being + pp (or to be told)

mistakes.wrong: This shirt needs to iron.
mistakes.right: This shirt needs to be ironed. / This shirt needs ironing.

points.title: Get passive: get married, get paid, get hurt
points.summary: In informal English, **get + past participle** can replace *be* in the passive, often for changes, accidents or things we don't control: *He got injured. We get paid on Fridays.*

blocks.md: ***Get*** + past participle is common in **informal** speech: *My bike **got stolen**. She **got promoted** last month.*
It's especially used for events that **happen** to someone (often unexpected or bad), and for changes: *get hurt, get lost, get caught, get fired, get married, get dressed*.
In questions and negatives, use *do / did* like a normal verb: ***Did** you **get invited**? I **didn't get paid**.*
*Get married, get dressed, get lost* are fixed and very common. In formal writing, use *be*: *The employee **was dismissed*** (not *got fired*).

examples.text: I **got stuck** in traffic.
My brother **got fired** last week.
We **get paid** at the end of the month.
They **got married** in 2019.

mistakes.wrong: He was got hurt.
mistakes.right: He got hurt.

mistakes.wrong: Did you got invited?
mistakes.right: Did you get invited?

points.title: Passives with two objects: I was given…, She was offered…
points.summary: With verbs like **give, offer, send, show, tell, teach**, the person usually becomes the subject: *I was given a present.* (more natural than *A present was given to me*)

blocks.md: Some verbs have two objects: a **person** and a **thing**: *They gave **me** **a present**.* There are two possible passives:

items: ***I was given** a present.* (person as subject: more common)
*A present **was given to me**.* (thing as subject)

blocks.md: Common verbs: *give, offer, send, show, tell, teach, promise, pay, lend, award, ask*.
Some verbs can't take the person as subject: *explain, describe, suggest, say*: *The problem **was explained to** me.* Not *I was explained the problem*.

examples.text: She **was offered** a job in London.
We **were shown** the new office.
The prize **was awarded to** a young scientist.
The rules **were explained to** us.

mistakes.wrong: I was explained the instructions.
mistakes.right: The instructions were explained to me.
mistakes.why: explain can't have the person as subject

mistakes.wrong: She was given a present to.
mistakes.right: She was given a present.

points.title: Complex passives: elected president, looked after, it was decided
points.summary: Passives with complements (*He was elected president*), prepositional verbs (*She was looked after*), and verbs that can't be passive (*happen, arrive, have*).

blocks.md: **Verb + object + complement**: the complement stays after the verb: *They elected her leader.* → *She **was elected** leader.* Also: *was considered (a genius), was named (after), was made (captain)*.

**Prepositional and phrasal verbs** keep the preposition: *They looked after the baby well.* → *The baby **was** well **looked after**.* *Nobody has dealt with the complaint.* → *The complaint **hasn't been dealt with**.*

**Intransitive verbs** (no object) can't be passive: *The accident **happened** at night* (not *was happened*). Also *arrive, die, exist, seem*. Some state verbs aren't used in the passive: *She **has** a car* (not *A car is had by her*).

*It + passive + that* is common for decisions and agreements: ***It was decided that** the meeting would be cancelled.* For *It is said that…*, see [Passive Reporting Structures](/blog/grammar/passive-reporting-structures/).

examples.text: He **was named** after his grandfather.
Our concerns **were** completely **ignored**.
The issue **is** still **being looked into**.
**It was agreed that** prices would rise.

mistakes.wrong: The accident was happened on Monday.
mistakes.right: The accident happened on Monday.

mistakes.wrong: The children were looked well.
mistakes.right: The children were well looked after.

items.prompt: I hate ___ when I'm watching a film.
The children are hoping ___ to the zoo this weekend.
He escaped from the prison without ___ (see).
Be careful on that ladder. You might ___ hurt.
Which sentence is the most informal?
options: My phone was stolen at the concert.
The theft of my phone occurred at the concert.
My phone got stolen at the concert.
Someone committed theft of my phone.

items.prompt: Did you ___ (get / invite) to Sara's party?
After the interview, Ali ___ the job.
Which sentence is NOT correct?
options: The problem was explained to me.
I was told about the problem.
items.explanation: *Explain* can't have the person as the subject.

items.prompt: Yesterday the students ___ (give) extra time to finish the test.

topics.summary: An action in progress at a moment in the past: At 9 last night I was reading.
intro: We use the **past continuous** (*was / were* + *-ing*) for an action that was **in progress** at a particular time in the past: *At nine o'clock last night I **was reading**.*
It often appears with the past simple: *I **was reading** when the phone **rang**.* That contrast has its own page: [Past Simple vs Past Continuous](/blog/grammar/past-simple-vs-past-continuous/).

points.title: Form and use: in the middle of an action
points.summary: **was / were + -ing**: the action was in progress at a past moment. *At 8 I was having dinner.*

blocks.md: The past continuous shows that an action **had started and hadn't finished** at a time in the past. We were in the middle of it.
Typical time phrases: *at 6 o'clock yesterday, at this time last week, all morning, when you called*.

The *-ing* spelling rules are the same as for the present continuous: *make → making, sit → sitting, lie → lying*. Stative verbs (*know, want, like*) are not usually used in the continuous: *I **knew** the answer* (not *was knowing*). See [Stative Verbs](/blog/grammar/stative-verbs/).

examples.text: At 7 o'clock this morning I **was running** in the park.
The children **were playing** in the garden all afternoon.
Sorry I missed your call. I **was driving**.
What **were** you **doing** at midnight?

mistakes.wrong: At 9 pm I was watch TV.
mistakes.right: At 9 pm I was watching TV.

mistakes.wrong: They was waiting outside.
mistakes.right: They were waiting outside.

mistakes.wrong: I was knowing the answer.
mistakes.right: I knew the answer.

points.title: Negatives and questions
points.summary: Negative: **wasn't / weren't + -ing**. Question: **Was / Were + subject + -ing?**

rows: Yes, … was / were. No, … wasn't / weren't.

blocks.md: Don't use *did* in past continuous questions: ***Were** you **working**?* Not *Did you working?*

examples.text: I **wasn't feeling** well, so I stayed at home.
**Was** it **raining** when you left? ~ Yes, it **was**.
Who **were** you **talking** to?
We **weren't expecting** so many people.

mistakes.wrong: Did you sleeping?
mistakes.right: Were you sleeping?
mistakes.why: No did in the past continuous.

mistakes.wrong: What you were doing?
mistakes.right: What were you doing?

mistakes.wrong: I didn't listening.
mistakes.right: I wasn't listening.

points.title: Two actions in progress at the same time: while
points.summary: Two longer actions happening at the same time: *While I **was cooking**, he **was watching** TV.*

blocks.md: When two longer actions were in progress at the same time, we can use the past continuous for both, often with ***while***: *While I **was cooking**, my husband **was setting** the table.*
*While* can go at the start or in the middle: *She was reading **while** the baby was sleeping.* Use a comma when the *while* clause comes first.

Use ***while*** (or *as*) with longer actions. For a short action that interrupts a longer one, use *when* + past simple: *I was cooking **when** the lights **went** out.* See [Past Simple vs Past Continuous](/blog/grammar/past-simple-vs-past-continuous/).

examples.text: **While** we **were having** dinner, it **was raining** outside.
Some students **were writing** notes, and others **were looking** at their phones.
I **was working** **while** my flatmate **was sleeping**.

mistakes.wrong: While I was cooking, he watching TV.
mistakes.right: While I was cooking, he was watching TV.

mistakes.wrong: During I was studying, she was working.
mistakes.right: While I was studying, she was working.

points.title: Setting the scene in a story
points.summary: Use the past continuous for the **background** of a story; use the past simple for the **events**.

blocks.md: At the start of a story, the past continuous describes the situation: what was happening around the main events. *It **was raining**. People **were hurrying** home. A man **was standing** at the corner.*
Then the past simple tells the events: *Suddenly he **turned** and **walked** towards me.*
This contrast is the heart of storytelling in English. For the complete set of story tenses, see [Narrative Tenses](/blog/grammar/narrative-tenses/).

examples.text: The sun **was shining** and the birds **were singing**.
We **were sitting** in the café when a strange man **came** in.
Everyone **was laughing** and **having** a good time.

mistakes.wrong: When I arrived, everyone danced and sang.
mistakes.right: When I arrived, everyone was dancing and singing.
mistakes.why: To describe the scene when you arrived: past continuous.

mistakes.wrong: The music was playing, and suddenly the lights were going out.
mistakes.right: The music was playing, and suddenly the lights went out.

points.title: Was always doing: annoying past habits
points.summary: **always / constantly + past continuous** for repeated past behaviour, often annoying: *He **was always losing** his keys.*

blocks.md: Just like the present continuous with *always* (*You're always complaining!*), the past continuous with ***always, constantly, forever*** describes behaviour that happened again and again, usually with a feeling of annoyance or surprise.
*My old flatmate **was always borrowing** my things without asking.* = He did it very often, and it annoyed me.

Compare: *He **always borrowed** my things* is a neutral fact. *He **was always borrowing** my things* adds feeling: it happened too often. For the present version, see [Present Continuous](/blog/grammar/present-continuous/#pc-always).

examples.text: My brother **was always taking** my phone.
She **was constantly checking** her messages during the meeting.
Our old car **was forever breaking** down.

mistakes.wrong: He always was complaining.
mistakes.right: He was always complaining.

mistakes.wrong: She was always borrow my pen.
mistakes.right: She was always borrowing my pen.

points.title: Temporary periods, repeated actions and duration
points.summary: The past continuous can show a temporary routine (*That summer I was working nights*) or stress duration (*I was cleaning all morning*).

blocks.md: **Temporary situations and routines.** We use the past continuous for something that was true for a limited period: *That year I **was cycling** to work every day. She **was living** with her parents while her flat was being repaired.*
**Duration.** With *all day, all morning, all week*, the past continuous stresses that the activity filled the time, often to explain a result: *I **was gardening** all afternoon, so I'm exhausted.*
**Not for a counted series.** When we say **how many times**, we use the past simple: *I **phoned** her five times.* Not *I was phoning her five times*.
The past simple is also possible in many of these sentences (*That year I cycled to work*). The past continuous adds the idea that the situation was temporary or in progress.

examples.text: When I was at university, I **was working** in a café at weekends.
It **was snowing** all day, so the roads were closed.
In those days we **were seeing** each other every weekend.
I **called** you three times last night!

mistakes.wrong: I was calling you three times.
mistakes.right: I called you three times.

mistakes.wrong: I was knowing her for years.
mistakes.right: I had known her for years.
mistakes.why: know is stative; up to a past time: past perfect.

points.title: I was wondering if…: polite requests and past plans
points.summary: *I **was wondering** if you could help* is a polite request about now. *She **was leaving** the next day* is a plan seen from the past.

blocks.md: **Politeness.** With verbs like *wonder, hope, think (of)*, the past continuous makes a request or suggestion softer and less direct. The meaning is **now**: *I **was wondering** if you could help me. We **were hoping** you might join us. I **was thinking** we could go to the coast.*

**Plans in the past.** The past continuous can describe an arrangement that was in the future at that time: *I couldn't stay late because I **was flying** to Paris the next morning.* See [Future in the Past](/blog/grammar/future-in-the-past/).
The degree of politeness, from direct to soft: *I wonder if…* → *I wondered if…* → *I **was wondering** if…* (softest).

examples.text: I **was wondering** if I could leave early today.
We **were hoping** you could come to dinner on Saturday.
She was nervous because she **was starting** a new job the next day.
**I was thinking** we could try that new restaurant.

mistakes.wrong: I was wondering if you can help me.
mistakes.right: I was wondering if you could help me.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows the speaker was annoyed?
options: My boss always changed his mind on Fridays.
My boss was always changing his mind.
My boss had changed his mind.

items.prompt: Our neighbour's dog was ___ (always / bark) at night. We couldn't sleep.
Which part is wrong?
items.correction: My old teacher was always forgetting our names.

topics.summary: An activity that continued up to a moment in the past: I'd been waiting for an hour when the bus came.
intro: We use the **past perfect continuous** (*had been* + *-ing*) for an activity that was going on **before** a moment in the past, often **up to** that moment: *When the bus finally came, I **had been waiting** for an hour.*
It is the past version of the present perfect continuous: *I**'ve been waiting** for an hour* (up to now) → *I**'d been waiting** for an hour* (up to then).

points.title: Form and use: up to a moment in the past
points.summary: **had been + -ing** for an activity that continued up to (or until shortly before) a past moment, often with *for*, *since* or *how long*.

rows: *She **had been working** there for ten years.*
*She**'d been working** there for ten years.*

blocks.md: The activity started before a past moment and continued up to that moment (or stopped just before it). We often say **how long** it continued:
*When I met Sam, he **had been living** in Toronto **for** five years.* (He started living there five years earlier and was still living there.)
Compare the present: *I**'ve been living** here for five years* (until now) and the past: *I**'d been living** there for five years* (until then).
*'d* can be *had* or *would*. After *'d* + *been* + *-ing* it is always *had*: *He'd been running.*

examples.text: We **had been driving** for six hours when we finally stopped.
examples.note: duration up to a past moment

examples.text: How long **had** you **been studying** English before you moved to Canada?
I **hadn't been feeling** well, so I went to the doctor.
It **had been raining** all night, and the roads were flooded.

mistakes.wrong: When I arrived, she was waiting for two hours.
mistakes.right: When I arrived, she had been waiting for two hours.
mistakes.why: Duration up to a past moment: had been + -ing.

mistakes.wrong: He had been work there for years.
mistakes.right: He had been working there for years.

mistakes.wrong: How long you had been waiting?
mistakes.right: How long had you been waiting?

points.title: Explaining what we saw: She'd been crying
points.summary: Use the past perfect continuous to explain a past situation by an activity that happened just before it: *His eyes were red. He'd been crying.*

blocks.md: When we describe a situation in the past, the past perfect continuous explains **the activity that caused it**. The activity has usually just stopped:

items: *The ground was wet. It **had been raining**.*
*She was out of breath because she **had been running**.*
*His hands were black. He**'d been repairing** the car.*

blocks.md: This is the past version of: *The ground is wet. It**'s been raining.***
The focus is on the **activity** (and what we could see), not on a finished result. For a finished result, use the past perfect simple: *The kitchen was clean. Someone **had cleaned** it.*

examples.text: The kitchen smelled wonderful. Mum **had been baking**.
When I came in, the kids looked guilty. They**'d been fighting**.
My legs hurt because I**'d been walking** all day.

mistakes.wrong: Her eyes were red because she has been crying.
mistakes.right: Her eyes were red because she had been crying.

mistakes.wrong: The ground was wet. It had rained been.
mistakes.right: The ground was wet. It had been raining.

points.title: Had been doing or had done?
points.summary: **had been doing** = the activity and how long. **had done** = a completed action, a result, or how many. State verbs use **had done**.

rows: *She **had been painting** the room.* (maybe not finished)
*I**'d been writing** emails all morning.* (how long)
*They**'d argued** and stopped speaking.* (a completed event)

blocks.md: With **how long** + an activity, the continuous is usual. With **how many / how much**, use the simple.

**State verbs** (*know, have* for possession, *be, like, believe, own*) are not normally used in the continuous: *I**'d known** her for years.* Not *I'd been knowing her*. See [Stative Verbs](/blog/grammar/stative-verbs/).
With *live* and *work*, both forms are often possible with *for* / *since*: *She **had lived / had been living** there for ten years.* The continuous suggests the situation was more temporary.

examples.text: I**'d been cleaning** for two hours, but the house still looked messy.
I**'d cleaned** the whole house, so I relaxed.
He**'d been taking** photos all day.
He**'d taken** over 500 photos.
We**'d known** each other since school.

mistakes.wrong: I'd been knowing him for ten years.
mistakes.right: I'd known him for ten years.

mistakes.wrong: She had been writing three letters before lunch.
mistakes.right: She had written three letters before lunch.

points.title: Was doing or had been doing?
points.summary: **was doing** = in progress **at** that moment. **had been doing** = in progress **up to** that moment, often with how long.

blocks.md: Both forms describe activities in progress in the past, but from a different point of view:

rows: *When I arrived, she **was cooking**.* (at that moment)
*When I arrived, she **had been cooking** for hours.* (up to that moment)
*It **was raining** when we left.* (it was raining then)
*It **had been raining**, so the roads were wet.* (before, maybe stopped)

blocks.md: When you say **how long** something continued up to a past moment, use the past perfect continuous: *I **had been waiting** for an hour.* Not *I was waiting for an hour when she arrived*.

examples.text: When I called, he **was having** dinner.
When I called, he **had been trying** to call me too.
The baby **was sleeping**, so we spoke quietly.
The baby **had been sleeping** for three hours when she woke up.

mistakes.wrong: When I arrived, they were playing for two hours.
mistakes.right: When I arrived, they had been playing for two hours.
mistakes.why: How long up to a past moment: had been + -ing.

mistakes.wrong: When I phoned, he had been having a shower, so he didn't answer.
mistakes.right: When I phoned, he was having a shower, so he didn't answer.
mistakes.why: In progress at that moment: was having.

points.title: Repeated activities and plans up to a past time
points.summary: The past perfect continuous can describe a **repeated** activity up to a past time (*She'd been phoning him all week*) and intentions: *I'd been meaning to call you.*

blocks.md: The activity doesn't have to be continuous. It can be **repeated** many times over a period before a past moment:

items: *She**'d been phoning** him all week, but he never answered.*
*We**'d been seeing** a lot of each other before he moved abroad.*

blocks.md: With ***mean, hope, plan, think of***, it describes an intention that existed before a past moment, often one that didn't happen: *I**'d been meaning** to call you, but I kept forgetting.* *They**'d been planning** to move, but then the prices went up.*

Don't use it for a **single, short** completed action: *The bomb **had exploded**.* Not *The bomb had been exploding*. With a short action, the continuous suggests repetition: *He'd been kicking the ball against the wall* (again and again).

examples.text: I**'d been going** to the gym every day before I hurt my knee.
examples.note: repeated up to a past time

examples.text: He**'d been sending** her flowers for months.
We**'d been hoping** to see you at the wedding.
The phone **had rung** once and then stopped.

mistakes.wrong: The guest had been arriving at 8.
mistakes.right: The guest had arrived at 8.
mistakes.why: A single short action: had arrived.

mistakes.wrong: I'd meaning to tell you.
mistakes.right: I'd been meaning to tell you.

points.title: In reported speech
points.summary: In reported speech, the present perfect continuous and the past continuous often become the past perfect continuous: *I've been waiting* → *She said she had been waiting.*

blocks.md: When the reporting verb is in the past, we often move the tense back:

rows: *She said she **had been working** all day.*
*They said they **had been watching** TV when it happened.*
*He asked me how long I **had been learning** English.*

blocks.md: For the past continuous, moving back is **optional** when the time is clear: *They said they **were watching** TV when it happened* is also correct.
If the situation is still true now, you don't have to move the tense back: *She said she**'s been feeling** better* (she still is). See [Reported Speech](/blog/grammar/reported-speech/).

examples.text: He told me he **had been trying** to call me for hours.
She admitted she **hadn't been paying** attention.
They asked us how long we **had been living** there.

mistakes.wrong: She said she has been waiting since 6. (the waiting is over)
mistakes.right: She said she had been waiting since 6.
mistakes.why: The situation is finished: move back.

mistakes.wrong: He asked me how long had I been studying.
mistakes.right: He asked me how long I had been studying.

items.prompt: When the plane finally took off, we ___ at the airport for five hours.
items.explanation: Duration up to a past moment: *had been waiting*.

items.prompt: How long ___ before she got her first job?
By the time the doctor saw me, I ___ (sit) in the waiting room for over an hour.
items.explanation: Duration up to a past moment: *had been sitting* (*had sat* is also possible).

items.prompt: Tom's clothes were covered in paint. He ___ the fence.
items.explanation: Evidence in the past: *had been painting*.

items.prompt: *When I got home, the TV was warm.* What's the best explanation?
items.explanation: The past situation is explained by an earlier activity.

items.prompt: She was hot and tired because she ___ (play) tennis.
items.explanation: The activity that caused it: *had been playing* is the usual choice; *had played* is also possible.

items.prompt: By noon, I ___ five kilometres.
items.explanation: *How many / how far* = completed amount: *had walked*.

items.prompt: By the time we got married, we ___ each other for six years.
My hands were dirty because I ___ (work) in the garden.
items.explanation: The activity explaining the situation: *had been working* is usual.

items.prompt: When I looked out, it ___. I could see the rain falling.
items.explanation: In progress at that moment (I could see it): *was raining*.

items.prompt: When I looked out, the streets were wet, but the sun was shining. It ___.
items.explanation: The rain had stopped before that moment: *had been raining*.

items.prompt: When we arrived at the party, people ___ (dance) for hours and were exhausted.
items.explanation: Duration up to the moment we arrived: *had been dancing*.

topics.summary: One step further back in the past: When I arrived, the film had started.
intro: We use the **past perfect** (*had* + past participle) for something that happened **before** another moment in the past: *When I arrived, the film **had** already **started**.*
It takes you one step further back than the past simple. If you need to review the past simple first, see [Past Simple](/blog/grammar/past-simple/).

points.title: Form and main use: something earlier in the past
points.summary: had + past participle for an action before another past moment.

rows: Had she called? – No, she hadn't.

blocks.md: *Had* is the same for every person: *I had, you had, she had, they had.* Use the **past participle**: *gone, eaten, seen, been* (not *went, ate, saw*). See the list of irregular verbs on [Past Simple](/blog/grammar/past-simple/).
Think of two past moments. The past perfect is the **earlier** one: *I couldn't get in* (past) *because I **had lost** my keys* (earlier).
In speech, *had* is often **'d**: *I'd forgotten. They'd gone.* Be careful: *'d* can also mean *would* (*I'd like*). If a past participle follows, it's *had*.

examples.text: I couldn't get in because I **had lost** my keys.
She was tired because she **had worked** all night.
I **hadn't seen** the film, so I didn't know the ending.
**Had** you **been** to Asia before that trip?
The streets were wet. It**'d rained** in the night.

mistakes.wrong: I had went to bed early.
mistakes.right: I had gone to bed early.

mistakes.wrong: Had you ate before you came?
mistakes.right: Had you eaten before you came?

mistakes.wrong: She was tired because she had work all day.
mistakes.right: She was tired because she had worked all day.

points.title: Past simple or past perfect? The order of events
points.summary: Past simple for events in order; past perfect for an event that happened earlier than the one you're talking about.

blocks.md: The tense changes the **order** of events:

items: *When I arrived, the film **started**.* = I arrived, then the film started.
*When I arrived, the film **had started**.* = The film started first, then I arrived.

blocks.md: When you tell events **in the order they happened**, use the past simple. Don't use the past perfect for every past action: *I **woke up**, **had** a shower and **left** the house.*

examples.text: When we got to the station, the train **had left**.
When we got to the station, the train **left**.
When I got home, someone **had eaten** my cake.
I **got up**, **made** breakfast and **went** for a run.
I didn't know the way because I **hadn't been** there before.

mistakes.wrong: I had woken up, had had breakfast and had left.
mistakes.right: I woke up, had breakfast and left.

mistakes.wrong: When I arrived, the film has started.
mistakes.right: When I arrived, the film had started.
mistakes.why: Earlier than a past moment: past perfect.

points.title: By the time, already, just, never … before
points.summary: by the time + past simple, then past perfect; already, just, never … before with the past perfect.

rows: *By the time we arrived, the concert **had finished**.*
*He **had just sat** down when the phone rang.*
*When she moved to Canada, she **had never seen** snow.*
***Had** you **ever** tried sushi before that night?*

blocks.md: *Already, just, never* and *ever* go between *had* and the past participle: *had **already** left, had **just** sat, had **never** seen.*

examples.text: By the time we got there, everyone **had gone** home.
She **had already ordered** when I arrived.
I**'d just got** into bed when the alarm went off.
He was nervous because he **had never flown** before.
By the time I finished my degree, my parents **had moved** to Canada.
