mistakes.wrong: By the time we got there, the shop closed.
mistakes.right: By the time we got there, the shop had closed.
mistakes.why: By the time + earlier event: past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: She had left already when I called.
mistakes.right: She had already left when I called.
mistakes.why: Already goes between had and the participle.

points.title: Present perfect or past perfect?
points.summary: have done = before now; had done = before a moment in the past.

rows: *Until I moved to Canada, I**'d** never **seen** snow.*

blocks.md: The present perfect connects the past to **now**. The past perfect connects an earlier past to **a moment in the past**.

examples.text: I can't come out. I **haven't finished** my homework.
I couldn't go out because I **hadn't finished** my homework.
Last summer I visited Rome. I**'d** never **been** there before.
When I met him, he **had been** in the army for ten years.

mistakes.wrong: Before I came to Canada, I have never seen snow.
mistakes.right: Before I came to Canada, I had never seen snow.
mistakes.why: Before a past moment: past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: I'm not hungry. I'd already eaten.
mistakes.right: I'm not hungry. I've already eaten.

points.title: It was the first time I'd…; states up to a past moment
points.summary: It was the first time / the best … I'd ever + past perfect; state verbs up to a past moment use the past perfect simple.

blocks.md: After *It was the first / second / third time…* and after superlatives (*the best, the worst…*) in the past, use the past perfect: *It was the first time I**'d been** on a plane. It was the best meal we**'d** ever **had**.*

To say **how long** a state continued up to a past moment, use the past perfect simple with state verbs: *They **had known** each other for years when they got married.* (not *had been knowing*). For actions, the past perfect continuous is common: *She **had been working** there for ten years when she left.*

examples.text: It was the first time she**'d been** on a plane.
That was the third time he**'d lost** his phone that month.
It was the most beautiful place I**'d** ever **seen**.
We **had known** each other for years before we started working together.
I**'d had** the car for only a month when it broke down.

mistakes.wrong: It was the first time I've been abroad.
mistakes.right: It was the first time I'd been abroad.
mistakes.why: It was the first time + past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: We had been knowing each other for ten years.
mistakes.right: We had known each other for ten years.
mistakes.why: Know is a state: past perfect simple.

points.title: When the past perfect is optional
points.summary: If the order is already clear (after, as soon as, before) the past simple is also fine; once the earlier time is set, you can continue in the past simple.

blocks.md: When a time word like *after, as soon as* or *before* already makes the order clear, the past simple is also correct and the meaning doesn't change: *After she **had finished** / **finished** work, she went home.*

When you have **set up** an earlier time with the past perfect, you don't have to keep using it. You can continue in the past simple: *I sold my old guitar last week. I**'d had** it since I was fifteen, and I **played** it almost every day.*

But keep the past perfect when the past simple would change the order: *When I got home, my son **had cooked** dinner* (it was ready) vs *When I got home, my son **cooked** dinner* (he started after I arrived).

examples.text: After the guests **had gone** / **went**, we cleaned up.
As soon as I**'d sent** / **sent** the message, I regretted it.
She asked about the salary before she **accepted** the job.
We**'d lived** in that flat for years. We **loved** it, but it was too small.
When the police arrived, the thief **had escaped**.

mistakes.wrong: After we have eaten, we went for a walk.
mistakes.right: After we had eaten (or After we ate), we went for a walk.
mistakes.why: A past sequence: past perfect or past simple, not present perfect.

points.title: Past perfect in reported speech and thoughts
points.summary: A present perfect becomes past perfect when reported in the past; a past simple can become past perfect or stay the same.

blocks.md: When we report words or thoughts in the past, a **present perfect** usually becomes **past perfect**: *'I've met him before.' → I was sure I**'d met** him before.*
A **past simple** can become past perfect, but it can also stay in the past simple, especially when the time is clear: *'I lost my keys.' → She said she **had lost** / **lost** her keys.*
If the situation is still true now, you can also keep the present perfect: *He told me he**'s** never **been** to Asia.* See [Reported Speech](/blog/grammar/reported-speech/).

examples.text: 'I've finished.' → She said she **had finished**.
'We haven't decided yet.' → They said they **hadn't decided** yet.
'I lost my phone.' → He said he **had lost** / **lost** his phone.
I realised I**'d left** my umbrella on the bus.
Police said twenty people **had been** / **were** injured.

mistakes.wrong: I was sure that I have met him before.
mistakes.right: I was sure that I had met him before.
mistakes.why: Reported in the past: present perfect → past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: She said she hasn't finish yet.
mistakes.right: She said she hadn't finished yet.
mistakes.why: Past perfect, with the past participle finished.

points.title: Plans that didn't happen: I had hoped to…
points.summary: had hoped / meant / intended / planned / wanted to = a plan or wish that didn't happen.

blocks.md: Use *had* + *hoped, meant, intended, planned, wanted, expected* + to-infinitive for a plan or wish that **didn't happen**: *I **had hoped** to finish by Friday, but my computer broke.*

The past simple and the continuous forms are also used with a similar meaning: *I **hoped** / **was hoping** / **had been hoping** to see you.* The past perfect makes it clearest that it didn't happen.

examples.text: We**'d hoped** to visit the museum, but it was closed.
I**'d meant** to call you, but I forgot.
She **had intended** to stay a week, but she left after two days.
They **had planned** to retire at 60, but they're still working.
I **was hoping** to see you at the party.

mistakes.wrong: I had hope to finish today, but I couldn't.
mistakes.right: I had hoped to finish today, but I couldn't.

mistakes.wrong: We had wanted visit you.
mistakes.right: We had wanted to visit you.

items.prompt: It was the first time I ___ a horse.
items.explanation: It was the first time + past perfect: *I'd ridden*.

items.prompt: It was the best meal we ___ in years.
items.explanation: A past superlative + past perfect: *we'd had*.

items.prompt: They ___ each other for ten years when they got married.
items.explanation: *Know* is a state: past perfect simple, *had known*.

topics.summary: I was walking home (in progress) when it started to rain (a short event).
intro: The **past simple** (*I walked*) tells us that an action happened and finished. The **past continuous** (*I was walking*) tells us that an action was **in progress** at a moment in the past.
We often use them together: *I **was walking** home **when** it **started** to rain.* This page shows how to choose between them, from the basic pattern to the differences in meaning.

points.title: A longer action and a short action
points.summary: Past continuous for the longer action in progress; past simple for the short action that happened in the middle of it.

blocks.md: Use the **past continuous** for the longer action (the background) and the **past simple** for the shorter action that interrupted it:

items: *I **was having** a shower **when** the phone **rang**.*
*We **were driving** to the airport **when** the car **broke** down.*

blocks.md: The longer action started first. The short action happened in the middle of it.

Some verbs are not normally used in the continuous: *know, want, like, believe, understand*. Say *I **knew** the answer*, not *I was knowing the answer*. See [Stative Verbs](/blog/grammar/stative-verbs/).

examples.text: I **was cooking** dinner **when** my sister **arrived**.
He **was cycling** to school **when** he **fell** off his bike.
When I **saw** them, they **were sitting** in the park.
examples.note: the short action can come first

mistakes.wrong: I cooked dinner when my sister was arriving.
mistakes.right: I was cooking dinner when my sister arrived.
mistakes.why: Longer action: past continuous; short action: past simple.

mistakes.wrong: When the phone was ringing, I had a shower.
mistakes.right: When the phone rang, I was having a shower.
mistakes.why: The ring is the short action.

mistakes.wrong: I was knowing the answer.
mistakes.right: I knew the answer.

points.title: When and while
points.summary: **While** usually goes before the longer action (past continuous). **When** usually goes before the shorter action (past simple).

blocks.md: Both words can join the two actions, but they usually go in different places:

items: ***while** + longer action*: *The phone rang **while** I **was having** a shower.*
***when** + shorter action*: *I was having a shower **when** the phone **rang**.*

blocks.md: *When* can also introduce a longer period or a state: ***When** I **was** a child, I lived in Mashhad. **When** we **were living** in Paris, we often went to museums.*
If both actions are short, use the past simple for both. With *when*, this means one action came **right after** the other: ***When** she **saw** the spider, she **screamed**.*
You can start with either clause. Use a comma after the first clause when *when* or *while* comes first: ***While** I was waiting, I read the news.* / *I read the news **while** I was waiting.*

examples.text: **While** we **were watching** the film, someone **knocked** at the door.
We **were watching** the film **when** someone **knocked**.
**When** the bell **rang**, everyone **stood** up.
examples.note: two short actions: one after the other

examples.text: **When** I **was** at university, I **worked** in a café.

mistakes.wrong: When I was waiting for the bus, I was seeing an accident.
mistakes.right: While I was waiting for the bus, I saw an accident.
mistakes.why: The accident is a short action: saw.

mistakes.wrong: During I was waiting, I read the news.
mistakes.right: While I was waiting, I read the news.

points.title: How the tense changes the meaning
points.summary: *When I arrived, they **had** lunch* = after I arrived. *When I arrived, they **were having** lunch* = it was already in progress.

blocks.md: With *when*, the tense of the second action tells you the **order**:

rows: *When Ana got home, her husband **cooked** dinner.*
Ana got home → then he cooked.
*When Ana got home, her husband **was cooking** dinner.*
He started before she got home and was still cooking.
*When Ana got home, her husband **had cooked** dinner.*
Dinner was ready before she got home.

blocks.md: The third sentence uses the past perfect. See [Past Perfect](/blog/grammar/past-perfect/).
Ask yourself: was the action **already in progress** at that moment? If yes, use the past continuous. If it **started at that moment** or after it, use the past simple.

examples.text: When the teacher came in, the students **were talking**.
When the teacher came in, the students **stopped** talking.
When I looked outside, it **was snowing**.
When we got to the station, the train **was leaving**.
examples.note: in progress: we could still see it

mistakes.wrong: When I woke up, the sun shone.
mistakes.right: When I woke up, the sun was shining.
mistakes.why: Already in progress when I woke up.

mistakes.wrong: When I saw the cake, I was eating it.
mistakes.right: When I saw the cake, I ate it.
mistakes.why: The reaction came after: past simple.

points.title: Finished or unfinished?
points.summary: The past simple often means the action was **completed**; the past continuous can mean it was **not completed**: *I read a book* vs *I was reading a book*.

blocks.md: The past simple usually presents an action as **complete**. The past continuous shows the action was **in progress**, so it may not have been finished:

rows: *I **was writing** a letter last night.* (maybe not finished)
*He **was drowning**, but a lifeguard saved him.* (it didn't happen)
*They **were building** a bridge when the money ran out.* (not finished)

blocks.md: This is why the past continuous is useful when something stopped an action before it was completed.
Verbs that describe a change or result (*die, drown, crash, fall, finish, build, fix*) show this difference most clearly.

examples.text: I **was crossing** the road when a car nearly hit me.
She **was dying**, but the doctors saved her.
We **painted** the kitchen on Saturday.
We **were painting** the kitchen when we ran out of paint.

mistakes.wrong: He drowned, but a lifeguard saved him.
mistakes.right: He was drowning, but a lifeguard saved him.
mistakes.why: He didn't die: the action was in progress.

mistakes.wrong: We were fixing the car yesterday, and now it works perfectly.
mistakes.right: We fixed the car yesterday, and now it works perfectly.
mistakes.why: The result is complete: past simple.

points.title: I was talking to… : introducing news and background
points.summary: We use the past continuous to introduce news or a report of what someone said: *I was talking to Ali yesterday, and he told me…*

blocks.md: In conversation, the past continuous often sets up a story or a piece of news. The **background** is in the past continuous; the **news** follows:

items: *I **was talking** to Maryam the other day and she **said** she's moving to Vancouver.*
*I **was reading** an article about sleep, and it **said** we need eight hours.*

blocks.md: With verbs of saying, the past continuous can also report something that was said recently, especially when we don't remember the exact words: *Hassan **was saying** that the office might close.* / *What **were** you **saying**?*
Compare: *I **talked** to Maryam* (a complete event, often as an answer to *What did you do?*) and *I **was talking** to Maryam* (background to what comes next).
The past continuous of *say, tell, talk* is common in spoken English when we come back to a topic: *As I **was saying**, the deadline is Friday.*

examples.text: I **was chatting** to my neighbour, and she **told** me about a great dentist.
We **were discussing** your idea at the meeting, and everyone **liked** it.
Sorry, what **were** you **saying**?
As I **was saying** before the interruption, we need more staff.

mistakes.wrong: I talking to Sara yesterday, and she said she's leaving.
mistakes.right: I was talking to Sara yesterday, and she said she's leaving.

mistakes.wrong: As I am saying, the deadline is Friday.
mistakes.right: As I was saying, the deadline is Friday.
mistakes.why: The fixed phrase is as I was saying.

items.prompt: The building ___, but the firefighters saved it.
items.explanation: It wasn't destroyed: the action was in progress, not completed.

items.prompt: *I was reading a novel last night.* Did I finish it?
options: Yes, and I read it again.
items.explanation: The past continuous doesn't say the action was completed.

items.prompt: They ___ (build) a new hospital, but the project stopped when the money ran out.

topics.summary: Verbs with a particle (up, down, on, off, out): get up, turn on, look after, run out of. Meaning, word order and common mistakes.
intro: A **phrasal verb** is a verb + a small word called a **particle** (*up, down, on, off, out, back, in, over*): *get **up**, turn **on**, look **after***. The particle often changes the meaning completely: *look* (see) / *look **for*** (try to find) / *look **after*** (take care of).
Phrasal verbs are very common in everyday English, so learn them in **real sentences**, not as lists. This page also explains **word order**: *turn it on*, not *turn on it*.

points.title: Get up, turn on, put on, look for
points.summary: Everyday phrasal verbs: **get up, wake up, sit down, stand up, turn on / off, put on, take off, look for, come back, go out**. The particle changes the meaning.

rows: start / stop a machine or light
***Put on** your coat. **Take off** your shoes.*

blocks.md: In English, you **turn on** a light or a TV (not *open the light*), and you **put on** clothes before you wear them.

examples.text: I usually **get up** at half past six.
**Turn on** the light, please.
It's cold. **Put on** a jumper.
She's **looking for** a new job.

mistakes.wrong: Can you open the light?
mistakes.right: Can you turn on the light?

mistakes.wrong: I'm looking my phone.
mistakes.right: I'm looking for my phone.

mistakes.wrong: Put off your shoes, please.
mistakes.right: Take off your shoes, please.

points.title: Turn it off, not turn off it: separable verbs
points.summary: With many phrasal verbs, a **noun** can go **before or after** the particle (*turn off the TV / turn the TV off*), but a **pronoun** must go **in the middle**: *turn **it** off* (not *turn off it*).

rows: *Turn on the TV.* / *Turn the TV on.*
*Pick up your toys.* / *Pick your toys up.*
*Fill in the form.* / *Fill the form in.*
*Wake up the kids.* / *Wake the kids up.*

blocks.md: Common separable phrasal verbs: *turn on / off, put on, take off, pick up, throw away, give back, fill in, write down, try on, put away, wake up* (someone), *call back*.
A **pronoun** (*it, them, me, him, her, us*) always goes **between** the verb and the particle.

examples.text: Can you **pick me up** at six?
**Write down** the address. / **Write** the address **down**.
Don't **throw it away**!
Can I **try these jeans on**?

mistakes.wrong: I'll pick up you at six.
mistakes.right: I'll pick you up at six.

mistakes.wrong: Turn off it, please.
mistakes.right: Turn it off, please.

mistakes.wrong: Can you fill in it?
mistakes.right: Can you fill it in?

points.title: Look after her, get on the bus: inseparable verbs
points.summary: Some phrasal verbs are **inseparable**: the object always goes **after** the particle, even a pronoun (*look after **her***, *come across **it***). Some have **no object** at all: *get up, grow up, break down*.

rows: *She **looks after** her grandma. She looks after **her**.*
enter / leave a bus or train

blocks.md: With inseparable verbs, never put the object in the middle: *look after **the baby*** (not *look the baby after*).
***Grow up*** has no object. To raise children, use ***bring up***: *She **brought up** three children.*

examples.text: Who **looks after** your dog when you travel?
I **came across** this café by chance.
The plane **took off** on time.
I'll **deal with** the problem tomorrow.

mistakes.wrong: Can you look your sister after?
mistakes.right: Can you look after your sister?

mistakes.wrong: I came an old letter across.
mistakes.right: I came across an old letter.

mistakes.wrong: She grew up three children.
mistakes.right: She brought up three children.

points.title: Look forward to, run out of, put up with
points.summary: **Three-part phrasal verbs** (verb + particle + preposition) can't be separated: **look forward to, get on with, run out of, put up with, come up with, catch up with, look up to, get away with, cut down on, keep up with**.

rows: be happy about something in the future
*It's hard to **keep up with** the news.*

blocks.md: The object always goes at the **end**: *I can't put up with **it***.
In ***look forward to***, *to* is a **preposition**, so use ***-ing***: *I'm looking forward to **seeing** you.*

examples.text: I'm **looking forward to** the weekend.
We **ran out of** petrol on the motorway.
How do you **put up with** him?
He **came up with** a clever solution.

mistakes.wrong: I'm looking forward to see you.
mistakes.right: I'm looking forward to seeing you.

mistakes.wrong: We've run out petrol.
mistakes.right: We've run out of petrol.

points.title: One phrasal verb, many meanings
points.summary: Many phrasal verbs have **several meanings**: *take off* (clothes / a plane / become successful), *pick up* (lift / collect / learn), *make up* (invent / become friends again), *work out* (exercise / solve), *put off* (postpone).

rows: remove clothes; leave the ground; become successful
***Take off** your coat. The plane **took off**. Her career **took off**.*
lift; collect someone; learn without studying
***Pick up** the box. I'll **pick** you **up** at 6. I **picked up** some Spanish.*
*He **made up** an excuse. They argued, then **made up**.*
*I **work out** at the gym. I can't **work out** this puzzle.*
postpone; make someone not want something
*They **put off** the meeting. The smell **put** me **off**.*

blocks.md: Use the **context** to understand the meaning.

In formal writing, a one-word verb often sounds better: *find out* → ***discover***, *put off* → ***postpone***, *carry out* → ***conduct***, *go up* → ***increase***, *look into* → ***investigate***.

examples.text: The plane **took off** at 6 am.
I **picked up** some Italian when I lived in Rome.
They had a fight but **made up** the next day.
The meeting has been **put off** until Friday.

mistakes.wrong: She gave up to smoke last year.
mistakes.right: She gave up smoking last year.

mistakes.wrong: He made up with a story about a lost wallet.
mistakes.right: He made up a story about a lost wallet.

points.title: Particle meanings, phrasal nouns, and passives
points.summary: Particles often have a **general meaning** (*up* = completely, *out* = to the end or disappear, *on* = continue, *off* = stop or leave, *down* = decrease). Many phrasal verbs make **nouns** (*a breakdown, an outbreak, a setback*) and can be **passive** (*It was called off*).

rows: *eat up, use up, tidy up; speed up, go up*
*sort out, run out, die out, wipe out, point out*
*carry on, keep on, go on, drag on*
leave or start; stop or cancel
*set off; call off, wear off, lay off*
*slow down, cut down; break down; write down*

blocks.md: **Phrasal nouns** are common in news and business English: *a **breakdown**, a **takeover**, an **outbreak**, a **setback**, a **turnout**, a **drawback**, a **cutback**, the **outcome**, the **input***. They're usually written as **one word** (sometimes with a hyphen: *a check-in*).
Phrasal verbs with an object can be **passive**: *The match **was called off**. The issue **is being looked into**.*

examples.text: The effect of the coffee soon **wore off**.
Many species have **died out**.
There has been an **outbreak** of flu.
The concert **was called off** because of the storm.

mistakes.wrong: The company is laying out 200 workers.
mistakes.right: The company is laying off 200 workers.

mistakes.wrong: We had a break down on the motorway.
mistakes.right: We had a breakdown on the motorway.

items.prompt: We've run ___ of coffee. Can you buy some?
I'm looking forward to ___ you next week.
I don't know how you put ___ with your noisy neighbours. (one word)
In *Her career really took off after her first film*, *took off* means:
Which is the most formal?
options: The meeting has been put off.

items.prompt: My grandfather gave ___ smoking when he was 50. (one word)

topics.h1: Possessive Pronouns: Mine, Yours, His, Hers
topics.summary: Using mine, yours, his, hers, ours and theirs instead of a possessive + noun: This bag is mine.
intro: **Possessive pronouns** (*mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs*) replace a **possessive adjective + noun**: *This is **my bag** → This bag is **mine**.*

For *my, your, his* and *her*, see [Subject Pronouns and Possessive Adjectives](/blog/grammar/subject-pronouns-possessive-adjectives/#spa-possessive). For *Ali's* and *my parents'*, see [Possessive 's](/blog/grammar/possessive-s/).

points.title: Mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs
points.summary: Use a **possessive pronoun** without a noun: *This phone is **mine**. Is this **yours**?* Use a **possessive adjective** before a noun: *This is **my** phone.*

blocks.md: Possessive pronouns stand **alone**; they never come before a noun: *This is **mine**.* (not *This is mine bag*)
There's **no apostrophe**: *yours, hers, ours, theirs* (not *your's, her's*).

examples.text: That's not my coffee. **Mine** is the big one.
Is this pen **yours**?
The red car is **hers**.
Their house is bigger than **ours**.

mistakes.wrong: This is mine book.
mistakes.right: This is my book.

mistakes.wrong: Is this your's?
mistakes.right: Is this yours?

mistakes.wrong: These seats are our.
mistakes.right: These seats are ours.

points.title: Whose is it? Whose bag is this?
points.summary: Ask about the owner with ***whose***: *Whose bag is this?* or *Whose is this bag?* Answer with a possessive pronoun or *'s*: *It's **mine**. It's **Ali's**.*

blocks.md: ***Whose*** can go **before a noun** (*Whose car is this?*) or **alone** (*Whose is this car?*).
Don't confuse ***whose*** (possession) with ***who's*** (= who is / who has).

examples.text: **Whose** coat is this?
**Whose** are these keys? ~ They're **mine**.
**Whose** turn is it? ~ It's **yours**.
**Who's** coming tonight?

mistakes.wrong: Who's bag is this?
mistakes.right: Whose bag is this?

mistakes.wrong: Whose is this bag? ~ It's of Ali.
mistakes.right: Whose is this bag? ~ It's Ali's.

mistakes.wrong: Who's are these?
mistakes.right: Whose are these?

points.title: My own, of my own, on my own
points.summary: ***Own*** emphasises possession: *my own room, a room of my own*. ***On my own*** = alone or without help (*I live on my own*). ***A friend of mine*** = one of my friends.

rows: *I have **my own** car. She runs **her own** business.*
*I'd like **a room of my own**. He has **no children of his own**.*
*She lives **on her own**.* = *She lives by herself.*

blocks.md: *Own* always follows a **possessive adjective** (*my, your, his…*) or *'s*: ***my** own room, **Ali's** own idea* (not *an own room*).

examples.text: I'd love to have **my own** flat.
They want **a house of their own**.
He travelled around Asia **on his own**.
**A friend of mine** is a pilot.

mistakes.wrong: I want an own room.
mistakes.right: I want my own room.

mistakes.wrong: She lives on herself.
mistakes.right: She lives on her own.

mistakes.wrong: He's a cousin of me.
mistakes.right: He's a cousin of mine.

points.title: Formal possessives: one's own, whose for things, of which
points.summary: In formal English, use ***one's own*** for people in general. ***Whose*** can refer to **things** (*a company whose profits rose*), and ***of which*** is a formal alternative. Possessive pronouns avoid repeating a noun in comparisons: *Her results were better than **his***.

rows: *It's a city **whose** history goes back 3,000 years.*
*a house, the roof **of which** needs repair*

blocks.md: ***Whose*** for things is correct and common: *a word **whose** meaning I don't know*. *The… of which* is more formal.
In comparisons, use possessive pronouns to avoid repeating the noun: *Your English is better than **mine*** (= my English).

examples.text: One must make **one's own** decisions.
She works for a company **whose** products are sold worldwide.
The building, the walls **of which** were cracked, was closed.
My car is older than **yours**.

mistakes.wrong: It's a country which history is very long.
mistakes.right: It's a country whose history is very long.

mistakes.wrong: My score was higher than your.
mistakes.right: My score was higher than yours.

items.prompt: My sister has ___ company. She started it in 2020.
I don't need help. I can do it on ___ own.
Leila is a colleague ___ mine. We work together. (one word)

topics.summary: How to show who something belongs to: Ali's phone, my parents' house, the end of the film, a friend of mine.
intro: Add ***'s*** to a person to show that something belongs to them: *This is **Sara's** bag.* For plural nouns ending in *-s*, add just an **apostrophe**: *my **parents'** house*.
For possessive words like *my, his, mine* and *hers*, see [Possessive Pronouns](/blog/grammar/possessive-pronouns/).

points.title: 's and s': my sister's car, my parents' house
points.summary: Add **'s** to a person or animal to show possession: *Ali's phone, my sister's car*. For regular plurals ending in *-s*, add only an **apostrophe**: *my parents' house*. Irregular plurals take **'s**: *the children's toys*.

blocks.md: The thing that is owned comes **after** the possessive: *Ali's **book*** (not *the book of Ali*).
Don't confuse possessive *'s* with *'s* = *is* or *has*: *Ali**'s** tired* (= Ali is tired). *Ali**'s** car* (possessive).

examples.text: This is **my brother's** bedroom.
**My parents'** house is near the sea.
The **children's** toys are everywhere.
Is this **Maryam's** coat?

mistakes.wrong: This is the car of my father.
mistakes.right: This is my father's car.

mistakes.wrong: My parent's house is big. (two parents)
mistakes.right: My parents' house is big.

mistakes.wrong: The childrens' room is upstairs.
mistakes.right: The children's room is upstairs.

points.title: At the doctor's, Ali and Sara's house
points.summary: Use **'s** for **shops and homes** without the noun: *at the doctor's, at my aunt's*. When two people **share** something, add *'s* to the **second** name: *Ali and Sara's flat*. For **separate** things, add it to both: *Ali's and Sara's phones*.

rows: *I'm going to **the hairdresser's / the dentist's / the chemist's**.*
*We had dinner **at my aunt's**.* (= at my aunt's house)

blocks.md: In American English, people often say *the dentist, the doctor* without *'s*. Both are correct.

examples.text: I've got an appointment **at the dentist's**.
We stayed **at my cousin's** for a week.
**Reza and Mina's** baby was born yesterday.
**Chris's** brother is a pilot.

mistakes.wrong: Ali's and Sara's wedding was lovely. (one wedding)
mistakes.right: Ali and Sara's wedding was lovely.

mistakes.wrong: We met at my grandma. (at her house)
mistakes.right: We met at my grandma's.

points.title: 's or of? My friend's name, the end of the film
points.summary: Use **'s** mostly for **people and animals** (*my friend's name*). Use **of** for **parts of things** (*the end of the street, the top of the page*). Both are possible with **places and organisations** (*Canada's capital / the capital of Canada*).

rows: parts of things: *the top of the page, the back of the room*
*the middle of the night, the end of the film*
places, organisations: *Toronto's mayor, the company's profits*
*the mayor of Toronto, the profits of the company*
long description: *the son of the woman who lives next door*

blocks.md: With **things**, *of* or a **compound noun** is usually more natural: *the end of the street, the car door, the kitchen window*. With *top, bottom, back, front, middle, end*, use *of*: *the back **of** the room* (not *the room's back*).
With a **long** description of the person, use *of*: *the phone number **of** the man I met at the party*.

examples.text: What's **your brother's** name?
I didn't understand **the end of the film**.
**Canada's** capital is Ottawa.
Write your name at **the top of the page**.

mistakes.wrong: I woke up in the night's middle.
mistakes.right: I woke up in the middle of the night.

mistakes.wrong: Let's sit at the room's back.
mistakes.right: Let's sit at the back of the room.

points.title: Today's news, a week's holiday, a friend of mine
points.summary: Use **'s / s'** with **time** expressions: *today's news, last week's meeting, a week's holiday, two hours' drive, in ten minutes' time*. Use **a friend of mine** or **a friend of my sister's** to mean *one of my friends*.

rows: *today's newspaper, yesterday's meeting, next month's exam*
*a week's holiday, an hour's drive, two weeks' notice, in five minutes' time*

blocks.md: With plural time words ending in *-s*, add only an apostrophe: *two **weeks'** holiday, three **days'** walk*.
***A friend of mine*** = one of my friends (I have more than one). *My friend* often means a particular friend the listener knows about.
A compound adjective with a hyphen is another common pattern: *a two-hour drive, a ten-minute walk*. See [Noun Modifiers and Compound Nouns](/blog/grammar/noun-modifiers-compound-nouns/).

examples.text: Did you see **yesterday's** match?
We had **a week's** holiday in Spain.
The hotel is **ten minutes'** walk from the beach.
**A friend of mine** works at Google.

mistakes.wrong: I read it in the today newspaper.
mistakes.right: I read it in today's newspaper.

mistakes.wrong: She's a friend of me.
mistakes.right: She's a friend of mine.

mistakes.wrong: two weeks holiday
mistakes.right: two weeks' holiday

points.title: Group possessives, else's, its and one's
points.summary: **'s** can attach to a whole **noun phrase**: *the King of Spain's visit, someone else's bag*. In formal writing, prefer *of* with long phrases. Possessive pronouns have **no apostrophe**: *its, hers, ours, theirs*.

rows: *the Prime Minister of Canada's speech, my brother-in-law's car*
*The company changed **its** name.* / ***It's*** (= it is) late.
*the man next door's dog* (informal) → *the dog that belongs to the man next door* (writing)

blocks.md: The *'s* goes at the **end of the whole phrase**, not on the main noun: *the head of department**'s** office* (not *the head's of department office*).
In formal writing, long *'s* phrases can sound clumsy. Use *of* or rephrase: *the speech **of** the Prime Minister of Canada* or *the Canadian Prime Minister's speech*.
Possessive **pronouns** never have an apostrophe: ***its, hers, ours, yours, theirs***.

examples.text: That's **someone else's** problem.
**My mother-in-law's** cooking is amazing.
The committee published **its** report.
**The Queen of Denmark's** visit was a success.

mistakes.wrong: That's somebody's else bag.
mistakes.right: That's somebody else's bag.

mistakes.wrong: The dog wagged it's tail.
mistakes.right: The dog wagged its tail.

mistakes.wrong: Their's is the white house.
mistakes.right: Theirs is the white house.

items.prompt: Have you read ___ newspaper?
He's a colleague ___.
The station is about ten ___ (minute) walk from here. (one word)

topics.summary: Saying where things are: in the box, on the table, at the door, under the bed, next to the window.
intro: **Prepositions of place** say **where** something is: *The keys are **on** the table. The cat is **under** the bed. I'm **at** the station.*
The three most important are ***in, on*** and ***at***, and they're also the most confusing. This page goes step by step.

points.title: In, on, under, next to, between, behind
points.summary: Basic prepositions of place: ***in*** (inside), ***on*** (on a surface), ***under, next to, between, behind, in front of, opposite, near***.

rows: *The car is **behind** the house. There's a tree **in front of** the house.*
*The school is **opposite** the park.* (on the other side of the road)

blocks.md: ***Next to*** and ***in front of*** need all their words: *next **to** the door, in front **of** the school*. ***Near*** doesn't need *to*: *near the door*.

examples.text: Your keys are **in** your bag.
There's a picture **on** the wall.
The shoes are **under** the bed.
I live **next to** a supermarket.

mistakes.wrong: The book is in the table.
mistakes.right: The book is on the table.

mistakes.wrong: She sat next me.
mistakes.right: She sat next to me.

mistakes.wrong: The park is in front the school.
mistakes.right: The park is in front of the school.

points.title: In, on or at? At the door, in the room, on the wall
points.summary: ***At*** = a **point** or a place where something happens (*at the bus stop, at work, at a party*). ***In*** = **inside** an area or space (*in the kitchen, in Toronto*). ***On*** = a **surface** or a **line** (*on the wall, on the second floor*).

rows: a point: *at the door, at the traffic lights*
inside: *in the box, in the car*
a surface: *on the table, on the wall*
an event or activity: *at a party, at work, at school*
a city or country: *in Tehran, in Canada*
a room or building (inside): *in the kitchen*
*on the left / right, on the map*

blocks.md: Use ***at*** for a building when you mean the **activity** or a **meeting point**: *I'll meet you **at** the cinema.* Use ***in*** when you mean **inside**: *It's cold **in** the cinema.*
***On*** + street (*on Queen Street*) but ***at*** + full address (*at 15 Queen Street*).

examples.text: I'll wait for you **at** the bus stop.
She lives **in** Vancouver.
Our flat is **on** the fifth floor.
He's **at** work until six.

mistakes.wrong: I live at Canada.
mistakes.right: I live in Canada.

mistakes.wrong: My office is in the second floor.
mistakes.right: My office is on the second floor.

mistakes.wrong: There were 100 people in the party.
mistakes.right: There were 100 people at the party.

points.title: On the bus, in the car, arrive in or at
points.summary: Use ***on*** for public transport and bikes (*on the bus, on a plane, on my bike*) and ***in*** for cars and taxis (*in the car*). ***Arrive in*** a city or country; ***arrive at*** a building or place (*arrive at the airport*). Never *arrive to*.

rows: *I read **on the bus**. She came **on her bike**.*
*get on / off* the bus or train
***Get off** the bus at the next stop.*
*get in(to) / out of* the car or taxi

blocks.md: ***By*** + transport, with no *the*: *by bus, by car, by plane* (but *on foot*).

examples.text: I met him **on the train** to Montreal.
Get **into** the taxi.
What time did you **arrive at** the airport?
We **arrived in** Canada in 2019.

mistakes.wrong: I arrived to the hotel late.
mistakes.right: I arrived at the hotel late.

mistakes.wrong: She was sitting on the car.
mistakes.right: She was sitting in the car.

mistakes.wrong: I go to work with bus.
mistakes.right: I go to work by bus.

points.title: Over, above, across, through, along, past
points.summary: ***Above / below*** = higher / lower. ***Over*** = above, often covering or moving to the other side. ***Across*** = from one side to the other of a flat surface. ***Through*** = inside, from one end to the other. ***Along*** = following a line. ***Past*** = going by.

rows: *The plane flew **above** the clouds. The temperature is **below** zero.*
*She put a blanket **over** the baby. He jumped **over** the wall.*
*The train went **through** the tunnel. We walked **through** the forest.*
*She jumped **into** the pool. Get **out of** the car.*

blocks.md: For **numbers** and levels, use ***above / below***: *above average, 10 degrees below zero*. ***Over*** often means *more than*: *over 100 people*.

examples.text: A helicopter flew **over** the city.
We swam **across** the lake.
The road goes **through** the mountains.
Walk **along** this street for 200 metres.

mistakes.wrong: We walked through the bridge.
mistakes.right: We walked across the bridge.

mistakes.wrong: The cat jumped in the table.
mistakes.right: The cat jumped onto the table.

mistakes.wrong: It's three degrees under zero.
mistakes.right: It's three degrees below zero.

points.title: Under pressure, on the brink of, beyond repair
points.summary: Prepositions of place are often used **figuratively**: ***under*** pressure / control / construction, ***on the verge / brink of***, ***beyond*** repair / belief, ***within*** reach / walking distance, ***among*** (in a group).

rows: affected by / in the process of
*The company is **on the brink of** collapse.*
*She was **among** the winners.* (a group) / *a secret **between** you and me*
*the problem **at the heart of** the debate*

blocks.md: ***Between*** is for clearly separate things, often two; ***among*** is for a group or crowd: *The house is hidden **among** the trees.*

examples.text: The new bridge is still **under construction**.
The species is **on the verge of** extinction.
My old phone is **beyond repair**.
The beach is **within walking distance**.

mistakes.wrong: The situation is in control now.
mistakes.right: The situation is under control now.

mistakes.wrong: The car is over repair.
mistakes.right: The car is beyond repair.

items.prompt: Look both ways before you walk ___ the road to the other side.
The train goes ___ a long tunnel under the mountain.
The temperature fell to ten degrees ___ zero last night. (one word)

topics.h1: Prepositions of Time: In, On and At
topics.summary: When to use at (at 7 pm), on (on Friday) and in (in May), plus for, during, by, until and within.
intro: Use ***at*** for exact **times**, ***on*** for **days and dates**, and ***in*** for **longer periods** like months, years and seasons: *at 7 pm, on Friday, in May*.
This page also covers *for, during, by, until* and *within*. For *for* and *since*, see [For, Since and Ago](/blog/grammar/for-since/).

points.title: At 6 o'clock, on Monday, in July
points.summary: ***At*** + times (*at 6 o'clock, at night*), ***on*** + days and dates (*on Monday, on 5 May*), ***in*** + months, years, seasons and parts of the day (*in July, in 2025, in the morning*).

rows: times: *at 6 o'clock, at 7.30, at noon, at midnight*
*on Monday morning, on New Year's Day*
special days: *on Christmas Day, on my wedding day*
parts of the day: *in the morning / afternoon / evening*

blocks.md: American English often says ***on the weekend***; British English says ***at the weekend***. Both are correct.
Use **no preposition** before *this, next, last, every, today, tomorrow, yesterday*: *I'll see you **next** Friday.* (not *on next Friday*)

examples.text: The film starts **at** 8 pm.
My birthday is **on** 12 March.
We're going to Spain **in** August.
I usually read **in** the evening.

mistakes.wrong: I was born on 1995.
mistakes.right: I was born in 1995.

mistakes.wrong: See you in Monday.
mistakes.right: See you on Monday.

mistakes.wrong: The meeting is at next Tuesday.
mistakes.right: The meeting is next Tuesday.

mistakes.wrong: I go to bed in midnight.
mistakes.right: I go to bed at midnight.

points.title: On Monday morning, at night, in ten minutes, on time
points.summary: ***In the morning***, but ***on*** + a specific day: ***on Monday morning***. ***At night*** (in general), but ***in the night*** (during one night). ***In*** + period = after that time from now: *in ten minutes*. ***On time*** = not late; ***in time*** = early enough.

rows: *The train leaves **in 10 minutes**.* (= 10 minutes from now)
*The bus was **on time**.* (at the planned time) / *We arrived **in time** for dinner.* (early enough)

blocks.md: ***On time*** = at the correct time, not late. ***In time*** = early enough for something.

examples.text: She called me **on Sunday evening**.
I can't sleep **at night**.
I'll be ready **in five minutes**.
The plane landed **on time**.

mistakes.wrong: I have an exam in Monday morning.
mistakes.right: I have an exam on Monday morning.

mistakes.wrong: I'll call you after ten minutes. (from now)
mistakes.right: I'll call you in ten minutes.

mistakes.wrong: We got there on time to see the start.
mistakes.right: We got there in time to see the start.

points.title: For, during or while?
points.summary: ***For*** + a period says **how long** (*for two hours*). ***During*** + a noun says **when**, inside a period (*during the film*). ***While*** + a clause (subject + verb): *while I was watching the film*.

rows: *I fell asleep **while** I was watching the film.*

blocks.md: Don't use *during* to say how long: *I lived there **for** three years* (not *during three years*).

examples.text: We stayed in Paris **for** a week.
Please don't talk **during** the exam.
My phone rang **while** I was driving.
It rained **during** the night.

mistakes.wrong: I studied English during five years.
mistakes.right: I studied English for five years.

mistakes.wrong: She called while the meeting.
mistakes.right: She called during the meeting.

mistakes.wrong: During I was cooking, the phone rang.
mistakes.right: While I was cooking, the phone rang.

points.title: By or until? From… to, within
points.summary: ***Until / till*** = up to a time (an action **continues**): *I'll wait **until** 6.* ***By*** = **not later than** (a deadline): *Please finish it **by** Friday.* ***Within*** = before the end of a period: *within 24 hours*.

rows: before the end of a period

blocks.md: A quick test: *by* answers “what's the deadline?”; *until* answers “how long does it continue?”.
***By the time*** + clause: ***By the time** we arrived, the film had started.*

examples.text: I'll be at the office **until** six.
The essay must be submitted **by** Friday.
You'll receive an answer **within** 48 hours.
She **didn't** wake up **until** 11.

mistakes.wrong: Please pay until the end of the month.
mistakes.right: Please pay by the end of the month.

mistakes.wrong: I'll wait for you by 8 o'clock.
mistakes.right: I'll wait for you until 8 o'clock.

mistakes.wrong: We work from 9 until to 5.
mistakes.right: We work from 9 to 5.

points.title: As of, over the last decade, on arrival
points.summary: Formal and advanced expressions: ***as of / as from*** (starting from), ***over*** + period (during the whole period), ***in the run-up to*** (in the period before), ***in the course of*** (during), ***on*** + noun / *-ing* (as soon as), ***at the turn of the century***.

rows: ***In the course of** the meeting, three issues came up.*
***On arrival**, please go to reception. **On hearing** the news, she cried.*
*The house was built **at the turn of the century**.*

blocks.md: ***On*** + *-ing* is formal and means *as soon as*: ***On receiving** your payment, we will send the goods.* (*Upon* is even more formal.)

examples.text: **As of** today, the office is closed on Fridays.
Unemployment has fallen **over** the past two years.
**On arrival**, guests will receive a welcome drink.
Prices rose **in the run-up to** Christmas.

mistakes.wrong: In arrival, please show your ticket.
mistakes.right: On arrival, please show your ticket.

mistakes.wrong: As of from Monday, the new rules apply.
mistakes.right: As of Monday, the new rules apply.

items.prompt: You must return the book ___ Monday.
The museum is open ___ 6 pm.
I didn't go to bed ___ 2 am. I was studying. (one word)

topics.h1: Present Perfect Continuous (I have been doing)
topics.summary: An activity that started in the past and continues now, or has just stopped: I've been waiting for an hour.
intro: We use the **present perfect continuous** (*have / has been* + *-ing*) for an activity that started in the past and is **still going on**, or has **just stopped**: *I**'ve been waiting** for an hour. You're wet! **Have** you **been swimming**?*

It focuses on the **activity** and **how long** it has lasted. The present perfect simple (*I've done*) focuses on the **result** or **how much**. This page covers both and the cases where the choice changes the meaning.

points.title: Form and use: still going on, how long
points.summary: **have / has been + -ing** for an activity that started in the past and continues now, often with *how long, for, since*.

rows: *I**'ve been learning** English for three years.*

blocks.md: The activity started in the past and is **still happening**: *It**'s been raining** all day* (and it's still raining). *How long **have** you **been learning** to drive?*
Common time words: *for, since, how long, all day, all morning, recently, lately*.
*She's been* = *she has been*. Don't confuse *she's been working* (present perfect continuous) with *she's working* (present continuous, now).

examples.text: I**'ve been studying** for this exam for weeks.
How long **has** it **been snowing**?
They**'ve been building** that bridge since 2022.
We **haven't been sleeping** well recently.

mistakes.wrong: I'm waiting for an hour.
mistakes.right: I've been waiting for an hour.
mistakes.why: How long up to now: present perfect continuous.

mistakes.wrong: She has been work here since May.
mistakes.right: She has been working here since May.

mistakes.wrong: How long you have been learning English?
mistakes.right: How long have you been learning English?

points.title: An activity that has just stopped: evidence now
points.summary: We use it for an activity that has **recently stopped** when we can see the **result** now: *You're out of breath. Have you been running?*

blocks.md: The activity may have **just finished**, but we can see or feel its effects now:

items: *Your eyes are red. **Have** you **been crying**?*
*I'm tired because I**'ve been working** in the garden.*
*The ground is wet. It**'s been raining**.*

blocks.md: The focus is on the **activity** (what you have been doing), not on a completed result.
For something that is finished and its **completed** result, use the simple: *I**'ve washed** the car.* (It's clean.) *I**'ve been washing** the car.* (That's why I'm wet.)

examples.text: Sorry I'm dirty. I**'ve been fixing** the car.
The kitchen smells of onions. **Have** you **been cooking**?
Why are you so tired? ~ I**'ve been running**.

mistakes.wrong: Your eyes are red. Have you been cry?
mistakes.right: Your eyes are red. Have you been crying?

mistakes.wrong: My hands hurt because I've been dig in the garden.
mistakes.right: My hands hurt because I've been digging in the garden.

points.title: Have been doing or have done?
points.summary: **have been doing** = the activity, how long, maybe not finished. **have done** = completed, a result, how many / how much.

rows: *She**'s been writing** emails all morning.* (how long)
*They**'ve been painting** the kitchen.* (that's why it smells)

blocks.md: Ask **how long?** → usually continuous: *How long **have** you **been playing** tennis?* Ask **how many / how much?** → simple: *How many matches **have** you **played**?*

With **for / since**, the continuous is common for activities: *I've been learning Persian **for** two years.* With *live* and *work*, both are possible: *I**'ve lived / 've been living** here for ten years.*
Don't use the continuous with a number of completed things: *I've drunk three coffees.* Not *I've been drinking three coffees*.

examples.text: I**'ve been cooking** all afternoon.
I**'ve cooked** dinner. Come and eat!
He**'s been saving** money for a new car.
He**'s saved** $5,000 so far.

mistakes.wrong: I've been reading three books this month.
mistakes.right: I've read three books this month.

mistakes.wrong: Look! I've been finishing my homework.
mistakes.right: Look! I've finished my homework.

points.title: Repeated actions and temporary situations
points.summary: The continuous can describe **repeated** actions over a period (*I've been going to the gym a lot*) and **temporary** situations (*I've been staying with friends*).

blocks.md: The activity doesn't have to be continuous. It can be **repeated** many times up to now: *I**'ve been playing** a lot of tennis recently. She**'s been calling** me every day.*
It also suggests a **temporary** situation: *I**'ve been staying** at my sister's since I came back.* (not permanent) Compare: *I**'ve lived** here all my life.* (permanent)
With *always*, use the simple: *I**'ve always lived** in Kerman.* Not *I've always been living*.
A single short action in the continuous suggests repetition: *He**'s been kicking** the ball against the wall* (again and again). *He**'s kicked** the ball over the fence* (once).

examples.text: I**'ve been going** to bed late recently.
We**'ve been using** my brother's car while ours is being repaired.
The phone**'s been ringing** all morning.
My grandparents **have lived** in this village all their lives.

mistakes.wrong: I've always been living in Toronto.
mistakes.right: I've always lived in Toronto.

mistakes.wrong: She's been phoning me twice today.
mistakes.right: She's phoned me twice today.

points.title: State verbs and verbs with two meanings
points.summary: State verbs use the **simple**: *I've known her for years.* Verbs like *have, think, see* can be continuous only in their action meaning: *I've been thinking about it.*

blocks.md: Verbs for **states** (*know, believe, like, love, want, own, belong, understand, be*) are not normally used in the continuous, even with *for* or *since*: *I**'ve known** him since school.* Not *I've been knowing him*.
Some verbs have a **state** meaning and an **action** meaning:
For the full list of state verbs, see [Stative Verbs](/blog/grammar/stative-verbs/).

examples.text: We**'ve known** each other for twenty years.
I**'ve wanted** a dog since I was a child.
I**'ve been thinking** of changing jobs.
They**'ve been having** a lot of fun on holiday.

mistakes.wrong: I've been knowing her since 2015.
mistakes.right: I've known her since 2015.

mistakes.wrong: She's been owning that shop for years.
mistakes.right: She's owned that shop for years.

points.title: Subtle differences: temporary, unfinished, annoyed
points.summary: The continuous can make a situation sound **temporary**, **unfinished**, or **annoying**: *Who's been using my computer?* The simple sounds more **permanent** or **complete**.

blocks.md: When both forms are grammatical, the continuous adds a nuance:

items: **Temporary vs permanent**: *She**'s been working** in sales* (maybe for now) / *She**'s worked** in sales for twenty years* (her career).
**Unfinished vs complete**: *I**'ve been reading** the report* (I'm in the middle) / *I**'ve read** the report* (I can discuss it).
**Complaint or surprise**: *Who**'s been using** my laptop? Someone**'s been eating** my chocolate!* (I can see signs, and I'm annoyed.)
**Repeated intention**: *I**'ve been meaning** to call you.* (I intended to many times, but didn't.)

blocks.md: In negative sentences, the simple often focuses on the gap since the last time: *I **haven't slept** for two days* (not at all). The continuous describes a pattern: *I **haven't been sleeping** well* (badly, recently).

In formal writing and reports, the simple is preferred for completed achievements: *The project **has reduced** costs by 15%.* The continuous suits ongoing processes: *We **have been monitoring** the results.*

examples.text: Someone**'s been reading** my diary!
I**'ve been meaning** to tell you something.
I **haven't eaten** since breakfast.
I **haven't been eating** well lately.

mistakes.wrong: I've been meaning tell you.
mistakes.right: I've been meaning to tell you.

mistakes.wrong: The company has been reducing costs by 15% so far. (a completed result)
mistakes.right: The company has reduced costs by 15% so far.

items.prompt: I ___ a lot of exercise lately. I feel great.
items.explanation: Repeated activity up to now: *have been doing*.

items.prompt: Which sentence suggests a temporary situation?
options: I've worked from home all my life.
I've been working from home this month.

items.prompt: My neighbour ___ (play) loud music every night this week.
How long ___ your boyfriend?
I ___ about what you said, and I think you're right.
She ___ (have) that bike since she was twelve.

topics.summary: I've lost my keys (connected to now) or I lost my keys yesterday (finished time).
intro: Both tenses talk about the past. The **past simple** (*I lost*) is about a **finished** time. The **present perfect** (*I've lost*) connects the past with **now**.
The most important question is: **do you say or mean a finished time?** If yes, use the past simple. This page goes from that basic rule to the cases where both are possible.

points.title: Finished time or up to now?
points.summary: Past simple with a **finished time** (*yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago*). Present perfect when there's **no finished time** and the past is connected to now.

headers: Present perfect (up to now / no time given)

blocks.md: Words with a **finished time** take the past simple: *yesterday, last night / week / year, ago, in 2015, on Monday, when I was a child, What time…? When…?*
Words that mean **up to now** often take the present perfect: *ever, never, already, yet, so far, since, for* (up to now).
You can't use the present perfect with a finished time: *I saw him yesterday.* Not *I've seen him yesterday*.

examples.text: I **lost** my phone **last week**.
I**'ve lost** my phone. Can you call it?
**When did** you **buy** that dress?
**Have** you **bought** the tickets?

mistakes.wrong: I've seen that film last night.
mistakes.right: I saw that film last night.
mistakes.why: last night is finished: past simple

mistakes.wrong: When have you got home?
mistakes.right: When did you get home?

mistakes.wrong: I have visited my aunt on Sunday.
mistakes.right: I visited my aunt on Sunday.
mistakes.why: on Sunday is finished: past simple

points.title: Have you ever…? Yes, I went there in…
points.summary: Use the present perfect to **ask about or introduce** an experience, then the past simple for the **details** (when, where, how).

blocks.md: Conversations about experiences often start with the present perfect and continue in the past simple:
*A: **Have** you ever **been** to Isfahan?*
*B: Yes, I **have**. I **went** there last spring.*
*A: Really? What **did** you **think** of it?*
*B: I **loved** it. We **stayed** near the bridge.*
The first question is about life up to now (no time). The follow-up questions are about a **specific** visit, so they use the past simple.
*Have you been…?* asks about the experience. *When did you go?* asks about the details.

examples.text: I**'ve met** a famous actor. I **met** him at the airport in Dubai.
**Have** you **tried** this café? ~ Yes, I **had** lunch there on Monday.
She**'s won** a lot of prizes. She **won** her first one when she was ten.

mistakes.wrong: Have you ever been to Japan? ~ Yes, I've been there in 2018.
mistakes.right: Have you ever been to Japan? ~ Yes, I went there in 2018.
mistakes.why: Details with a time: past simple.

mistakes.wrong: I've seen the match. It has been fantastic.
mistakes.right: I've seen the match. It was fantastic.
mistakes.why: Details about the match: past simple.

points.title: Still true now, or finished?
points.summary: *I**'ve lived** here for ten years* = I still live here. *I **lived** there for ten years* = I don't now. People who are dead: past simple.

blocks.md: With *for* and with situations, the tense tells you if the situation is **still true**:

rows: *He**'s worked** at the bank for five years.* (he still does)
*He **worked** at the bank for five years.* (he doesn't now)

blocks.md: When we talk about people who are **no longer alive**, or periods that are over, we use the past simple: *Hafez **wrote** beautiful poetry.* For living people whose work continues, the present perfect is common: *This author **has written** twelve novels* (and may write more).
Think about **now**: Is the situation still going on? Can the person still do it? If not, use the past simple.

examples.text: My grandfather **lived** in Tabriz all his life.
My parents **have lived** in Tabriz all their lives.
Picasso **painted** thousands of works.
She**'s** already **written** three books, and she's only 25.

mistakes.wrong: I've worked there for three years, but then I left.
mistakes.right: I worked there for three years, but then I left.

mistakes.wrong: Einstein has won the Nobel Prize.
mistakes.right: Einstein won the Nobel Prize.
mistakes.why: He's no longer alive: past simple.

points.title: Today, this morning, this year: finished or not?
points.summary: *this morning, today, this week* take the present perfect if the period **isn't over** and the past simple if it **is over**.

blocks.md: Some time phrases can mean a finished or an unfinished period. It depends on **when you are speaking**:

With ***today, this week, this month, this year***, the present perfect is the usual choice while the period continues: *It**'s been** a busy week.* At the end of a period, people often use the past simple: *(on Friday evening) It **was** a busy week.*
If you mention a specific time **within** the unfinished period, use the past simple: *I**'ve** spoken to her **today**. I **spoke** to her **at 9**.*

examples.text: (at 11 am) I**'ve sent** ten emails this morning.
(at 6 pm) I **sent** ten emails this morning.
I**'ve** seen her **today**. We **had** lunch together **at one**.
We**'ve had** a lot of rain **this year**.

mistakes.wrong: (at 9 pm) Have you seen the doctor this morning?
mistakes.right: (at 9 pm) Did you see the doctor this morning?
mistakes.why: At 9 pm the morning is over.

mistakes.wrong: I've phoned him at 10 o'clock today.
mistakes.right: I phoned him at 10 o'clock today.

points.title: American and British English
points.summary: In American English, the past simple is common with *just, already, yet* and *ever*: *I just ate. Did you finish yet?* British English prefers the present perfect.

blocks.md: Both varieties use the present perfect, but American English often uses the **past simple** where British English uses the present perfect, especially with *just, already, yet, ever* and for recent news:

rows: ***Did** you ever **go** to Mexico?* / ***Have** you ever **been**…?*

blocks.md: Both forms are correct. In exams and international English, the present perfect is the safer choice with these words. With a **finished time** (*yesterday, ago*), both varieties use the past simple.
American English also uses *gotten* as a past participle of *get* in some meanings: *It's **gotten** colder.* British English: *It's **got** colder.*

examples.text: (BrE) *Have you **had** lunch yet?* / (AmE) *Did you **have** lunch yet?*
(BrE) *She**'s just left**.* / (AmE) *She **just left**.*
(both) *She **left** ten minutes ago.*

mistakes.wrong: (in any variety) I've just finished it ten minutes ago.
mistakes.right: I finished it ten minutes ago.
mistakes.why: With ago, only the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: (in any variety) Did you see him yet yesterday?
mistakes.right: Did you see him yesterday?
mistakes.why: yet doesn't go with a finished time.

points.title: When both are possible: the meaning changes
points.summary: Sometimes both tenses are correct, with a different focus: *I've always wanted* (still) vs *I always wanted* (not now); *Have you heard?* vs *Did you hear?*

blocks.md: In some contexts, both tenses are grammatical. The choice shows how the speaker sees the event:

items: *I**'ve always wanted** to visit Japan.* (I still want to.) / *I **always wanted** to visit Japan.* (Maybe I've visited now, or I've given up.)
***Have** you **heard**? They're getting married!* (news, now) / ***Did** you **hear** the news this morning?* (a specific occasion)
*I**'ve recently started** running.* / *I **recently started** running.* (Both are fine with *recently*.)
*Who**'s eaten** my sandwich?* (I've just noticed; the result) / *Who **ate** my sandwich?* (also natural, especially in American English)

blocks.md: Speakers also switch tense to show **distance**: *I **haven't seen** him since the party* (up to now) / *I **didn't see** him at the party* (one occasion).

With ***already, just, yet, ever*** and ***recently***, both tenses are acceptable in modern English, though the present perfect is the standard in British English. With **finished time expressions**, only the past simple is correct.

examples.text: My father **has always loved** gardening.
My father **always loved** gardening.
examples.note: he has probably died, or it's no longer true

examples.text: **Have** you **seen** my glasses? I can't find them.
**Did** you **see** my glasses when you were in the kitchen?

mistakes.wrong: I always wanted to try sushi, and I still want to.
mistakes.right: I've always wanted to try sushi, and I still want to.

mistakes.wrong: Have you heard the president's speech last night?
mistakes.right: Did you hear the president's speech last night?

items.prompt: Which sentence is correct in both British and American English?
options: I've already done my homework yesterday.
I already have did my homework.
items.explanation: The present perfect with *already* is correct everywhere.

items.prompt: An American friend says *I just got here.* What is the British English equivalent?
options: I had just got here now.
items.explanation: BrE: present perfect *I've just got here.*

items.prompt: (British English) ___ (you / see) the new Batman film yet?

topics.h1: Quantifiers: All, Most, Each, Every, None
topics.summary: Words that say how many: all students, most of my friends, every day, each of them, both, neither, none.
intro: **Quantifiers** tell us how many or how much: *all, most, some, none, each, every, both, either, neither*. Many can be used with or without ***of***: *most people / most of the people*.

For *much, many, a few* and *a little*, see [Much, Many, A Few, A Little](/blog/grammar/much-many-a-few-a-little/). For *both… and* and *either… or*, see [Both… And, Either… Or](/blog/grammar/both-either-neither-not-only/).

points.title: All, most, some, no: with or without of
points.summary: Use ***all / most / some / no*** + noun for things **in general** (*Most people like music*). Use ***all of / most of / some of / none of*** + ***the / my / these*** + noun, or a pronoun, for a **specific** group (*Most of my friends live here*).

rows: ***All (of) the** children in my class are friendly.*
***Most of the** people I know work hard.*
***Some of the** shops in my street are closed.*

blocks.md: With a **pronoun**, always use *of*: ***most of them**, **some of us**, **all of it**, **none of you***.
***All*** can drop *of* before *the / my / these*: ***all the** students = **all of the** students*. *Most* and *some* can't: ***most of the** students* (not *most the students*).

examples.text: **Most** people in Canada speak English.
**Most of my** friends are married.
**All of us** were tired.
**None of the** shops were open.

mistakes.wrong: Most of people like chocolate.
mistakes.right: Most people like chocolate.

mistakes.wrong: Most the students passed.
mistakes.right: Most of the students passed.

mistakes.wrong: All of them is here.
mistakes.right: All of them are here.

points.title: Each or every?
points.summary: ***Each*** and ***every*** + **singular** noun + **singular** verb. ***Every*** = all of a group, seen together (*Every student passed*). ***Each*** = one by one, separately (*Each child got a present*). Only ***each*** can be used with ***of*** or alone.

rows: one by one: *Each player has a number.*
all together: *Every player wants to win.*
also for two: *She had a ring on each hand.*

blocks.md: Both take a **singular** verb: ***Every** room **has** a TV. **Each** of the rooms **has** a TV.*
For things that happen regularly, use ***every***: ***every** morning, **every** two weeks* (not *each two weeks*).

examples.text: **Every** child needs love.
The teacher spoke to **each** student individually.
**Each of** my parents has a car.
I go to the gym **every** other day.

mistakes.wrong: Every of the students has a laptop.
mistakes.right: Each of the students has a laptop.

mistakes.wrong: Every students are here.
mistakes.right: Every student is here.

mistakes.wrong: I visit my parents each two weeks.
mistakes.right: I visit my parents every two weeks.

points.title: Both, either, neither (of)
points.summary: For **two** things: ***both*** = the one and the other (+ plural); ***either*** = one or the other (+ singular); ***neither*** = not one and not the other (+ singular). With ***of***: *both of / either of / neither of* + ***the / my / them***.

rows: *both of the children, both of them*
*either of the days, either of them*
*neither of the answers, neither of them*

blocks.md: ***Neither*** is already negative, so use a **positive** verb: ***Neither** of them **came**.* (not *didn't come*). In negative sentences, use ***either***: *I **don't** like **either** of them.*
After ***neither of / either of***, a **singular** verb is more formal and a plural verb is common in speech: *Neither of my parents **speaks / speak** English.*
For **more than two**, use *all, any* and *none*: *None of my three brothers…*

examples.text: **Both** my brothers live in Toronto.
You can park on **either** side of the street.
**Neither** restaurant was open.
I don't like **either** of these shirts.

mistakes.wrong: Both of them is teachers.
mistakes.right: Both of them are teachers.

mistakes.wrong: Neither of them didn't come.
mistakes.right: Neither of them came.

mistakes.wrong: I don't want neither of them.
mistakes.right: I don't want either of them.

points.title: All or whole? All, everything, no and none
points.summary: ***The whole*** + singular noun = all of one thing (*the whole day, the whole cake*). ***All*** goes with uncountable and plural nouns (*all the money, all the people*). ***Everything*** is more natural than *all* alone. ***None*** stands alone; ***no*** needs a noun.

rows: *I spent **the whole** day at home. She ate **the whole** pizza.*
***Everything** is fine.* (*All is fine* sounds old-fashioned)
***All** I want is some rest.* (= the only thing)

blocks.md: ***All day / all night / all week*** (no *the*) = the whole day: *I worked **all day**.*
***All*** goes **before** the main verb but **after** *be* and auxiliaries: *We **all** love it. We're **all** tired. They've **all** gone.*

examples.text: I read **the whole** book in one night.
**All** my friends came.
**Everything** went well.
**All** we need is a little more time.
How many tickets are left? ~ **None**.

mistakes.wrong: She spent whole day shopping.
mistakes.right: She spent the whole day shopping.

mistakes.wrong: There are none tickets.
mistakes.right: There are no tickets.

points.title: None of them is or are? All of whom, each and every
points.summary: ***None of*** + plural takes a **singular** verb in formal style and a **plural** verb in everyday English. In relative clauses, use ***all / most / none / both of whom / which***. ***Each and every*** is emphatic. ***Not all*** ≠ ***none***.

rows: ***None of** the candidates **was / were** suitable.* (singular = formal)
*She has three sons, **all of whom** are doctors. I bought two books, **neither of which** was cheap.*
***Each and every** one of you has helped.*
***Not all** students passed.* (some failed) / ***None** of the students passed.*
*every other day* (= every second day), *every few weeks*
***all of us*** (not *all us*); *us all* after a verb: *She thanked **us all**.*

blocks.md: *All… not* can be ambiguous: *All the students didn't pass* may mean *not all*. Write ***Not all** the students passed* or ***None** of the students passed* to be clear.
After a comma, *all of them / both of them* + verb starts a new clause, so it needs *and* or a full stop. In one sentence, use ***of whom / of which***.

examples.text: **None of** the reports **has** been published yet.
I have two brothers, **both of whom** live abroad.
**Not all** doctors agree with this.
I see my parents **every other** weekend.

mistakes.wrong: I have three sisters, all of them are married.
mistakes.right: I have three sisters, all of whom are married.

mistakes.wrong: All us were tired.
mistakes.right: All of us were tired.

items.prompt: I was so hungry that I ate ___ pizza.
How much money is left? ~ ___. We spent it all.
I didn't sleep at all last night. I was awake ___ night. (one word)

topics.h1: Question Tags (…, isn't it? …, don't you?)
topics.summary: Short questions at the end of a sentence to check or ask for agreement: It's cold, isn't it? You like coffee, don't you?
intro: A **question tag** is a short question at the end of a sentence: *It's a nice day, **isn't it**?* We use tags to **check** information or to ask the listener to **agree**.
Usually, a **positive** sentence has a **negative** tag, and a **negative** sentence has a **positive** tag. The tag uses the same auxiliary as the sentence.

points.title: Positive sentence, negative tag (and the other way)
points.summary: Positive + negative tag: *You're Iranian, **aren't you**?* Negative + positive tag: *She doesn't eat meat, **does she**?* Use the same auxiliary as the sentence.

blocks.md: Use the **auxiliary** from the sentence (*be, have, can, will…*). If there's no auxiliary, use ***do / does / did***.
The tag uses a **pronoun**, not a name: *Ali works here, doesn't **he**?* (not *doesn't Ali*)

examples.text: It's hot today, **isn't it**?
You like football, **don't you**?
Your sister lives in Rome, **doesn't she**?
They didn't call, **did they**?

mistakes.wrong: You're tired, isn't it?
mistakes.right: You're tired, aren't you?
mistakes.why: same verb and subject: aren't you

mistakes.wrong: She went home, wasn't she?
mistakes.right: She went home, didn't she?

mistakes.wrong: Tom is here, isn't Tom?
mistakes.right: Tom is here, isn't he?

points.title: Intonation: a real question or asking for agreement?
points.summary: **Rising** intonation (↗) = a real question, I'm not sure. **Falling** intonation (↘) = I'm sure, I want you to agree.

blocks.md: The meaning of a tag depends on your voice:

items: **Rising** (↗): you don't know the answer and really ask: *You're coming tonight, aren't you? ↗* (I'm not sure.)
**Falling** (↘): you're fairly sure and want the listener to agree: *It's a lovely day, isn't it? ↘* (I'm sure it is.)

blocks.md: Tags with falling intonation are very common in small talk, about the weather, food, or shared experiences.

examples.text: It's really cold, isn't it? ↘
You've got the tickets, haven't you? ↗
That was a fantastic film, wasn't it? ↘
The meeting's at three, isn't it? ↗

mistakes.wrong: It's a lovely day, is it? (asking for agreement)
mistakes.right: It's a lovely day, isn't it?

points.title: Special tags: aren't I, let's… shall we, imperatives, there is
points.summary: **I am → aren't I?** **Let's → shall we?** Imperatives → **will you? / won't you? / can you?** **There is → isn't there?** **Everybody → they**.

blocks.md: After ***everyone, everybody, someone, nobody***, the tag uses ***they***: *Somebody called, didn't **they**?* After ***everything, nothing***, use ***it***: *Everything's ready, isn't **it**?*

examples.text: I'm right, **aren't I**?
Let's have a break, **shall we**?
Pass me the salt, **would you**?
There's no milk, **is there**?
examples.note: there is + negative word → is there

mistakes.wrong: I'm late, amn't I?
mistakes.right: I'm late, aren't I?

mistakes.wrong: Let's go, don't we?
mistakes.right: Let's go, shall we?

mistakes.wrong: Nobody came, did he?
mistakes.right: Nobody came, did they?

points.title: Never, hardly, no one: negative words take a positive tag
points.summary: Sentences with **never, hardly, rarely, no, nobody, nothing** are negative, so the tag is **positive**: *You never call me, **do you**?*

blocks.md: Words like ***never, seldom, rarely, hardly, scarcely, no, nobody, nothing, nowhere*** make the sentence **negative**, even without *not*. So use a **positive** tag: *She hardly eats anything, **does she**?*
Remember the pronoun rules: *Nobody knows, do **they**? Nothing happened, did **it**?*

examples.text: You **never** listen to me, **do you**?
He **hardly** ever smiles, **does he**?
**No one** was hurt, **were they**?
There's **nothing** we can do, **is there**?

mistakes.wrong: You never call me, don't you?
mistakes.right: You never call me, do you?

mistakes.wrong: Nobody saw it, didn't they?
mistakes.right: Nobody saw it, did they?

points.title: Same-way tags and tags in requests
points.summary: **Positive + positive** tags show surprise, interest or irony: *So you're the new boss, **are you**?* Negative sentence + positive tag in polite requests: *You couldn't help me, **could you**?*

blocks.md: **Same-way tags** (positive sentence + positive tag) don't really ask for information. They show **surprise, interest, or sarcasm**, and they often follow *so* or *oh*: *Oh, you're a chef, **are you**? So you think it's funny, **do you**?*
In polite **requests**, a negative statement with a positive tag sounds tentative and polite: *You **couldn't** lend me £10, **could you**? You **wouldn't** have a pen, **would you**?*
***I don't suppose … , do you / could you?*** is another tentative pattern: *I don't suppose you know where she is, **do you**?*
Same-way tags with an angry tone can sound aggressive: *Oh, you want a fight, do you?* Use them carefully.

examples.text: So you've finally arrived, **have you**?
You're moving to Japan, **are you**? How exciting!
You couldn't open the window, **could you**?
I don't suppose you've seen my keys, **have you**?

mistakes.wrong: You couldn't help me, couldn't you?
mistakes.right: You couldn't help me, could you?

items.prompt: I'm in the right room, ___?
Let's watch a film, ___?
There's a bank near here, ___? (two words)
You've never been to Spain, ___?
She hardly ever goes out, ___?
Nobody called while I was out, ___? (two words)

topics.summary: How to make questions: Are you…? Do you…? Where do you live? Who called you? What is it like? Don't you like it?
intro: In English questions, the **auxiliary verb** (*be, do, have, can, will…*) usually comes **before** the subject: ***Are** you hungry? **Do** you like tea? **Can** she swim?*

With question words (*what, where, when…*), the word goes first: ***Where do** you live?* This page goes from basic questions to negative and echo questions. For *Do you know where…?*, see [Indirect Questions](/blog/grammar/indirect-questions/).

points.title: Yes/no questions: Are you…? Do you…? Can you…?
points.summary: Put **be** or an **auxiliary** (*do, does, did, can, will, have*) before the subject: *Are you ready? Does she work here? Can you swim?*

blocks.md: With *be* and modals, just change the order. With other verbs, add ***do / does / did*** and use the **base verb**: ***Does** she **like** it?* Not *Does she likes it?*
Short answers repeat the auxiliary: *Yes, she **does**. / No, I **can't**. / Yes, they **are**.*

examples.text: **Are** you a student? ~ Yes, I **am**.
**Do** you speak English? ~ Yes, I **do**.
**Did** they win the match? ~ No, they **didn't**.
**Have** you finished? ~ Not yet.

mistakes.wrong: You are hungry? (in writing)
mistakes.right: Are you hungry?

mistakes.wrong: Does she likes coffee?
mistakes.right: Does she like coffee?

mistakes.wrong: Do you can swim?
mistakes.right: Can you swim?

points.title: Wh- question words: what, where, when, who, why, how
points.summary: Put the question word **first**, then the auxiliary and the subject: *Where do you live? What is your name? Why did she leave?*

blocks.md: Order: **question word + auxiliary / be + subject + main verb**: ***Where do** you **work**?* ***What are** you **doing**?*

examples.text: **What** is your phone number?
**Where** did you go on holiday?
**Why** is the shop closed?
**Whose** keys are these?

mistakes.wrong: Where you live?
mistakes.right: Where do you live?

mistakes.wrong: What time the film starts?
mistakes.right: What time does the film start?

mistakes.wrong: Why you are sad?
mistakes.right: Why are you sad?

points.title: How much, how many, how long, how often, how far
points.summary: **How + adjective / adverb** asks about amount, time and frequency: *How much is it? How long does it take? How often do you exercise?*

blocks.md: ***How long does it take** (to…)?* asks about the time a journey or job needs: *How long does it take to get to the airport? ~ It takes about 40 minutes.*
***How much*** goes with uncountable nouns (*money, time, water*); ***how many*** with plural nouns (*people, books*).

examples.text: **How much** does this jacket cost?
**How many** brothers and sisters do you have?
**How long** does it take to walk there?
**How often** do you visit your parents?

mistakes.wrong: How many money do you have?
mistakes.right: How much money do you have?

mistakes.wrong: How long it takes to get there?
mistakes.right: How long does it take to get there?

points.title: Who saw you? or Who did you see? Subject and object questions
