points.summary: When **who / what** is the **subject**, don't use *do / did*: *Who called you?* When it's the **object**, use *do / did*: *Who did you call?*

blocks.md: Ask yourself: is the question word the person or thing that **does** the action? If yes, it's the **subject**: use normal word order, no *do*: ***Who broke** the window? ~ Tom did.*
If the question word is the person or thing that **receives** the action, use *do / does / did*: ***Who did** Tom **see**? ~ He saw Maria.*

examples.text: **Who told** you that?
**Who did** you **tell**?
**What happened** at the meeting?
**Which team won** the match?

mistakes.wrong: What did happen?
mistakes.right: What happened?

mistakes.wrong: Who did break the window? (asking who did it)
mistakes.right: Who broke the window?

mistakes.wrong: Who you saw at the party?
mistakes.right: Who did you see at the party?

points.title: Who is she talking to? What is it like? Prepositions at the end
points.summary: In questions, prepositions usually go at the **end**: *Who are you talking **to**? Where are you **from**?* **What is it like?** = describe it.

blocks.md: When a verb has a preposition (*talk to, look at, come from, wait for, think about*), the preposition goes at the **end** of the question: *What are you looking **at**? Who is this present **for**?*
***What is … like?*** asks for a **description**: *What's your new school **like**? ~ It's big and modern.* It's different from *Do you like…?* (Do you enjoy it?)
In very formal English, the preposition can go first: ***To whom** did you speak?* In normal English, *Who did you speak to?* is much more common.

examples.text: **Where** are you **from**?
**What** are you thinking **about**?
**Who** is the letter **from**?
**What's** the weather **like** in Vancouver?

mistakes.wrong: From where are you?
mistakes.right: Where are you from?

mistakes.wrong: How is your new boss like?
mistakes.right: What is your new boss like?

points.title: What or which? What kind of…?
points.summary: **which** = a choice from a small, known group: *Which colour do you want, red or blue?* **what** = an open choice: *What colour is your car?*

blocks.md: Use ***which*** when there is a **limited** number of options, often mentioned or obvious: ***Which** of these bags is yours? **Which** way is the station, left or right?*
Use ***what*** for an **open** question with many possible answers: ***What** music do you like? **What** time is it?*
***Which one(s)?*** and ***which of*** + plural: ***Which one** do you want? **Which of** your friends is coming?* (Not *what of*.)
***What kind of / what sort of*** asks about a type: ***What kind of** films do you like?*

examples.text: **Which** do you prefer, tea or coffee?
**What** do you want for your birthday?
**Which of** these photos do you like best?
**What kind of** job are you looking for?

mistakes.wrong: What of these is yours?
mistakes.right: Which of these is yours?

mistakes.wrong: What one do you want?
mistakes.right: Which one do you want?

points.title: Negative questions: Don't you…? Isn't it…?
points.summary: Negative questions (*Don't you…? Isn't it…? Haven't you…?*) show **surprise**, ask for **agreement**, or check something we **expect** to be true.

blocks.md: Negative questions are used:

items: for **surprise**: ***Don't** you **like** chocolate?* (I'm surprised.)
to ask for **agreement**: ***Isn't** it a beautiful day?* (I think it is.)
to check what we **expect**: ***Haven't** we **met** before?* (I think we have.)
in **complaints**: ***Can't** you be quiet?*

blocks.md: Answering: answer about the **fact**, not the question form: *Don't you like coffee? ~ **No**, I don't. (= I don't like it) / **Yes**, I do. (= I like it)*
In formal English, *not* can go after the subject: ***Do you not** agree?*

examples.text: **Don't** you **remember** me?
**Isn't** this view amazing?
**Haven't** you **finished** yet?
**Wouldn't** it be better to wait?

mistakes.wrong: Don't you like it? ~ No, I like it.
mistakes.right: Don't you like it? ~ Yes, I do. / Yes, I like it.

mistakes.wrong: Do you don't want it?
mistakes.right: Don't you want it?

points.title: Echo questions and statement questions: You did what?
points.summary: **Echo questions** repeat part of what someone said to show surprise or check: *She's moving to Peru. ~ She's moving where?* **Statement questions** keep normal word order with rising intonation: *You're leaving?*

blocks.md: An **echo question** repeats the sentence and replaces the surprising part with a question word, with strong stress: *I paid $500 for it. ~ You paid **how much**?* *He married his boss. ~ He married **who**?*

A **statement question** uses normal word order with **rising** intonation. It checks or expresses surprise about something we think we heard or understood: *You've finished **already**?* *So you're not coming?*
Short **reply questions** show interest: *I've just got engaged. ~ **Have you**? Congratulations!* See [So Do I, Neither Do I](/blog/grammar/so-do-i-neither-do-i/).
These are spoken forms. In writing, use normal questions, except in dialogue.

examples.text: I've sold the car. ~ You've sold **what**?
They're getting married in Bali. ~ **Where**?
You're not hungry? I made a huge dinner!
He's 90. ~ **Is he**? He looks much younger.

mistakes.wrong: You paid how much? (in a formal essay)
mistakes.right: How much did you pay?

items.prompt: ___ tired? You've been working for ten hours!
*Don't you eat meat?* ~ ___ I'm a vegetarian.
items.explanation: Answer about the fact: *No, I don't.*

items.prompt: ___ (it / not / be) a lovely evening?

topics.summary: Words that make adjectives weaker or stronger: a bit cold, fairly good, quite nice, pretty busy, rather expensive.
intro: ***Fairly, quite, pretty*** and ***rather*** go before adjectives and adverbs to mean “more than a little, but not very”: *The test was **fairly** easy. It's **pretty** cold today.*
Their exact meaning depends on the word after them, on your voice, and on British or American English.

points.title: A bit, fairly, quite, very: how strong?
points.summary: From weaker to stronger: ***a bit / a little*** < ***fairly*** < ***quite / pretty*** < ***very / really*** < ***extremely***.

rows: more than a little, not very
a bit more than *fairly* (*pretty* is informal)

blocks.md: ***A bit*** is common with **negative** adjectives: *It's **a bit** expensive. I'm **a bit** tired.*
These words come **before** the adjective: *It's **quite** big.* With a noun, the usual order is ***quite a*** + adjective + noun: *It's **quite a** big house.*

examples.text: I'm **a bit** hungry.
My English is **fairly** good.
The restaurant was **pretty** busy.
She's **really** kind.

mistakes.wrong: It's very much cold.
mistakes.right: It's very cold.

mistakes.wrong: I'm a few tired.
mistakes.right: I'm a bit tired.

points.title: Quite: fairly or completely?
points.summary: With most adjectives, ***quite*** = **fairly** (*quite good*). With **extreme** or **absolute** adjectives (*amazing, impossible, sure, right*), ***quite*** = **completely** (*quite impossible, quite right*). ***Quite a lot / quite a few*** = a fairly large amount.

rows: I like it, but not very much

blocks.md: In **American English**, *quite* often means *very*: *The food was **quite** good* (= very good). In British English, it often means *fairly*.
***Not quite*** = almost: *I haven't **quite** finished.*

examples.text: The hotel was **quite** nice.
Are you **quite** sure?
I've read **quite a lot of** his books.
I'm **not quite** ready. Give me two minutes.

mistakes.wrong: I quite am sure.
mistakes.right: I'm quite sure.

mistakes.wrong: There were quite much people.
mistakes.right: There were quite a lot of people.

points.title: Rather and pretty: rather expensive, pretty good
points.summary: ***Rather*** is like *quite*, but it often sounds **negative** or **surprised**: *It's rather expensive.* With positive words, it means *surprisingly*: *The film was rather good.* ***Pretty*** is informal: *pretty good, pretty tired*.

rows: *It was **rather a** long day.* = *a **rather** long day*

blocks.md: ***Rather*** is more common in British English and in writing. In everyday American English, *pretty* is more common.
Don't confuse *rather* (= fairly) with ***would rather*** (= prefer): *I'd rather stay at home.*

examples.text: The instructions were **rather** confusing.
I **rather** liked the film.
It was **rather a** strange evening.
I'm **pretty** sure he'll come.

mistakes.wrong: It was a rather good.
mistakes.right: It was rather good.

mistakes.wrong: The test was rather more easy.
mistakes.right: The test was rather easier.

points.title: Somewhat, relatively, reasonably: formal alternatives
points.summary: In formal English, use ***somewhat, slightly, reasonably, moderately*** and ***relatively*** instead of *a bit, quite* or *pretty*: *The results were **somewhat** disappointing. Prices are **relatively** low.* ***Rather*** and ***quite*** can also go with verbs: *I **rather** like it. I **quite** understand.*

blocks.md: ***I quite understand*** = I understand completely (polite). ***I quite like it*** (BrE) = I like it, but not very much.
***Somewhat*** and ***relatively*** are common in academic writing: *These results are **relatively** reliable.*

examples.text: The new system is **somewhat** slower.
Housing is **relatively** cheap in this region.
The restaurant is **reasonably** priced.
I **quite** understand your concern.

mistakes.wrong: The results were somewhat of disappointing.
mistakes.right: The results were somewhat disappointing.

mistakes.wrong: It's relatively a cheap area.
mistakes.right: It's a relatively cheap area.

items.prompt: It's ___ cold in here. Can you close the window?
I'm ___ sure he'll be late again. He always is.
The exam was ___ easier than I expected. (one word)

topics.summary: Myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves, and each other.
intro: Use a **reflexive pronoun** when the subject and the object are the **same** person: *I cut **myself**. She taught **herself** English.*
Use ***each other*** when two or more people do something **to one another**: *They love **each other**.*

points.title: Myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves
points.summary: Use a **reflexive pronoun** when the **subject and object are the same**: *I hurt **myself**. They enjoyed **themselves**.*

blocks.md: Compare: *She looked at **her**.* (another woman) / *She looked at **herself**.* (in the mirror)
Spelling: singular *-self*, plural *-selves*. Say *himself* and *themselves* (not *hisself, theirselves*).

examples.text: I cut **myself** while I was cooking.
Be careful! Don't hurt **yourself**.
The cat is washing **itself**.
We introduced **ourselves** to the new neighbours.
She taught **herself** to play the guitar.

mistakes.wrong: He hurt hisself.
mistakes.right: He hurt himself.

mistakes.wrong: They enjoyed theirselves.
mistakes.right: They enjoyed themselves.

mistakes.wrong: We looked at ourself in the mirror.
mistakes.right: We looked at ourselves in the mirror.

points.title: Enjoy yourself, help yourself, by myself; relax, feel, meet
points.summary: Some verbs often take a reflexive pronoun: ***enjoy yourself, help yourself, behave yourself, introduce yourself***. Many verbs usually **don't** in English: *relax, feel, concentrate, meet, wash, get dressed*. ***By myself*** = alone.

blocks.md: ***Enjoy*** needs an object: *Did you **enjoy yourself**? Did you **enjoy the party**?* (not *Did you enjoy?*)
Use *wash, shave* and *get dressed* without *myself* unless you want to emphasise it: *I got up, **washed** and **got dressed**.*

examples.text: Enjoy **yourselves**!
Please **help yourself** to coffee.
I **feel** much better today.
She lives **by herself**.

mistakes.wrong: Relax yourself and sit down.
mistakes.right: Relax and sit down.

mistakes.wrong: I feel myself tired.
mistakes.right: I feel tired.

mistakes.wrong: We met ourselves at university.
mistakes.right: We met at university.

mistakes.wrong: Did you enjoy?
mistakes.right: Did you enjoy yourself?

points.title: Each other and one another
points.summary: Use ***each other*** (or ***one another***) when two or more people do something **to the other(s)**: *Ali and Sara love **each other**.* Compare: *They blamed **themselves*** (each blamed himself or herself) / *They blamed **each other*** (A blamed B, and B blamed A).

rows: *They blamed **themselves**.* (each one blamed himself or herself)
*They blamed **each other**.* (A blamed B, B blamed A)

blocks.md: ***Each other's*** = possessive: *They borrowed **each other's** notes.*
***One another*** means the same and is a little more formal: *The students helped **one another**.*
Some verbs don't need *each other*: *They **met** in 2010. They **kissed**. They **got married**.*

examples.text: My brother and I call **each other** every day.
They don't talk to **each other** any more.
We read **each other's** essays.
The team members support **one another**.

mistakes.wrong: They love themselves very much. (meaning A loves B)
mistakes.right: They love each other very much.

mistakes.wrong: We send messages each other.
mistakes.right: We send messages to each other.

mistakes.wrong: They know each others.
mistakes.right: They know each other.

points.title: Emphatic myself: I did it myself
points.summary: Use a reflexive pronoun for **emphasis**: *I made the cake **myself*** (= I made it, not someone else). *The manager **herself** called me* (= the manager, not her assistant).

rows: the president, not someone less important

blocks.md: An emphatic reflexive can be removed and the sentence is still correct: *I made it (myself).* This is the difference from normal reflexives (*I hurt myself*).
Compare: *She **herself** told me.* (she, not another person) / *She told **herself**…* (she said it to herself)

examples.text: Did you make this dress **yourself**?
The hotel **itself** was nice, but the area was noisy.
I **myself** have never been to Japan.
We built the shed **ourselves**.

mistakes.wrong: I fixed the car by me.
mistakes.right: I fixed the car by myself.

mistakes.wrong: The director hisself answered the phone.
mistakes.right: The director himself answered the phone.

points.title: Me or myself? Reflexives after prepositions
points.summary: Don't use ***myself*** instead of ***me / I*** to sound polite: *Please contact **me*** (not *contact myself*). After **prepositions of place**, use an **object pronoun**: *She put the bag **beside her***. Use a reflexive when the object is the same person as the subject: *He's talking **to himself***.

rows: *He was talking to him.* (= to another man)

blocks.md: ***Myself*** as an object is correct when the subject is ***I*** (*I hurt myself*) or for emphasis (*I did it myself*). Using it as a “polite” subject or object is a common mistake in business English.

After prepositions of **place**, use object pronouns: *She looked **around her**. He put his bag **next to him**.* Use a reflexive when the meaning is “the same person”: *She was angry **with herself**.*

examples.text: If you have questions, please ask **me**.
**My colleague and I** will present the results.
She looked **around her** nervously.
He was very pleased **with himself**.

mistakes.wrong: Please send the report to myself.
mistakes.right: Please send the report to me.

mistakes.wrong: Myself and Ali organised the event.
mistakes.right: Ali and I organised the event.

mistakes.wrong: She had no money with herself.
mistakes.right: She had no money with her.

items.prompt: Did you paint this picture ___? It's beautiful!
The food was fine, but the restaurant ___ was dirty.
Nobody helped me. I did it all ___. (one word)

topics.h1: Reporting Verbs (She promised to…, He denied…)
topics.summary: Verbs that report what someone said and how: She promised to call. He denied taking it. They suggested going by train.
intro: Instead of *say* and *tell*, we can use **reporting verbs** that show the speaker's purpose: *promise, refuse, warn, admit, suggest*. *“I'll definitely call you.” → She **promised to call** me.*

Each verb has its own **pattern**: *to* + verb, object + *to*, *-ing*, preposition + *-ing*, or a *that* clause. This page groups them. For the basics, see [Reported Speech](/blog/grammar/reported-speech/).

points.title: Verb + to: agree, offer, promise, refuse, threaten
points.summary: **agree / offer / promise / refuse / threaten / decide / claim + to + verb**: *He offered to help me. She refused to answer.*

blocks.md: The negative is ***not to***: *He **promised not to** tell anyone.*
These verbs are followed directly by *to* + verb, with **no object**: *She offered **to help** me.* Not *She offered me to help*.

examples.text: My brother **offered to drive** us to the airport.
The manager **refused to give** me a refund.
She **promised not to be** late again.
They **threatened to leave** if nothing changed.

mistakes.wrong: He offered me to help.
mistakes.right: He offered to help me.

mistakes.wrong: She refused answering the question.
mistakes.right: She refused to answer the question.

points.title: Verb + object + to: advise, remind, warn, encourage, invite
points.summary: **advise / ask / tell / remind / warn / encourage / invite / persuade / order + person + to + verb**: *She reminded me to call my mum.*

rows: *“Would you like to come to dinner?”*
*He **encouraged me to apply** for the job.*

blocks.md: These verbs need a **person** (object) before *to*: *She advised **me** to rest.* Not *She advised to rest* (in this pattern).
The negative is ***not to***: *The doctor **warned him not to** drink alcohol.*

examples.text: My teacher **encouraged me to enter** the competition.
The police **warned people not to travel**.
She **persuaded her father to buy** a new car.
They **invited us to stay** for the weekend.

mistakes.wrong: She advised to me see a doctor.
mistakes.right: She advised me to see a doctor.

mistakes.wrong: He reminded me that I call him.
mistakes.right: He reminded me to call him.

points.title: Verb + -ing and verb + preposition + -ing: deny, admit, apologise for, accuse of
points.summary: **deny / admit / recommend / mention + -ing**. **apologise for / insist on / blame for / accuse of / congratulate on / thank for + -ing**.

blocks.md: After *deny* and *admit*, we can also use ***having + past participle*** for the past: *He **denied having taken** it.* Both forms are correct.
With *accuse, blame, congratulate, thank*, the person comes first: *She **blamed me for** the mistake.*

examples.text: The minister **denied lying** to Parliament.
I **apologise for** not **calling** you back.
She **thanked me for helping** her.
They **blamed the driver for causing** the accident.

mistakes.wrong: He denied to steal the car.
mistakes.right: He denied stealing the car.

mistakes.wrong: She apologised to be late.
mistakes.right: She apologised for being late.

mistakes.wrong: They accused him for lying.
mistakes.right: They accused him of lying.

points.title: Verb + that: explain, admit, claim, complain, agree, insist
points.summary: **explain / admit / claim / complain / agree / insist / point out / announce + (that) + clause**: *She explained that the train was late.*

blocks.md: Many reporting verbs can be followed by a ***that*** clause: *He **complained that** the room was too cold. They **announced that** the shop would close.*
*That* is often left out after common verbs (*say, explain, admit*), but it is usually kept after more formal verbs (*announce, claim, point out*).
Some verbs have **two patterns**: *She **admitted taking** it. / She **admitted that** she had taken it.* *He **agreed to come**. / He **agreed that** it was a good idea.*
With *explain*, the person needs *to*: *She **explained to me** that…* Not *She explained me that…*

examples.text: She **explained (to me) that** the office was closed.
He **complained that** the food was cold.
The company **announced that** it would cut 200 jobs.
My friend **pointed out that** I had made a mistake.

mistakes.wrong: He explained me that the bus was late.
mistakes.right: He explained to me that the bus was late.

mistakes.wrong: She complained the food was cold to the manager that.
mistakes.right: She complained to the manager that the food was cold.

points.title: Suggest and recommend: the right patterns
points.summary: **suggest / recommend + -ing**, **+ (that) + someone + (should) + verb**, or **+ noun**. Not *suggest someone to do*.

rows: *She **suggested that we should go** to the beach.* (BrE)
*She **suggested we went** to the beach.* (BrE, informal)

blocks.md: ***Suggest*** and ***recommend*** can't take *person + to + verb*: *She suggested **that I see** a doctor* / *She suggested **seeing** a doctor.* Not *She suggested me to see a doctor*.
***Recommend*** works the same way: *I **recommend booking** early. I **recommend that you book** early.* (*Recommend someone to do* is heard in British English but is often considered incorrect.)

examples.text: My friend **suggested trying** the new café.
The doctor **suggested that I get** more sleep.
I **recommend that** everyone **should** read this book.
Can you **suggest** a good hotel?

mistakes.wrong: He suggested me to buy a new car.
mistakes.right: He suggested (that) I buy a new car. / He suggested buying a new car.

mistakes.wrong: She suggested to go out.
mistakes.right: She suggested going out.

points.title: Reporting with nouns and adjectives: the claim that, her refusal to
points.summary: Many reporting verbs have noun forms with the same patterns: **the claim that…, her refusal to…, his insistence on…, my suggestion that…**. Adjectives too: **sure that, aware that, adamant that**.

rows: *The **claim that** the drug is safe is false.*
*I liked your **suggestion that** we leave early.*

blocks.md: These nouns are common in **formal writing and news**: *The government's **decision to** raise taxes… The **announcement that** the factory would close…*
Adjectives can report attitudes: *She was **adamant that** she was right. He was **confident that** he would win. They were **aware that** it was risky.*

examples.text: The **news that** the president had resigned shocked everyone.
Her **refusal to** cooperate made things difficult.
There was **no mention of** the problem in the report.
He was **adamant that** he hadn't seen anything.

mistakes.wrong: His insistence to pay was annoying.
mistakes.right: His insistence on paying was annoying.

mistakes.wrong: Her refusal of answering surprised us.
mistakes.right: Her refusal to answer surprised us.

items.prompt: *“I won't sign the contract.”* → She ___ the contract.
*“I'll lend you my car if you need it.”* → He ___ me his car.
*“I'll never do it again, I promise.”* → He promised ___ (not / do) it again.
*“Remember to lock the door!”* → My mum ___ the door.
*“Don't touch the wire.”* → The electrician ___ the wire.
*“Why don't you join the club?”* → She encouraged me ___ (join) the club.
*“It wasn't me! I didn't break it.”* → He ___ it.
*“I'm so sorry I forgot your birthday.”* → She ___ my birthday.
*“You cheated in the exam!”* → The teacher accused him ___ (cheat) in the exam.
*“The lift is broken,”* he said. → He ___ the lift was broken.
Which sentence is correct?
options: She explained us that the meeting was postponed.
She explained that us the meeting was postponed.
She explained to us the meeting postponing.
She explained to us that the meeting was postponed.

items.prompt: The president ___ (announce) that he would not run again.

topics.h1: Should Have, Could Have, Would Have, Needn't Have
topics.summary: Talking about the past that didn't happen: I should have studied. You could have called. You needn't have bought it.
intro: We use ***modal + have + past participle*** to talk about things in the past that **didn't happen** or that we **regret**: *I **should have** left earlier.* (I didn't, and now I'm late.)

For deductions about the past (*must have, can't have, might have*), see [Modals of Deduction](/blog/grammar/modals-of-deduction/#md-past-must-cant). For *if* sentences about the past, see [Third Conditional](/blog/grammar/third-conditional/).

points.title: Should have / shouldn't have: regrets and criticism
points.summary: **should have + past participle** = it was a good idea, but it didn't happen. **shouldn't have** = it happened, but it was a mistake.

rows: it didn't happen (but it was a good idea)
it happened (but it was a bad idea)

blocks.md: We use these forms for **regrets** about our own actions and **criticism** of other people's: *We **should have** booked a table. You **shouldn't have** shouted at him.*
***Ought to have*** means the same as *should have* but is more formal: *You **ought to have** told me.*
In speech, *should have* sounds like /ˈʃʊdəv/ (*should've*). Never write *should of*.

examples.text: I **should have** brought a jacket. I'm freezing.
You **shouldn't have** eaten all that cake.
They **should have** checked the weather before they left.
**Should** I **have** told her?

mistakes.wrong: I should have went to the doctor.
mistakes.right: I should have gone to the doctor.

mistakes.wrong: You should of called me.
mistakes.right: You should have called me.

mistakes.wrong: I should studied more.
mistakes.right: I should have studied more.

points.title: Could have: a chance you didn't take
points.summary: **could have + past participle** = it was possible, but it didn't happen: *I **could have** gone to university, but I started working.*

blocks.md: *Could have* describes a **possibility** or **opportunity** in the past that **didn't happen**: *We **could have** stayed longer, but we were tired.*

It's also used for **criticism** (*you didn't do it, and you should have*): *You **could have** told me you were coming!* And for things that nearly happened: *That was dangerous. You **could have** had an accident.*
***Couldn't have*** = it wasn't possible: *I **couldn't have** come. I was in hospital.*

examples.text: She **could have** been a professional singer.
You **could have** asked for help!
The accident **could have** been much worse.
I **couldn't have** finished without you.

mistakes.wrong: I could have go to the party, but I was too tired.
mistakes.right: I could have gone to the party, but I was too tired.

mistakes.wrong: You could helped me.
mistakes.right: You could have helped me.

points.title: Would have: what you were willing to do
points.summary: **would have + past participle** = you were ready or willing to do something, but it didn't happen: *I **would have** helped you, but you didn't ask.*

blocks.md: Outside *if* sentences, *would have* still describes an **imagined past**: something that was going to happen or that you were willing to do, but didn't: *I **would have** called, but my phone was dead.*
Often the *if* part is hidden: *I **would have** come (if you had invited me).*
***Wouldn't have*** + past participle = you were not willing, or it wasn't going to happen: *I **wouldn't have** said yes anyway.*

examples.text: I **would have** bought it, but it was too expensive.
She **would have** loved this place.
We **would have** stayed, but the kids were tired.
He **wouldn't have** agreed, even if you'd asked.

mistakes.wrong: I would have came, but I was sick.
mistakes.right: I would have come, but I was sick.

points.title: Needn't have or didn't need to?
points.summary: **needn't have + past participle** = you did it, but it wasn't necessary. **didn't need to** = it wasn't necessary (you probably didn't do it).

rows: *I **didn't need to** cook. We went to a restaurant.*

blocks.md: ***Needn't have*** + past participle means you **did** something that **wasn't necessary**: *You **needn't have** brought flowers.* (You brought them, but it wasn't necessary.)
***Didn't need to*** + base verb says it **wasn't necessary**, and usually you didn't do it: *I **didn't need to** wear a coat. It was warm.*
*Needn't have* is mainly British English. In American English, people usually say *didn't need to* (or *didn't have to*) for both meanings: *I **didn't need to** cook, but I did.*

examples.text: You **needn't have** hurried. The meeting started late.
We **didn't need to** book. There were lots of free tables.
I **needn't have** worried. The exam was easy.
She **didn't need to** wait long. The bus came quickly.

mistakes.wrong: I needn't have worry about the test.
mistakes.right: I needn't have worried about the test.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't need to brought an umbrella.
mistakes.right: I didn't need to bring an umbrella.

points.title: You shouldn't have!, should have for expectations, might have for annoyance
points.summary: *You **shouldn't have**!* = a polite thank you for a gift. *They **should have** arrived by now* = expected. *You **might have** warned me!* = annoyance.

blocks.md: Some past modal forms have special meanings:

items: ***You shouldn't have!*** is a polite, warm reaction when someone gives you a present or does something kind. It doesn't mean they did something wrong: *Oh, flowers! You **shouldn't have**!*

***Should have*** + past participle can describe an **expectation** about the past: *The parcel **should have arrived** yesterday.* (It was expected, but it hasn't arrived.) / *They **should have landed** by now.*
***Might have / could have*** + past participle can express **annoyance**: *You **might have** told me you weren't coming!*

blocks.md: The meaning depends on the context and the tone of voice.

examples.text: A cake for me? Oh, you **shouldn't have**!
The train **should have left** ten minutes ago. Why are we still here?
You **might have** asked before you took my car!
By now they **should have finished** the building.

mistakes.wrong: You shouldn't have bought me. (meaning thank you)
mistakes.right: You shouldn't have! / You shouldn't have bought me anything!

items.prompt: I ___ you to the airport, but my car was at the garage.
items.explanation: Willing, but it didn't happen: *would have driven*.

items.prompt: What does *My father would have loved this restaurant* suggest?
options: He never saw it (he's probably no longer alive).

items.prompt: We ___ (would / come) to the party, but we didn't know about it.
I took a taxi to the station, but the train was late. I ___ a taxi. (British English)
items.explanation: I took it, but it wasn't necessary: *needn't have taken*.

items.prompt: The museum was free, so we ___ tickets. We just walked in.
items.explanation: It wasn't necessary, so we didn't: *didn't need to buy*.

items.prompt: You ___ (need / not / bring) a present, but thank you!
items.explanation: You brought one, but it wasn't necessary.

topics.h1: Should, Ought To and Had Better
topics.summary: Giving advice and saying what is right or expected: You should see a doctor. You'd better hurry. It should arrive tomorrow.
intro: We use ***should*** to give **advice** and to say what we think is **right**: *You **should** drink more water.* ***Ought to*** means almost the same, and ***had better*** is stronger, often a warning.

*Should* is weaker than *must*: it's advice, not a rule. For obligation, see [Must and Have To](/blog/grammar/must-have-to/). For past regrets (*I should have…*), see [Should Have, Could Have, Needn't Have](/blog/grammar/should-have-could-have-neednt-have/).

points.title: Should and shouldn't for advice
points.summary: **should / shouldn't + base verb** for advice and opinions: *You **should** go to bed earlier. You **shouldn't** eat so much sugar.*

rows: *I think you **should** apologise. I **don't think** you **should** go.*

blocks.md: *Should* is the same for every person and is followed by the **base verb**: *She **should** rest.* Not *She shoulds rest* or *She should to rest*.
To give a softer opinion, we often use ***I think … should*** or ***I don't think … should***: *I **don't think** you **should** buy it.* (more natural than *I think you shouldn't buy it*)

examples.text: You **should** try the fish. It's delicious.
You **shouldn't** drive when you're tired.
What **should** I wear to the wedding?
I **think** we **should** leave now.

mistakes.wrong: You should to see a doctor.
mistakes.right: You should see a doctor.

mistakes.wrong: She shoulds study more.
mistakes.right: She should study more.

mistakes.wrong: Do I should call him?
mistakes.right: Should I call him?

points.title: Ought to
points.summary: **ought to + base verb** = should. It's a little more formal and is less common in questions and negatives: *You **ought to** call your mother.*

blocks.md: ***Ought to*** has the same meaning as *should* for advice and what's right: *You **ought to** tell the truth.* = *You **should** tell the truth.*
Unlike *should*, it has ***to***: *ought **to** go* (not *ought go*). It is the same for every person: *She **ought to** go.*
The negative ***ought not to / oughtn't to*** exists but sounds formal. Questions with *ought* (*Ought I to…?*) are rare. Most people use *should* for both: *You **shouldn't** go. **Should** I go?*
*Ought to* often suggests a duty or what is morally right: *We **ought to** help them.* In American English, *should* is much more common.

examples.text: You **ought to** apologise to her.
We **ought to** be more careful with money.
You **ought not to** park there.
Ought I to tell him? → **Should** I tell him?

mistakes.wrong: You ought apologise.
mistakes.right: You ought to apologise.

mistakes.wrong: She oughts to know.
mistakes.right: She ought to know.

points.title: Had better: strong advice and warnings
points.summary: **had better ('d better) + base verb** = strong advice for a particular situation, often with a warning: *You**'d better** hurry or you'll miss the train.*

blocks.md: ***Had better*** is stronger than *should*. It suggests that something **bad** will happen if you don't follow the advice: *You**'d better** take an umbrella. It's going to rain.*
It's about a **specific situation now or soon**, not general advice: *You**'d better** go now* (not *You'd better eat vegetables in general*).
Form: ***had better*** (usually ***'d better***) + base verb. Negative: ***had better not***: *You**'d better not** be late.* Even though it uses *had*, it's about the **present or future**.

examples.text: We**'d better** leave now. The traffic is terrible.
You**'d better not** tell Mum about this.
I**'d better** call my wife. She's waiting for me.
You**'d better** be careful. That dog bites.

mistakes.wrong: You'd better to go now.
mistakes.right: You'd better go now.

mistakes.wrong: You hadn't better be late.
mistakes.right: You'd better not be late.

mistakes.wrong: You would better hurry.
mistakes.right: You'd better hurry.

points.title: Should for expectations: It should arrive tomorrow
points.summary: **should** also means *probably will* or *is expected to*: *The package **should** arrive tomorrow. They **should** be here by now.*

blocks.md: *Should* can say that something is **likely** or **expected**, because it's normal or planned: *The meeting **should** finish at five.* (That's the plan.) *This test **should** be easy for you.* (I expect it.)
***Should be + -ing*** / ***should have + past participle*** for expectations now or in the past: *They **should be arriving** soon. The parcel **should have arrived** yesterday.* (but it didn't)
With *by now*, *should* often suggests that the expected thing hasn't happened: *It's 9 o'clock. Jo **should** be here by now.* (Where is she?)

Compare *should* (I expect, but I'm not sure) and *must* (I'm sure, from evidence): *She **should** be home soon* vs *Her car is outside. She **must** be home.* See [Modals of Deduction](/blog/grammar/modals-of-deduction/).

examples.text: The train **should** be here in five minutes.
You've studied a lot. You **should** pass easily.
It's 7 pm. The shops **should** be open until 8.
The repair **should have taken** an hour, but it took all day.

mistakes.wrong: The bus should to arrive soon.
mistakes.right: The bus should arrive soon.

points.title: Be supposed to
points.summary: **be supposed to + verb** = what is expected, arranged or the rule (often not what really happens): *We're **supposed to** wear a tie. You **were supposed to** call me!*

blocks.md: ***Be supposed to*** says what **should** happen because of a rule, an arrangement or what people expect: *You**'re supposed to** check in an hour before the flight.*
It often suggests that the thing **doesn't** happen, or didn't happen: *I'm **supposed to** be on a diet, but I love cake!* *You **were supposed to** be here at six!* (You weren't.)
It can also mean *people say*: *This film **is supposed to** be very good.*
***Not supposed to*** = not allowed: *You**'re not supposed to** park here.*
Don't forget the ***-d***: *supposed to* (not *suppose to*). In speech the *d* is almost silent, but it is always written.

examples.text: We**'re supposed to** finish this by Friday.
You **weren't supposed to** tell anyone!
This restaurant **is supposed to** be the best in town.
What **are** we **supposed to** do now?

mistakes.wrong: We're suppose to arrive at 9.
mistakes.right: We're supposed to arrive at 9.

mistakes.wrong: You supposed to call me.
mistakes.right: You were supposed to call me.

points.title: Should in that-clauses and for surprise
points.summary: After verbs like **suggest, insist, recommend** and adjectives like **important, essential**, British English often uses **should**: *I suggest that you **should** apply.* **Should** also shows surprise: *It's strange that she **should** say that.*

blocks.md: After verbs and adjectives of **suggestion, demand and importance**, we can use ***should*** + base verb in the *that* clause (especially in British English): *They recommended that we **should** book early. It's essential that everyone **should** attend.*

The **subjunctive** (base verb with no *should*) is also correct and is more common in American English and formal writing: *They recommended that we **book** early.* See [Subjunctive](/blog/grammar/subjunctive/).
***Should*** after expressions of **feeling** (*strange, odd, surprising, a pity*) adds surprise or emotion: *It's odd that you **should** mention her. I was just thinking about her!*

Both *should* and the subjunctive are correct after *suggest / insist / important*: *I insisted that he **should** come / he **come**.* The ordinary present (*he comes*) is also common in informal British English.

examples.text: The doctor suggested that I **should** rest for a week.
It's important that every child **should** have access to education.
It's a pity that you **should** feel that way.
I find it surprising that he **should** say such a thing.

mistakes.wrong: I suggest that you should to apply.
mistakes.right: I suggest that you should apply.

mistakes.wrong: It's essential that he should arrives on time.
mistakes.right: It's essential that he should arrive on time.

items.prompt: You ___ supposed to use your phone in the cinema.
The train was supposed to leave at 8, but it ___.
items.explanation: *Was supposed to* often means it didn't happen.

items.prompt: That new pizza place ___ (be) supposed to be amazing. Shall we try it?

topics.h1: Short Answers, So Do I, Neither Do I, I Think So
topics.summary: Short replies with auxiliary verbs: Yes, I do. So am I. Neither can I. Have you? I think so.
intro: In conversation, we often answer with just the **auxiliary verb** instead of repeating the whole sentence: *Do you like jazz? ~ Yes, I **do**. I'm tired. ~ So **am** I.*
This makes English sound natural and less repetitive. The auxiliary must match the verb in the first sentence: *be → am / is / are*, present simple → *do / does*, past simple → *did*, and so on.

points.title: Short answers: Yes, I do. No, she isn't.
points.summary: Answer yes/no questions with **Yes / No + pronoun + auxiliary**: *Are you hungry? ~ Yes, I **am**. Do they live here? ~ No, they **don't**.*

blocks.md: Use the **same auxiliary** as in the question. Don't contract positive short answers: *Yes, I **am**.* Not *Yes, I'm*.
A short answer alone (*Yes.*) can sound abrupt. *Yes, I do* is more polite and natural.

examples.text: Are you from Iran? ~ Yes, I **am**.
Does your brother work? ~ No, he **doesn't**.
Did you enjoy the film? ~ Yes, we **did**.
Will you be home tonight? ~ No, I **won't**.

mistakes.wrong: Are you hungry? ~ Yes, I'm.
mistakes.right: Are you hungry? ~ Yes, I am.
mistakes.why: no contraction in positive short answers

mistakes.wrong: Do you like it? ~ Yes, I like.
mistakes.right: Do you like it? ~ Yes, I do.

mistakes.wrong: Is it cold? ~ Yes, it's.
mistakes.right: Is it cold? ~ Yes, it is.

points.title: So do I, Neither can I, Me too, Me neither
points.summary: To agree: **So + auxiliary + I** (positive): *I'm hungry. ~ So am I.* **Neither + auxiliary + I** (negative): *I can't swim. ~ Neither can I.*

blocks.md: Word order: ***So / Neither + auxiliary + subject***: *So **do I**. Neither **have we**.* Not *So I do*.
***Nor*** is also used like *neither*, especially in British English: *I don't like it. ~ **Nor do I**.*
To **disagree**, use the opposite auxiliary: *I love horror films. ~ Really? I **don't**. / I don't like coffee. ~ Oh, I **do**.*

examples.text: I'm from Shiraz. ~ **So am I**!
We went to the concert. ~ **So did we**.
I haven't seen it. ~ **Neither have I**.
I can't wait for the holidays. ~ **Me neither**!

mistakes.wrong: I like tea. ~ So I do.
mistakes.right: I like tea. ~ So do I.

mistakes.wrong: I don't eat meat. ~ So don't I.
mistakes.right: I don't eat meat. ~ Neither do I.

mistakes.wrong: I can't swim. ~ Me too.
mistakes.right: I can't swim. ~ Me neither.

points.title: Reply questions: Have you? Really? Is she?
points.summary: Short **reply questions** (*Have you? Did she? Is it?*) show interest or surprise: *I've just got married! ~ Have you? Congratulations!*

blocks.md: To show you're **listening** and **interested**, reply with *auxiliary + pronoun* as a question: *I live in Calgary. ~ **Do you**? I've been there!*
The auxiliary matches the statement: positive → positive, negative → negative: *I don't eat meat. ~ **Don't you**? I didn't know that.*
Your intonation shows your feeling: rising for interest or surprise, falling for something you already guessed.

examples.text: I'm learning Japanese. ~ **Are you**? That's great!
She passed her driving test. ~ **Did she**? Wow!
I can't swim. ~ **Can't you**? I'll teach you!
We've bought a house. ~ **Have you**? Where?

mistakes.wrong: I've been to Peru. ~ Did you?
mistakes.right: I've been to Peru. ~ Have you?

mistakes.wrong: She lives in Rome. ~ Is she?
mistakes.right: She lives in Rome. ~ Does she?

points.title: I think so, I hope so, I'm afraid not, I don't think so
points.summary: Use **so** / **not** instead of repeating a clause: *Is it going to rain? ~ I hope not. Will she come? ~ I think so.*

blocks.md: ***So*** replaces a positive clause: *Is the shop open? ~ I **think so**.* (= I think it's open.)

With *think, expect, believe, suppose*, the negative is usually ***I don't think so***. With ***hope*** and ***be afraid***, use ***not***: *I **hope not**. I'm **afraid not**.* (not *I don't hope so*)

examples.text: Will it be sunny tomorrow? ~ I **hope so**.
Are we late? ~ I **don't think so**.
Did you lose the match? ~ I'm **afraid so**.
Can you come on Friday? ~ I'm **afraid not**.

mistakes.wrong: Will it rain? ~ I don't hope so.
mistakes.right: Will it rain? ~ I hope not.

mistakes.wrong: Is it true? ~ I think it.
mistakes.right: Is it true? ~ I think so.

points.title: Using auxiliaries to avoid repetition: She can, but I can't
points.summary: Use an **auxiliary** alone to avoid repeating a verb phrase: *I haven't seen it, but my brother **has**. She speaks French and **so does** her son.*

blocks.md: After the first clause, the auxiliary can stand for the whole verb phrase: *I wasn't tired, but everyone else **was**.* (= was tired)
Use *do / does / did* for simple tenses: *I don't like coffee, but my wife **does**. He said he'd call, and he **did**.*
This is common in contrasts with ***but***, additions with ***and so / and neither***, and replies: *Who can help? ~ I **can**.*

examples.text: I can't swim, but my sister **can**.
Tom didn't come, but Lisa **did**.
I've finished, and **so has** Mina.
We don't eat meat, and **neither do** our kids.

mistakes.wrong: I don't smoke, but my dad smokes does.
mistakes.right: I don't smoke, but my dad does.

mistakes.wrong: She's tired and so I am.
mistakes.right: She's tired and so am I.

points.title: Nor, so it is, and other auxiliary patterns
points.summary: **Nor** + inversion adds a negative point formally (*He didn't apologise, nor did he explain*). **So it is / So I did** confirms with surprise. Stressed **do** adds emphasis (*I do like it!*).

blocks.md: ***Nor / neither + auxiliary + subject*** can join two negative ideas in formal speech and writing: *The government didn't reduce taxes, **nor did it** increase spending.*
***So + subject + auxiliary*** (no inversion) **confirms** something with surprise: *Look, it's snowing! ~ **So it is**!* (= You're right, it is!) Compare *So is it* (= it is too).
A stressed ***do / does / did*** in a positive sentence adds **emphasis** or contrast: *I **do** like your new haircut! She **did** call you, I promise.*

examples.text: I didn't see the accident, **nor did** anyone else.
You've got paint on your shirt. ~ Oh, **so I have**!
I **do** think you should apologise.
He doesn't like sport, **nor does** he watch it.

mistakes.wrong: He didn't call, nor he wrote.
mistakes.right: He didn't call, nor did he write.

mistakes.wrong: Look, the sun is out! ~ So is it!
mistakes.right: Look, the sun is out! ~ So it is!

items.prompt: I don't like horror films, but my friends ___.
Mina has visited Paris, and so ___ her brother.
I wasn't invited, but my sister ___. (one word)

topics.summary: Making adjectives stronger (so tired, such a long day), showing results (so cold that…) and purpose (so that I can…).
intro: ***So*** and ***such*** make a description stronger: *I'm **so** tired! It was **such** a long day!* Add a ***that***-clause to show the **result**: *It was **so** cold **that** we stayed inside.*
Don't confuse them with ***so that***, which shows **purpose**: *I left early **so that** I could catch the train.*

points.title: So or such? So hot, such a hot day
points.summary: Use ***so*** + adjective or adverb (*so tired, so quickly*). Use ***such*** + (*a / an*) + (adjective) + noun (*such a nice man, such good weather*).

rows: *such a / an* + adjective + singular noun: *It's **such a** cold day!*
*so much / so many* + noun: ***so many** people*

blocks.md: Both make the meaning **stronger**, like *very*, but they sound more emotional: *I'm **so** happy! You're **such** a good friend.*

examples.text: The film was **so** boring.
It was **such a** boring film.
They're **such** lovely people.
There were **so many** people at the party.

mistakes.wrong: It was so a good party.
mistakes.right: It was such a good party.

mistakes.wrong: The weather was such nice.
mistakes.right: The weather was so nice.

mistakes.wrong: It was a such long day.
mistakes.right: It was such a long day.

points.title: So… that, such… that: results
points.summary: ***so*** + adjective + ***that*** and ***such*** + noun phrase + ***that*** show a **result**: *It was so cold that we stayed inside. It was such a cold day that we stayed inside.* *That* can be left out in informal English.

rows: *The film was **so** long **(that)** I fell asleep.*
*It was **such a** long film **(that)** I fell asleep.*
*There was **so much** traffic **that** we were late.*

blocks.md: The *that*-clause gives the **result** of the strong feeling or situation.

examples.text: She was **so** tired **that** she fell asleep at her desk.
It was **such** an easy exam **that** everyone passed.
I had **so much** work **that** I couldn't go out.
The music was **so** loud I couldn't hear you.

mistakes.wrong: It was so hot day that we went to the beach.
mistakes.right: It was such a hot day that we went to the beach.

mistakes.wrong: He spoke such quickly that I didn't understand.
mistakes.right: He spoke so quickly that I didn't understand.

points.title: So (result) or so that (purpose)?
points.summary: ***so*** + clause = **result** (*It was late, so I took a taxi*). ***so that*** + clause, often with *can / could*, = **purpose** (*I took a taxi so that I wouldn't be late*).

rows: *It started to rain, **so** we went home.*
*I left early **so that** I could catch the train.*

blocks.md: After ***so that***, use ***can / will*** for the present or future, and ***could / would*** for the past: *I wrote it down **so that** I **wouldn't** forget.* More examples: [Infinitive of Purpose](/blog/grammar/infinitive-of-purpose/#ip-so-that).
In speech, *so* alone can mean *so that*. A comma before *so* usually signals a **result**.

examples.text: The shop was closed, **so** we went home.
I turned the music down **so that** the baby could sleep.
She studied hard, **so** she passed.
Write your email address here **so that** we can contact you.

mistakes.wrong: I saved money so that I can buy a car last year.
mistakes.right: I saved money so that I could buy a car last year.

mistakes.wrong: I was hungry so that I made a sandwich.
mistakes.right: I was hungry, so I made a sandwich.

points.title: So good a book, such was the demand, so loud was the music
points.summary: Formal patterns: ***so*** + adjective + ***a*** + noun (*so good a book*), ***Such*** + *be* at the start with inversion (*Such was the noise that…*), ***So*** + adjective + *be* + subject (*So strong was the wind that…*), and ***such that*** (= in a way that).

rows: *It was **so good a book** that I read it twice.* (= such a good book)
***Such was** the demand **that** tickets sold out in minutes.*
***So loud was** the music **that** the neighbours complained.*
*The design is **such that** it can be used anywhere.*

blocks.md: These patterns are **formal** and mostly written. In speech, *such a good book* and *The music was so loud that…* are normal.

examples.text: **Such was** her talent **that** she won every prize.
**So heavy was** the rain **that** the roads flooded.
It was **so difficult a question** that nobody answered.
The problem is **such that** we need outside help.

mistakes.wrong: So was the wind strong that trees fell.
mistakes.right: So strong was the wind that trees fell.

mistakes.wrong: It was so a difficult question.
mistakes.right: It was so difficult a question.

items.prompt: The test was ___ difficult that nobody finished it.
It was ___ terrible weather that the flight was cancelled.
There were so ___ people that we couldn't get in. (one word)
I was hungry, ___ I made a sandwich.
Last night I set two alarms so that I ___ oversleep.
It was raining, ___ we stayed at home. (one word: so or because)

topics.summary: When to use some and any: I've got some money. Have you got any money? I haven't got any money.
intro: ***Some*** and ***any*** talk about an amount that isn't exact. Use them with **plural** nouns (*some eggs*) and **uncountable** nouns (*some milk*).

The basic rule is ***some*** in positive sentences and ***any*** in negatives and questions, but there are important exceptions. For countable and uncountable nouns, see [Countable and Uncountable Nouns](/blog/grammar/countable-uncountable-nouns/).

points.title: Some in positive sentences, any in negatives and questions
points.summary: Use ***some*** in **positive** sentences (*I've got some apples*). Use ***any*** in **negatives** (*I haven't got any apples*) and most **questions** (*Have you got any apples?*).

blocks.md: Use *some / any* with **plural** and **uncountable** nouns. With a singular countable noun, use *a / an*: *Is there **a** bank near here?* (not *any bank*)

examples.text: I bought **some** bread.
We don't have **any** homework today.
Are there **any** good restaurants near here?
There's **some** juice in the fridge.

mistakes.wrong: I don't have some money.
mistakes.right: I don't have any money.

mistakes.wrong: There are any chairs in the room.
mistakes.right: There are some chairs in the room.

mistakes.wrong: Have you got any pen?
mistakes.right: Have you got a pen?

points.title: Some in offers and requests: Can I have some water?
points.summary: Use ***some*** in **questions** when you **offer** something or **ask for** something, or when you expect the answer *yes*: *Would you like **some** coffee? Can I have **some** water?*

rows: *Can I have **some** water, please? Could you lend me **some** money?*
*Did you buy **some** bread?* (I think you did.)

blocks.md: Compare: *Have you got **any** questions?* (an open question) / *Would you like **some** more tea?* (an offer).

examples.text: Would you like **some** biscuits?
Can I have **some** more rice, please?
Could you give me **some** advice?
Are there **any** messages for me?

mistakes.wrong: Can I have any water, please?
mistakes.right: Can I have some water, please?

points.title: Someone, anything, nowhere, everybody
points.summary: ***Some-, any-, no-, every-*** combine with ***-one / -body*** (people), ***-thing*** (things) and ***-where*** (places): *someone, anything, nowhere, everybody*. Use them like *some* and *any*.

blocks.md: ***No-*** words already have a negative meaning, so use a **positive** verb: *I saw **nobody**.* = *I didn't see **anybody**.* (not *I didn't see nobody*)
These words take a **singular** verb: ***Everyone is** here. **Nothing has** changed.*
Don't use *to* before *somewhere / anywhere* after *go*: *Let's go **somewhere** quiet.*

examples.text: **Someone** is knocking at the door.
I didn't buy **anything**.
There's **nowhere** to park.
**Everybody** loves her.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't say nothing.
mistakes.right: I didn't say anything.

mistakes.wrong: Everyone are happy.
mistakes.right: Everyone is happy.

mistakes.wrong: I want to go to somewhere warm.
mistakes.right: I want to go somewhere warm.

points.title: Any = it doesn't matter which; any after if
points.summary: In **positive** sentences, ***any*** means **it doesn't matter which**: *Call me **any** time.* Use ***any*** after ***if*** and with words that have a **negative meaning** (*never, hardly, without*).

rows: *Choose **any** colour you like. **Anyone** can learn to cook.*

blocks.md: With this meaning, *any* can go with a **singular** noun: ***Any** child can do it. Take **any** bus from here.*
***Not… any*** = ***no***: *There **aren't any** chairs.* = *There **are no** chairs.* Use only **one** negative.

examples.text: You can sit **anywhere**.
**Any** bus from this stop goes to the centre.
If you need **anything**, just ask.
There were **hardly any** people at the party.

mistakes.wrong: You can come some time you like.
mistakes.right: You can come any time you like.

mistakes.wrong: There is hardly some food.
mistakes.right: There is hardly any food.

mistakes.wrong: I don't have no time.
mistakes.right: I don't have any time.

points.title: Some 200 people, some idiot, any better, no faster
points.summary: ***Some*** + number = **about** (*some 200 people*). ***Some*** + singular noun = an **unknown** person or thing (*Some idiot parked in my space*). ***Any / no*** + comparative = *at all* (*Is he any better? It's no faster.*).

rows: ***SOME** people think it's a good idea.* (but not everyone)
*Are you feeling **any** better? It isn't **any** easier.*
*The new phone is **no** faster than the old one.*

blocks.md: Use ***no*** or ***none***, not *not any*, at the **start** of a sentence: ***No** students passed. **None** of my friends came.* (not *Not any students passed*)
***Any*** + comparative is common in questions and negatives: *Can't you drive **any** faster?*

examples.text: **Some** 50,000 fans watched the match.
**Some** man called, but he didn't leave his name.
Is your cold **any** better today?
**No** one knows the answer.

mistakes.wrong: Not any of the students passed.
mistakes.right: None of the students passed.

mistakes.wrong: The traffic isn't no better today.
mistakes.right: The traffic isn't any better today.

items.prompt: ___ 5,000 people took part in the march.
Is the traffic ___ better today?
___ students passed the exam. It was far too difficult. (one word)

topics.summary: Verbs for states, not actions: I know (not I'm knowing), and when the continuous is possible.
intro: **Stative verbs** (state verbs) describe states, not actions: thoughts, feelings, senses, possession and existence.
We don't normally use them in continuous tenses: *I **know** the answer.* (not *I'm knowing*) *She **wants** a new phone.* (not *She's wanting*)

points.title: Verbs we don't use in the continuous
points.summary: know, want, like, need, understand, believe, belong… use the simple form, even for now.

rows: know, believe, understand, remember, forget, mean, realise, recognise
like, love, hate, prefer, want, need

blocks.md: Use the simple form **even when you mean now**: *I'm hungry. I **want** something to eat.* (not *I'm wanting*) *Do you **understand** what I mean?*
*Have* for possession is a state: *I **have** a car.* But *have* in phrases like *have lunch, have a shower, have fun* is an action, so the continuous is fine: *We**'re having** lunch.*

examples.text: I **don't understand** this question.
This bag **belongs** to my sister.
Do you **remember** her name?
How much **does** this jacket **cost**?
We**'re having** dinner at the moment.

mistakes.wrong: I'm knowing the answer.
mistakes.right: I know the answer.

mistakes.wrong: This book is belonging to me.
mistakes.right: This book belongs to me.

mistakes.wrong: I'm having a car.
mistakes.right: I have a car.

points.title: Verbs with two meanings: think, have, see, taste
points.summary: Some verbs are states with one meaning and actions with another; only the action meaning can be continuous.

rows: *She**'s having** lunch / a shower / a good time.*

blocks.md: With *feel* (= how your body or mood is), both forms are fine: *I **feel** tired. / I**'m feeling** tired.* But *feel* = think is a state: *I **feel** you're right.*

examples.text: I**'m thinking** of moving to Montreal.
What **do** you **think** of my new haircut?
We**'re having** a great time.
This coffee **tastes** a bit strange.
Look! The cat **is looking** at the bird.

mistakes.wrong: I'm thinking this is a good idea.
mistakes.right: I think this is a good idea.

mistakes.wrong: What do you think about? You look worried.
mistakes.right: What are you thinking about? You look worried.

mistakes.wrong: This soup is tasting delicious.
mistakes.right: This soup tastes delicious.
mistakes.why: Taste = the flavour it has: a state.

points.title: He's being rude: be in the continuous, and states in perfect tenses
points.summary: is being + adjective = behaviour right now; state verbs stay simple in perfect tenses (I've known, not I've been knowing).

blocks.md: *Be* is normally a state: *He **is** rude* = that's his character. But *be* + adjective in the continuous describes **behaviour at the moment**: *He**'s being** rude* = he is behaving rudely now (maybe that's not normal for him).
We only do this with adjectives about behaviour: *silly, rude, kind, careful, patient, difficult, quiet.* Not with things you can't control: *He's tall* (not *He's being tall*).

The same rule applies to **perfect continuous** tenses: use the perfect simple with state verbs: *I**'ve known** him for years.* (not *I've been knowing*) *They **had owned** the house for twenty years.* (not *had been owning*)

examples.text: You**'re being** very quiet today. Is everything OK?
Stop it! You**'re being** silly.
She**'s** a very patient person.
I**'ve known** Sam since primary school.
We **had** only **had** the car for a month when it broke down.

mistakes.wrong: I've been knowing her for years.
mistakes.right: I've known her for years.
mistakes.why: Know is a state: perfect simple.

mistakes.wrong: He's being tall for his age.
mistakes.right: He's tall for his age.
mistakes.why: Being + adjective is only for behaviour.

points.title: State verbs in the continuous for emphasis or change
points.summary: Informally, some state verbs take the continuous to stress a temporary feeling or a gradual change: We're loving it, I'm regretting it.

blocks.md: With some state verbs, the continuous is possible to stress that a situation is **temporary or around now**: *The kids **are loving** their new school.* *You**'re looking** great these days.* This is common in informal English.

With verbs of **mental states** (*regret, realise, understand, find*), the continuous can show a feeling that is **growing or new**: *I**'m regretting** my decision more every day. I**'m** slowly **understanding** how the system works.* *Consider* (= think about carefully) is usually continuous: *He**'s considering** a move to Vancouver.*

Some verbs are still very rarely continuous, even informally: *believe, doubt, own, belong, consist of, know.* In exams and formal writing, use the simple form with state verbs unless you have a clear reason not to.

examples.text: We**'re loving** our new flat!
You**'re looking** great these days.
I**'m regretting** that I said yes.
He**'s considering** early retirement.
We**'re hoping** to finish by Friday.

mistakes.wrong: I'm believing you now.
mistakes.right: I believe you now.

mistakes.wrong: This box is consisting of three parts.
mistakes.right: This box consists of three parts.

items.prompt: He ___ very rude today. That's not like him.
I ___ her for ten years.
items.explanation: *Know* is a state: perfect simple, *I've known*.

items.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: He's being tall for his age.
He's being taller for his age.
He being tall for his age.
items.explanation: *Being* + adjective is only for behaviour, not for height.

topics.summary: I, you, he, she, it, we, they and my, your, his, her, its, our, their: who does something and who it belongs to.
intro: **Subject pronouns** (*I, you, he, she, it, we, they*) come before the verb: ***She** works in a bank.* **Possessive adjectives** (*my, your, his, her, its, our, their*) come before a noun: ***Her** bank is near **my** house.*
For *me, him, her, us, them*, see [Object Pronouns](/blog/grammar/object-pronouns/). For *mine, yours, hers*, see [Possessive Pronouns](/blog/grammar/possessive-pronouns/).

points.title: Subject pronouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
points.summary: Use a **subject pronoun** before the verb: *I, you, he, she, it, we, they*. English sentences **need** a subject: *It's raining.* (not *Is raining*)

rows: *he* (a man / boy), *she* (a woman / girl), *it* (a thing / animal)

blocks.md: English always needs a subject, even when the verb shows who it is in other languages: ***I** am tired.* (not *Am tired*). ***It** is cold today.*
Don't repeat the subject with a pronoun: *My brother lives in Ottawa.* (not *My brother he lives…*)
*I* is always a capital letter.

examples.text: **I**'m a student.
**She** is my sister.
**They** live in Toronto.
**It**'s very hot today.

mistakes.wrong: My father he is a doctor.
mistakes.right: My father is a doctor.

mistakes.wrong: Is very expensive.
mistakes.right: It is very expensive.

mistakes.wrong: i am from Iran.
mistakes.right: I am from Iran.

points.title: Possessive adjectives: my, your, his, her, its, our, their
points.summary: Use **possessive adjectives** before a noun to show who something belongs to: *my bag, your phone, his car, her house, its tail, our school, their children*.

blocks.md: The possessive adjective agrees with the **owner**, not the thing: *Ali loves **his** mother.* (Ali = he → his). *Sara loves **her** father.* (Sara = she → her).
Possessive adjectives don't change for plural nouns: *my book, my books*.

examples.text: This is **my** brother.
Sara is in **her** room.
Reza lives with **his** parents.
The dog is eating **its** food.

mistakes.wrong: Maryam is visiting his grandmother.
mistakes.right: Maryam is visiting her grandmother.
mistakes.why: the owner is a woman: her

mistakes.wrong: They love they children.
mistakes.right: They love their children.

mistakes.wrong: Is this you bag?
mistakes.right: Is this your bag?

points.title: Its or it's? Their, there or they're? Your or you're?
points.summary: Don't confuse possessive adjectives with short forms: ***its*** (possessive) / ***it's*** (= it is / it has); ***their*** (possessive) / ***there*** (place) / ***they're*** (= they are); ***your*** / ***you're*** (= you are).

blocks.md: Possessive adjectives **never** have an apostrophe: *its, your, their, whose*.
A quick test: can you say *it is, they are, you are, who is*? Then use the apostrophe form.

examples.text: The tree lost **its** leaves.
**It's** a beautiful day.
**They're** at **their** friend's house over **there**.
**You're** going to love **your** new room.

mistakes.wrong: The dog hurt it's paw.
mistakes.right: The dog hurt its paw.

mistakes.wrong: Their going to be late.
mistakes.right: They're going to be late.

mistakes.wrong: Is this you're coat?
mistakes.right: Is this your coat?

points.title: It for weather, time and distance; it as an empty subject
points.summary: Use ***it*** as an **empty subject** for weather, time, dates and distance (*It's raining. It's 5 o'clock. It's 10 km to the city.*), before *adjective + to / that* (*It's important to sleep well*), and with ***it takes*** + time.

rows: ***It's** about 5 km from here to the beach.*
***It's** easy to learn. **It's** strange that he didn't call.*
***It takes** an hour to get there.*

blocks.md: English needs a subject even when there's no real “doer”: ***It** is raining* (not *Is raining* or *Rains*).
Put a long *to*-infinitive subject at the end with ***it***: *To learn a language is hard* → ***It's** hard **to learn** a language.* (more natural)

examples.text: **It**'s windy today.
**It**'s ten past nine.
How far is **it** to the airport?
**It**'s nice to meet you.

mistakes.wrong: Is very hot today.
mistakes.right: It's very hot today.

mistakes.wrong: This is important to drink water.
mistakes.right: It's important to drink water.

mistakes.wrong: It needs two hours to get there.
mistakes.right: It takes two hours to get there.

points.title: Singular they, generic you and one
points.summary: Use ***they / their*** for **one person** when you don't know, or don't want to say, if the person is male or female: *Someone left **their** phone.* Use ***you*** (informal) or ***one*** (very formal) for **people in general**: *You never know.*

rows: *Someone called, but **they** didn't leave a message.*
***You** can't smoke here. **You** never know what will happen.*

blocks.md: Singular ***they*** uses a **plural verb**: *Someone left their bag. **They are** probably looking for it.*
*He or she* is also possible in formal writing, but singular *they* is now standard in most style guides.

examples.text: If a student is late, **they** must sign in at reception.
Everybody did **their** best.
**You** have to be 18 to vote here.
**One** must respect the law.

mistakes.wrong: If a customer complains, they is always right.
mistakes.right: If a customer complains, they are always right.

mistakes.wrong: Somebody left there bag.
mistakes.right: Somebody left their bag.

items.prompt: Someone left ___ umbrella on the bus.
If anyone calls, tell ___ I'll be back at five.
A good teacher always listens to ___ students. (one word)

topics.summary: Matching the verb to the subject: She works. They work. Everyone is here. One of my friends lives in Paris.
intro: The verb must **agree** with its subject: a **singular** subject takes a **singular** verb (*She **works***), and a **plural** subject takes a **plural** verb (*They **work***).

This is easy with short subjects, but harder with words like *everyone, each* and *one of*, and with long subjects. For group nouns like *team* and *family*, see [Plural Nouns](/blog/grammar/plural-nouns/#pn-group-nouns).

points.title: He works, they work; there is, there are
points.summary: In the present, use **-s** with *he, she, it* and singular nouns (*My brother works*). With *I, you, we, they* and plural nouns, there's no *-s* (*My brothers work*). Use **there is** + singular and **there are** + plural.

blocks.md: ***There is*** + singular or uncountable noun: *There **is** a bank. There **is** some milk.* ***There are*** + plural: *There **are** two banks.*
The past of *be* also changes: *I / he / she / it **was***; *you / we / they **were***. And ***has*** with *he, she, it*: *She **has** a car.*

examples.text: My sister **lives** in Toronto.
My parents **live** in Shiraz.
**There is** a park near my house.
**There are** three bedrooms in our flat.

mistakes.wrong: My brother work in a bank.
mistakes.right: My brother works in a bank.

mistakes.wrong: The children is in the garden.
mistakes.right: The children are in the garden.

mistakes.wrong: There is two cafés on my street.
mistakes.right: There are two cafés on my street.

points.title: Everyone is, each student has, one of my friends is
points.summary: ***Everyone, everybody, someone, nobody, everything*** take a **singular** verb (*Everyone is here*). So do ***each*** and ***every*** + noun. ***One of*** + plural noun also takes a **singular** verb (*One of my friends lives in Paris*).

blocks.md: The verb agrees with ***one***, not with the plural noun after *of*: ***One** of the students **is** late.*
After *everyone / someone*, we often use *they / their* to refer back: *Everyone **has** **their** own room.*

examples.text: **Everyone is** welcome.
**Every child needs** love.
**One of my friends works** at the airport.
**Each of** the hotels **has** a pool.

mistakes.wrong: Everybody are tired.
mistakes.right: Everybody is tired.

mistakes.wrong: One of my cousins live in Dubai.
mistakes.right: One of my cousins lives in Dubai.

mistakes.wrong: Every students has a book.
mistakes.right: Every student has a book.

points.title: Long subjects: the list of names is, either… or
points.summary: The verb agrees with the **main noun** of the subject, not the noun closest to it: *The list of names **is** on the wall.* With ***as well as / along with***, it agrees with the **first** subject. With ***either… or / neither… nor***, it agrees with the **nearest** subject.

rows: *The **people** who live next door **are** very kind.*
*as well as, along with, together with*
*The **teacher**, as well as the students, **is** here.*
*Neither my sister nor my **parents are** coming. Either Ali or **Sara is** coming.*
***The number** of students **is** rising. **A number of** students **are** absent.*

blocks.md: Find the **head noun** and ignore *of*-phrases and relative clauses: *The **box** of chocolates **is** on the table.*
***The number of*** = the total (singular verb). ***A number of*** = several (plural verb).

examples.text: The **price** of these shoes **is** too high.
The **students** in my class **come** from ten countries.
**A number of** people **have** complained.
Neither the manager nor **the staff were** happy.

mistakes.wrong: The quality of the products are excellent.
mistakes.right: The quality of the products is excellent.

mistakes.wrong: The number of tourists are increasing.
mistakes.right: The number of tourists is increasing.

mistakes.wrong: The manager, as well as his assistants, are coming.
mistakes.right: The manager, as well as his assistants, is coming.

points.title: Amounts, what-clauses and none of them is or are
points.summary: **Amounts** of money, time and distance usually take a **singular** verb (*Ten dollars is enough*). ***What***-clauses usually take a singular verb (*What we need is more time*). With ***none of*** + plural, both singular and plural are used.

rows: ***Two hours is** too long to wait. **Five kilometres is** a long way.*
*None of my friends **has / have** a car.* (singular = more formal)
agrees with the noun: *Most of the **cake is** gone. Most of the **students are** here.*

blocks.md: With ***percentages, fractions*** and ***most / some / all / half of***, the verb agrees with the noun after *of*: *Half of the **money is** gone. Half of the **guests are** here.*

***None of*** + plural: the **singular** verb is traditional and formal; the **plural** is very common and accepted. A ***what***-clause takes a singular verb before a singular complement (*What I need **is** a holiday*); before a plural complement, a plural verb is also common (*What we need **are** new ideas*).

examples.text: **Fifty dollars is** a lot for a T-shirt.
**What surprised me was** his attitude.
**Most of the information is** out of date.
**More than one student has** failed.

mistakes.wrong: Fifty kilometres are a long way to drive.
mistakes.right: Fifty kilometres is a long way to drive.

mistakes.wrong: The majority of the work are done.
mistakes.right: The majority of the work is done.

mistakes.wrong: More than one person have called.
mistakes.right: More than one person has called.

items.prompt: The price of houses in this city ___ very high.
A number of students ___ asked for extra help.
The people who work in this office ___ (be) very friendly.

topics.h1: The Subjunctive (I Insist That He Be…)
topics.summary: The base form after suggest, insist and essential that (that he see, that she be), were for unreal situations, and fixed expressions like if need be.
intro: The **subjunctive** is a special verb form. The most common type is the **base form** after verbs like *suggest, insist, recommend* and adjectives like *essential*: *I suggest **that he see** a doctor.* (not *sees*) *It's vital **that she be** on time.* (not *is*)

The subjunctive is **formal** and more common in **American English**. British English often uses ***should*** instead: *I suggest that he **should see** a doctor.* For suggest + *-ing*, see [Reporting Verbs](/blog/grammar/reporting-verbs/#rv-suggest).

points.title: Suggest that he see, insist that she be
points.summary: After ***suggest, recommend, insist, demand, request, propose, ask*** + ***that***, use the **base form** for every person: *They insisted **that he leave**. I recommend **that she be** careful.* British English also uses ***should*** + base form.

rows: past main verb: still base form

blocks.md: The base form doesn't change for *he / she / it* (**no -s**) and doesn't change for the **past**: *We **recommended** that she **take** the job.*
In informal British English, a normal tense is also heard (*I suggest that he sees…*), but in formal writing use the base form or *should*.

examples.text: I suggest **that you book** early.
The teacher insisted **that every student be** on time.
They recommended **that he take** a few days off.
The judge ordered **that the money be** returned.

mistakes.wrong: The doctor recommended that he takes a holiday. (formal)
mistakes.right: The doctor recommended that he take a holiday.

mistakes.wrong: She suggested me to see a doctor.
mistakes.right: She suggested that I see a doctor.

points.title: It's essential that he be…, it's vital that
points.summary: After ***essential, vital, important, crucial, imperative, necessary, advisable*** + ***that***, formal English uses the **subjunctive** (base form): ***It is essential that** every child **have** access to education.* Also after nouns like ***the suggestion / requirement / insistence that***.

rows: *It is essential / vital that* + base form
***It is vital that** he **be** told the truth.*
*It is important / crucial that* + base form
***It is imperative that** the work **be** finished today.*
***The requirement that** all visitors **sign** in is strict.*
*It is essential that he **should be** told.*

blocks.md: Compare: *It's important **to arrive** early* (general) / *It's important **that she arrive** early* (a specific person, formal).

examples.text: **It is essential that** the patient **rest** for a week.
**It is crucial that** nobody **find** out.
**It's important that** he **not be** late.
She ignored **the suggestion that** she **apply** for the job.

mistakes.wrong: It is vital that he is informed immediately. (formal)
mistakes.right: It is vital that he be informed immediately.

mistakes.wrong: It's essential that she arrives on time. (formal written)
mistakes.right: It's essential that she arrive on time.

points.title: That he not be told, that it be done
points.summary: The **negative** subjunctive is ***not*** + base form (no *do*): *I suggest that he **not go**.* The **passive** subjunctive is ***be*** + past participle: *They demanded that the law **be changed**.*

rows: *We asked that she **not tell** anyone.* (not *doesn't tell*)
*She requested that her name **not be published**.*

blocks.md: Don't use *don't / doesn't* in the subjunctive: *…that he **not leave*** (not *that he doesn't leave*).

examples.text: The doctor advised that he **not drive** for a week.
The report recommends that the factory **be closed**.
She asked that her address **not be** given to anyone.
We insist that the problem **be solved** immediately.

mistakes.wrong: I suggest that he doesn't go alone. (formal)
mistakes.right: I suggest that he not go alone.

mistakes.wrong: They demanded that the rules are changed. (formal)
mistakes.right: They demanded that the rules be changed.

points.title: If I were you, I wish it were, as if he were
points.summary: The ***were*** subjunctive is used for **unreal** situations with **all** persons, especially after ***if, I wish, if only, as if / as though, suppose***: *If I **were** you… I wish he **were** here. He acts as if he **were** the boss.* In informal English, *was* is also common.

rows: *She talks as if she **were** an expert.*
***Were** it not for your help, we'd have failed.*
*If I **was** rich, I'd buy a house.*

blocks.md: ***If I were you*** is a fixed expression for advice: use ***were***, even in informal English.
For more on these patterns, see [Second Conditional](/blog/grammar/second-conditional/) and [Unreal Past](/blog/grammar/unreal-past/).

examples.text: **If I were** you, I'd talk to her.
I wish my brother **were** here.
He behaves as if he **were** the manager.
**Were** it not for the rain, we'd go out.

mistakes.wrong: If I would be you, I'd go.
mistakes.right: If I were you, I'd go.

mistakes.wrong: I wish it is summer.
mistakes.right: I wish it were summer.

points.title: If need be, as it were, heaven forbid, long live
points.summary: Some **fixed expressions** keep old subjunctive forms: ***if need be*** (= if necessary), ***as it were*** (= so to speak), ***heaven forbid*** (= I hope it never happens), ***long live…***, ***God bless***, ***woe betide***, ***the powers that be***.

rows: *She's the boss of the family, **as it were**.*
***Heaven forbid** that anything should happen to him.*
***The powers that be** have decided to close the school.*

blocks.md: These are **fixed**: don't change the verb form (*if need be*, not *if need is*).

examples.text: We'll take a taxi, **if need be**.
He was, **as it were**, a second father to me.
**Heaven forbid** we should ever need it.
**Woe betide** anyone who forgets her birthday!

mistakes.wrong: I'll stay longer, if need is.
mistakes.right: I'll stay longer, if need be.

mistakes.wrong: Long lives the Queen!
mistakes.right: Long live the Queen!

items.prompt: (Formal) The doctor recommended that she ___ more exercise.
(Formal) They insisted that he ___ present at the meeting.
(Formal) I suggest that he ___ (call) the company directly.
