topics.summary: When English uses no article (I love music. She's at work. I live in Canada.) and when you need the (the music in this film, the Nile, the Hilton).
intro: In English, many nouns have **no article** at all. This is called the **zero article**: *I love **music**. **Dogs** are friendly. She's **at work**.* This page shows when to use ***the*** and when to use **nothing**.
For *a / an* and the basic uses of *the*, see [A, An and The](/blog/grammar/a-an-the/).

points.title: General or specific? Music or the music
points.summary: No article for things **in general** (plural and uncountable nouns): *I love music. Cats are clever.* Use **the** for **specific** things: *The music at the party was great.*

rows: ***The dogs** next door bark all night.*

blocks.md: With **plural** and **uncountable** nouns, no article means all of them, in general: ***Children** need sleep. **Water** is important.*
***The*** makes it specific: a particular group or thing that we can identify: *the children in my class, the water in this bottle*.
Many languages use *the* for general ideas. In English, general = no article: ***Love** is blind. **Nature** is beautiful.*

examples.text: **Vegetables** are good for you.
**The vegetables** from my garden are delicious.
I'm not interested in **politics**.
**The people** at the meeting were very friendly.

mistakes.wrong: The life is beautiful.
mistakes.right: Life is beautiful.

mistakes.wrong: I love the nature.
mistakes.right: I love nature.

mistakes.wrong: Money can't buy the happiness.
mistakes.right: Money can't buy happiness.

points.title: At home, go to work, in bed, by bus, have lunch
points.summary: No article in fixed phrases with **home, work, school, bed, hospital, prison, church, university**, with **meals** (*have breakfast*) and with **by + transport** (*by bus*).

blocks.md: These phrases are about the **purpose** of the place: *go to school* = to study; *in hospital* = as a patient. Use ***the*** when you mean the **building**: *My mother went to **the school** to talk to the teacher.* (She isn't a student.)
With an adjective or a specific meal, use an article: *We had **a** great lunch. **The** dinner at the wedding was amazing.*
American English usually says *in **the** hospital*. Both are correct.

examples.text: I usually get **home** at six.
She's **at work** until five.
We had **breakfast** in the garden.
He goes to work **by bike**.
Dad went to **the hospital** to visit Grandma.

mistakes.wrong: I go to the bed at eleven.
mistakes.right: I go to bed at eleven.

mistakes.wrong: We came to home late.
mistakes.right: We came home late.

mistakes.wrong: She goes to work by the bus.
mistakes.right: She goes to work by bus.

points.title: Countries, cities, rivers and mountains
points.summary: No article for most **countries, cities, streets, lakes, single mountains and continents** (*Canada, Lake Ontario, Mount Everest*). Use **the** for **rivers, seas, oceans, mountain ranges, island groups, deserts** and plural names (*the Nile, the Alps, the USA*).

rows: *the UK, the USA, the Netherlands, the Philippines*
seas and oceans: *the Caspian Sea, the Pacific*
streets and squares: *Oxford Street, Times Square*

blocks.md: Use ***the*** with country names that include *Republic, Kingdom, States* or *Union*, or are **plural**: *the Czech Republic, the United Kingdom, the United States, the Netherlands*.
Use ***the*** with *north, south, east, west* as regions: *the north of Iran, the Middle East*. But compass words that are part of a name have no article: *North America, South Korea*.

examples.text: I live in **Canada**, near **Lake Ontario**.
**The** Danube flows into **the** Black Sea.
They went skiing in **the** Alps.
My cousin lives in **the** United States.

mistakes.wrong: I visited the Canada last year.
mistakes.right: I visited Canada last year.

mistakes.wrong: We swam in Caspian Sea.
mistakes.right: We swam in the Caspian Sea.

mistakes.wrong: She climbed the Mount Kilimanjaro.
mistakes.right: She climbed Mount Kilimanjaro.

points.title: Names of buildings, organisations and newspapers
points.summary: Use **the** with hotels, museums, theatres, newspapers and names with **of** (*the Hilton, the Louvre, the Guardian, the University of Toronto*). No article with **place name + airport / station / university / park** (*Pearson Airport, Oxford University, Central Park*) or company names.

rows: hotels, theatres, museums: *the Hilton, the Louvre*
names with *of*: *the University of Toronto, the Bank of Canada*
newspapers: *the Globe and Mail, the Times*
names with *'s*: *McDonald's, Harrods, St Paul's Cathedral*

blocks.md: Organisations known by their initials often take *the* when we say the letters: *the BBC, the UN, the EU*. Names said as words usually don't: *NATO, UNESCO*.
Names with *'s* (often the founder's name) have no article: *McDonald's, St Paul's Cathedral, Harrods*.

examples.text: We stayed at **the** Marriott.
I flew into **Pearson Airport**.
She studies at **the** University of Tehran.
My dad reads **the** Guardian every morning.

mistakes.wrong: We visited St Paul's Cathedral and the Harrods.
mistakes.right: We visited St Paul's Cathedral and Harrods.

mistakes.wrong: We visited British Museum.
mistakes.right: We visited the British Museum.

mistakes.wrong: He works for the Google.
mistakes.right: He works for Google.

points.title: Fixed pairs, roles, headlines and decades
points.summary: No article in **fixed pairs** (*arm in arm, from start to finish*), for **unique roles** after verbs like *elect, appoint, become* (*She became CEO*), and in **headlines**. Use **the** for decades (*the 1990s*), and say **at night** (in general) but **in the night** (one night).

rows: *hand in hand, face to face, day after day, from top to bottom, husband and wife*
*She was elected **president**. He became **head** of the department.*
*Storm hits coast. Exit. Turn left at end of road.*
*at night* (in general) / *in the night* (one night); *next week* / *the next week*

blocks.md: **Roles**: if only one person can have the role, the article is often dropped after *be, become, elect, appoint, make, name*: *They appointed her **director**.* With a role that many people have, keep *a*: *She became **a** director* (one of several).
**Next / last**: *next week* = the week after this one; *the next week* = the week after another point in time: *I arrived on Monday, and **the next week** was very busy.*

examples.text: They walked along the beach **hand in hand**.
He was appointed **captain** of the team.
Fashion changed a lot in **the** 1960s.
I woke up twice **in the night**.

mistakes.wrong: We met in 1990s.
mistakes.right: We met in the 1990s.

mistakes.wrong: I often work in night.
mistakes.right: I often work at night.

items.prompt: We spent the whole day in ___.
Which is correct?
options: My sister studies at University of Toronto.
My sister studies at a University of Toronto.
My sister studies at the University Toronto.
My sister studies at the University of Toronto.

items.prompt: I read about it in ___ Guardian this morning. (one word)

topics.h1: Third Conditional (If I had known…, I would have…)
topics.summary: Imaginary past: things that didn't happen and their results. If I had known, I would have helped.
intro: We use the **third conditional** to imagine a **different past**: something that didn't happen, and what the result would have been. *If I **had known** you were ill, I **would have visited** you.* (I didn't know, so I didn't visit.)

It's often used for regrets, criticism and relief. For imaginary situations now, see [Second Conditional](/blog/grammar/second-conditional/). To mix past and present, see [Mixed Conditionals](/blog/grammar/mixed-conditionals/).

points.title: Form and use: if + past perfect, would have + past participle
points.summary: **if + had + past participle, would have + past participle** for an imaginary past: *If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.*

blocks.md: Both halves are about the **past**, and both are **not real**: *If I had studied harder, I would have passed* = I didn't study hard, and I didn't pass.
Don't use *would have* in the *if* clause: *If I **had known**…* Not *If I would have known…*
The *if* clause can come second: *I **would have called** you if I **had had** your number.* (*had had* = the past perfect of *have*.)

examples.text: If it **hadn't rained**, we**'d have had** a picnic.
If you **had asked** me, I **would have said** yes.
She **wouldn't have got** lost if she **had taken** a map.
What **would** you **have done** if you **had missed** the flight?

mistakes.wrong: If I would have known, I would have come.
mistakes.right: If I had known, I would have come.
mistakes.why: No would in the if clause.

mistakes.wrong: If you had told me, I would help you.
mistakes.right: If you had told me, I would have helped you.
mistakes.why: Past result: would have + past participle.

mistakes.wrong: If we had leave earlier, we would have arrived on time.
mistakes.right: If we had left earlier, we would have arrived on time.

points.title: 'd = had or would? Contractions in the third conditional
points.summary: In *If I'd known, I'd have called*, the first **'d = had**, the second **'d = would**. *'d* + past participle = had; *'d have* = would have.

blocks.md: In speech, both *had* and *would* are shortened to ***'d***: *If I**'d** known, I**'d** have called you.*
How to tell them apart: ***'d* + past participle** = *had* (*I'd known* = I had known). ***'d have* + past participle** = *would have* (*I'd have called* = I would have called).
*Would have* is often pronounced /ˈwʊdəv/ and written informally as *would've*. Never write *would of*.

examples.text: If you**'d** asked me, I**'d have** helped.
She**'d have** come if she**'d** known.
If we**'d** left at six, we**'d have** missed the traffic.
I **would've** told you if I'd remembered.

mistakes.wrong: If I'd of known, I'd of come.
mistakes.right: If I'd known, I'd have come.

mistakes.wrong: If I'd have known, I'd have come.
mistakes.right: If I'd known, I'd have come.

points.title: Could have, might have in the result
points.summary: **could have** + past participle = would have been able to; **might have** = perhaps would have: *If you'd asked, I could have helped.*

blocks.md: Instead of *would have*, the result clause can use:

items: ***could have*** + past participle = *would have been able to*: *If I'd had a car, I **could have driven** you.*
***might have*** + past participle = *perhaps would have*: *If you'd apologised, she **might have forgiven** you.*

blocks.md: In the *if* clause, ***had been able to*** means *could*: *If I **had been able to** find a taxi, I would have come.*
*Couldn't have* and *might not have* are common too: *If you hadn't helped me, I **couldn't have finished** on time.*

examples.text: If we'd left earlier, we **could have seen** the sunset.
If you'd been more careful, you **might have won**.
Without your help, I **couldn't have done** it.
If she **had been able to** get a visa, she would have come.

mistakes.wrong: If I had known, I could helped you.
mistakes.right: If I had known, I could have helped you.

mistakes.wrong: If you had tried, you might have win.
mistakes.right: If you had tried, you might have won.

points.title: Continuous forms: If I hadn't been driving so fast…
points.summary: Use **had been + -ing** or **would have been + -ing** for actions in progress: *If I hadn't been driving so fast, I wouldn't have crashed.*

blocks.md: Use the **past perfect continuous** in the *if* clause for an action that was **in progress**: *If I **hadn't been driving** so fast, I wouldn't have had the accident.*
Use ***would have been + -ing*** in the main clause for an imagined action in progress: *If you hadn't called, I **would have been sleeping** all afternoon.*

examples.text: If he **hadn't been texting**, he would have seen the car.
If you **had been listening**, you would have understood.
If I hadn't taken this job, I **would have been working** in my dad's shop.
If it **hadn't been raining**, we would have played outside.

mistakes.wrong: If I wasn't driving so fast, I wouldn't have crashed.
mistakes.right: If I hadn't been driving so fast, I wouldn't have crashed.

mistakes.wrong: If she had been pay attention, she would have seen it.
mistakes.right: If she had been paying attention, she would have seen it.

points.title: If it hadn't been for…, But for…, Without…
points.summary: **If it hadn't been for** + noun = without this thing, the past would have been different: *If it hadn't been for you, I'd have failed.*

blocks.md: ***If it hadn't been for*** + noun shows that one thing made the difference: ***If it hadn't been for** the seat belt, he would have been killed.* (The seat belt saved him.)

Shorter and more formal alternatives: ***But for** the seat belt…* / ***Without** the seat belt…* The inverted form is very formal: ***Had it not been for** the seat belt…* See [Inverted Conditionals](/blog/grammar/inverted-conditionals/).
Compare the present version: ***If it weren't for** you, I'd be lonely* (now). See [Second Conditional](/blog/grammar/second-conditional/#sc-were-to).

examples.text: **If it hadn't been for** the traffic, we'd have arrived on time.
**But for** her quick thinking, the fire would have spread.
**Without** your advice, I would have made a terrible mistake.
**Had it not been for** the rain, the match would have finished.

mistakes.wrong: If it wasn't for the traffic, we would have arrived on time.
mistakes.right: If it hadn't been for the traffic, we would have arrived on time.

mistakes.wrong: But for his help, I will fail.
mistakes.right: But for his help, I would have failed.
mistakes.why: Past result: would have + past participle.

items.prompt: If I'd had more money, I ___ a better hotel, perhaps.
If you'd called me, I ___ you up from the station.
items.explanation: Would have been able to: *could have picked*.

items.prompt: If it hadn't rained, we ___ (might / go) to the beach.
If you ___ attention during the test, you wouldn't have made that mistake.
items.explanation: Action in progress in the past: *had been paying*.

items.prompt: If they hadn't invited me to the coast last weekend, I ___ at home the whole time.
items.explanation: Imagined activity in progress: *would have been sitting*.

items.prompt: If the driver ___ (not / use) his phone, the accident wouldn't have happened.
items.explanation: *Hadn't been using* (in progress); *hadn't used* is also possible.

topics.summary: Pointing to things near and far: this book, that house, these shoes, those people.
intro: Use ***this*** (singular) and ***these*** (plural) for things **near** you, and ***that*** (singular) and ***those*** (plural) for things **far** from you: ***This** is my bag. **That** car over there is my dad's.*
They're also used for time (*this week, in those days*), in conversation (*That's great!*) and in writing to refer back to ideas (*This means that…*).

points.title: This, that, these, those: near and far
points.summary: ***This*** + singular and ***these*** + plural = **near**. ***That*** + singular and ***those*** + plural = **far**.

blocks.md: Use them **before a noun** (*this phone*) or **alone** (*What's **this**?*).
The verb agrees: ***This is**… / **These are**…* and ***That is**… / **Those are**…*

examples.text: **This** coffee is really hot.
**These** shoes are too small.
Can you see **that** bird?
**Those** houses are very old.

mistakes.wrong: This shoes are new.
mistakes.right: These shoes are new.

mistakes.wrong: Those is my car.
mistakes.right: That is my car.

mistakes.wrong: These book is interesting.
mistakes.right: This book is interesting.

points.title: This is…, that's great, this one
points.summary: Use ***this*** to introduce people (*This is my friend*) and on the phone (*Hi, this is Sara*). ***That's*** reacts to what someone has just said (*That's great!*). ***This one / that one*** replace a noun.

rows: *I passed! ~ **That's** great! That's a good idea.*

blocks.md: *That* often refers to something **just said**: *I'm getting married. ~ Really? **That's** wonderful!*
*This one / that one* avoid repeating the noun: *Which cake do you want? ~ **That one**, please.* With plurals, *these / those* alone is more common than *these ones*.

examples.text: **This is** my colleague, David.
Hi, **this is** Sara. Can I speak to Leila?
I've found a new job. ~ **That's** fantastic!
Not that one, **this one**.

mistakes.wrong: These is my parents.
mistakes.right: These are my parents.

mistakes.wrong: Hello, I am Sara speaking. (on the phone)
mistakes.right: Hello, this is Sara.

points.title: This morning, that day, these days, in those days
points.summary: ***This*** + time = the **present** or a **near** time (*this morning, this week*). ***That*** + time = a **past** time we've mentioned (*that day, that night*). ***These days*** = nowadays; ***in those days*** = at that time in the past.

rows: the morning of today / the current week / year
a time in the past that we've mentioned
at that time in the past

blocks.md: When telling a story, use ***that***: *We met in 2015. **That** summer was amazing.*
In reported speech, *this* often changes to *that*: *“I'm busy this week.” → She said she was busy **that** week.* See [Reported Speech](/blog/grammar/reported-speech/).

examples.text: I'm really busy **this week**.
I remember **that day** very well.
**These days**, everyone has a smartphone.
**In those days**, there was no internet.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't sleep well this night. (meaning last night)
mistakes.right: I didn't sleep well last night.

mistakes.wrong: In these days, people worked longer hours. (in the past)
mistakes.right: In those days, people worked longer hours.

points.title: This and that in writing: this means, those who
points.summary: In writing, ***this*** often refers to an idea **just mentioned** (*This means that…*). ***That*** refers to what another person said. ***Those who*** = the people who; ***that of / those of*** replace a noun (*higher than those of last year*).

rows: *A: Let's leave early. B: **That**'s a good idea.*
***Those who** arrived late missed the talk.*
*Our prices are lower than **those of** our competitors.*

blocks.md: In formal writing, ***this*** + a summary noun is clearer than *this* alone: *this **situation**, this **change**, this **approach***.
***That of / those of*** replace a noun to avoid repeating it: *The climate of Vancouver is milder than **that of** Toronto.* (= the climate of) Use *those of* for plurals.

examples.text: Sleep improves memory. **This** is why students should rest before exams.
**Those who** want to join should sign up today.
The climate here is warmer than **that of** northern Europe.
You'll fail? Don't say **that**!

mistakes.wrong: Them who arrived late missed the start.
mistakes.right: Those who arrived late missed the start.

mistakes.wrong: Our results are better than these of last year.
mistakes.right: Our results are better than those of last year.

mistakes.wrong: The population of Toronto is bigger than Montreal.
mistakes.right: The population of Toronto is bigger than that of Montreal.
mistakes.why: compare the same things: that of

points.title: Storytelling this, shared that, and not that hungry
points.summary: In informal stories, ***this*** introduces something **new** (*So this man comes up to me…*). ***That*** refers to **shared memories** or shows dislike (*Remember that café? I hate that noise.*). ***That*** + adjective = *very / so* (*I'm not that hungry*).

rows: *There was **this** strange guy on the bus…* (like *a*, but more vivid)
*I'm not **that** hungry. I didn't know it was **that** expensive.*

blocks.md: ***That*** + adjective (informal) means *so* or *very*: *The film wasn't **that** good.* (= not very good)
***It*** simply refers back to something already mentioned. ***This*** draws attention or points forward to new information: *Here's the plan. **This** is what we'll do.*

examples.text: So I'm in a shop, and **this** woman starts shouting at me.
Remember **that** little restaurant near the beach?
The film wasn't **that** good.
Listen to **this**: I've got the job!

mistakes.wrong: It wasn't that much good.
mistakes.right: It wasn't that good.

items.prompt: ___ who finish early can leave.
Unemployment fell last year. ___ was good news for the government.
The weather in Vancouver is milder than ___ of Toronto. (one word)

topics.summary: Words that show when things happen and in what order: when, while, before, after, as soon as, until, then, finally.
intro: **Time conjunctions** join two actions and show **when** they happen: *I had dinner **when** I got home. **While** I was cooking, the phone rang. Wash your hands **before** you eat.*
This page is about time linkers in general and in the past. For the rule *when I **get** home* (present for the future), see [Future Time Clauses](/blog/grammar/future-time-clauses/).

points.title: When, while, before, after
points.summary: ***When*** = at that time. ***While*** = during a longer action (often with the past continuous). ***Before*** and ***after*** show the order. The time clause can go **first** (with a comma) or **second**.

rows: ***When** I got home, I made dinner.*
*The phone rang **while** I was having a shower.*
*Brush your teeth **before** you go to bed.*
***After** we finished lunch, we went for a walk.*

blocks.md: When the time clause comes **first**, put a **comma** after it: ***When** the film ended**,** we went home.* No comma when it comes second: *We went home **when** the film ended.*
***Before*** and ***after*** can also take ***-ing***: ***Before leaving**, turn off the lights. **After finishing** work, I went to the gym.*

examples.text: **When** I saw her, I smiled.
I fell asleep **while** I was watching TV.
Check the price **before** you buy it.
**After** the meeting finished, we had coffee.

mistakes.wrong: While I watched TV, the phone was ringing.
mistakes.right: While I was watching TV, the phone rang.

mistakes.wrong: After finish work, I go to the gym.
mistakes.right: After finishing work, I go to the gym.

points.title: As soon as, until, since, once, by the time
points.summary: ***As soon as*** = immediately after. ***Until*** = up to that time. ***Since*** = from that time to now (with the present perfect). ***Once*** = after (when something is finished). ***By the time*** = before or at the moment that.

rows: *I called you **as soon as** I heard the news.*
***Once** you've paid, you'll get a receipt.*
***By the time** we arrived, the film had started.*

blocks.md: After ***since***, use a past time (*since 2019*, *since I left school*); the main clause is usually in the **present perfect**: *I**'ve known** him **since** we were children.*

examples.text: She left **as soon as** the lesson ended.
I stayed in bed **until** 10.
We've been friends **since** we met at university.
**By the time** I got to the station, the train had left.

mistakes.wrong: I know him since I was a child.
mistakes.right: I've known him since I was a child.

mistakes.wrong: Wait here until I will come back.
mistakes.right: Wait here until I come back.

points.title: First, then, after that, finally, in the end, at last
points.summary: To tell a story or give instructions in order: ***first***, ***then / next / after that***, ***finally***. ***In the end*** = after a long time or many changes. ***At last*** = after waiting a long time (relief). ***Eventually*** = after a long time.

rows: ***Then** add the onions. **After that**, add the rice.*
the final result after problems or changes
*We looked at ten flats. **In the end**, we chose the first one.*

blocks.md: Don't confuse ***in the end*** (finally) with ***at the end of*** (the last part of something): ***At the end of** the film, everyone cried.*

examples.text: **First**, open the app. **Then**, create an account.
**After that**, we had lunch in a café.
**In the end**, we decided to stay at home.
**At last**, the exams are over!

mistakes.wrong: In the end of the lesson, we had a quiz.
mistakes.right: At the end of the lesson, we had a quiz.
mistakes.why: the last part: at the end of

mistakes.wrong: After, we went to the cinema.
mistakes.right: After that, we went to the cinema.

points.title: The moment, every time, as, whenever
points.summary: ***The moment / the minute*** = as soon as. ***Every time / whenever*** = each time. ***As*** = at the same time as (two things changing or happening together). ***Hardly … when*** = something happened immediately after.

rows: ***The moment** I saw him, I knew something was wrong.*
***Every time** I see that photo, I smile.*
***As** I was leaving, the phone rang. **As** you get older, you worry less.*
*I had **hardly** sat down **when** the doorbell rang.*

blocks.md: ***As*** is common with **changes that happen together**: ***As** the population grows, cities get bigger.*

examples.text: **The minute** she walked in, everyone stopped talking.
**Whenever** I go to Paris, I visit the Louvre.
The rain started **just as** we left the house.
**As** prices rise, people spend less.

mistakes.wrong: Every times I call him, he's busy.
mistakes.right: Every time I call him, he's busy.

mistakes.wrong: I had hardly arrived than it started raining.
mistakes.right: I had hardly arrived when it started raining.

points.title: No sooner … than, upon arrival, prior to, following
points.summary: Formal time expressions: ***no sooner … than*** and ***hardly / scarcely … when*** (often with inversion), ***upon / on*** + *-ing* or noun, ***prior to***, ***following***, ***having*** + past participle.

rows: *We had **no sooner** arrived **than** it started to rain.* / ***No sooner had** we arrived **than** it started to rain.*
***Scarcely had** she left **when** the phone rang.*
***Upon arriving**, guests are given a key. **On arrival**, …*
***Prior to** the meeting, please read the report.*
***Having finished** the report, she went home.*

blocks.md: When ***no sooner***, ***hardly*** or ***scarcely*** start the sentence, use **inversion** (*had + subject*). See [Inversion After Negative Adverbials](/blog/grammar/inversion-negative-adverbials/).
Remember: ***no sooner*** goes with ***than***; ***hardly / scarcely*** go with ***when***.

examples.text: **No sooner had** I sat down **than** the phone rang.
**Upon** receiving the results, the team celebrated.
Please arrive 30 minutes **prior to** departure.
**Following** the storm, many roads were closed.

mistakes.wrong: No sooner had I arrived when they left.
mistakes.right: No sooner had I arrived than they left.

mistakes.wrong: No sooner I had arrived than they left.
mistakes.right: No sooner had I arrived than they left.

items.prompt: ___ I hear this song, I think of my grandmother.
The train left just ___ we got to the platform.
The ___ I saw the house, I knew I wanted to buy it. (one word)

topics.h1: Unreal Past (It's time we went, I'd rather you didn't…)
topics.summary: Past forms that don't mean past: It's time we went. I'd rather you stayed. He acts as if he owned the place.
intro: In some structures, a **past** form doesn't talk about past time. It shows that a situation is **unreal**, **imagined** or **wanted**: *It's time we **went**.* (We should go now.)

You already know this from [Second Conditional](/blog/grammar/second-conditional/) and [Wish and If Only](/blog/grammar/wish-if-only/). This page covers the other common structures: *it's time, would rather, as if, suppose* and *what if*.

points.title: It's time…: it's time to go, it's time we went
points.summary: **It's time + to-infinitive** or **It's time + subject + past simple**: *It's time to go. It's time we went.* **High / about time** = it should have happened already.

blocks.md: There are two patterns:

items: ***It's time + to + verb***: *It's late. **It's time to go**.* / ***It's time for** + noun*: ***It's time for** bed.*
***It's time + subject + past simple***: *It's late. **It's time we went** home.* The meaning is **now**, not the past.

blocks.md: ***It's high time*** and ***it's about time*** + subject + past simple are stronger. They suggest it's **late** and the thing should have happened already, often as a complaint: ***It's about time** you **found** a job!*
After *It's time* + subject, don't use the present: *It's time we **left**.* Not *It's time we leave* (heard informally, but avoid it in exams and writing).

examples.text: **It's time to** start the meeting.
**It's time** the kids **went** to bed.
**It's high time** you **cleaned** your room!
**It's about time** the council **did** something about the roads.

mistakes.wrong: It's time we go.
mistakes.right: It's time we went.

mistakes.wrong: It's high time to you started.
mistakes.right: It's high time you started.

points.title: Would rather: I'd rather stay, I'd rather you stayed
points.summary: **would rather + base verb** (your own preference). **would rather + another person + past simple** (what you want someone else to do).

rows: what I want you to do (now / future)

blocks.md: When the subject is the **same** person (*I'd rather I…*), use the base verb: *I'd rather **go** by train.* When it's **another** person, use the past simple: *I'd rather **you went** by train.*
***would rather … than***: *I'd rather **walk than take** the bus.*
*Would rather* is close to *would prefer*, but the patterns are different: *I'd prefer **to stay**.* / *I'd rather **stay**.* See [Would Like, Would Rather and Prefer](/blog/grammar/would-like/).

examples.text: I**'d rather** have tea, please.
I**'d rather** you **didn't** tell anyone about this.
My parents **would rather** I **studied** medicine.
examples.note: what they want me to do

examples.text: We**'d rather** walk **than** wait for a taxi.

mistakes.wrong: I'd rather to stay at home.
mistakes.right: I'd rather stay at home.

mistakes.wrong: I'd rather you don't call me at work.
mistakes.right: I'd rather you didn't call me at work.

mistakes.wrong: I'd rather you to come tomorrow.
mistakes.right: I'd rather you came tomorrow.

points.title: As if / as though: real or unreal?
points.summary: **as if / as though** + present for something that seems **true** (*It looks as if it's going to rain*). + past for something **unreal** (*He talks as if he knew everything*).

blocks.md: ***As if*** and ***as though*** describe how someone or something **seems**. They mean the same.
Use a **normal tense** when the situation is probably **true**: *You look **as if** you **haven't slept**.* (Maybe you really haven't.) *It looks **as if** it**'s going** to rain.*
Use a **past** form to show that the comparison is **unreal** or **unlikely**: *He talks **as if** he **knew** everything.* (He doesn't.) *She treats me **as though** I **were** a child.* (I'm not.)
In informal English, ***like*** is often used instead of *as if*: *It looks **like** it's going to rain.* In formal writing, *as if* is better.

examples.text: You sound **as if** you**'ve got** a cold.
He spends money **as if** he **were** a millionaire.
It feels **as though** we**'ve known** each other for years.
Don't talk to me **as if** I **was** stupid.

mistakes.wrong: It looks as it's going to rain.
mistakes.right: It looks as if it's going to rain.

mistakes.wrong: She looks as she's tired.
mistakes.right: She looks as if she's tired.

points.title: Suppose, supposing, imagine, what if
points.summary: **suppose / supposing / imagine / what if** + present = a real possibility. + past = an imaginary or less likely situation. + past perfect = an imaginary past.

blocks.md: These words introduce a hypothetical situation, often as a question or to make a suggestion: ***Supposing** we **took** the train instead?* (= a suggestion)
The tense shows how real the speaker thinks the situation is, like in conditionals: ***What if** it **rains**?* (it might) / ***What if** it **rained** every day?* (imaginary).

examples.text: **Suppose** your boss **found out**. What would you say?
**What if** the shop **is** closed?
**Supposing** we **went** to Spain this summer?
**Imagine** you **had missed** that plane. You'd have been in the crash.

mistakes.wrong: Suppose you would win, what would you buy?
mistakes.right: Suppose you won, what would you buy?

mistakes.wrong: What if we had more time tomorrow, we will finish.
mistakes.right: If we had more time tomorrow, we would finish.

points.title: Unreal past about the past: past perfect
points.summary: To talk about an unreal **past**, use the **past perfect**: *I'd rather you **hadn't told** him. He looked as if he **had seen** a ghost.*

blocks.md: All the unreal structures move back a step for the past:

items: ***would rather*** + person + past perfect: *I'd rather you **hadn't invited** her.* (You did, and I'm not happy.)
***as if*** + past perfect: *She looked **as if** she **had been** crying.*
***suppose / imagine / what if*** + past perfect: ***What if** I **hadn't come**?*
***wish / if only*** + past perfect: *I **wish** I **had known**.* See [Wish and If Only](/blog/grammar/wish-if-only/#wio-past).

blocks.md: The past perfect here means something **didn't** happen, or we imagine it differently.

examples.text: I'd rather you **hadn't mentioned** my age.
He talked **as if** nothing **had happened**.
**What if** we **hadn't met** that day?
**Suppose** the police **had stopped** you.

mistakes.wrong: I'd rather you didn't tell her yesterday.
mistakes.right: I'd rather you hadn't told her yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: He looked as if he saw a ghost.
mistakes.right: He looked as if he had seen a ghost.

items.prompt: I'd rather you ___ the window. It's cold in here.
I'm tired. I'd rather ___ in tonight.
My mother would rather I ___ (live) closer to home.
He's not my boss, but he gives orders as if he ___ my boss.
Look at those dark clouds. It looks as if it ___ to rain.
She treats her cat as though it ___ a baby.

topics.summary: Past habits and states that are not true now: I used to live in Shiraz.
intro: We use ***used to*** + base verb for things that happened regularly or were true in the past, but are **not true now**: *I **used to play** the piano.* (I don't now.) *She **used to live** in Isfahan.* (She doesn't now.)
This page goes from the basic form to the difference between *used to* and *would*, and how *will* and *would* describe typical behaviour.

points.title: Used to: past habits and states
points.summary: **used to + base verb** for something that was true or happened regularly in the past but doesn't now.

blocks.md: ***Used to*** is the same for every person: *I / you / he / she / we / they **used to** + base verb.*

items: **Past habits** (repeated actions): *I **used to walk** to school every day.*
**Past states** (situations): *We **used to have** a dog. There **used to be** a cinema here.*

blocks.md: The meaning is always: this was true in the past, but it's **different now**. *I used to smoke* = I smoked in the past, but I don't now.
*Used to* exists only in the past. For present habits, use the present simple: *I **usually** walk to work.* Not *I use to walk to work*.

examples.text: I **used to live** in a small village.
My father **used to work** in a bank.
We **used to go** camping every summer.
There **used to be** a park here. Now it's a car park.

mistakes.wrong: I use to play football when I was young.
mistakes.right: I used to play football when I was young.
mistakes.why: Spell it used to in positive sentences.

mistakes.wrong: She used to lives in Paris.
mistakes.right: She used to live in Paris.

mistakes.wrong: I used to play tennis now.
mistakes.right: I usually play tennis now.
mistakes.why: used to is only for the past.

points.title: Didn't use to and Did you use to…?
points.summary: Negative: **didn't use to**. Question: **Did … use to…?** (no *d* after *did*).

blocks.md: After *did* and *didn't*, write ***use to*** (without *-d*), like other verbs: *didn't **go**, didn't **use to** go*.
You can also make the negative with *never*: *I **never used to** eat vegetables.* This is very common in speech.

examples.text: I **didn't use to** like coffee, but now I love it.
**Did** you **use to** live in Tabriz?
Where **did** you **use to** go on holiday?
He **never used to** do any sport.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't used to watch TV.
mistakes.right: I didn't use to watch TV.

mistakes.wrong: Did you used to play chess?
mistakes.right: Did you use to play chess?

mistakes.wrong: Used you to live here?
mistakes.right: Did you use to live here?

points.title: Used to or past simple?
points.summary: Use *used to* for repeated actions or long situations. Use the **past simple** for one action, a number of times, or an exact length of time.

blocks.md: *Used to* only describes **repeated** actions or situations that lasted a long time. For other past actions, use the past simple:
For repeated past actions, the past simple is also correct: *I **went** to the gym every day when I was a student.* *Used to* adds the idea that this is **not true now**.
Don't use *used to* with *for + period* or with *how long*: *How long **did** you **live** there?* Not *How long did you use to live there?*

examples.text: I **used to play** chess with my grandfather.
I **played** chess with my grandfather last Sunday.
We **lived** in Kerman for ten years.
She **called** me five times yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: I used to go to Spain last year.
mistakes.right: I went to Spain last year.

mistakes.wrong: He used to work there for twenty years.
mistakes.right: He worked there for twenty years.

mistakes.wrong: I used to call her three times.
mistakes.right: I called her three times.

points.title: Used to do or be used to doing?
points.summary: *I **used to work** at night* = in the past (not now). *I**'m used to working** at night* = it's normal for me, not strange.

blocks.md: These look similar but mean different things:

rows: a past habit or state, not now
*I **used to live** alone.* (but now I don't)
something is familiar and not strange or difficult
*I**'m used to living** alone.* (it's normal for me)
*I'm **getting used to living** alone.* (it's becoming easier)

blocks.md: After *be used to* and *get used to*, *to* is a preposition, so it's followed by a **noun** or an ***-ing*** form: *I'm used to **the cold**. I'm used to **getting up** early.*
For more on *be used to* and *get used to* in all tenses, see [Be Used To and Get Used To](/blog/grammar/would-be-get-used-to/).

examples.text: I **used to drive** to work, but now I take the train.
I'm **used to driving** on the right.
She **isn't used to** the noise of the city yet.
You'll soon **get used to** the food.

mistakes.wrong: I'm used to get up early.
mistakes.right: I'm used to getting up early.

mistakes.wrong: I used to getting up early when I was a student.
mistakes.right: I used to get up early when I was a student.
mistakes.why: past habit: used to + base verb

points.title: Would for past habits
points.summary: **would** + base verb can describe repeated **actions** in the past, especially in stories: *Every summer we would go to the lake.* Not for states.

blocks.md: In stories and memories, we often use ***would*** for repeated past actions, usually after the scene has been set with *used to* or the past simple:
*When I was a kid, we **used to** spend the summer at my grandparents' farm. Every morning, we **would get up** early and **would help** with the animals.*
*Would* can't be used for **states** (*be, have* for possession, *live, like, know, believe*). Use *used to* or the past simple for states.
Don't start a story with *would* alone, because it can be confused with other meanings (*I would go* = conditional). First make the time clear: *When we were children, … / Every summer, …*

examples.text: Every evening my father **would read** us a story.
On Fridays we **would visit** my aunt.
I **used to have** a red bicycle.
She **used to be** very quiet.

mistakes.wrong: When I was young, I would have a cat.
mistakes.right: When I was young, I used to have a cat.
mistakes.why: have (possession) is a state: used to.

mistakes.wrong: We would live in a small flat in those days.
mistakes.right: We used to live in a small flat in those days.
mistakes.why: live is a state: used to.

points.title: Will and would for typical behaviour
points.summary: **will / would** can describe typical or characteristic behaviour: *She'll sit there for hours.* Stressed **would** can show criticism: *He WOULD say that!*

blocks.md: We can use ***will*** (present) and ***would*** (past) to describe what someone or something **typically** does:

items: *My cat **will** sleep anywhere.* (it's typical of her)
*On a good day, the shop **will** sell 300 coffees.*
*My grandfather **would** sit in the garden for hours, just watching the birds.*

blocks.md: When ***would*** (or ***will***) is **stressed** in speech, it often shows that the speaker finds the behaviour annoying and predictable: *He **WOULD** forget my birthday!* (= that's typical of him, and I'm annoyed). *She **WILL** leave her shoes in the hall.*
***Used to*** can also refer to things that **no longer exist**: *This building **used to be** a cinema.* *Would* is not used like this.
This *will* is not about the future: *Boys **will** be boys* means boys typically behave like this.

examples.text: She**'ll** talk to anyone who listens.
In the evenings, my father **would** fall asleep in front of the TV.
Of course he was late. He **WOULD** be!
Oil **will** float on water.

mistakes.wrong: This shop would be a bakery when I was a child.
mistakes.right: This shop used to be a bakery when I was a child.
mistakes.why: A past state: used to, not would.

mistakes.wrong: She would to sit by the window for hours.
mistakes.right: She would sit by the window for hours.

items.prompt: When I was a child, I ___ a lot of friends in my street.
Every Sunday my grandmother ___ a big lunch for the whole family.
items.explanation: A repeated action in a memory: *would* + base verb.

items.prompt: Which part is wrong?
items.correction: In those days my parents used to own a small shop.

topics.h1: The Verb To Be (Am, Is, Are)
topics.summary: The most important verb in English: I am, you are, he is. Forms, negatives, questions, and common mistakes.
intro: ***Be*** is the most common verb in English. In the present, it has three forms: ***am, is, are***: *I **am** a student. She **is** from Iran. We **are** happy.* In the past: ***was, were***.
This page covers the present forms and uses of *be*. For the past, see [Was and Were](/blog/grammar/was-were/).

points.title: I am, you are, he is: forms and contractions
points.summary: ***I am*** (I'm), ***you / we / they are*** ('re), ***he / she / it is*** ('s). In speaking, we usually use the **short forms**.

blocks.md: With a **noun** subject, use *is* (singular) or *are* (plural): *My brother **is** a doctor. My parents **are** teachers.*
Don't confuse ***it's*** (= it is) and ***its*** (possessive): ***It's** a nice car. **Its** colour is red.*

examples.text: **I'm** a student.
**She's** from Canada.
**We're** in the kitchen.
My friends **are** very kind.

mistakes.wrong: I is a teacher.
mistakes.right: I am a teacher.

mistakes.wrong: They is my friends.
mistakes.right: They are my friends.

points.title: I'm not, isn't, aren't; Are you…?
points.summary: **Negative**: ***I'm not, he isn't (is not), they aren't (are not)***. **Questions**: put *be* first: ***Are** you OK? **Is** she here?* Short answers: *Yes, I am. No, she isn't.*

blocks.md: Say ***I'm not*** (not *I amn't*). Both ***he isn't*** and ***he's not*** are correct.
In positive short answers, don't use contractions: *Yes, I **am**.* (not *Yes, I'm.*)

examples.text: I'**m not** hungry.
**Is** this your bag?
They **aren't** at school today.
**Are** you from Spain? ~ No, I'**m not**.

mistakes.wrong: I amn't tired.
mistakes.right: I'm not tired.

mistakes.wrong: You are ready?
mistakes.right: Are you ready?

mistakes.wrong: Yes, I'm.
mistakes.right: Yes, I am.

points.title: I'm 25, I'm hungry, I'm cold: be, not have
points.summary: English uses ***be*** (not *have*) for **age** (*I'm 25*), **feelings** (*I'm hungry, I'm cold, I'm afraid*), **jobs** (*She's a doctor*), **nationality**, and **be born** (*I was born in 1990*).

rows: *I born in Shiraz. / I am born in Shiraz.*

blocks.md: ***Be born*** is in the **past** for when you came into the world: *I **was born** in 1995.*

examples.text: My son **is** seven.
Are you **cold**? I can close the window.
You**'re right**. I'm sorry.
My father **was born** in Isfahan.

mistakes.wrong: I have 30 years.
mistakes.right: I'm 30 (years old).

mistakes.wrong: I have cold. Close the window.
mistakes.right: I'm cold. Close the window.

mistakes.wrong: I born in 1998.
mistakes.right: I was born in 1998.

points.title: I agree, not I'm agree: be or do?
points.summary: Don't use ***be*** with other verbs in the present simple: *I **agree*** (not *I'm agree*), *I **don't understand*** (not *I'm not understand*), ***Do** you like…?* (not *Are you like…?*). Use ***be*** with **adjectives**, **nouns** and **-ing**.

blocks.md: Ask yourself: is there **another verb**? Then use ***do / does*** for questions and negatives: *Do you **live** here?* Is there **no other verb** (just an adjective or noun)? Then use ***be***: *Are you **tired**?*

examples.text: I **agree** with you completely.
**Do** you **know** him?
**Are** you **happy** here?
He **doesn't eat** meat.

mistakes.wrong: I'm agree with you.
mistakes.right: I agree with you.

mistakes.wrong: Are you like football?
mistakes.right: Do you like football?

mistakes.wrong: She is live in Toronto.
mistakes.right: She lives in Toronto.

points.title: He's being silly: be in the continuous
points.summary: ***Be*** can be continuous (***am / is / are being***) to talk about **temporary behaviour**: *You're **being** very rude today.* (= you're acting rudely now). It's also used in the **passive continuous**: *The road **is being** repaired.*

blocks.md: Use ***being*** + adjective for **actions and behaviour**: *silly, rude, kind, careful, lazy, stupid, difficult, nice*. Not for states like *tall* or *tired*: *He's tired* (not *He's being tired*).

examples.text: Stop it! You're **being** silly.
She's usually shy, but today she's **being** very friendly.
My car **is being** fixed this week.
**Being** a parent is hard work.

mistakes.wrong: He's being tall.
mistakes.right: He's tall.

mistakes.wrong: The bridge is be repaired.
mistakes.right: The bridge is being repaired.

items.prompt: Why ___ so difficult today? You're not usually like this.
The museum ___ renovated, so it's closed until June.
Be careful! You ___ (be) very careless with that knife.

topics.summary: Which preposition comes after a verb: listen to, wait for, depend on, thank someone for, think about.
intro: Many verbs are followed by a **fixed preposition**: *I'm **waiting for** the bus. It **depends on** the weather. Can you **listen to** me?* Learn the verb and its preposition **together**.

Some verbs take **no preposition** at all (*discuss the problem*, not *discuss about*), and some change meaning with a different preposition (*look at, look for, look after*). For adjectives, see [Adjectives and Prepositions](/blog/grammar/adjectives-and-prepositions/).

points.title: Listen to, wait for, look at, depend on
points.summary: Common pairs: **listen to**, **wait for**, **look at**, **ask for**, **pay for**, **talk to / about**, **think about**, **belong to**, **depend on**, **agree with**.

blocks.md: The preposition stays with the verb in questions, often at the **end**: *Who are you **waiting for**? What are you **looking at**?*

examples.text: She's **listening to** a podcast.
I'm **waiting for** my friend.
**Look at** the sky!
It **depends on** the weather.

mistakes.wrong: I'm listening music.
mistakes.right: I'm listening to music.

mistakes.wrong: Wait me here.
mistakes.right: Wait for me here.

mistakes.wrong: It depends of the price.
mistakes.right: It depends on the price.

points.title: Discuss, enter, marry, call: no preposition
points.summary: Some verbs take a **direct object** with **no preposition**: **discuss** a problem, **enter** a room, **marry** someone, **call / phone** someone, **answer** a question, **reach** a place, **approach** someone, **lack** something.

blocks.md: But the **nouns** often have a preposition: *a **discussion about** the plan, the **answer to** the question, a **lack of** experience*.
***Explain*** something **to** someone (not *explain me*): *Can you **explain** the rule **to me**?*

examples.text: Let's **discuss** your ideas tomorrow.
She **married** her best friend.
Please **call** me when you arrive.
We **reached** the top of the mountain.

mistakes.wrong: We need to discuss about the budget.
mistakes.right: We need to discuss the budget.

mistakes.wrong: Can you explain me this word?
mistakes.right: Can you explain this word to me?

mistakes.wrong: I'll phone to you later.
mistakes.right: I'll phone you later.

points.title: Thank someone for, remind someone of, spend money on
points.summary: **Verb + object + preposition**: **thank / blame** someone **for**, **accuse** someone **of**, **remind** someone **of / about**, **spend** money **on**, **provide** someone **with**, **protect / prevent** someone **from**, **congratulate** someone **on**, **borrow** something **from**.

rows: *You **remind** me **of** my sister. **Remind** me **about** the meeting.*

blocks.md: After the preposition, use a noun or ***-ing***: *Thank you **for helping**. They prevented us **from leaving**.*

examples.text: Thank you **for** your help.
He **spends** hours **on** his phone.
This song **reminds** me **of** my childhood.
We **congratulated** them **on** their wedding.

mistakes.wrong: Thank you for help me.
mistakes.right: Thank you for helping me.

mistakes.wrong: Sunscreen protects you of the sun.
mistakes.right: Sunscreen protects you from the sun.

mistakes.wrong: I borrowed some money of my brother.
mistakes.right: I borrowed some money from my brother.

points.title: Look at, look for, look after; think of or about
points.summary: The **preposition** can change the **meaning**: *look **at** / **for** / **after***, *think **of** / **about***, *hear **about** / **of** / **from***, *care **about** / **for***, *agree **with** / **to** / **on***, *dream **of** / **about***.

rows: see / try to find / take care of
***Look at** me. I'm **looking for** my keys. She **looks after** her mum.*
consider / have an idea or opinion
*I'm **thinking about** moving. What do you **think of** my dress?*
get news / know it exists / get a message
*Did you **hear about** the fire? I've never **heard of** him. I **heard from** Sara yesterday.*
think it's important / look after or like
*I **care about** the environment. She **cares for** her sick father.*
same opinion / accept a request / decide together
*I **agree with** you. He **agreed to** the plan. We **agreed on** a price.*
*I **dream of** living by the sea. I **dreamt about** you last night.*

blocks.md: ***Think of*** is also used for **ideas**: *Can you **think of** a name for the dog?*

examples.text: I'm **looking for** a new flat.
Who **looks after** your kids when you're at work?
Have you **heard from** your brother?
Finally, we **agreed on** a date for the wedding.

mistakes.wrong: She dreams to become a doctor.
mistakes.right: She dreams of becoming a doctor.

mistakes.wrong: I agree to you.
mistakes.right: I agree with you.

mistakes.wrong: Can you look for my cat while I'm on holiday?
mistakes.right: Can you look after my cat while I'm on holiday?

points.title: Comply with, refrain from, account for, attribute to
points.summary: Formal verb + preposition pairs: **comply with**, **adhere to**, **abide by**, **refrain from**, **account for**, **attribute** something **to**, **cope / contend with**, **object to + -ing**, **capitalise on**, **embark on**, **dispose of**.

rows: *Tourism **accounts for** 10% of the economy. How do you **account for** the delay?*
*I **object to** being treated like a child.*

blocks.md: In ***object to***, ***be committed to*** and ***look forward to***, *to* is a **preposition**, so use ***-ing***: *I **object to paying** for this.*

examples.text: Visitors must **adhere to** the safety guidelines.
Young people **account for** half of our customers.
He **attributes** his long life **to** a good diet.
Guests are asked to **refrain from** using phones.

mistakes.wrong: I object to pay for something I didn't order.
mistakes.right: I object to paying for something I didn't order.

mistakes.wrong: All products must comply to the new standards.
mistakes.right: All products must comply with the new standards.

items.prompt: Can you look ___ the children for an hour? I need to go out.
I've never heard ___ that singer. Is she famous?
Can you think ___ a good name for our new cat? (one word)

topics.h1: Verbs that Change Meaning with -ing or To
topics.summary: Some verbs mean different things with -ing and to: I remember locking the door. Remember to lock the door!
intro: Most verbs take either *-ing* or *to*, but some can take **both**. With some of them (*like, start, begin*), the meaning hardly changes. With others (*remember, forget, stop, try, regret, mean*), the meaning is **very different**: *I stopped **smoking*** (I don't smoke now) / *I stopped **to smoke*** (I stopped what I was doing so that I could smoke).
For the general patterns, see [Gerund or Infinitive](/blog/grammar/gerund-or-infinitive/).

points.title: Like, love, start, begin, continue: little or no difference
points.summary: **like, love, hate, prefer, start, begin, continue** can take **-ing** or **to** with little difference: *It started raining / to rain.*

blocks.md: With these verbs, both forms are correct and the meaning is almost the same: *I **love cooking** / I **love to cook**. She **began working** / **to work** at 18.*
There are a few small differences:

items: In British English, ***like + -ing*** often means *enjoy*, and ***like + to*** can mean *think it's a good idea*: *I **like to see** the dentist twice a year.* (I don't enjoy it, but it's sensible.)
After ***would like / would love / would prefer***, only ***to*** is possible: *I'd like **to** go.* See [Would Like](/blog/grammar/would-like/).
Avoid two *-ing* forms together: *It's **starting to rain*** (not *It's starting raining*).

examples.text: It **started raining** / **to rain** at noon.
I **love swimming** / **to swim** in the sea.
I **like to pay** my bills on time.
The baby is **beginning to walk**.

mistakes.wrong: I'd love going to Japan one day.
mistakes.right: I'd love to go to Japan one day.

mistakes.wrong: It's starting snowing.
mistakes.right: It's starting to snow.

points.title: Remember and forget: -ing or to?
points.summary: **remember / forget + -ing** = a memory of the past. **remember / forget + to** = a duty, something you need to do (before you do it).

rows: I did it, and I have the memory
*I **remember locking** the door.* (I locked it; I can remember it.)
I didn't forget to do it
*I **remembered to lock** the door.* (I locked it, as I needed to.)
lose the memory of something you did (often *I'll never forget*)
not do something you needed to do

blocks.md: Think about the **order**: with ***-ing***, the action comes **first** and the remembering comes later. With ***to***, the remembering comes **first**, then the action.

examples.text: I **remember visiting** my grandparents every summer.
Please **remember to call** your mother.
I **forgot to send** the email!
I'll **never forget seeing** the sea for the first time.

mistakes.wrong: Remember locking the door when you go out!
mistakes.right: Remember to lock the door when you go out!

mistakes.wrong: I remember to go to Paris when I was a child.
mistakes.right: I remember going to Paris when I was a child.

points.title: Stop and go on: -ing or to?
points.summary: **stop + -ing** = not do it any more. **stop + to** = stop one thing in order to do another. **go on + -ing** = continue. **go on + to** = do something next.

rows: pause in order to do something
*He finished school and **went on to study** law.*

blocks.md: *Stop + to* is really an infinitive of **purpose**: *We stopped (the car) **in order to** buy petrol.*

examples.text: He **stopped working** at 65.
On the way home, I **stopped to buy** some flowers.
The teacher **went on explaining** for an hour.
After the introduction, she **went on to describe** the results.

mistakes.wrong: I've stopped to drink coffee. (meaning I don't drink it now)
mistakes.right: I've stopped drinking coffee.

mistakes.wrong: We stopped buying petrol on the motorway. (meaning we paused to buy)
mistakes.right: We stopped to buy petrol on the motorway.

points.title: Try and need: -ing or to?
points.summary: **try + to** = make an effort (it's difficult). **try + -ing** = do it as an experiment to see if it works. **need + to** = it's necessary for me. **need + -ing** = it needs to be done (passive meaning).

rows: *I **tried to open** the window, but it was stuck.*
*If you can't sleep, **try drinking** warm milk.*
it's necessary for the subject to do it
it needs to be done (passive meaning)
*My room **needs cleaning**.* (= needs to be cleaned)

blocks.md: *Need + -ing* is mainly British English. Both British and American English use ***need to be*** + past participle: *The car **needs washing** / **needs to be washed**.*

examples.text: I **tried to lift** the box, but it was too heavy.
The printer didn't work, so I **tried turning** it off and on.
I **need to call** the bank.
Your hair **needs cutting**.

mistakes.wrong: I tried calling, but I couldn't because my phone was dead. (making an effort)
mistakes.right: I tried to call, but I couldn't because my phone was dead.

mistakes.wrong: The windows need to clean.
mistakes.right: The windows need cleaning / to be cleaned.

points.title: Regret and mean: -ing or to?
points.summary: **regret + -ing** = be sorry about something you did. **regret + to** = be sorry to give bad news (formal). **mean + -ing** = involve. **mean + to** = intend.

rows: I did it and I'm sorry
formal: I'm sorry to give bad news
*We **regret to inform** you that the flight is cancelled.*
*A new job **means moving** to another city.*
*I **meant to call** you, but I forgot.*

examples.text: I **regret not studying** harder at school.
We **regret to announce** that the concert has been cancelled.
Saving money **means spending** less.
Sorry, I didn't **mean to** hurt you.

mistakes.wrong: We regret informing you that your application was unsuccessful. (formal letter)
mistakes.right: We regret to inform you that your application was unsuccessful.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't mean hurting you.
mistakes.right: I didn't mean to hurt you.

points.title: Afraid to or afraid of -ing? Sorry to or sorry for -ing?
points.summary: **afraid to do** = you don't do it because it's dangerous or scary. **afraid of doing** = afraid that something might happen. **sorry to** = sorry about now. **sorry for / about -ing** = sorry about the past.

rows: don't want to do it (because of fear)

blocks.md: Compare: *I was **afraid to** tell him* (I didn't tell him because I was scared) / *I was **afraid of** hurting his feelings* (that was the possible result I was worried about).
*I'm sorry to* + verb can also apologise for something happening now: *I'm **sorry to** interrupt, but…*
Similar pairs: ***interested in -ing*** (find it interesting) / ***interested to hear*** (want to know), ***certain / sure to*** (it will happen) / ***certain of / about -ing*** (I feel sure).

examples.text: I was **afraid to** say anything.
Many people are **afraid of** losing their jobs.
I'm **sorry to** hear that.
I'm **sorry for** shouting at you yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: I'm afraid of to fly.
mistakes.right: I'm afraid of flying. / I'm afraid to fly.

mistakes.wrong: I'm sorry for interrupt.
mistakes.right: I'm sorry to interrupt. / I'm sorry for interrupting.

items.prompt: Did you remember ___ the windows before we left?
I remember ___ the Eiffel Tower when I was six. It was amazing.
Oh no! I forgot ___ (buy) bread.
I was tired, so I stopped ___ a rest.
My doctor told me to stop ___.
After winning the national title, she went on ___ (win) an Olympic medal.
I tried hard ___ the jar, but the lid was too tight.
The headache didn't go away, so I tried ___ a glass of water.
This shirt needs ___ (iron).
items.explanation: Passive meaning: *needs ironing / to be ironed*.

items.prompt: I regret ___ so much money on clothes. Now I'm broke.
I'm sorry, I didn't mean ___ you.
Getting a dog means ___ (walk) it twice a day.

topics.summary: The future with will: predictions, decisions, offers and promises. I'll help you. It will be cold tomorrow. Shall I open the window?
intro: ***Will*** + base verb is one of the main ways to talk about the future in English: *I**'ll** call you tomorrow. It **will** be sunny at the weekend.*

But *will* isn't the only future form, and it isn't always the right one. For plans, see [Be Going To](/blog/grammar/be-going-to/), and for choosing, see [Will vs Going To](/blog/grammar/will-vs-going-to/).

points.title: Will and won't: form and future facts
points.summary: **will / won't + base verb**, the same for every person: *I'll be 30 next year. She won't be here tomorrow.*

blocks.md: *Will* is the same for all persons and is followed by the **base verb**, with no *to*: *She **will come**.* Not *She wills come* or *will to come*.
We use it for **facts** about the future and things we're sure about: *Tomorrow **will** be Monday. The sun **will** set at 6.45.*

examples.text: I**'ll** be 25 next month.
The shop **won't** be open on Sunday.
**Will** you be at home this evening? ~ Yes, I **will**.
My parents **will** arrive at ten.

mistakes.wrong: She will comes tomorrow.
mistakes.right: She will come tomorrow.

mistakes.wrong: I will to help you.
mistakes.right: I will help you.

mistakes.wrong: Will you to be there?
mistakes.right: Will you be there?

points.title: Instant decisions, offers, promises and requests
points.summary: Use **will** when you decide at the moment of speaking (*I'll have the soup*), and for offers (*I'll help*), promises (*I'll call you*) and requests (*Will you…?*).

rows: *Your bags look heavy. I**'ll** carry one.*

blocks.md: When we decide something **at the moment of speaking**, we use *will*, not the present simple: *The phone's ringing. ~ I**'ll** get it.* Not *I get it*.
If the decision was made **before**, use *be going to*: *I**'m going to** paint the kitchen this weekend.* (I decided last week.) See [Will vs Going To](/blog/grammar/will-vs-going-to/).

examples.text: I**'ll** have the chicken, please.
Don't worry, I**'ll** pick you up from the station.
I**'ll** always love you.
**Will** you pass me the salt?

mistakes.wrong: The phone's ringing. ~ I answer it.
mistakes.right: The phone's ringing. ~ I'll answer it.

mistakes.wrong: I promise I call you tomorrow.
mistakes.right: I promise I'll call you tomorrow.

points.title: Predictions: I think it will…, probably
points.summary: Use **will** for predictions based on opinion or experience, often with *I think, I'm sure, probably, I expect*: *I think it'll be a great party.*

blocks.md: We often use *will* to say what we **think** or **believe** about the future: *I think Brazil **will** win the World Cup. You**'ll** love this film.*
Common phrases: *I think / I don't think, I'm sure, I expect, I hope, probably, definitely, perhaps*.
Word order: ***probably / definitely*** go **after** *will* but **before** *won't*: *She**'ll probably** be late. She **probably won't** come.*
For a negative prediction, say ***I don't think … will***, not *I think … won't*: *I **don't think** it **will** rain.* (more natural than *I think it won't rain*)

examples.text: I think you**'ll** pass the exam.
I'm sure they**'ll** enjoy the trip.
He**'ll probably** be late again.
I **don't think** she**'ll** like it.

mistakes.wrong: I think it won't snow.
mistakes.right: I don't think it will snow.

mistakes.wrong: She will be probably late.
mistakes.right: She'll probably be late.

mistakes.wrong: He won't probably come.
mistakes.right: He probably won't come.

points.title: Shall: offers, suggestions and formal rules
points.summary: **Shall I / shall we** + base verb for offers and suggestions (mainly British). In formal documents, **shall** = must: *The tenant shall pay the rent monthly.*

blocks.md: ***Shall I…?*** offers help, and ***Shall we…?*** makes a suggestion: ***Shall I** carry your bag? **Shall we** go for a walk?* It's also used to ask for advice: *What **shall** I do?*
*Shall* with *I / we* for the future (*I shall be there*) is formal and old-fashioned in British English. Most people say *I'll* or *I will*.
In **legal and formal documents**, ***shall*** expresses an obligation: *The company **shall** provide training to all staff.*
In American English, *shall* is rare in conversation. Americans usually say ***Should I…?*** or ***Do you want me to…?*** for offers, and ***Should we…?*** or ***Let's…*** for suggestions.

examples.text: **Shall I** turn the heating on?
**Shall we** meet at the café at six?
What **shall** we do this weekend?
Payment **shall** be made within 30 days.

mistakes.wrong: Shall I to help you?
mistakes.right: Shall I help you?

mistakes.wrong: Shall you come with us? (a suggestion)
mistakes.right: Will you come with us? / Shall we go together?
mistakes.why: shall is used with I / we

points.title: Won't for refusals: The door won't open
points.summary: **won't** = refuses to (people) or doesn't work (things): *He **won't** listen to me. The car **won't** start.*

blocks.md: ***Won't*** can mean **refuse to** or **be unwilling to**: *My son **won't** eat vegetables. She **won't** tell me what happened.*
With **things**, *won't* means *doesn't work* even when we try: *The door **won't** open. My laptop **won't** turn on.*
For the past, use ***wouldn't***: *He **wouldn't** listen. The car **wouldn't** start this morning.*

examples.text: My phone **won't** charge.
The baby **won't** stop crying.
They **won't** let me in without a ticket.
The car **wouldn't** start yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: The window doesn't will open.
mistakes.right: The window won't open.

mistakes.wrong: Yesterday the car won't start.
mistakes.right: Yesterday the car wouldn't start.

points.title: Will for habits and characteristic behaviour
points.summary: **will** can describe typical behaviour or habits (*She'll sit there for hours*) and, when stressed, annoying insistence (*He **will** leave his socks on the floor!*).

blocks.md: ***Will*** + base verb can describe what someone or something **typically** does: *My cat **will** sleep anywhere. Boys **will** be boys.* (= that's how they are)
When *will* is **stressed** in speech (/wɪl/, not *'ll*), it shows that the habit is **annoying**: *He **WILL** play his music so loud!*
In the past, use ***would*** for the same meanings: *My grandfather **would** tell us stories every night.* See [Used To](/blog/grammar/used-to/#ut-characteristic).
The habit use is also common in general statements: *Oil **will** float on water. A good teacher **will** listen to students.*

examples.text: My grandmother **will** spend hours in the garden.
She **will** keep interrupting me!
Children **will** always copy their parents.
Water **will** freeze at zero degrees.

mistakes.wrong: He'll always leaves the door open.
mistakes.right: He'll always leave the door open.

items.prompt: I've tried everything, but this jar ___ open.
Yesterday my son ___ do his homework. We argued for an hour.
My computer ___ (will / not / turn) on. Can you help?

topics.summary: Wanting things to be different: I wish I had more time. I wish I hadn't said that. If only it would stop raining!
intro: We use ***wish*** and ***if only*** to say that we want a situation to be **different** from what it is or was: *I **wish** I **had** more time.* (I don't have enough time.)

The verb after *wish* moves **one step back** in time: present → past simple, past → past perfect. The same happens in [Second Conditional](/blog/grammar/second-conditional/) and [Third Conditional](/blog/grammar/third-conditional/).

points.title: Wish + past simple: things you want to be different now
points.summary: **wish + past simple** for a present situation you don't like: *I **wish** I **lived** near the sea.* (I don't.)

rows: I live in a small flat.
*I wish I **didn't live** in a small flat.*

blocks.md: After *wish*, the **past simple** talks about the **present**. It shows the situation isn't real.
With *be*, both ***were*** and ***was*** are used after *I / he / she / it*. *Were* is more formal: *I wish I **were** on holiday.*
Don't use *will* or the present after *wish* for a present situation: *I wish I **had** more money.* Not *I wish I have more money*.

examples.text: I **wish** I **spoke** French.
She **wishes** she **didn't have** to work on Saturdays.
I **wish** it **were** summer.
Do you ever **wish** you **lived** somewhere else?

mistakes.wrong: I wish I have a bigger house.
mistakes.right: I wish I had a bigger house.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I am taller.
mistakes.right: I wish I were (was) taller.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I will know the answer.
mistakes.right: I wish I knew the answer.

points.title: Wish + could: abilities and possibilities
points.summary: **wish + could** for something you can't do now: *I **wish** I **could** swim. I **wish** I **could** come to your party.*

blocks.md: Use ***could*** after *wish* when you're talking about **ability** or **possibility**: *I can't drive.* → *I **wish** I **could** drive.*
It's also used to say politely that you can't do something: *I **wish** I **could** help, but I'm busy.*

examples.text: I **wish** I **could** play the piano.
We **wish** we **could** stay longer, but our flight is tonight.
I **wish** I **could** remember where I put my keys.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I can speak Japanese.
mistakes.right: I wish I could speak Japanese.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I would swim.
mistakes.right: I wish I could swim.

points.title: Wish or hope?
points.summary: **hope** = something that is **possible**: *I hope you pass.* **wish** = something that **isn't** true or likely: *I wish I were younger.*

blocks.md: After ***hope***, use normal tenses, including the present and *will*: *I hope she **calls**. I hope she**'ll call**.*
After ***wish***, the verb moves back: past simple, past perfect, *could*, *would*.
***Wish*** + person + noun is used for good wishes: *We **wish you** a happy new year. I **wish you** good luck!* Here *wish* means *hope you have*.

examples.text: I **hope** you **enjoy** the film.
I **wish** you **didn't live** so far away.
I **hope** they **won**. I haven't seen the score.
**Good luck!** I **wish you** all the best.

mistakes.wrong: I wish you have a good trip.
mistakes.right: I hope you have a good trip.

mistakes.wrong: I hope I was taller.
mistakes.right: I wish I were (was) taller.

points.title: Wish + past perfect: regrets about the past
points.summary: **wish + past perfect** for something in the past you regret: *I **wish** I **hadn't eaten** so much.* (I ate too much.)

blocks.md: Use the **past perfect** after *wish* to talk about the **past**. It expresses **regret**: we can't change it.
Don't use *would have* after *wish*: *I wish I **had known**.* Not *I wish I would have known* (heard in informal American English, but avoid it in writing and exams).
For the same regret with a modal, use *should have*: *I **should have** studied.* See [Should Have, Could Have, Needn't Have](/blog/grammar/should-have-could-have-neednt-have/).

examples.text: I **wish** I **had gone** to the concert. Everyone says it was amazing.
She **wishes** she **hadn't sold** her old car.
I **wish** you**'d told** me earlier.
Do you **wish** you **had studied** something else?

mistakes.wrong: I wish I didn't say that yesterday.
mistakes.right: I wish I hadn't said that yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I would have known.
mistakes.right: I wish I had known.

points.title: Wish + would: wanting someone or something to change
points.summary: **wish + would** to complain about someone's behaviour or a situation you want to change: *I **wish** you **would** stop interrupting!*

blocks.md: Use ***wish + somebody + would*** when you want someone (or something) to **change** their behaviour. It often shows annoyance: *I **wish** my neighbours **would** turn the music down.*
It can also be about the weather or a situation: *I **wish** it **would** stop raining.*
Don't use *I wish I would…* or *we wish we would…* (you can't wish yourself to change like this). Use *could* or the past simple: *I **wish** I **could** stop smoking. I wish I **didn't smoke**.*
Compare: *I wish you **didn't smoke*** (I don't like the fact that you smoke) and *I wish you **would** stop smoking* (I want you to make a change).

examples.text: I **wish** you **would** listen to me!
I **wish** the bus **would** come. We've been waiting for ages.
She **wishes** her son **would** tidy his room.
I **wish** you **wouldn't** leave your shoes in the hall.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I would have more time.
mistakes.right: I wish I had more time.

mistakes.wrong: I wish you will stop.
mistakes.right: I wish you would stop.

points.title: If only: a stronger wish
points.summary: **If only** = a stronger, more emotional *I wish*: *If only I had more time! If only I hadn't said that! If only he would call!*

blocks.md: ***If only*** works like *wish*, with the same tenses, but it's more emotional and dramatic:

items: present: ***If only** I **knew** the answer!*
past: ***If only** we **had left** earlier!*
change: ***If only** it **would** stop raining!*

blocks.md: *If only* often stands alone as an exclamation. It can also start a conditional: ***If only** you'd told me, I could have helped.*

Don't confuse ***if only*** (a strong wish) with ***only if*** (the one condition): *I'll go **only if** you come.* See [Unless, As Long As, Provided](/blog/grammar/conditionals-unless-provided/#cup-unless-limits).

examples.text: **If only** I **had** a car!
**If only** I **hadn't lost** my phone!
**If only** the baby **would** sleep!
**If only** I **could** see her again.

mistakes.wrong: If only I have more money!
mistakes.right: If only I had more money!

mistakes.wrong: If only I didn't miss the plane yesterday!
mistakes.right: If only I hadn't missed the plane yesterday!

points.title: Formal wish: I wish to…, wish for…
points.summary: In formal English, **wish + to-infinitive** = *want*: *I **wish to** complain.* **wish for** + noun = want something you don't have.

blocks.md: ***Wish + to + verb*** means *want* or *would like*, and it's formal: *I **wish to** speak to the manager. Passengers who **wish to** change their seats should contact the crew.*
***Wish for*** + noun = to want something (often something hard to get): *She has everything she could **wish for**. What would you **wish for** if you had three wishes?*
***Wish*** + object + adjective/adverb in fixed phrases: *We **wish him well**.*
In everyday speech, *I'd like to* or *I want to* are more natural than *I wish to*: *I'd like to speak to the manager.*

examples.text: I **wish to** make a complaint.
Customers who **wish to** return items must keep the receipt.
We couldn't **wish for** better neighbours.
Everyone at the office **wishes you well** in your new job.

mistakes.wrong: I wish speaking to the director.
mistakes.right: I wish to speak to the director.

mistakes.wrong: She wished a new bike for her birthday.
mistakes.right: She wished for a new bike for her birthday.

items.prompt: I failed the test. I wish I ___ harder.
I wish you ___ me about the problem. I could have helped.

options: I wish you would help me.

items.prompt: It's been raining all week. I wish it ___ (stop).
items.explanation: A situation we want to change: *would stop*.
